ingredients.text: 2 kg beef leg and knuckle bones, cut across
800 g beef brisket in one piece
6 litres cold water, plus more for blanching

steps.text: Cover the bones and brisket with cold water, boil hard 10 minutes, then throw the water away and scrub both the bones and the pot until nothing grey clings to either.
Char the unpeeled onion and ginger straight on a gas flame or under a hot grill until blistered black on every face and smelling sweet, then rub off the loose ash.
Toast the star anise, cassia, black cardamom, coriander, cloves and fennel in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until fragrant and just beginning to darken, and tie them in muslin.

Cover the clean bones and brisket with the 6 litres of cold water, bring to 90C (195F) and hold there, skimming every 20 minutes for the first hour. Pull the brisket at 90 minutes, when a skewer slides out with no resistance, and chill it in cold water.
Simmer the bones 5 hours more with the charred aromatics, adding the spice bag only for the last 90 minutes, then season off the heat with the fish sauce, rock sugar and salt.

note: Two opposite heats. The first is a hard ten minute blanch that boils the blood and marrow scum out of the bones, and that water is thrown away with the foam. After the scrub the pot never boils again, because agitation drives the same fine particles back into suspension and pho is judged on being seen through. The spices go in late for the same reason they are toasted: their aroma is volatile, and five hours of simmering leaves a broth tasting of dust and medicine.

ingredients.text: 2.5 litres cold chicken stock, fully degreased and set to a jelly
400 g lean chicken leg meat, minced

steps.text: Mix the minced chicken, egg whites, chopped vegetables, tomato and aromatics into a loose slurry and chill it hard for 30 minutes. Everything that goes into the pot must be cold.

Whisk the slurry into the cold jellied stock in a tall heavy pot, then stir constantly over medium heat until it reaches 55-60C and turns thick and cloudy. Stop stirring at that moment and do not touch it again.

Let the raft rise and knit for 10 minutes, cut a 5 cm chimney in it with the back of a ladle, and drop the heat until a single bubble breaks through the chimney every second or two, around 82C (180F).
Hold 55 minutes untouched, until the liquid seen down the chimney runs transparent amber and the raft above has gone grey and firm.
Ladle out through the chimney into a double layer of muslin, never pouring, then blot the surface with paper to take the last beads of fat. Season at the end.

note: The raft is a filter that builds itself. Egg white and the myosin in lean mince coagulate as the pot climbs through 55-60C, knitting into a mesh that floats up and takes every clouding particle with it. It only forms from cold stock, stirred until it thickens and then left completely alone. Boil it and the raft tears and drops its cargo back through; press or pour it and you push grey silt into clear liquid. Ladle through the chimney, always.

ingredients.text: 20 g dried kombu, two pieces about 10 cm square

steps.text: Wipe the kombu with a dry cloth and leave the white bloom on it. That is mannitol and it is flavour, not mould, so do not rinse it.
Toast the soybeans in a dry pan over medium heat for about 4 minutes, until they smell nutty and one or two split.
Submerge the kombu, shiitake and soybeans in the cold water, cover, and refrigerate 8 to 12 hours, until the water is pale gold and smells of sea and forest floor.
Set over the lowest heat and bring to 60C (140F), then hold between 60C and 70C (140F-158F) for 45 minutes, never letting a bubble rise anywhere in the pot.
Lift out the kombu and strain through a fine sieve without squeezing the mushrooms. A squeezed shiitake gives bitterness and cloud. Keep the caps for another dish.

note: Two umami compounds that multiply rather than add: glutamate from the kombu, 5'-guanylate from the shiitake. The guanylate is not in the dry mushroom. An enzyme builds it during a slow warm soak, and that enzyme is dead above roughly 70C, so a fast pot destroys the flavour before it exists. Kombu has its own ceiling: past 80C it releases alginates that go slimy and a bitterness no straining removes. Built cold, held warm, and ruined by hurry.
techniques: Dry-pan toasting: spices, seeds and nuts

ingredients.text: 1 kg salmon side, skin on, pin bones pulled
25 g fine sea salt (2.5% of the trimmed fish weight)
3 g coriander seed, toasted and cracked
40 g dill, stalks and all, roughly chopped

steps.text: Weigh the trimmed fish and scale the salt and sugar to it, 2.5% and 2%, rather than reaching for a fixed spoonful.
Rub the spirit over the flesh, press on the salt, sugar and cracked spice, then pack the dill over the top.
Seal in a vacuum bag, or wrap tight in two layers of film in a tray, and hold at 4C (39F) for 48 hours, turning the parcel every 12 hours.
Open it when the flesh has gone deep translucent orange throughout and a fingertip pressed into the thick end springs back instead of denting.
Scrape off the dill, pat dry, and slice paper thin at a shallow angle down toward the skin, leaving the grey line behind.

note: Salt does not soak in. It pulls water out by osmosis, that water makes a brine in the bag, and the brine carries salt back into the muscle until both sides even out. Weigh the fish and the cure cannot overshoot the percentage you chose. Bury the same side in loose salt instead and it keeps giving up water, so a thin tail turns chalky and ham-like while the loin is still raw. Turn the parcel so both faces sit in brine.

ingredients.text: 1.4 kg salmon side, skin on, pin bones pulled, held at -20C (-4F) for 7 days first
42 g coarse sea salt (3% of the fish weight)
2 large handfuls oak or alder smoking dust

steps.text: Mix the salt, sugar and pepper, rub it over the flesh side, and cure skin down in a tray at 4C (39F): 24 hours for a thin side, 36 for a thick one.
Rinse briefly, pat dry, then leave uncovered on a rack in the fridge for 12 hours until the surface turns tacky and faintly glossy and you can tap it without wetting a finger.
Cold smoke below 30C (86F) for about 6 hours, in two sessions if the box warms up, until the flesh is the colour of old brass.
Wrap and rest in the fridge for 48 hours so the smoke moves inward and stops smelling like a bonfire.
Slice long and thin off the skin with the knife held almost flat.

note: Smoke sticks to a pellicle, the dry tacky protein film that forms in cold moving air. Smoke a wet fillet and the phenols dissolve in surface water and run off, leaving patchy colour and a sooty edge. Hold the box under 30C (86F): warmer and the proteins set and you have hot smoked fish instead. Lox is the other branch of the family, a salt brined belly cut, never smoked at all.

steps.text: Bury the breast in the salt in a non-reactive dish, covered above and below, and refrigerate 24 hours for a 350 g breast, 30 for a heavy magret.
Rinse every grain of salt off, pat bone dry, and weigh it now: this is the number every later weighing is measured against.
Rub with the pepper, thyme and bay, wrap in a double layer of muslin, tie, and hang somewhere 12-15C (54-59F) with air moving over it.
Weigh it every few days. It is finished at 30% loss from that post-cure weight, usually 10 to 21 days, when the thick end feels like the heel of your hand.
Slice across the grain, thin enough to see light through.

note: This is a box cure: buried in loose salt the meat never reaches equilibrium, so time is the only control and thickness sets the clock. Run it an extra day and the outer centimetre goes hard and salty. Weight loss, not the calendar, says when the drying is done, because at 30% the water activity is low enough that nothing grows. That is also why a small muscle drying fast in moving air needs no nitrite. Go thicker or slower and it does.

ingredients.text: 1.2 kg beef eye of round, every scrap of silverskin and fat trimmed off
1 beef bung, large collagen casing or drying net

steps.text: Weigh the trimmed muscle and scale every cure ingredient to that weight, then rub the lot on and seal it in a vacuum bag with the wine.
Cure at 4C (39F) for 12 days, flipping the bag daily so the liquor washes both ends.
Wipe the meat down, case it or truss it tight in netting, and hang at 12-14C (54-57F) and 70-75% humidity.
Weigh it weekly. It is ready at 38% weight loss, four to eight weeks, when the whole muscle feels evenly firm with no soft give at the core.
Slice across the grain as thin as the knife allows and let it warm on the plate before serving.

note: Nitrate earns its place here. A thick anaerobic muscle drying for weeks at cellar temperature is exactly where botulism grows, and cure no. 2 releases nitrite slowly across the whole run rather than all at once. The other failure is case hardening: dry air shrinks the outside into a shell that traps water in the middle, which then spoils. Hold humidity at 70-75%, and if a crust does form, vacuum bag the piece for a week to let the moisture even out.

ingredients.text: 1.5 kg pork jowl, skin on, glands and bruised meat cut away

steps.text: Square off the jowl so it dries evenly, then weigh it and scale the cure to that weight.
Rub the cure into every face, seal in a bag or covered tray, and refrigerate 7 days at 4C (39F), turning daily.
Wipe off the wet cure, pierce one corner and thread string through, then hang at 12-15C (54-59F) at about 70% humidity.
Give it 3 to 5 weeks, until it has lost 30% of its weight and the lean seam at the thick end is firm under a thumb.
Wipe any bloom off with a vinegar cloth, wrap in paper, and keep it in the fridge, cutting only what you need.

note: Jowl is mostly fat, and fat holds almost no water, so the weight comes out of the lean seams and comes out slowly. That is why the cure runs a week and the hang runs a month: you are seasoning fat and drying a little meat, not dehydrating a muscle. Powdery white mould is Penicillium and belongs there. Green fuzz or black patches do not, so wipe with vinegar, raise the airflow, and check nothing is touching its neighbour.

ingredients.text: 1 kg thick cod loin, skin on, pin boned

steps.text: Lay a 1 cm bed of salt in a perforated tray set over a dish, put the cod on it skin down, and bury it completely in more salt.
Refrigerate. Each day pour off the brine that has collected and replace the wet salt with dry, because the fish must never sit in its own liquor.
By day 7 the loin should be stiff, amber at the edge and about half its starting weight. Rack it another 5 days in a cold airy place if you want it board hard.
To cook with it, rinse the surface salt away and soak in a large bowl of cold water in the fridge for 48 hours, changing the water four times.
Poach a sliver to test: it should taste seasoned, not salty. Thin tail pieces need only 24 hours, so soak those separately.

note: Salting to saturation drags water activity under 0.85, below which spoilage bacteria simply stop, which is how a fish crossed oceans before refrigeration. Soaking runs that gradient backwards, and it stalls the moment the water around the fish gets salty, so volume and changes matter far more than hours. Soak in warm water, or too little of it, and the outside goes woolly while the middle stays a salt lick.

steps.text: Toss the legs with the salt, pepper, thyme, bay and garlic, then cure uncovered on a rack in the fridge for 24 hours.
Wipe off the cure and aromatics and pat the legs dry, because salt crystals left clinging will make the fat too salty to reuse.
Melt the fat in a deep pan, settle the legs in fully submerged, and hold at 85C (185F), one lazy bubble every few seconds and no more, for 3 hours.
They are done when a skewer meets no resistance at the thigh joint and the drumstick meat has pulled back from the bone.
Cool in the fat, lift the legs into a jar, pour the strained fat over to cover by 1 cm, and refrigerate at least a week before eating.

note: Confit preserves twice: salt lowers water activity at the surface, and the set fat cap keeps oxygen out. What breaks it is the jelly. Meat juices sink below the fat in the pan, and if that layer goes into the jar you have sealed a growth medium under an airtight lid. Pour the fat off the jelly, or chill and lift the fat cake clean. Hold 85C (185F): above 95C (203F) the fibres squeeze shut and the meat goes stringy.

ingredients.text: 1 kg pork shoulder, boned and cut into 4 cm cubes

steps.text: Toss the pork and back fat with the salt and spices and leave in the fridge overnight, a short cure rather than a long one.
Put the meat, aromatics, wine and water in a heavy casserole, cover, and cook at 130C (265F) for 4 hours.
It is ready when a cube collapses under the back of a spoon with no push behind it and the fat has run clear above the liquid.
Lift out the meat, pick out thyme stalks and bay, and shred with two forks or in a mixer on its lowest speed until it is strands, never paste.
Beat in enough strained cooking fat and juice to make it spoonable, then chill a teaspoonful and taste that before you correct the salt.
Pack into jars, pressing out air pockets, seal with 5 mm of melted fat, and keep 3 days before eating.

note: Two things go wrong. A food processor shears the fibres into wallpaper paste, so pull the meat and keep the strands. And seasoning judged hot always lands flat, because fat coats the tongue and blunts salt more as it chills: season, chill a spoonful, taste the cold one. The fat seal is not decoration either. Any pocket of trapped air turns the meat beneath it grey within a week.

ingredients.text: 1 kg beef silverside, cut with the grain into strips 25 mm thick
60 ml brown malt or cider vinegar
20 g coriander seed, toasted and coarsely cracked

steps.text: Dip each strip in the vinegar, let it drain, then toss it in the salt, coriander, sugar and pepper.
Stack in a non-reactive dish and refrigerate 6 hours, turning once, until the surface has gone dull and firm.
Wipe each strip with a vinegar-dampened cloth, hook it, and hang in a warm box at 25-30C (77-86F) with a fan pulling air past every face, nothing touching.
Weigh the batch daily. Medium biltong, still red in the middle, is 50% weight loss and takes 3 to 4 days. Dry sticks are 60%.
Slice across the grain and store in paper, not plastic, or it sweats and softens.

note: Biltong is not jerky. Jerky is thin slices cooked dry in a warm oven; biltong is a thick strip cured raw and dried by moving air, so the vinegar does real work, dropping surface pH under 5 while the interior takes days to lose its water. Salt sits at only 2.5% because the drying, not the brine, preserves. Stalled air is the failure: a strip touching its neighbour sweats at the contact point and sours from the inside out.

ingredients.text: 500 g fresh anchovies, held at -20C (-4F) for 48 hours first

steps.text: Pinch off each head and pull it downward to draw the guts with it, open the fish along the belly, and lift the backbone out from the head end, leaving the fillets joined at the tail.
Rinse the fillets in cold water, changing it until the water stays clear, because leftover blood turns the finished fish grey.
Lay them skin down in a shallow dish, pour over the vinegar, water and salt, and refrigerate 4 hours for small fish, 6 for fat ones.
Cut one fillet across to check: the moment no translucent line is left at the centre, drain the lot.
Layer in a container with the garlic and parsley, cover completely with the oil, and leave a day before eating. Use within five days.

note: This is an acid cure, not a salt one. Acetic acid unfolds the muscle proteins much as heat does, which is why the flesh goes white and firm with no pan involved, and the change front travels in from both faces, so thickness sets the time and the clock only follows it. Leave them in past white and they go chalky and taste of nothing but vinegar. Oil is the stop: drained and covered, the acid has nothing left to work on.

ingredients.text: 1.2 L light beef or chicken stock, held at a bare simmer
60 g beef marrow, scooped from the bone and diced

steps.text: Steep the saffron in 60 ml of the hot stock and leave it while you start, until the liquid is deep orange and smells of hay rather than dust.
Melt the marrow with the onion in a wide pan over low heat until the onion is translucent and slippery with no colour at all, about 6 minutes.
Add the rice and toast it, stirring, until the grains rattle, feel hot to the back of the hand and turn glassy at the edges around an opaque white core. Pour in the wine and let it vanish.

Add simmering stock a ladle at a time, stirring often and keeping the pan at a lazy boil; stir in the saffron at minute 12 and stop when a grain bends without snapping but still shows a chalk line at its centre, 16 to 18 minutes.
Pull the pan off the heat, count to sixty, then beat in the cold butter and the cheese hard until the rice is glossy and settles in a slow wave when you knock the pan. Season and serve at once.

note: The sauce is not cream: it is the rice's own surface starch, rubbed loose by the grains turning against the pan and suspended in hot stock. Add the stock in stages and keep it simmering, because cold stock drops the pan off the boil and the starch stops shedding. Mantecatura goes off the heat with cold butter; beaten into a boiling pan the butter splits and the risotto turns greasy instead of glossy.

ingredients.text: 600 g chicken, jointed into small bone-in pieces
400 g rabbit, jointed into small bone-in pieces
200 g flat green beans, topped and halved
150 g cooked garrofo or butter beans
200 g ripe tomato, grated to a pulp

steps.text: Heat the oil in a 42 cm pan over medium and brown the chicken and rabbit hard on every side until the meat is mahogany and no longer sticks, 12 to 15 minutes, then push it out to the rim.

Fry the beans in the clear centre, add the grated tomato and cook it down until it darkens and the oil runs red at the edges, then stir in the pimenton and count to ten only, since it burns almost immediately.
Pour in the water with the saffron, rosemary, garrofo and salt; boil 25 to 30 minutes until the level sits just below the pan rivets and the broth tastes a shade too salty.

Rain the rice across the pan in a cross and shake it level, no deeper than 2 cm. Do not stir again. Boil hard for 8 minutes, then drop to a bare simmer for 8 to 10 more, until the surface liquid is gone and small craters open.
Raise the heat for 60 to 90 seconds until you hear a fine even crackle and smell toasted grain; cut the heat the moment the smell sharpens, cover with a cloth and rest 5 minutes.

It only forms if the rice sits still: stir after the grains go in and you strip starch into the liquid and get risotto in a paella pan. ingredients.text: 700 g goat shoulder on the bone, in 4 cm pieces

4 green cardamom, 1 black cardamom, 5 cm cassia bark, 4 cloves, 2 bay leaves

Soak the rice 30 minutes and drain. Boil the water hard with the rest of the salt and the whole spices, drop in the rice and cook 3 to 4 minutes only, until a grain crushed between finger and thumb is soft outside with a firm white core. Drain at once.
Spread the marinated meat in an even layer in a heavy pot, pile the drained rice over it without pressing, and scatter on the rest of the fried onion, the saffron milk and the remaining melted ghee.
Roll the dough into a rope, press it round the rim and clamp the lid on. Cook 5 minutes on high to raise steam, then on the lowest flame, or on a tava, for 45 minutes.
Rest it sealed off the heat for 15 minutes, break the crust, and lift the biryani out in wedges with a flat spoon from the bottom of the pot rather than stirring.

Use basmati aged a year: the drier grain elongates rather than splitting.

ingredients.text: 600 g ripe plum tomatoes, or 400 g tinned plum tomatoes

steps.text: Blend the tomatoes, bell pepper, scotch bonnet and half the onion smooth, then boil the puree hard in a wide pan for 15 to 20 minutes until it turns from scarlet to brick and stops smelling raw and green.
In a heavy pot fry the remaining onion in the oil until soft, add the tomato paste and fry it 5 minutes until it darkens to rust and the oil floats free around it.
Add the reduced puree, curry powder, thyme, bay and salt and fry, stirring, for 10 to 15 minutes more, until the oil separates at the edges again and the base tastes sweet rather than sharp.

Rinse the rice and stir it through until every grain is coated red, then add the hot stock so the liquid sits exactly level with the rice. Cover with foil, then the lid, and cook on the lowest heat for 30 minutes without stirring or peeking.
Lift the lid, raise the heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the base smells faintly of smoke, then kill the heat, fork the rice through from the sides and leave it covered 10 minutes.

ingredients.text: 200 g jasmine or other long grain rice
8 g salt, plus more to finish
250 g pork loin, rubbed with 6 g salt and chilled overnight

steps.text: Rinse the rice until the water runs milky rather than white, drain it well, then toss it with the oil and salt and leave it 30 minutes; an hour in the freezer does the same job faster.
Bring the water to a rolling boil in a tall pot, add the rice and ginger, return it to the boil, then hold a lively simmer with the lid ajar, scraping up from the base every few minutes.
After 50 to 70 minutes the grains will have burst and lost their edges, and the congee should fall off the spoon in a sheet rather than in drops. Slacken with boiling water if it gets ahead of you.
Slice the salted pork thin across the grain, stir it in with half the century egg and simmer 5 minutes, just until the pork turns opaque and firms.
Season with the white pepper and more salt, then ladle out and top with the remaining century egg, the spring onion and the fried shallots.

note: Congee is a starch suspension, not rice sitting in soup, and agitation is what builds it: stirring shears starch off the grains until the liquid thickens on its own. The oil and salt rub, or a spell in the freezer, damages the grain surface so it collapses sooner. Work at about 1:12 rice to water by weight and stop it looser than you want to eat it, because congee sets hard as it cools.

ingredients.text: 700 g cooked short grain rice, cooled to just warm
200 g beef sirloin, sliced 3 mm thick
45 ml toasted sesame oil, plus 40 ml for the bowls
60 g gochujang, loosened with 20 ml water and 10 g sugar

steps.text: Cook and dress each vegetable on its own: spinach blanched 30 seconds and wrung out dry, sprouts boiled 3 minutes, carrot, courgette and shiitake fried separately until just limp. Season each with a little garlic, sesame oil and salt and keep them apart.
Marinate the beef 20 minutes in the soy, sugar, garlic and sesame oil, then sear it in a dry hot pan in one layer until the edges catch and darken.
Set the stone bowls on a medium flame and heat them 5 minutes, until a flicked drop of water skitters and disappears on contact, then swirl 10 ml of sesame oil around the inside of each.
Press the warm rice firmly against the base and walls in an even layer and leave it completely alone for 3 to 4 minutes, listening for the sizzle to tighten into a fine crackle.

Lay the vegetables and beef over the top in wedges, slide on a fried egg, and carry the bowl to the table still ticking. The diner mixes in the gochujang, which lifts the crust off the stone in shards.

note: The crust, nurungji, is dextrinised starch and Maillard browning against the stone, and it needs a dry surface to start. Use rice that has stood and given off its steam, not wet rice straight from the cooker, and once it is pressed in do not touch it. A bowl that is not properly hot glues the layer on instead of browning it and the crust tears. Oil the stone and load it at once, or the sesame oil smokes and the bowl tastes bitter.

ingredients.text: 0.3 g saffron, ground with a pinch of sugar and steeped in 60 ml hot water

steps.text: Rinse the rice in several changes of cold water until the water runs clear, then soak it in salted water for 1 to 2 hours and drain.

Boil the 4 L of water with the salt, drop the rice in and cook it 4 to 6 minutes, until a grain is soft at the outside but still snaps at a firm needle in the centre. Drain and rinse briefly under tepid water.

Beat the yogurt with the yolk, half the saffron water and two ladles of the parboiled rice. Pour the oil and half the melted ghee into the pot and spread this mixture over the base in an even layer about 1 cm deep.

Mound the rest of the rice on top loosely in a pyramid, punch five holes down to the base with the handle of a spoon, and pour over the remaining ghee, the rest of the saffron water and 3 tablespoons of water.

Wrap the lid in a tea towel and clamp it on. Cook on medium 8 to 10 minutes until you hear a steady sizzle, then on the lowest heat for 45 to 50 minutes. Stand the pot on a wet cloth for 2 minutes to release the crust, then invert onto a plate.

note: Parboiling in heavily salted water and draining carries off the surface starch, which is why chelow steams into separate grains instead of clumping. The yogurt layer is the tahdig itself: its protein and milk sugar brown where plain rice would only harden, and it releases as one disc. Punch steam vents to the base or the mound cooks wet, and wrap the lid so condensation is absorbed rather than raining back down.

ingredients.text: 1.2 kg chicken thighs and drumsticks, bone in and skin on
200 g tomato, grated to a pulp
3 g ground annatto, or 0.2 g saffron
80 g green olives, with 30 ml of their brine

steps.text: Salt the chicken and brown it skin down in the oil in a wide heavy pot until the skin lets go of the pan by itself and is deep brown, about 8 minutes, then 2 minutes on the other side. Lift it out.

Cook the onion, pepper and garlic in the same fat over medium until translucent and sweet smelling, then add the tomato, oregano, bay and annatto and cook until the mixture darkens and the oil runs orange around the edge.
Stir in the rice and turn it in the fat for 2 minutes until every grain is coated and the edges go slightly translucent, then pour in the wine and let it boil away.

Add the hot stock, the olives and their brine and taste: it should be a shade saltier than you want. Settle the chicken back on top, bring it to a boil, cover, and cook on the lowest heat 18 to 20 minutes without lifting the lid.
Scatter the peas over, put the lid back and leave the pot off the heat for 10 minutes, then fork the rice up from the edges.

note: This is the pilaf method: coating each grain in hot fat before any liquid arrives slows water into the starch and keeps the grains separate. Count every source of liquid, the wine, the tomato and the juice the chicken will give up, and err dry, because the covered ten minute rest moves moisture from the sodden base up to the drier top. Lift the lid mid cook and the pot falls out of steam, leaving the top layer chalky.

steps.text: Wash the rice in cold water, turning it with an open hand and changing the water four or five times, until it runs faintly cloudy rather than clear. Over-washing chips the grains. Drain in a sieve for 30 minutes.

Cook it with the measured water and the kombu laid on top; lift the kombu out as the water comes to the boil, cover, cook on the lowest heat 12 minutes, then leave the lid on off the heat for 10 minutes more.
Warm the vinegar, sugar and salt together just until the crystals dissolve, no further, or the acid boils off.

Tip the hot rice into a wide wooden or plastic tub, pour the seasoning over the back of a paddle so it lands spread out, and cut through the rice at a slant, folding rather than stirring, while fanning it.
Stop when the rice is at body temperature, about 37C (99F), the grains gloss individually and a squeezed handful holds together. Cover with a damp cloth and use it within the hour.

note: Season the rice hot: the starch granules are still swollen and open, and they drink the vinegar in. Let it cool first and the seasoning sits on the outside and reads harsh. Cut with the edge of the paddle instead of stirring, since crushed grains give paste, and fan to drive off surface moisture so the rice glosses rather than sweats. Never refrigerate it. Near 4C (39F) the starch retrogrades and goes chalky for good.

steps.text: Dry roast the moong dal in a pan over medium heat, shaking it, for 3 to 4 minutes until it smells nutty and a few grains freckle brown, then rinse it with the rice until the water runs clear.

Heat half the ghee in a heavy pot and crackle the cumin until the seeds darken a shade and stop spitting, then add the asafoetida, ginger and chilli and stir for 30 seconds only, since asafoetida scorches fast.

Add the rice, dal, turmeric, salt and water, bring to a boil and simmer covered for 25 minutes, or pressure cook to 3 whistles, until the grains have lost their edges and the mass drops off a spoon in a soft ribbon.
Beat in the rest of the ghee off the heat and loosen with boiling water until it pours slowly, then serve straight away.

note: Khichdi is the opposite of pilaf: at 1:4 grain to water the rice goes past absorption into full gelatinisation, and collapse is the point, so wash it but do not chase separate grains. Roasting the dal dry first sets its surface protein and stops it dissolving into slime. Add the second half of the ghee off the heat, where it stays aromatic instead of cooking flat, and serve it looser than looks right; it tightens within minutes of leaving the pot.

ingredients.text: 1 whole cauliflower, 900 g to 1.1 kg, leaves trimmed, stem left whole

steps.text: Bring the water, salt, sugar, bay and coriander seed to the boil in a pot deep enough to submerge the head, then lower the cauliflower in stem down and weight it with a small plate so it stays under.
Simmer gently 12 to 15 minutes, until a thin knife slides into the thickest part of the stem with only slight resistance and the florets have gone from chalk white to faintly translucent.
Lift it out onto a rack, stem up so the hollows drain, and leave 20 minutes until the surface is dry to the back of a finger; wet cauliflower will steam, not colour.
Rub all over with 40 ml of the olive oil, set on a tray and roast at 220C (425F) for 30 to 40 minutes, turning once, until the florets are mahogany with black tips.
Whisk the miso, lemon, remaining oil and chilli, brush over the head for the last 8 minutes only, and carve at the table in thick vertical slabs.

ingredients.text: 1 celeriac, about 800 g, scrubbed hard, root hairs left on

steps.text: Work the flour, salt and thyme with the water to a stiff, smooth dough, adding the last of the water only if it will not come together; rest it 15 minutes so it rolls without tearing.
Roll to 8 mm, wrap the celeriac completely with no thin patches, pinch the seams and patch any split with a scrap: every crack is a steam leak.
Bake at 200C (390F) for 2 to 2 hours 15 minutes, until a skewer pushed through the crust meets no resistance at the centre and comes out steaming.
Rest the sealed parcel 20 minutes so the heat evens out, then crack the crust with the back of a knife and lift the celeriac clear, brushing off any salt that clings.
Toast the hazelnuts until they smell of biscuit, crush them and whisk with oil, vinegar, mustard and parsley; peel the celeriac, cut into thick wedges and spoon the dressing over while hot.

note: The salt crust seasons almost nothing: it is a sealed ceramic shell that turns the celeriac into its own steamer, holding it just above 100C in its own moisture so the sugars concentrate instead of leaching into a pan of water. A cracked crust vents that steam and the outer centimetre dries to cork, so patch every split before it goes in and rest the parcel before you break it open.

ingredients.text: 250 g king oyster mushrooms, cut in 3 mm dice
25 g dried red chillies, soaked and chopped
20 g fermented black beans, rinsed and roughly chopped

steps.text: Soak the shiitake in the hot water 30 minutes, squeeze them dry over the bowl, chop to 3 mm dice and keep 100 ml of the strained soaking liquid.
Warm the oil to about 140C (285F), fry the shallots until pale gold and lift them out, then the garlic and ginger for 60 seconds only, and set both aside; they will keep browning off the heat.
Fry the two mushrooms in the same oil, 12 to 15 minutes, until the loud bubbling of escaping water quietens to a slow fizz and the pieces are shrunken and chewy at the edge.

Return the aromatics with the chillies, black beans and kombu powder, add the soy, sugar, vinegar and reserved soaking liquid and cook 10 minutes more, until the liquid has gone and the oil sits clear on top.
Cool completely and jar with the oil covering the solids by 5 mm; it keeps 3 weeks refrigerated and tastes better after two days.

note: XO tastes bottomless because glutamate and nucleotides multiply each other rather than simply add: dried shiitake brings guanylate, kombu and soy bring glutamate, and the dried scallop of the original is not doing anything a mushroom cannot. The risk is the frying. Each addition dumps water, the oil temperature drops, then spikes as it dries, and garlic burns in the ten seconds after the bubbling goes quiet. Fry in stages, by moisture content.

steps.text: Halve the aubergines lengthways, salt the cut faces and leave 15 minutes, then blot dry; steam them cut side up for 10 to 12 minutes, until a skewer passes through the shoulder without pushing back.
Cool 5 minutes, then score the cut faces in a 1 cm diamond, cutting halfway into the flesh but never through the skin.

Heat the oil in a heavy pan until it shimmers, lay the halves cut side down and press flat with a spatula for 4 to 5 minutes, until the whole face is lacquer brown and the flesh has collapsed to a custard.
Simmer the miso, mirin, sugar, sake, ginger and vinegar for 2 minutes to a glossy paste that falls from the spoon in a ribbon.
Turn the halves skin down, spoon the glaze over the scored faces and grill close to the element for 90 seconds, until it blisters and darkens at the ridges; scatter spring onion and sesame.

note: Raw aubergine is a sponge, much of its volume air, and it will drink a hot pan dry and then weep the oil back out when the cells finally collapse: greasy, beige and still squeaky. Collapse that structure first with moist heat, and the second cooking becomes a sear that browns on a spoonful of oil in four minutes. Glaze at the very end and watch it: the miso mix is roughly a quarter sugar and goes from blistered to acrid in under a minute.

ingredients.text: 6 beetroot, 150 to 180 g each, scrubbed, unpeeled, tails left on
2 kg hardwood charcoal or a hardwood fire burnt down

steps.text: Burn the fire down until the flames are gone and the coals are red under a grey ash skin; flame gives you a charcoal shell over a raw middle.
Nestle the beetroot directly into the embers, heap more coals over the tops, and turn them every 15 minutes so no face sits still against the hottest spot.
Cook 45 to 60 minutes, until a skewer runs to the centre with no resistance and the skins are blistered black and lifting away from the flesh.
Rest 10 minutes, then rub the skins off in a dry cloth; they should come away in sheets with the charred layer.
Quarter while still hot, dress at once with vinegar, oil, horseradish, toasted walnuts, dill, salt and pepper, and turn them once in the bowl as they cool.

note: The skin is the cooking vessel. Sealed, the beet steams in its own water while radiant heat caramelises the sugar just beneath it, and beetroot carries more sugar than almost any other vegetable you will roast. Foil gives you a boiled flavour and no char; live flame gives a burnt shell over a raw core. Use embers with grey edges. Dress while hot: a warm beet pulls vinegar into the flesh, a cold one sheds it onto the plate.

steps.text: Trim the roots flat but leave the root plate attached, cut off the coarse dark green, then split each leek lengthways to within 2 cm of the root and fan the layers under cold running water until no grit remains.
Simmer in the salted water 12 to 16 minutes, until a knife tip enters the thickest white and meets nothing; a leek that squeaks against the teeth is undercooked, not al dente.
Lift onto a tray lined with a folded cloth, cut side down, lay another cloth on top and press with a light tray for 10 minutes.
Whisk the mustard with the vinegar and a pinch of salt, then beat in the oil in a thin stream until it thickens, and stir through shallot, capers and parsley.
Arrange the halves still warm, spoon the vinaigrette along the length and leave 20 minutes before serving so they drink it in.

Then the water: a leek holds it between its layers, and a wet leek sheds vinaigrette straight into a puddle on the plate. Press the halves on a cloth, then dress them warm. ingredients.text: 4 large king oyster mushrooms with thick stems, about 450 g

steps.text: Steep the kombu in the water at 60C (140F) for 20 minutes, lift it out before it turns slippery, add soy and mirin and reduce to 60 ml of syrupy glaze.
Cut the stems into 3 cm cylinders, score a 2 mm crosshatch about 1 mm deep on both flat faces, salt them and rest 10 minutes, then blot the beads of moisture away.
Get a heavy pan properly hot, add the neutral oil, and lay the cylinders down spaced apart; leave them completely alone 3 to 4 minutes, until the underside is deep brown and lifts without sticking.
Turn, add olive oil, garlic and thyme, and baste for 2 minutes as the second face colours and the mushroom goes springy rather than soft.
Spoon on the kombu glaze off the heat, let it bubble to a shine, and finish with lemon zest and a squeeze of juice.

note: A mushroom is around 90% water held in walls of chitin, and chitin does not dissolve with heat, which is why this takes a sear that would reduce any other vegetable to a slick. It just cannot brown until the water has gone. Salting the cut faces and blotting means you start already partly dry. Crowd the pan or start it lukewarm and they release their water, stew grey and turn rubbery. The scoring is not decoration: it holds the glaze.

ingredients.text: 1 hispi or pointed cabbage, about 800 g
25 g capers, rinsed and drained dry

steps.text: Quarter the cabbage through the root so each wedge holds together, salt the cut faces and leave 15 minutes, then blot.

Heat a heavy pan until a drop of water skitters, add the oil and lay the wedges on one cut face; do not move them for 4 to 5 minutes, until the face is mahogany with black frilled edges, then repeat on the second face.
Transfer the pan to a 200C (390F) oven for 8 to 10 minutes, until a knife slips into the root end without effort while the leaf edges stay crisp.

Melt the butter in a pale pan over medium heat and cook until it stops foaming, the solids on the base go the colour of hazelnut skin and it smells of toasted nuts, then drop in the capers and breadcrumbs and pull it off the heat immediately.
Add the lemon juice to stop the butter cooking, stir in the parsley and pour the whole pan over the wedges.

Fast dry heat browns the sugars before that chemistry gets going, which is why a black-edged wedge tastes sweet and a simmered one does not. Then watch the butter. Once its water has boiled off the milk solids brown at around 150C, and the gap between hazelnut and burnt is about twenty seconds; the lemon is the brake.

ingredients.text: 2 kg floury potatoes such as Maris Piper or russet
2 garlic cloves, crushed to a paste

steps.text: Melt the butter without stirring, let it settle 5 minutes and pour off the clear fat, leaving the milky solids behind; you want about 230 g of clarified butter, and the solids would burn later.
Peel the potatoes and slice 2 mm thick on a mandolin straight into a bowl with the butter, garlic, salt, thyme and pepper, and do not rinse them at any point.
Line a 900 g loaf tin with baking paper, then layer the slices flat and overlapping, pressing each layer down with your palm so no air is trapped, and level the top.
Cover tightly with foil and bake at 160C (320F) for 1 hour 45 minutes to 2 hours, until a skewer meets no resistance anywhere from top to base.
Press with a board and a 2 kg weight, cool, then refrigerate overnight; turn out, cut into bars and fry in the oil over medium heat until all four long faces are glassy and crisp.

note: Do not rinse the slices. The starch you would wash away is the glue: amylose gelatinises between the layers as they cook and sets as the terrine cools, and that, not the butter, is what makes the block sliceable. Waxy potatoes never do it and slide apart on the knife. Press while warm to drive out the air, then chill overnight so the starch retrogrades and firms. Salt every layer, because there is no seasoning the middle afterwards.

ingredients.text: 2 kg very ripe tomatoes, the softest you can find

steps.text: Core and roughly chop the tomatoes, blitz with the salt in short pulses to a coarse, still-lumpy purée; a smooth blend makes a fine suspension that will drive pulp through the cloth.
Stir in the kombu and basil sprig, cover and leave at room temperature 30 minutes for the salt to draw the water out.
Line a sieve with a doubled muslin, set it over a deep bowl, tip in the purée and refrigerate 8 to 12 hours, letting it drip; never squeeze or twist the cloth.
Discard the pulp and taste the liquid, which will be pale gold: correct with the vinegar and more salt until it tastes distinctly seasoned, well past where you would stop with a soup that had body.
Serve cold at 8C, or warmed to no more than 60C (140F), poured at the table over cherry tomatoes, cucumber, torn basil and a thread of olive oil.

note: It runs clear because it drips, not because of any raft, so never squeeze the bag: pressure forces pectin-bound pulp through the weave and cloudy tomato water tastes flat. Salt at 1% of the fruit weight seasons and pulls water out osmotically, taking the yield to around 60%. With the pulp goes all the body, so it needs more salt, more acid and the kombu glutamate to stand up. Do not boil it; the aroma of raw tomato leaves above about 70C.

ingredients.text: 1 tsp salt, for the grinding jar

steps.text: Rub the steaks with 1 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and leave 15 minutes, until water beads stand on the cut faces and the flesh firms to the touch.

Soak both mustards in warm water 20 minutes, drain, then grind with 4 green chillies, 1 tsp salt and 3 tbsp cold water in short pulses, stopping the moment the paste smells sharp and clean rather than dull. Push it through a sieve and discard the husk.
Heat 75ml mustard oil in a kadai until the raw pungency flattens and a thin white wisp lifts off the surface, then take the pan off the flame for 30 seconds.

Return it to a low flame, pour in the sieved paste with the water, remaining turmeric and salt, and cook 4 minutes until it thickens to a loose custard and oil beads yellow around the rim. Never let it gallop.

Slide the fish in one layer, spoon gravy over each piece, cover and cook 7 minutes until the flesh parts from the backbone under a fork. Trail the last 15ml raw mustard oil and the whole chillies over, cover, and rest 5 minutes off the heat.

note: Mustard pungency is made, not stored: crushing puts myrosinase onto sinigrin and the reaction wants cold water and a minute. Grind long and the jar warms, the volatile isothiocyanate blows off, and the husk gives up bitter phenols in its place. So soak the seeds, pulse briefly with salt and a green chilli, sieve out the husk, and never boil the gravy hard once the paste is in.

steps.text: Rub the fish with 1.5 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt and leave 15 minutes until the surface goes tacky.

Fry the potato and potol in the same oil until the cut edges turn gold and translucent, then lift them out.

The turmeric and salt rub pulls surface moisture out, and hot oil then sets a thin denatured protein crust that holds the steak together through the simmer. ingredients.text: 1.2kg goat on the bone, shoulder and leg, in 4cm pieces

steps.text: Marinate the goat with the yoghurt, turmeric, ginger, garlic, salt and 1 tbsp of the mustard oil for at least 2 hours.

Heat the rest of the oil until the pungency flattens, add the sugar and let it foam to the colour of dark honey, then the whole spices, then the onions. Fry 20 minutes until they collapse into a jammy brown mass that no longer catches on the spoon.
Tip in the meat with its marinade over a high flame and stir until the pieces tighten, go grey-brown, and the yoghurt breaks into a rough curd around them.

Now kosha it. Let the mass dry out and stick, splash in 60ml water, scrape the brown fond off the base and stir it back through. Repeat 5 or 6 times across 30 minutes, until the meat is dark mahogany and oil pools red at the rim of the pan.
Add the hot water, cover, and cook on the lowest flame 50 minutes until the meat gives at the bone. Stir in the ghee and garam masala and rest 10 minutes.

note: Koshano is a browning technique disguised as stirring. Each cycle of drying out and splashing lets onion sugars and yoghurt proteins scorch onto the pan, then lifts that fond back into the meat, so colour and depth build in layers. Add all the water at once and the pot never climbs past 100C (212F), nothing browns, and you get a pale thin jhol. Stop only when oil separates and runs red at the edge.

flavor.sentence: Leads with warm spice humming through the middle, aromatics blooming from the first bite, settling low and earthy.

steps.text: Soak the posto in hot water for 30 minutes, drain, then grind with 2 green chillies, a pinch of salt and 3 tbsp cold water until the paste ribbons off the spoon and feels smooth, not sandy, between finger and thumb.
Heat 45ml mustard oil until the raw bite flattens, drop the flame to medium and crackle the kalojeere for 10 seconds.
Add the potato, turmeric and salt and fry over medium heat 8 minutes until the cut faces are gold and the edges have gone translucent.
Pour in the water, cover, and cook 8 minutes until a cube yields to a spoon but still holds its corners.

Take the pan off a hard boil, stir the posto paste through with the sugar, and cook gently 4 minutes until it tightens around the potato and oil beads on the surface. It must stay ivory. Finish off the heat with the last 15ml raw mustard oil and the remaining chillies, slit.

note: Poppy seed is around 45 per cent oil inside a hard shell, so it becomes a paste only if the shell is softened by soaking and then ground wet and cool. Grind it dry or hot and the oil cracks out: what you get is a gritty, greasy sludge that will not bind to anything. In the pan there is a second trap. Past pale ivory the paste scorches, and scorched posto tastes bitter and sandy. Low flame, short cook.
techniques: Frying the paste until the oil splits

ingredients.text: 2 tsp white poppy seeds ground to a paste with 1 tsp yellow mustard seeds

steps.text: Fry the bori in the mustard oil until they puff and go biscuit-gold, then lift them out. Fry the uchche slices by themselves until the edges crisp and darken, and set them aside on their own plate.
Fry the remaining vegetables in batches until the cut edges take colour but the centres are still raw, then lift them out.

Temper the panch phoron and bay leaves in the same oil over a low flame, and judge the pan by the methi: pull it the second the fenugreek darkens one shade, because ten seconds later the whole tempering is acrid.
Return every vegetable except the gourd, add the ginger, the poppy and mustard paste, salt, sugar and water, cover, and simmer 15 minutes until a drumstick gives up its pulp to a fingernail.
Drop the flame, stir the milk in below a simmer and cook 3 minutes until the gravy turns opaque white and just coats a spoon.
Fold the fried gourd and bori back in, finish with the ghee and ground radhuni, and rest 5 minutes so the bori soften without going to mush.

note: Shukto opens the meal because bitterness sharpens the palate for the rice, dal and fish that follow, so that bitterness has to stay a note and not a wash. The cucurbitacins in uchche are water-soluble: simmer the gourd from the start and the whole white gravy turns bitter. Fry it alone, fold it back at the end, and hold the milk below a simmer, since heat plus ginger will curdle it into grains.

steps.text: Soak the dal 2 hours, drain, then boil with the turmeric, bay, salt and water, skimming the grey foam, 25 minutes, until a grain crushes between finger and thumb yet is still visibly a separate grain.
Fry the coconut chips in the ghee until the edges go the colour of pale toast, then lift them out before they darken and turn bitter.
In the same ghee temper the cumin, dried chillies, cassia, cardamom and cloves until the cumin darkens a shade and the cardamom smells sweet rather than green.
Pour the tempering and the ginger into the dal, stir in the jaggery, and simmer 8 minutes until the dal holds a spoon trail for two full seconds.
Fold in the coconut, raisins and garam masala and rest off the heat 5 minutes.

note: This is the dal you eat with luchi, so it has to stay grain-distinct: boiled to the point where a grain crushes on the palate but has not surrendered its skin. The trap is the gur. Sugar competes with the starch for water and firms the seed coat, so dal cooked sweet from the start never softens further, however long it sits. Soften and salt first, sweeten at the end.

steps.text: Score a shallow lattice into both faces of each round, rub in the turmeric, chilli, salt and sugar, and leave 20 minutes until beads of water stand on the surface.
Blot the rounds dry on a cloth, or that water will spit and drag the oil temperature down.
Heat the mustard oil in a flat pan until the sharp raw smell flattens and a white wisp lifts off, then drop the flame to medium and let it settle for 30 seconds.
Lay the rounds in without crowding and leave them alone 3 minutes, until the underside is deep mahogany and the flesh at the rim has gone translucent. Turn once and give the second side 2 minutes.
Drain the slices standing on edge on a rack rather than flat on paper, and salt them while they are still hot.

note: Raw mustard oil is a condiment, not a frying medium: it carries allyl isothiocyanate and a high free fatty acid load, and both taste raw and catch at the back of the throat. Take it to the smoke point, around 250C (480F), until the sharpness flattens and a wisp lifts, then drop to medium. Fry below that and aubergine, which is mostly air, drinks oil faster than its pectin can collapse.

ingredients.text: 600g bagda chingri (tiger prawns), shell and head on
1 tsp turmeric and 1.5 tsp salt, for the prawns
2 bay leaves, 4 green cardamom, 5cm cassia bark, 4 cloves
150g onion, ground to a smooth paste

steps.text: Devein the prawns through the back, leaving the shell and head on, and rub them with the first lot of turmeric and salt.
Heat the mustard oil until the raw pungency flattens, then sear the prawns 40 seconds a side, until they turn opaque coral and curl into a loose C. Lift them out while they are still slightly under.
Temper the whole spices until the cardamom smells sweet, add the onion paste, and fry 10 minutes until the raw smell goes and the oil separates and runs orange at the edge.
Stir in the ginger, turmeric, chilli powder and sugar with 2 tbsp water and fry 2 minutes, until the paste no longer smells of raw spice.

Pour in the thin coconut milk and simmer gently 6 minutes until it coats a spoon, then add the thick coconut milk, the prawns and the chillies and hold the pan at a lazy shiver, never a boil, for 3 minutes. Finish off the heat with the ghee and garam masala.

note: Coconut milk is a protein-stabilised emulsion, not cream. Boil it hard and those proteins coagulate, the fat breaks out as an oily slick, and the gravy goes grainy. Prawns want exactly the same restraint: their muscle sets near 60C (140F) and starts wringing out water above 70C (158F). Sear for colour, pull them early, and return them only to a shivering pan. A prawn curled to a C is done; an O is a rubber band.
techniques: Frying the paste until the oil splits

ingredients.text: 700ml refined oil or ghee, for frying

steps.text: Rub the ghee into the flour and salt with your fingertips until the mixture looks like damp sand and holds its shape when squeezed in a fist.
Work in the water in stages and knead 5 minutes to a dough noticeably firmer than chapati dough, smooth and tight. Smear the surface with oil, cover, and rest 30 minutes.
Divide into 16 balls and roll each into a 10cm disc of even thickness, using a smear of oil on the board rather than a dusting of flour.

Bring the frying oil to 190C (375F), the point where a scrap of dough surfaces in two seconds. Slide a luchi in and press its centre gently under with the back of a slotted spoon until it balloons, about 10 seconds.
Flip it, give it 10 seconds more, and lift it out while it is still puffed and pale. A browned luchi is an overcooked one. Drain them standing on edge.

note: The puff is trapped steam, so everything you do protects the seal. Moyan, the ghee rubbed into the flour, shortens the gluten for tenderness, but past roughly one part fat to eight of maida the sheet can no longer hold pressure and the luchi lies flat and greasy. Roll evenly on an oiled board, never a floured one, since loose flour burns and darkens the oil. At 190C (375F) the skin sets before the steam finds a way out.

ingredients.text: 60g live plain yoghurt, at room temperature

steps.text: Reduce the milk over a medium flame, scraping the skin off the sides back in every few minutes, for 30 minutes, until it is down to about 1 litre and has turned the colour of ivory.

Melt the sugar with the water in a dry pan until it is the colour of strong tea and smells nutty, then stand back and kill it with a ladle of the hot milk. Stir the caramel and the gur into the pot until both dissolve.
Cool the sweetened milk to 45C (113F). Against the inside of the wrist it should read warm, not hot.
Whisk the starter yoghurt smooth with a little of the warm milk, fold it into the rest without beating air in, and pour into unglazed earthenware pots.
Cover and hold undisturbed at 35C to 40C (95F to 104F) for 7 hours, until the surface wobbles as one piece and pulls cleanly from the side of the pot, then chill 4 hours before serving.

note: The set is casein flocculating once the culture drags the milk down to about pH 4.6, and that culture only works between 35C and 45C (95F to 113F). Stir the starter into milk above 50C (122F) and you kill it; below 30C (86F) it stalls and you are left with sweet soup. Reducing the milk by a third raises the solids so the gel is firm without any thickener. While it sets, do not move the pots: shearing a young gel makes it weep whey.
techniques: Dry-pan toasting: spices, seeds and nuts
The wobble & the skewer: testing a bake

ingredients.text: 8 scallops on the half shell, 400 g total
40 g fun see (mung bean glass noodles)
60 g garlic, half chopped raw and half chopped and fried golden
3 spring onions, green parts finely shredded
1 red chilli, deseeded and finely diced

steps.text: Soak the fun see in cold water for 15 minutes until the strands are pliable and dull white, cut into 5 cm lengths and coil a small nest into each shell under the scallop.

Fry half the garlic in the oil over low heat until it is pale straw and the fizzing stops, about 3 minutes, then pull it off the heat and stir in the raw garlic, soy, wine, sugar, pepper and water: the mix should end up warm, not sizzling.
Spoon the garlic oil over the scallops and hold the plate back until the steamer water is at a hard rolling boil that rattles the lid.

Steam covered on the highest heat for 3 minutes 30 seconds for scallops 3 cm thick, and pull them the moment the outside has turned from glassy to chalk white while the centre still reads faintly translucent.
Shower with spring onion and chilli, pour 2 tablespoons of smoking oil over the greens so they hiss and collapse, and serve at once.

note: Scallop adductor is nearly pure muscle with almost no collagen, so it crosses from set to squeaky in under a minute. The lid must already be rattling when the plate goes in: a slow climb through 50 to 60C (120 to 140F) contracts the fibres gradually and wrings the liquor out into the shell. Load into full steam, time from the moment the lid is back down, and pull while the centre still looks glassy.

ingredients.text: 2 litres iced water, for the plunge

steps.text: Bring the soys, water, rock sugar, wine, ginger, spring onion and whole spices to a boil in a pot just wide enough to hold the bird, then drop the heat until only a bubble or two breaks the surface every few seconds, around 85C (185F).

Lower the chicken in breast down, holding the legs so the cavity floods, and lift it clear twice in the first two minutes so the cold cavity liquid drains and is replaced: the brine must never climb back to a rolling boil.

Poach 25 minutes for a 1.4 kg bird, then kill the heat and leave it covered in the brine off the stove for 20 minutes, until the thickest part of the thigh reads 72C (162F) and runs clear amber juice when pierced.
Lift the bird into iced water for 3 minutes, until the skin tightens and squeaks under a finger, then hang it to drip for 10 minutes.
Chop through the bone into 2 cm strips, rebuild the bird on the plate, brush with sesame oil and spoon over 100 ml of the hot brine.

note: The bird cooks on the brine's stored heat, not on boiling. Past about 90C (194F) the skin's collagen shrinks and splits and the breast muscle squeezes out its water and goes stringy. So hold the pot at a shiver, cut the heat early and let carryover finish the thigh. The iced plunge then contracts the skin so it sits tight and glossy instead of sagging away from the meat.

ingredients.text: 1.5 kg pork belly in one piece, skin on, ribs removed, 4 cm thick
20 g fine sea salt, for the flesh
25 g naam yu (fermented red bean curd), mashed
400 g coarse rock salt, for the skin cap

steps.text: Blanch the belly skin side up in boiling water for 4 minutes, until the skin turns from waxy to matte and firm, then dry it and prick the skin all over, 40 to 50 punctures per 10 cm square, through the skin but never down into the meat.

Rub the salt, sugar, five spice, pepper, naam yu and wine into the flesh and cut sides only, keeping every trace off the skin, then sit the piece skin up on a rack and refrigerate uncovered for 24 hours.
Wipe the skin with the vinegar, wall the meat in a tight foil boat so only the skin is exposed, pack the rock salt over the skin in a 1 cm slab and roast at 200C (390F) for 40 minutes.

Lift the salt cap off in one piece, scrape the skin clean, then raise the oven to 250C (480F) and cook 12 to 20 minutes more, turning the tray, until the whole skin has puffed into fine blisters and rings hollow when tapped with a spoon.
Rest 15 minutes, then chop skin side down through the crackling with one heavy cleaver stroke per cut into 3 cm squares, and scatter with flaky salt.

note: Crackling is skin dried until its last water flashes to steam and inflates the collagen into a foam. Leave surface moisture and you get leather instead. So the skin dries uncovered overnight, takes a vinegar wipe that evaporates fast and carries water out with it, and wears a rock salt cap that wicks and holds it under 100C (212F) while the meat roasts. Pull the cap, then blast the dry skin at 250C (480F).

ingredients.text: 450 g fresh flat ho fun rice noodles, at room temperature
250 g beef flank, sliced 3 mm across the grain
10 ml light soy sauce, for the beef
20 ml groundnut oil, for the beef
45 ml groundnut oil, for the wok
4 spring onions, cut into 6 cm batons

steps.text: Slap the bicarbonate and water into the beef until every slice has drunk it and the pile turns tacky, rest 20 minutes, rinse well and squeeze dry, then work in the soy, cornflour and 20 ml oil until the slices are slick and fall apart singly.

Pull the ho fun into single strands with your fingers, rubbing a teaspoon of oil through as you go: they must be loose and at room temperature, so steam them for 1 minute first if they came straight from the fridge.

Get the wok smoking with a thin film of oil, lay the beef out in one layer and leave it until the underside browns and it releases on its own, about 45 seconds, turn once and tip it out still pink inside.

Wipe the wok, heat the rest of the oil until it shimmers and the first wisp of smoke rises, give the onion 30 seconds, then add the noodles and press them flat against the metal in 20 second stretches until you smell scorched starch and see brown freckles on the strands.

Pour the soys, sugar and wine down the hot side of the wok so they caramelise before they reach the noodles, return the beef, throw in the sprouts and spring onion and toss six or seven times: out of the wok while the sprouts still squeak.

note: Two things make this dish. Bicarbonate raises the beef's pH so the myosin cannot contract tight and wring out water, which is what velveting means. And gon chau means dry: no stock, no cornflour slurry, because any added liquid parks the wok below the roughly 200C (390F) at which scorched starch and vaporised soy give you wok hei. Cold noodles have retrograded and will snap, so warm them first.
techniques: Resting meat & slicing against the grain

ingredients.text: 20 ml groundnut oil, plus more for the tray

steps.text: Whisk the rice flour, wheat starch, tapioca starch, cornflour and salt into the water until there is not a lump left, stir in the oil and rest 30 minutes: the batter should run off the whisk as thin as single cream.
Simmer the soys, water, rock sugar, ginger and spring onion for 5 minutes until the sugar has gone and the ginger smells sweet, then strain and keep warm.

Oil a flat metal tray, sit it on a trivet in a wok of hard boiling water, stir the batter up from the bottom, ladle in 60 ml and tilt to a 2 mm film, then cover and steam 3 minutes until the sheet is translucent, blistered all over and no longer milky in the middle.
Slide the tray into cold water for 5 seconds to shock the base, scrape the sheet up with an oiled scraper and roll it into a loose three-fold log: it should feel slippery and slack, never springy.
Cut into 6 cm lengths, pour the warm sauce over, finish with sesame seeds and eat within a few minutes while the rolls are still soft.

note: The slip comes from the starch blend, not the rice alone. Rice flour sets the sheet, wheat starch keeps it clear and tender, tapioca supplies the stretch. Too much rice flour and it tears as you roll; too much tapioca and it eats like chewing gum. The batter also separates within a minute of standing, so stir it up from the bottom before every single ladle: an unstirred pot pours a gluey sheet, then a sheet too thin to lift.

ingredients.text: 300 g boneless chicken thigh, in 3 cm pieces
2 lap cheong (Chinese cured sausage), sliced on the angle

steps.text: Soak the glutinous rice in cold water for 4 hours, until a grain crushes to powder between your nails, then drain; soak the lotus leaves in hot water until leathery and pliable and wipe both faces.
Marinate the chicken in the oyster sauce, both soys, sugar, cornflour, wine and pepper for 20 minutes, until the pieces look glazed and cling to each other.

Fry the ginger, dried shrimp and shiitake in the oil until the shrimp smells sweet and the mushrooms have squeaked and gone slack, add the soaking liquid, boil 2 minutes, then fold the lot through the drained raw rice until every grain is stained brown.
Cup 150 g of rice into each leaf, bury chicken, lap cheong and half an egg yolk in the middle, cover with more rice and fold the leaf into a tight brick with no gap at the seam.
Steam over a hard boil for 60 minutes, then open one: the rice should be glossy and hold its shape under a press, with no chalky white core.

note: Glutinous rice is almost pure amylopectin. Boiled, it never takes on enough water to cook through: it goes to paste outside and stays chalky in the centre. It has to soak cold for hours so water enters the grain slowly, then steam so it gelatinises evenly. The leaf is not decoration either; it seals the parcel so the rice cooks in its own trapped steam and picks up that tea-like smell.

ingredients.text: 600 g squid, cleaned, tubes opened flat and tentacles left whole
5 g fine salt, for the squid
8 g fine salt, for the seasoning

steps.text: Score the inside of the tubes in a 5 mm crosshatch two thirds of the way through, cut into 4 cm pieces, toss with the wine and salt for 10 minutes, then dry every piece hard between cloths until the surface is matte and takes a fingerprint.
Toast the seasoning salt, white pepper, five spice and sugar in a dry pan for 40 seconds, until the pepper turns sharply floral, then tip it straight out so it stops cooking.
Dredge the squid in the mixed potato starch and cornflour, then shake it in a sieve until only a chalk-thin coat is left clinging.
Fry at 190C (375F) in two batches for 60 to 75 seconds, until the coating goes from white to pale gold and the pieces have curled and float high in the oil.

Drain, then flash the garlic, chillies and spring onion in a nearly dry wok for 20 seconds until fragrant but uncoloured, return the squid, shower with the toasted seasoning and toss three times before it hits the plate.

note: Squid has two edible windows: under about 2 minutes, or over 30. In between, the collagen in the mantle shrinks and squeezes the water out and the flesh goes to rubber. Frying at 190C (375F) keeps you inside the first window, but only if the squid is bone dry. Wet squid drops the oil temperature, so it sits far longer and crosses into the rubber zone while the crust is still pale.

ingredients.text: 2 lap cheong (Chinese cured sausage), sliced 3 mm on the angle
300 g boneless chicken thigh, in 3 cm pieces
10 ml light soy sauce, for the chicken
45 ml light soy sauce, for the sauce

steps.text: Rinse the rice until the water runs almost clear and soak it 30 minutes; meanwhile marinate the chicken in the oyster sauce, light soy, cornflour, wine, ginger and pepper, and simmer the sauce ingredients until the rock sugar dissolves.
Drain the rice, bring it to a boil with the 360 ml water in an oiled clay pot, uncovered, until craters open across the surface and the free water has gone.

Lay the chicken and lap cheong over the rice, cover and cook on the lowest flame for 12 minutes: the sausage fat should render down through the grains and the pot should smell of caramel, never of smoke.
Drizzle 30 ml of oil down the inside wall of the pot, raise to a medium flame and rotate the pot a quarter turn every 45 seconds for 3 minutes, listening for a steady crackle rather than a hiss.
Rest off the heat 5 minutes, lay the choy sum on top, pour the sauce over and cut straight down to the base with a spoon: the fan jiu crust should lift away in deep amber sheets you can hear.

note: The crust is not burnt rice. It is the layer touching the clay that ran out of free water first, so it climbs past 100C (212F) and browns while the grains above are still only steaming. Oil down the wall carries heat into that layer and stops it welding to the pot. Rotate the pot as it forms, because a pot left still cooks one hot spot black while the rest of the base stays pale and soft.

ingredients.text: 30 ml groundnut oil, for the blanching water
45 ml groundnut oil, for the finish
5 g caster sugar, for the sauce

steps.text: Split any stem thicker than a pencil down its length so stem and leaf finish together, and trim the dry base.
Bring the water to a hard rolling boil with the salt, sugar and 30 ml oil: it has to stay boiling when the greens go in, so work in two batches if the pan is small.

Blanch 90 seconds for medium stems, until a stem bends without snapping and the leaves have flipped to a hard bright green, then lift them straight out and stand them upright to drain, with no ice bath, which only waterlogs them.
Warm the ginger in the remaining oil for about 90 seconds, until it fizzes gently and smells sweet rather than raw, and stir the soy, water and sugar together in a separate bowl.
Lay the greens in one direction on a warm dish, spoon the soy onto the plate rather than over the leaves, pour the ginger oil across the greens and eat while the stems still steam.

note: Blanching drives the air out of the leaf so the green underneath reads through clearly. Keeping it short matters because the cells release acid as they break down, and that acid strips the magnesium out of chlorophyll and turns everything olive. A big, hard-boiling, lightly salted and oiled pot does all of this at once: in a small pot the water stalls off the boil, the greens stew, and the acid wins.

ingredients.text: 600 ml whole milk, at least 3.5 percent fat
200 g old fibrous ginger, to yield 90 ml juice

steps.text: Grate the ginger finely and squeeze it through a cloth for 90 ml of juice, then divide 15 ml into each of six bowls and leave them to stand while you heat the milk.
Heat the milk with the sugar, stirring, to 75C (167F): the surface should shiver and steam but never carry a bubble. Take it off and let it fall to 70C (158F).

Stir the settled white sediment back up through the juice in each bowl, then pour the milk in from about 20 cm above in one steady stream so it slams into the juice and mixes itself. Do not stir afterwards.
Leave the bowls undisturbed for 10 minutes: the curd is set when you can tilt one to 45 degrees and the surface holds, taking a spoon like a soft panna cotta.

note: A protease in ginger clips the kappa casein off the milk's micelles exactly as rennet does, and the bared micelles then link into a gel. That enzyme is wrecked above roughly 80C (176F) and too sluggish below 65C (149F), so you pour between 70 and 75C (158 and 167F). Old fibrous ginger carries far more of it than young, and it settles out with the starch, so restir the juice. Stirring after the pour shears the gel and it will never set.

ingredients.text: 300 g farina 00, plus more for the board
3 whole eggs, 55 g to 60 g each, at room temperature
1 capon, about 1.8 kg, or a 1.5 kg boiling hen
1 onion, 1 carrot, 1 celery stalk, left whole
150 g pork loin, in 2 cm cubes
120 g Parmigiano Reggiano, 24 month, grated fine
10 g fine salt for the broth

steps.text: Cover the capon, beef and vegetables with 4 litres of cold water and hold at 90C (194F), never a rolling boil, skimming until the surface is clear and the liquid is pale gold, about 3 hours; strain, chill, and lift off the set disc of fat.

Brown the pork loin in the butter until the cubes are deep gold and stiff to the press, cool, then mince fine with the mortadella and prosciutto and work in the Parmigiano, egg and nutmeg until the paste holds a fingerprint without weeping.
Mound the flour, break in the eggs, knead 10 minutes until the ball is smooth and springs back slowly, then rest it under an upturned bowl for 30 minutes.
Roll with a long pin, turning and stretching outward, until you can read newsprint through the sheet; cut 3 cm squares and keep the rest under cloth.

Put a chickpea of filling on each square, fold to a triangle pressing the air out from the filling to the edge, then wrap it round your little finger and pinch the two points until the cuff stands up on its own.
Drop them into barely trembling broth and cook until they rise and the chalky core at the pinched knot is gone, 3 to 4 minutes.

note: A hand sheet is stretched outward in every direction under the pin, so it keeps a fine nap that holds broth; a roller compresses and polishes it, and polished pasta arrives at the table naked. The other failure is trapped air: it expands in the hot broth and splits the seam. Press the fold down onto the filling and out to the edge before you close the cuff.

ingredients.text: 150 g dry breadcrumb, ground fine from stale unsalted bread
150 g Parmigiano Reggiano, 30 month, grated fine
20 g farina 00, only if the dough is slack

steps.text: Rub the breadcrumb, Parmigiano, nutmeg and lemon zest together, then work the eggs in with your fingers until the mass is uniform and squeezes into a lump with no dry crumb left in the bowl.
Wrap and rest 30 minutes so the crumb takes up the egg; the dough should now feel like firm putty and hold a ridge when pinched, not stick to the hand.
Bring the broth to a bare tremble, press the dough through a passatelli iron or a ricer with 4 mm holes, and cut the strands off at 4 cm as they fall in.
Cook until they float and the surface turns from matte to satiny, about 2 minutes, then ladle broth and passatelli together into warm bowls.

note: There is no gluten here. The strands hold together only because egg and Parmigiano protein set as they heat, so a rolling boil tears them into cloudy porridge before they ever firm up. Keep the broth at a bare tremble. Slack dough disintegrates the same way, and the usual cause is soft fresh breadcrumb: use dry crumb from stale bread, which absorbs rather than smears.

ingredients.text: 100 g cooked spinach, squeezed bone dry and pureed
80 g pancetta, chopped to a paste
200 g soffritto: onion, carrot and celery in equal weight, diced fine
300 g beef skirt or chuck, minced coarse
1 litre whole milk, for the besciamella
70 g unsalted butter and 70 g farina 00, for the besciamella
60 g unsalted butter, for the dish

steps.text: Render the pancetta slowly, add the soffritto and sweat it 20 minutes until it collapses to a sweet jammy base with no raw onion smell, then raise the heat and brown the beef and pork until the pan is dry and the meat catches brown on the bottom.

Deglaze with the wine and cook until the sharpness is gone, stir in the tomato concentrate, then feed in the milk and broth a ladle at a time over 3 hours at a lazy blip, until the sauce is brick brown and a spoon leaves a clean track across the pan.

Knead the flour, eggs and spinach 10 minutes to a firm green dough, rest 30 minutes, roll by hand to 1 mm, then blanch the sheets 20 seconds, chill them in cold water and lay them flat on cloths until the surface is dull and dry.
Cook the besciamella out until it coats the spoon and tastes only of milk and nutmeg, with no chalk of raw flour on the tongue.

Build 6 thin layers, each barely veiled with ragu and besciamella and dusted with Parmigiano, dot the top with butter and bake at 180C (350F) until the edges are lacquered dark and the centre trembles when you shake the dish, about 40 minutes.

note: Tomato is a seasoning here, not the sauce: 30 g of concentrate against 450 g of meat. Body comes from milk fed in over hours, whose sugars brown and whose casein slackens the meat fibres. Lead with tomato and the sauce stays thin and acid, and that acid will also curdle the milk into grains. Add milk only once the wine has cooked off, and never let the pan come above a blip.

ingredients.text: 30 g Parmigiano Reggiano, grated, for the dough
120 g prosciutto di Parma, an end piece, in 5 mm ribbons
60 g Parmigiano Reggiano, grated, to finish

steps.text: Knead the flour, eggs, Parmigiano and nutmeg 10 minutes until the dough is tight and a cut face shows no marbling, then rest it covered 30 minutes.

Roll by hand to about 1 mm, cut 4 cm squares, and lay each square on the comb corner first; roll it up on a pencil-thick dowel, pressing so the ridges bite, and slide it off with the seam sealed and the surface deeply grooved.

Melt the butter and warm the prosciutto just until the ribbons turn opaque and perfume the pan, no colour, then add the peas and a splash of pasta water and cook until they are bright green and just yield.
Boil the garganelli 2 to 3 minutes until they float and the seam is tender, then finish them in the pan off the heat with the cream and Parmigiano until the sauce clings and the grooves are filled.

note: The comb exists to make surface. Ridges plus the nap left by a hand pin give the sauce something to key into, which is why an extruded tube of the same shape comes to the plate bare. The prosciutto is the other trap: held over heat its collagen tightens and it turns to salty leather, so it goes into warm butter and comes out before it takes any colour.

ingredients.text: 400 g gramigna, fresh egg gramigna if you can get it
350 g coarse Emilian pork sausage, casings removed

steps.text: Crumble the sausage into cold butter and bring the heat up slowly so the fat runs before the meat sets, breaking it small until the pieces are gold and loose rather than welded into a patty.
Add the onion and sweat until translucent and sweet, then pour in the wine and reduce until the pan smells of sausage and not of alcohol.
Stir in the tomato concentrate and the milk and hold at a lazy blip for 20 minutes, until the sauce is pale russet and the fat beads at the edge.
Boil the gramigna, drain it a minute early, and finish it in the pan with a ladle of pasta water and the Parmigiano until the curls are coated and no sauce pools on the plate.

note: Sausage meat dropped into a hot pan seizes on contact: the proteins set before the fat renders and you get grey pellets rattling in a dry pan. Start it cold and let the fat come out to fry the meat in. Milk is the sauce here, not tomato. The 20 g of concentrate is for colour and depth only; more turns the dish sharp and buries the fennel and pepper in the sausage.

ingredients.text: 400 g Swiss chard leaves, stalks removed
250 g fresh ricotta, drained overnight in a sieve

steps.text: Wilt the chard in only the water clinging to the leaves, then wring it in a cloth until nothing more runs out and the ball is dense and dark; chop it fine.
Fold the chard, ricotta, Parmigiano, yolk and nutmeg together and season; the filling should sit on a spoon in a soft mound and hold its shape rather than slump.
Knead the flour and eggs 10 minutes to a firm dough, rest 30 minutes, then roll by hand to a sheet you can see your fingers through, working fast so it does not dry and crack.
Place walnut-sized mounds along the sheet, fold it over, press the air out from the fold outward, and cut with a fluted wheel so the crimped edge seals itself.
Boil 3 minutes until they float and the sealed edge turns translucent, then dress with butter melted to a nut-brown foam and a heavy hand of Parmigiano.

note: Chard carries far more water than it looks. Leave it in and the filling steams inside the parcel, softening the seal from within until it splits in the pot, so wring the leaves until the cloth runs dry. Undrained ricotta does the same. Judge it on the spoon: a filling that slumps there will slump on the sheet, and no crimp will hold a seam it is pushing apart.
