ingredients.text: 1 kg Swiss chard, leaves and tender stalks
80 g pancetta or lardo, in small dice

steps.text: Rub the cold strutto into the flour and salt to a coarse crumb, add the water and work briefly to a smooth slack dough, then rest it 30 minutes so it will stretch thin without tearing.
Blanch the chard 2 minutes, refresh it, and wring it in a cloth to a tight dark ball; chop it and season hard with salt and pepper.
Fry half the pancetta with the onion, garlic and parsley until the fat runs clear and the garlic smells sweet, then fold it through the chard with the Parmigiano and egg.
Roll two thin sheets, line an oiled tray with one, spread the filling 2 cm deep, cover with the second, seal the rim and prick the lid all over; scatter the remaining raw pancetta on top.
Bake at 200C (400F) on the oven floor until the lid is blistered and crackling brown and the base lifts crisp off the tray, 30 to 35 minutes.

note: This crust is short, not layered: cold lard coats the flour and blocks gluten, which is why it stays crisp instead of turning to leather. Steam is its enemy. Wet chard boils under the lid, lifts the top sheet off the filling and leaves the base grey and sodden. Wring the leaves until the cloth runs dry, prick the lid so steam can leave, and bake low in a hot oven.

ingredients.text: 80 g prosciutto di Parma, sliced thin

steps.text: Beat the cutlets between two sheets to an even 6 mm; thicker than that and the crumb burns long before the centre is hot.
Flour, egg and crumb them, pressing the crumb on firmly, then rest them 15 minutes so the coating sets and will not slide off in the pan.
Fry in clarified butter over moderate heat until both faces are an even hazelnut brown and the crust sounds hollow when tapped, about 3 minutes a side.

Lay a slice of prosciutto and a drift of Parmigiano on each, pour the broth around the cutlets and no more than a third of the way up, then cover and hold at the lowest heat until the cheese has slumped and the broth is syrupy, 5 minutes.

note: The whole point of the finish is that the crust survives it. Broth poured over the top dissolves the crumb in seconds, so it goes around the cutlets and stays low: the base softens into the sauce while steam alone melts the Parmigiano above. Clarified butter matters for the same reason. The milk solids in whole butter blacken well before the crumb is properly brown.

steps.text: Rub the strutto into the flour, salt and bicarbonate until it looks like damp sand, add the milk and knead 5 minutes to a soft dough that is smooth but still takes a fingerprint.
Divide into 6, roll into balls and rest them covered 30 minutes, until they no longer spring back when pressed.
Roll each into a 25 cm disc about 3 mm thick and prick it lightly all over with a fork.
Cook on a dry cast iron plate at 250C (480F), about 90 seconds a side, turning when the underside is freckled with brown blisters and the rim has stiffened.
Stack them under a cloth as they come off the iron so their own steam keeps them pliable.

note: There is no yeast: the lift is bicarbonate and steam, so the window is short and hot. On a cool plate the water leaves before the disc can blister and you get a cracker that snaps instead of folding. Get the iron properly hot and keep each side under two minutes. Lard, not oil, is what keeps it supple as it cools, because it stays soft at room temperature.

ingredients.text: 300 g savoiardi, or day-old pan di Spagna cut in fingers

steps.text: Infuse the milk with the lemon zest at 80C (176F) for 10 minutes, then lift the zest out.

Whisk the yolks, sugar and flour to a pale ribbon, temper in the hot milk, and cook it back over moderate heat, stirring into the corners of the pan, until it thickens and then blips once at 85C (185F).
Divide the hot cream, beat the cocoa into one half until it is glossy and free of lumps, and press cling film onto the surface of both so no skin forms.
Cut the alchermes with the water, dip each savoiardo in and out in a single second, and layer the biscuits with alternating pale and chocolate cream in a glass dish, finishing with cream.
Chill at least 6 hours, until a spoon lifts a clean edge and the biscuit is moist through with no dry white core.

note: Two things break this. A flour-thickened crema that never reaches a blip is still full of live amylase from the yolks, which digests the starch overnight and leaves you soup in the morning, so take it to 85C (185F) and let it bubble once. The second is the dip: savoiardi drink alarmingly fast, and more than a second in the alchermes gives you paste that will not hold a layer.

ingredients.text: 800 g skin-on pork belly, cut into 4 cm cubes

steps.text: Cover the belly with cold water, bring it up slowly with a slice of ginger and a splash of the wine, and lift the cubes out once the grey scum stops rising; drain and pat every face dry or the sugar will spit at you.

Melt the rock sugar in the oil over a low flame and watch it go from clear syrup to weak tea to the colour of dark honey, about 90 seconds from the first colour; the moment it smells nutty, tip in the pork.
Toss hard until every cube is lacquered mahogany and the fat has started to run clear at the edges.

Splash the Shaoxing down the hot side of the pot, add both soys, the aromatics, the salt and just enough boiling water to cover, then hold at a bare tremble for 60 minutes until a chopstick passes through the skin with no resistance.
Take the lid off, raise the heat and reduce, spooning the liquid back over the cubes, until it hangs on them in a glossy sheet and the oil runs clear red round the rim.

note: Tang se is caramel, not soy sauce. Rock sugar melts near 185C (365F) and browns, and that browning gives the red plus a faint bitterness that keeps the dish off pure syrup. Past roughly 195C it goes acrid and nothing added later covers it. Work by colour and smell with the pork already at hand: tipping it in is what stops the sugar cooking.

ingredients.text: 1 kg skin-on pork belly in one slab

steps.text: Blanch the slab from cold water for 5 minutes, lift it when the foam stops rising, cool it, then cut 5 cm squares and tie each one in a cross with string so the fat cannot slide off the skin.
Build a close raft of whole spring onions and ginger across the base of a clay pot and sit the squares on it skin down, so no pork touches the pot itself.
Pour in the wine, both soys and the rock sugar, lid on, and hold at the barest tremble for 90 minutes until a skewer goes through the skin without catching.

Turn every square skin up, lift them into individual bowls with a ladle of the braising liquid, and steam hard for 30 minutes until the fat is translucent amber and the square shivers when you knock the bowl.
Reduce what is left in the pot to a syrup that ribbons off the ladle and spoon it over each square.

note: The pot holds wine and sugar and almost no water, so anything resting on bare metal scorches long before the pork is tender: the spring onion and ginger raft is a heat break first and a seasoning second. The finish is steam because a rolling braise batters the square until the fat parts from the skin. Steam renders that fat with nothing moving, so the block keeps its corners.

ingredients.text: 300 g pork shoulder, minced, about 30 percent fat
150 g pork skin aspic (pi dong), diced 5 mm
60 ml cold ginger and spring onion water

steps.text: Work the flour, yeast, sugar and warm water into a firm dough, knead it smooth, and rest it 40 minutes only: you want it half risen, still springy, slow to fill a thumb dent.

Beat the soy, wine, salt, pepper and cold ginger water into the pork a spoonful at a time, always turning one way, until the mince is sticky and drags at the spoon; fold in the spring onion and the diced aspic and chill it hard.
Roll 25 g discs thicker in the middle than at the rim, pleat 25 g of filling shut and pinch the seam properly closed; the seam is a weld, not a decoration.
Set the buns seam down in a cold oiled pan a thumb apart and fry over medium heat for 3 minutes, until the bases are deep gold and sound hard under a chopstick.

Pour in the water, lid on at once, and steam 9 minutes until the pan runs dry and starts hissing again and the tops are matt and dry to the touch; scatter the sesame and spring onion and give the base 1 minute more.
Rest them 2 minutes before anyone bites, because the soup inside is at boiling point.

note: The soup is not poured in: it is diced pork skin aspic, which sets hard cold and slumps to liquid near 35C (95F), so it is solid while you pleat and broth by the time the bun is hot. Proof the dough halfway only. A fully risen bun is too weak and open to hold that liquid, so the seam blows, the soup boils off in the pan and you get a dry bun on a burnt base.

ingredients.text: 500 g pork, two parts belly to one part shoulder
100 ml cold ginger and spring onion water

steps.text: Chop the fat and the lean separately, then together, until the meat is loose grains the size of pomegranate seeds; a machine smears the fat through the lean and the ball comes out dense and bouncy.
Add the wine, salt, pepper, egg white and starch, then beat in the cold ginger water 20 ml at a time, one direction only, until the meat is glossy and clings to an upturned palm.
Fold through the water chestnuts and shape four balls of about 170 g, slapping each from palm to palm a dozen times until the surface is smooth and no air pockets are left.

Line the pot with the outer cabbage leaves, lower the balls onto them and pour in stock to cover; bring it to 85C (185F) and hold it there, covered, for 90 minutes, never letting the surface do more than shiver.
Drop the cabbage hearts in for the last 20 minutes and serve everything in the broth, which should still be clear enough to read the pattern on the bowl.

note: Salt plus beating in one direction pulls myosin out of the lean, and that protein sets into a net around 60C (140F) that holds both the water you beat in and the fat as it renders. So keep the pot at a shiver. At a true boil the fat leaves faster than the net can trap it and the ball turns from silky to crumbly and grey. Nothing here is browned; it is meant to stay pale.

ingredients.text: 1 mandarin fish (gui yu), about 700 g, scaled and gutted

steps.text: Take the head off in one cut and keep it, then run the knife along the backbone to lift two fillets, leaving them joined at the tail with the skin on.
Lay each fillet skin down and score it in 1 cm diamonds at 45 degrees, cutting through the flesh to the skin but never into it; salt, wine, and rest 10 minutes.
Blot the fillets dry and rub starch down into every cut with your fingers, then shake them hard so the squares fall open and none stay glued shut.

Hold the tail and lower a fillet into 180C (350F) oil so the squares spring open into spikes, let go and fry 4 minutes until rigid and pale gold, then lift and return it for 40 seconds at 200C (390F) until it rings when tapped.

Boil the sugar, vinegar, tomato paste, soy and water, thicken with a starch slurry until it ribbons off the ladle and coats the back of it, stir in the peas, bamboo and pine nuts and pour it over at the table for the hiss.

note: Cut to the skin and never through it. Skin contracts hard in the oil while the scored blocks do not, and that difference is what stands the squares up. Cut through and the fillet shreds as it fries; stop short of the skin and it comes out flat. Starch has to reach the bottom of every cut, or the wet faces weld back together and the fish fries as a plank.

steps.text: Rub the bird inside and out with the 25 g of salt and leave it uncovered in the fridge for 4 hours, until the skin feels dry and tacky rather than wet.

Slide it into water held at 85C (185F) with the ginger and spring onion, keep it there 25 minutes, then kill the heat and steep 25 more, until juice from the thigh joint runs clear and the meat at the bone is just set.
Plunge the bird into iced water for 10 minutes until the skin is taut and slippery, then joint it into large pieces, bone in.
Cool 500 ml of the poaching liquid to fridge cold, stir in the wine, brine salt, rock sugar and goji, and taste it: it should read a shade too salty on its own.
Submerge the pieces, weight them under the surface and refrigerate 24 hours at least; serve cold with the set jelly spooned over.

note: The wine goes into cold stock and nothing is ever warmed again. Ethanol denatures surface protein on contact, so a warm brine turns the outside of the meat chalky and grainy, and heat drives off the esters that carry huadiao's smell. Cold, the alcohol travels inward slowly alongside the salt; give it a full day in the fridge and the flavour reaches the bone.

ingredients.text: 400 g freshwater river shrimp, shelled to about 250 g meat
4 g Longjing tea leaves, pre-Qingming if you have them

steps.text: Rinse the shelled shrimp in salted water until it runs clear, then wring them in a cloth until the surface squeaks; a wet shrimp sheds its coating in the oil.
Mix them with the salt until tacky, work in the egg white, then the starch, then a spoonful of the oil, and chill 30 minutes.
Steep the tea in the 80C (175F) water for exactly 1 minute, keep the opened leaves and 60 ml of the pale liquor, and throw the rest away.
Slip the shrimp into oil at 120C (250F), stirring them apart, and lift them the second they go opaque and curl into a loose C, around 30 seconds.
Wipe the wok, splash in the wine, return the shrimp with the leaves and the liquor and toss 15 seconds until everything is glossy and barely wet. No soy, no colour, nothing else.

note: Two clocks run here. The shrimp poach in barely warm oil at 120C (250F) because once they pass about 60C inside they tighten from crisp to rubber within seconds: pull them at a loose C, never a closed ring. The tea is a one minute infusion at 80C (175F); boiling water strips catechins out of the leaf and the whole dish turns brown and bitter instead of green and sweet.
techniques: Chilling to firm: the fridge as binder

ingredients.text: 400 g salt cured pork belly (xian rou)
500 g fresh pork belly or ribs

steps.text: Soak the cured pork in cold water for 3 hours with two changes, then boil a slice for a minute and taste it; if it stings, soak it longer, because this is the only salt the pot will get.
Blanch both meats from cold water, skimming until the grey foam stops rising, then rinse the meat and the pot.
Simmer the meats with the ginger, spring onion and wine at a bare tremble for 60 minutes, skimming as you go, then push it to a rolling boil for 20 minutes until the broth turns opaque and milky.

Peel the shoots to the pale core, roll cut them and blanch 3 minutes to take the scratch out, then add them with the tofu knots and simmer 20 minutes until the shoots are translucent at the edge and the knots are heavy with broth.
Taste it before it goes to the table and add nothing but more of its own liquid if it falls short.

note: Nothing in this pot gets seasoned. The cure in the xian rou is the only salt, and it concentrates as the broth reduces, so a three hour soak with two changes of water is most of the work; an unsoaked piece leaves broth no one can drink. The milky colour is not cream but rendered fat and collagen emulsified by a hard boil, so simmer throughout and it stays thin and clear.

ingredients.text: 600 g spring bamboo shoots, still in the sheath

steps.text: Strip the sheaths back to the pale core, cut away the woody base and roll cut into wedges, so every piece carries a slanted face for the glaze to catch on.
Blanch 3 minutes in hard boiling water and drain them well.
Fry in the oil over a high flame for 5 minutes without crowding the pan, until the cut faces are blistered and gold at the edges.
Add the wine, both soys, the rock sugar and the water and braise uncovered for 12 minutes, tossing, until the liquid is a dark syrup hanging off the wedges and the pan hisses more than it bubbles.
Off the heat, sesame oil, and leave it until warm rather than hot: the glaze tightens as it cools.

note: Spring shoots carry oxalic acid, which is what scratches the throat and turns the pan grey, and three minutes in hard boiling water takes it out. The braise runs uncovered because the point is to lose the liquid, not to soften the shoots any further. Stop when the bubbles go slow and glassy: past that the sugar is alone in a dry pan and burns within seconds.

ingredients.text: 2 sections lotus root (lian ou), about 800 g, fat with short nodes
150 g glutinous rice (nuo mi), soaked 2 hours and drained
60 g dark brown sugar slab (pian tang)

steps.text: Cut a 2 cm lid off one end of each root and keep it, then rinse the open channels out under the tap.

Stand the root upright and push the rice into the channels with a chopstick, tapping the root down on the board to settle it, filling to about nine tenths and no further; replace the lids and pin them with cocktail sticks.
Lay the roots in a stainless or clay pot, cover with the water, add both sugars and the dates, and simmer covered for 2 hours until a skewer slides in easily and the cut faces have gone deep garnet.
Leave them to cool in the liquid overnight, then lift them out and slice 5 mm thick.
Reduce the cooking liquid to a loose syrup, take it off the heat, stir in the osmanthus and spoon it over the slices.

note: Pack the channels loosely and only to the shoulder: glutinous rice takes up around half its own weight in water and will split the root open if it has nowhere to swell. Cook in stainless or clay, never iron or aluminium, or the root's tannins bind with the metal and it goes slate grey instead of garnet. Osmanthus goes in off the heat, at the end; its aroma boils away to nothing.

ingredients.text: 700 g seer fish (neymeen) steaks, 2 cm thick
1 tsp turmeric powder, plus 1/2 tsp for the gravy

steps.text: Rub the steaks with 1 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp salt and leave them while you build the base; the surface should go tacky and the flesh firm slightly.

Pop the mustard seeds in coconut oil until they jump and turn grey, drop in the curry leaves until they crackle and go glassy, then sweat shallots, ginger, garlic and green chilli until translucent and slumped with no colour anywhere.
Stir in the remaining turmeric, pour in the thin coconut milk and simmer uncovered until it reduces by a quarter and lightly coats the back of a spoon.
Slide in the fish in one layer and poach, tilting the pan rather than stirring, until the flesh turns opaque to the bone and a skewer meets no resistance.
Lay the tomato rounds on top, pull the pan off the heat, then stir in the thick coconut milk and swirl until the gravy is a uniform pale gold that steams without a single bubble breaking the surface.
Finish with lime juice and cracked pepper and leave to sit five minutes before serving with appam.

note: Onnam paal is an emulsion held by coconut protein, and much above 80C (176F) that protein denatures, the droplets coalesce and the gravy splits into white grains under an oil slick. Randam paal is dilute enough to boil, so it does the reducing and the cooking. The thick milk goes in off the heat and is only warmed through.

ingredients.text: 700 g seer fish (neymeen) steaks, 2 cm thick

steps.text: Soak the kudampuli in 100 ml warm water until the pieces are soft and the water runs amber.

Warm the coconut oil in a manchatti over low heat, pop the mustard and fenugreek until the seeds crackle and the fenugreek turns one shade darker, then add curry leaves, shallots, ginger and garlic and cook until the shallots are soft and smell sweet, with no browning.
Take the pot off the fire, stir in the chilli powder and turmeric so they bloom in the residual heat until the paste smells toasted rather than acrid.
Return to low heat, add the water plus the kudampuli and its soaking liquid, and simmer until the gravy darkens to brick red and the raw chilli smell has gone.
Slide in the fish, cover and cook without stirring, swirling the pot by its rim, until the flesh flakes at a fork and clear red oil beads at the edge.
Take off the heat and leave the pot uncovered to settle for at least an hour.

note: Kudampuli is not tamarind: its acid firms fish protein and keeps the curry sound for days, but more than about six pieces turns it bitter and metallic. The unglazed manchatti holds a bare simmer through its own mass and does not react with that acid the way thin aluminium does. Once the fish is in, never stir; swirl the pot by the rim or the steaks shred into threads.

ingredients.text: 300 g raw white rice (pachari), soaked 4 hours and drained
1 tbsp sugar, plus 1 tsp for the yeast
200 ml water, plus 60 ml warm water for the yeast
coconut oil, for wiping the pan

steps.text: Grind the soaked rice with the cooked rice, grated coconut and 200 ml water until the batter is smooth between finger and thumb with only a faint grit left, like wet silk over sand.
Whisk the yeast and 1 tsp sugar into the warm water until it foams and caps, then stir it through the batter, holding back the salt.
Cover and ferment at 28C to 30C (82F to 86F) until the batter has doubled, domed and smells of sour bread and toddy, six to eight hours.
Knock it down and beat in the remaining sugar, the salt and the thick coconut milk to the consistency of single cream that ribbons off the ladle.

Pour a ladleful into a hot, lightly oiled appachatti, lift the pan and rotate it once so the batter climbs and clings to the wall, then cover and cook until the rim is lace crisp and dry and the centre is a set white sponge. Do not flip.

note: The cooked rice is the whole trick: its gelatinised starch gives the batter enough body to cling in a thin film when you swirl the pan, and that film crisps to lace while the yeasted pool at the centre steams into a sponge. Salt and thick coconut milk go in after fermenting, because salt slows the yeast and the milk sours over eight hours. Never flip it; the top sets in trapped steam.

ingredients.text: 400 g coarse roasted rice flour (puttu podi)

steps.text: Dissolve the salt in the water, then sprinkle it over the flour in stages, raking with your fingertips, until the flour darkens evenly and a squeezed fistful holds its shape but shatters when you poke it.
Rub the damp flour between your palms and push it through a coarse sieve so every lump breaks back into loose crumb, then cover and rest it ten minutes.
Layer the puttu kutti with a spoonful of grated coconut, then a loose handful of flour, alternating and never pressing, and finish with coconut.
Set the mould over hard boiling water and steam until a straight plume of steam blows from the top and holds for a full minute, six to eight minutes.
Push the cylinder out with the handle of a wooden spoon; it should stand up on the plate, then break into hot loose crumbs under a fork.

note: Puttu is a hydration problem: about 45 percent water to flour weight, added in stages so every grain wets evenly. Squeeze a fistful and it must hold, then shatter under a finger. Wetter than that and the steam cannot climb through, so you get a gluey plug; drier and it collapses to sand. Never pack the mould, because compressed layers block the steam that is meant to cook them.

flavor.sentence: A quiet dish that lets its main ingredient speak: season well and stand aside.

ingredients.text: 150 g elephant foot yam (chena), in 5 cm batons
150 g raw plantain, in 5 cm batons
150 g ash gourd, in 5 cm batons
80 g yardlong beans, in 5 cm lengths
120 g thick sour curd, whisked smooth

Pound or pulse the coconut with green chilli, cumin and shallots to a damp, gritty crumb, stopping well short of a smooth paste.
Fold the crumb through, shaking the pot by its handles rather than stirring, and cook two minutes more until the raw coconut smell turns sweet and the liquid clings to the batons instead of pooling.
Pull the pot off the heat, let the steam die back, then beat in the curd so it disappears without a single grain forming.
Pour on the raw coconut oil, tear in the curry leaves, cover and leave five minutes so the oil perfumes the whole pot.

note: Avial is bound by ground coconut, not milk, so keep the paste coarse: the fragments hold their own oil and coat the batons instead of dissolving into gravy. Curd goes in off the heat, since its proteins seize into grains above a simmer and the dish turns watery. The finishing coconut oil is never cooked, because its aroma compounds are volatile and heat drives them off in seconds.

ingredients.text: 500 g kaima rice (jeerakasala), rinsed and drained 20 minutes
1 kg chicken on the bone, in 8 pieces
30 g ginger and 30 g garlic, ground to a paste
6 green chillies, ground with the paste
30 g coriander leaf and 15 g mint, chopped
1 tsp Malabar garam masala (cinnamon, clove, green cardamom, fennel)

steps.text: Fry the cashews and raisins in half the ghee until the nuts are pale gold and the raisins swell, lift them out, then fry two thirds of the shallots in the same fat until crisp and mahogany, pulling them before they go past that.

In that fat with the coconut oil, cook the remaining shallots with the ginger, garlic and chilli paste until the raw smell goes and the oil pulls away at the edge, add tomato and half the herbs and cook to a thick masala, then the chicken, garam masala and salt until the chicken is done and the pan is almost dry.

In a second pan, fry the drained rice in the rest of the ghee until the grains turn chalky and rattle loose, pour on the boiling water and salt, cover and cook until the water is gone and craters open on the surface.
Spread the rice over the masala, scatter the fried shallots, nuts, raisins, remaining herbs and the lime juice across the top.
Seal the pot with a tight lid under a weight, set it on a tawa over the lowest flame and leave it on dum for twenty minutes, until the steam escaping at the rim smells of ghee and cardamom.
Rest sealed for ten minutes, then cut down through the layers with the edge of a spoon rather than stirring.

note: Kaima is a short, fat aromatic grain, not basmati: it drinks about one and a half times its volume and goes to paste if you soak it, so rinse, drain and fry it in ghee to set the surface starch before any water. On dum the heat must come from below through a tawa, or the masala scorches while the top rice is still raw. Seal the pot; the trapped steam is doing all the remaining cooking.

ingredients.text: 800 g beef shin or chuck, in 2 cm cubes
100 g fresh coconut, in thin slivers (thengakothu)

steps.text: Cook the beef with turmeric, chilli, coriander, half the pepper, fennel, salt and the water, covered, until a cube crushes between thumb and finger and only a syrupy liquor is left.
Fry the coconut slivers in the coconut oil until they are the colour of weak tea, then lift them out before they go any darker.
In the same oil fry the curry leaves until they blister, then the shallots, ginger, garlic and green chilli until the shallots collapse and brown at the edges.
Tip in the beef with its liquor and stir over medium heat until the liquid disappears, the cubes begin to stick and a dark crust builds on the pan floor.
Keep going, scraping that crust back onto the meat every minute or so, until the cubes are nearly black, glossy and dry, and clear oil beads out at the edge.
Off the heat, fold back the coconut slivers with the garam masala and the reserved pepper.

note: Ularthu means to stir until dry, and the flavour is entirely fond: as the liquor goes, sugar and protein lacquer onto the pan, and every time you scrape that back onto the cubes they darken a shade further. Stop while it is still saucy and you have a curry instead. The coconut slivers come out before the browning starts, since they scorch bitter inside a minute, and half the pepper goes in off the heat because piperine's aroma boils away.

Add the beans and cook until they turn bright green and lose their raw squeak.
Lift the pan off the heat, stir in the thick coconut milk and swirl until the ishtu is glossy and ivory and steaming, with no bubble breaking the surface.

note: An ishtu is white, so nothing is allowed to brown: the spices go in whole and bruised rather than ground, and the shallots are sweated only to translucent. Onnam paal goes in off the heat; boil it and the emulsion splits into oil above and white grains below.

ingredients.text: 700 ml thin coconut milk (second and third pressings)
60 g fresh coconut, in thin chips

steps.text: Pour boiling water over the ada and leave it until the pieces are pliable and fall apart from each other, then drain and rinse under cold water so they stop sticking.
Melt the jaggery with the water, strain the syrup through a sieve to leave the grit behind, then reduce it until it just threads off the back of a spoon.
Fry the coconut chips, cashews and raisins in the ghee until the chips are amber and the raisins puff, and lift them out, leaving the ghee in the pan.

Toss the drained ada in that ghee for two minutes, add the jaggery syrup and the thin coconut milk, and simmer, stirring often, until the ada turns translucent and the payasam coats a spoon and darkens to old bronze.
Off the heat, stir in the thick coconut milk, cardamom, dried ginger, cumin and salt, then the fried coconut and nuts; it should still pour.

note: Coconut is milked three times: the first pressing is thick and fragile, the second and third are thin and take a hard boil. Jaggery carries acid, and acid plus heat curdles that first pressing on contact, so the ada is cooked and the syrup reduced entirely in thin milk. Onnam paal goes in with the pan off the fire. Serve it looser than you want it, because the ada starch keeps setting as it cools.

ingredients.text: 500 g high-gluten wheat flour, 12 to 13 percent protein
4 g penghui alkaline water, or 3 g food-grade sodium carbonate dissolved in 15 g water
30 g neutral oil, for coating the dough
900 g beef shin, in one piece
400 g white radish, in half moons
30 g coarse dried chilli flakes, for the la you
120 g beef tallow or neutral oil, for the la you
a handful of coriander and garlic greens, chopped, to finish

steps.text: Dissolve the fine salt in the water, mix it into the flour until no dry flour is left, then knead 8 minutes until the dough is cohesive but still tears with a ragged edge rather than a clean one. Cover and rest 30 minutes.

Work the penghui solution in over three additions, slapping the dough flat on the bench between each, until it turns slack, faintly grey and glossy and will stretch to a translucent window without splitting. Oil it, cover, and rest 2 hours.

Meanwhile cover bones and shin with cold water, bring to the boil and skim until the scum runs thin and white, then add ginger, radish and spices and hold at a bare tremble for 3 hours, until the shin gives to a skewer with no spring back.
Warm the tallow to 140C (285F) and pour it over the chilli flakes in three goes, stirring; it should foam and smell toasted, never acrid, then settle to a deep red oil.

Roll a piece of dough into a rope, hold both ends, pull it and slap the belly of it against the bench, then twist, fold in half and repeat for 6 to 8 rounds, dusting with flour, until the strands hang even and ring faintly against the wood.

Drop the noodles into hard boiling water for 40 to 60 seconds, until they float and the chalky core is gone, then lift into bowls, ladle over broth strained clear, and spoon the la you on so it beads red across the surface.

note: Alkali is what makes the pull possible: sodium carbonate raises the dough's pH, which loosens the gluten network so it yields under tension instead of snapping back. Overdo it and the dough goes yellow, soapy and slack, tearing on the third fold. Underdo it, or cut the two hour rest short, and the rope recoils and breaks. Slapping the bench is not theatre; the impact stretches the strands faster than they can recover.

ingredients.text: 500 g plain wheat flour, about 11 percent protein
600 g ripe tomatoes, scored, peeled and roughly chopped
4 eggs (about 220 g), beaten with 2 g salt
4 spring onions, whites sliced and greens reserved
200 g green bok choy, cut in lengths

steps.text: Rub the salt and water into the flour and knead hard for 10 minutes; this dough fights back. Stop when it is dense and smooth and barely takes a fingerprint, like modelling clay. Wrap and rest 40 minutes, then shape into a fat loaf and rest 20 minutes more.
Pour the eggs into hot oil, let them puff and set at the edges, break them into large curds and lift them out while still glossy.

Fry ginger, garlic and spring onion whites for 30 seconds, add the tomatoes, sugar and salt and cook down 10 minutes, until they collapse to a jam and the oil separates and runs orange at the edge. Return the egg, kill the heat and stir in the vinegar.
Hold the loaf on your forearm over a pan at a hard rolling boil and shave with a curved blade in long flicks, so each noodle flies in as a leaf, thick along the spine and thin at the wings.
Boil 90 seconds, until the leaves float and the spine loses its chalky centre, adding the bok choy for the last 20 seconds, then drain and fold through the sauce with a spoonful of chilli oil.

note: This dough is deliberately underhydrated at about 45 percent, stiff enough to hold a cut edge under the blade. Wetter and the loaf slumps, the knife drags and you shave lumps rather than leaves. Each leaf is thick at the spine and thin at the wing, so one noodle gives two textures, but that only survives if the water is at a hard rolling boil when it lands. Add the aged vinegar off the heat: boiled, its aroma flattens and only sourness is left.

ingredients.text: 800 g pork belly, skin on, in one piece
600 g suan cai (northeastern fermented napa cabbage)
100 g sweet potato glass noodles, soaked 30 minutes
200 g pork blood sausage, sliced 5 mm (optional)
30 g jiucai hua (fermented chive flower sauce)

steps.text: Cover the belly with the water, add ginger, spring onion, star anise and wine, bring it up and then drop the heat so the surface only trembles. Hold it there 60 minutes, until a skewer meets no resistance at the thickest point and the skin has gone translucent.
Lift the belly out, press it under a weight and chill 2 hours, until it is firm enough to slice 2 mm thin without the layers sliding apart. Keep the broth.

Rinse the suan cai once, squeeze it hard in both hands and shred it very fine along the grain, then simmer it in the strained broth for 40 minutes, until it turns from squeaky to yielding and the broth smells clean and sour rather than sharp.
Slide in the sliced belly, the glass noodles and the blood sausage if using, and simmer 10 minutes more, until the noodles turn clear and the fat on the pork has gone glassy.
Whisk furu, sesame paste, chive flower sauce, garlic and chilli oil into a dipping sauce, scatter coriander over the pot, and let each person dip slice by slice.

note: Two long stages, neither of which can be hurried. The belly goes into water that only trembles: at a rolling boil the muscle fibres contract and squeeze out their water, so the slices turn dry and collapse on the board. Then the shredded suan cai needs its forty minutes in that broth, long enough for the lactic acid to soften the cabbage's pectin and spread through the fat. Cut it short and you get squeaky cabbage in a broth that is merely sour.

ingredients.text: 400 g pork loin, sliced 4 mm thick across the grain
20 g neutral oil, to loosen the batter
a few coriander stems, cut in lengths

steps.text: Stir the potato starch into the cold water and leave it 30 minutes, until it settles into a hard white cake under clear water. Pour the water off and work the cake with the 20 g of oil into a batter the texture of thick cream.
Season the pork with salt and wine, then fold it through the batter until every slice hangs heavy and fully cloaked.
Fry at 150C (300F), sliding the slices in one at a time so they cannot weld together, for about 2 minutes, until set and pale with no colour at all. Lift out and rest 3 minutes.
Fry again at 200C (390F) for 40 seconds, until the crust blisters, goes glassy and rattles against the spider. Drain.

Boil sugar, vinegar, soy and water in a clean wok until it just turns syrupy and coats the back of a spoon, then kill the heat and throw in the ginger, garlic, spring onion, carrot and coriander stems.
Return the pork and toss for no more than ten seconds, until every piece is lacquered and still audibly crackling, then plate at once.

note: Potato starch, not cornflour: its large granules gelatinise into a glassy, brittle shell that shatters, where cornflour goes sandy. Let the slurry settle and use the wet cake, which carries far more starch than a pourable batter ever could. The dish then lives or dies in the last ten seconds, because that crust is porous and drinks sauce. Reduce the sauce to a syrup first, kill the heat, toss briefly and plate. Any longer in the pan and it is soft.
techniques: Resting meat & slicing against the grain

flavor.sentence: Leads with aromatics blooming from the first bite, acid holding everything up to the light, on a rich, rounded finish.

ingredients.text: 1 kg pork belly, skin on, cut in 5 cm pieces
spice bag: 2 star anise, 3 g cassia bark, 4 bay leaves, 5 g fennel seed, 3 g huajiao, 2 cracked caoguo, 4 cloves
3 g fine salt, for the dough
a small bunch of coriander, chopped

steps.text: Start the belly in cold water, bring it to the boil and skim until the scum runs thin and white, then drain and rinse the pieces clean.

Return them to fresh water with rock sugar, wine, soy, ginger, salt and the spice bag, and hold at a bare simmer for 2 hours, until a chopstick slides through the skin without pressure and the fat wobbles. Leave the meat to cool in its liquid.

Mix 100 g of the flour with 65 g of the water and all the yeast into a soft sponge and leave it 60 minutes, until domed and webbed underneath, then knead it into the remaining flour, water and salt to make a firm dough and rest it 20 minutes.
Divide into six, roll each piece into a long rope, coil the rope flat like a snail and press it out to a 10 cm disc so the layers spiral inside.
Bake dry in a heavy pan over medium heat, 4 minutes a side, until tiger stripe scorch marks appear and the bun sounds hollow, then finish 6 minutes at 200C (390F) so the centre sets.

Chop the hot belly on the board, skin, fat and lean together, with a spoonful of the braising liquid, fold in chilli and coriander, split each bun through the equator without cutting it in two, and pack it while both are still steaming.

note: Baijimo is a half leavened dough: only a third of the flour is yeasted, so the crumb is tender but tight. That matters, because a fully risen, open bun is a sponge; the braising liquid soaks straight through and the bread slumps to wet pulp within a minute of filling. Dry pan first, oven second, sets a crisp skin that holds. Chop the meat rather than slice it, so skin, fat and lean land in every bite.
techniques: The bare simmer: holding liquid below the boil
Resting dough: the pause that does the work
The wobble & the skewer: testing a bake

flavor.sentence: Leads with richness that coats and comforts, a sweet edge rounding the corners, opening aromatic and staying there.

ingredients.text: 60 g dried sea cucumber (6 medium), rehydrated to about 600 g
300 g dacong (large Shandong scallion), white parts only, in 6 cm batons
8 g potato starch slaked in 20 g water

steps.text: Soak the dried sea cucumbers in cold water for 3 days in a scrupulously clean bowl, changing the water twice daily and giving them a 40 minute simmer on the second day. They are ready when they have swollen to four times their dry size and a finger sinks into the flank with a slight spring.

Fry the dacong batons slowly in the oil over low heat for about 12 minutes, turning them, until they collapse, go deep amber and the oil smells sweet and toasted. Lift the scallions out and keep both them and the oil.
Blanch the sea cucumbers 30 seconds in a little of the stock with the wine and ginger to drive off any raw sea smell, then drain them.

Bring the remaining stock, both soys, oyster sauce, sugar and pepper to a simmer, slide in the sea cucumbers and the fried scallions, and braise gently 8 minutes, until the flesh darkens, turns springy and the liquid has reduced by a third.

Pull the pan back off the boil, swirl in the starch slurry until the sauce coats and lifts to a mirror gloss, then finish with sesame oil and the reserved scallion oil so it pools bright across the top.

note: The body wall is almost pure collagen, and it will only swell in clean cold water. A trace of oil, salt or acid in the soaking bowl halts uptake, and the cucumber stays shrunk and rubbery however long you leave it, so keep hands, bowl and knife free of grease. At the other end, boiling it hard breaks that collagen down to slime. The braise stays at a tremble, and the endpoint you want is springy, not soft.
techniques: Soaking dried goods back to life

ingredients.text: 400 g plain wheat flour, for the dough
90 g plain wheat flour, for the yousu
70 g neutral oil, for the yousu
40 g maltose, loosened with 40 g hot water

steps.text: Mix the dough ingredients and knead 8 minutes, until smooth and able to stretch to a rough window, then cover and prove 60 minutes until doubled.

Heat the 70 g of oil to 150C (300F) and pour it over the yousu flour, salt, huajiao and five spice, stirring to a loose paste with the texture of wet sand that holds a ribbon for a second before sinking.

Roll the dough into a large thin rectangle, spread the yousu edge to edge, roll it into a tight log and cut it into 8, then stand each piece on its cut end, coil it and press it flat so the layers spiral inside.
Brush the tops with the loosened maltose and press them face down into the sesame; the maltose should be tacky rather than runny, or the seeds slide straight off.
Bake at 220C (430F) for 15 to 18 minutes, until the sesame is gold, clear seams open along the sides, and the bun feels surprisingly light for its size.

note: The yousu is what makes leaves rather than one loaf. Oil at 150C (300F) poured onto flour cooks the starch and coats each granule in fat, so the dough sheets cannot weld together and steam prises them apart in the oven. Use cold oil, or a paste thin enough to run, and it soaks into the dough and bakes as one dense brick. Maltose for the wash, not honey: it stays tacky enough to grip sesame and browns without scorching.
techniques: Proofing: the rise before the oven

ingredients.text: 400 g fresh hawthorn (shanzha), stems removed and cores pushed out

steps.text: Dry every hawthorn thoroughly on a cloth and thread 5 or 6 onto each skewer, all facing the same way. Any surface water left on the fruit will seize the syrup into a cloudy crust.
Put sugar, water and maltose in a wide pan, bring it to the boil and then leave the spoon out of it entirely, washing stray crystals down the sides with a wet brush.
Cook to 150C (300F): the syrup goes still, the bubbles turn small and slow, and a drop into cold water sets to a shard that snaps cleanly rather than bending.
Tilt the pan, roll each skewer through the syrup in a single unbroken pass and lay it on oiled parchment, scattering sesame while the coat is still wet.
Leave 5 minutes, until the glass has gone clear and rings against a fingernail.

note: Sugar wants to crystallise, and one stray crystal or a stir of the spoon will seed the whole pan cloudy and grainy. So it goes on the heat and is left alone, with the maltose there to interrupt the crystal lattice. Take it to 150C (300F): below about 145C (295F) the coat stays tacky and pulls at the teeth instead of shattering. Dry the fruit properly, because surface water chills the syrup where it lands and leaves a dull, sticky patch.

flavor.sentence: Leads with toasted, nutty warmth throughout, real fire that builds and stays.

ingredients.text: 1.6 kg turkey legs and thighs, jointed
2.5 L turkey or chicken stock, hot
120 g chilhuacle negro, stemmed and seeded, seeds reserved
80 g chile pasilla mexicano, stemmed and seeded, seeds reserved
80 g chile mulato, stemmed and seeded, seeds reserved
60 g chile guajillo, stemmed and seeded, seeds reserved
1 very ripe plátano macho (200 g), peeled and sliced
60 g pan de yema and 1 stale corn tortilla, torn
400 g ripe tomatoes and 250 g miltomate, husked
200 g white onion in wedges, 40 g garlic cloves, unpeeled
1 stick canela, 5 cloves, 6 allspice berries, 10 black peppercorns, 3 g oregano de monte
90 g chocolate de metate, 40 g piloncillo, fine salt

steps.text: Toast the four chillies on a dry comal, pressing them flat, until they blister and go almost black, about a minute a side; open a window first, they will smoke.

Burn the reserved seeds in the same dry pan, stirring, until they are true charcoal, then tip seeds and chillies into hot water, soak 30 minutes and drain, throwing away every drop of that black water.

Fry the almonds, peanuts, sesame, raisins, plantain, bread and tortilla in the lard in that order, lifting each out as it turns gold, then char the onion, garlic, tomatoes and miltomate on the comal until blistered black in patches and slumping.
Blend the drained chillies with a little stock and sieve them until no grit stays in the mesh, then blend and sieve the fried solids and charred vegetables with the spices and avocado leaves.
Reheat the lard until it shimmers, pour in both pastes and fry, stirring, 20-25 minutes, until the mole darkens, holds a channel behind the spoon and black fat runs at the edge.

Thin with hot stock to the body of pouring cream, melt in the chocolate and piloncillo, salt it, and simmer the turkey in it for 30 minutes until the surface goes glossy and a slick of fat sits on top.

note: The black is burnt carbon, and carbon is bitter, so the seeds go all the way to charcoal and are then soaked and drained: the acrid phenols are water soluble and leave with the black water, while the colour and the smoke stay in the solids. Keep that soaking water to save time and the pot turns harsh, and no amount of chocolate pulls it back.
techniques: Soaking dried goods back to life

ingredients.text: 120 g chile ancho, stemmed and seeded
80 g chile guajillo, stemmed and seeded
150 g white onion, in thick wedges

steps.text: Toast the chillies on a dry comal 15-20 seconds a side until they puff, smell like toasted bread and lighten a shade inside, then soak in hot water 20 minutes until limp enough to tear with a fingernail.
Char the tomatoes, onion and garlic on the same comal until the skins blister black in patches and the tomatoes collapse and weep.
Fry the plantain, almonds and sesame in 40 g of the lard until deep gold, then blend the lot with the drained chillies, spices and half the stock and push it through a sieve.

Heat the rest of the lard until a drop of paste hisses hard, add all the paste at once and fry, stirring without stopping, 15-20 minutes: it darkens to brick red, tightens, and clear fat separates and pools at the edge.
Only now thin with the remaining hot stock, melt in the chocolate and piloncillo, season, and simmer 20 minutes until it coats a spoon and tastes round rather than raw.

note: A mole is fried before it is thinned, and that is not ceremony. In hot fat the paste reaches temperatures water cannot: sugars and proteins brown, the raw starch of nut and plantain cooks out, and the fat soluble pigments bloom red. Thin it first and it can only stew, staying thin, sour and gritty however long you give it. Fry until the fat pools, then add liquid.
techniques: Soaking dried goods back to life

ingredients.text: 30 g chile costeño amarillo, stemmed and seeded
20 g chile guajillo, stemmed and seeded
4 cloves, 6 black peppercorns, 2 g cumin seed
250 g fresh nixtamal masa, for thickening
200 g fresh nixtamal masa, for the chochoyotes

steps.text: Toast the three chillies on a dry comal 15 seconds a side, until they smell of toast and no darker, soak them in hot water 20 minutes, then blend with the miltomate, onion, garlic and spices and sieve.
Fry the sieved sauce in a hot dry pot for 8 minutes until it darkens, tightens and no longer smells raw, then add the stock and the chicken and simmer until the meat is just firm.

Slake the 250 g of masa in 300 ml of cold stock, working it with your fingers until not one lump is left, and pour it into the pot through a sieve while stirring; it thickens in 3-4 minutes and then needs a gentle boil for 5 more to lose its chalky edge.

Work the lard and a good pinch of salt into the remaining masa, roll walnut sized balls, press a deep dimple into each with your little finger and drop them in; they are ready when they float and the dimple no longer looks wet.
Add the chayote, beans and potato, tuck in the torn hoja santa, and cook 12 minutes until a knife slides into the chayote and the pot smells of aniseed.

note: Amarillo is thickened with masa, not fat, so the masa is slaked in cold liquid first: tipped straight into hot broth the outside of every grain gelatinises at once and seals a raw core, which is why lumpy mole never smooths out again. Once in, it wants a gentle boil for five minutes. Pulled off early it tastes chalky and slackens as it stands.
techniques: Frying the paste until the oil splits

ingredients.text: 60 g asiento, the unrefined lard from the bottom of the rendering pot
400 g cooked frijoles negros, with a little of their liquor
400 g tasajo, beef leg cut in a 4 mm sheet and salted
150 g salsa de chile pasilla oaxaqueño

steps.text: Toast the avocado leaves on the comal until brittle and smelling of aniseed, crumble them into the beans, and fry the beans down in 20 g of the asiento for 8 minutes to a paste stiff enough to hold a line.
Grill the tasajo over hot charcoal: cut that thin it takes 40 seconds a side and is ruined at 90, so pull it while the centre is still juicy, then chop it coarse.
Warm a tlayuda on the comal until it turns pliable, smear asiento right to the rim, spread the beans and scatter the quesillo.

Fold it over, lay it on the grill well back from the flame and turn it every 30 seconds for 3-4 minutes, until it is rigid, blistered and cracks under a press of the thumb, and the cheese pulls in threads.
Open it up, load in the cabbage, tomato, avocado, onion and tasajo, and eat with salsa and lime while the base is still crisp.

note: A tlayuda is not just a big tortilla: it is cooked twice and left leathery and dry, and that low moisture is what lets charcoal turn it to glass instead of steaming it floppy. The asiento seals the surface against wet toppings. Keep it back from the flame, because hard direct heat tightens the aligned protein of the quesillo and weeps its fat out greasy instead of stringing.

flavor.sentence: Leads with char used as punctuation, wood-smoke running underneath, with a clean, bright snap.

ingredients.text: 150 g salsa de chile de árbol or salsa verde de miltomate

steps.text: Work the masa with a splash of warm water until a ball flattened between your palms holds a smooth edge with no cracks, then divide it into 60 g pieces.
Pat each piece into a disc 10 cm across and 7 mm thick, twice the thickness of a tortilla, and lay it on a comal at about 200C (390F).

Cook 90 seconds a side until the surface goes dry and matt and pale brown freckles come up, then lift it and, while it is still too hot to hold comfortably, pinch a wall up around the rim with wet fingertips.
Smear the hot inside with asiento until it soaks in and the masa looks translucent, then spread the beans with the crumbled avocado leaf worked through them.
Back on the comal, scatter the quesillo, cover for a minute until it strings, and finish with salsa and raw onion.

note: The rim is pinched inside a narrow window. Straight off the comal the masa starch has gelatinised enough to hold a shape but has not yet dried, so it folds like clay; wait two minutes and the same rim splits and shales away. Wet fingertips stop it sticking so you can work fast. Roll the base too thin and the wall tears through and the asiento runs out.

ingredients.text: 80 g chile guajillo, stemmed and seeded
40 g chile ancho, stemmed and seeded
20 g chile costeño rojo, stemmed and seeded
200 g green beans, in 2 cm lengths
tostadas and crumbled queso fresco, to serve

steps.text: Toast the chillies on a dry comal 10-15 seconds a side, pressing them down: they should darken half a shade and smell like toasted bread, and any that smoke or blacken go in the bin.
Cover them with hot water, soak 20 minutes until floppy, then blend with the garlic, spices, vinegar and 150 ml of the soaking water until smooth and push through a sieve.
Fry the sauce in the oil over medium heat 8-10 minutes, stirring, until it darkens, thickens and red oil rises at the edge; salt it hard, there is a lot of vegetable to season.
Boil the vegetables separately in salted water, lifting each one the moment a knife tip meets slight resistance, and spread them on a tray to cool fast.
Fold the cold vegetables through the warm sauce, rest at least two hours, and pile onto tostadas with queso fresco.

note: Toasting is for aroma, not colour. A few seconds of dry heat volatilises the chilli aromatics and makes the brittle skin blend smooth, but the sugars scorch fast and scorched chilli is permanently acrid, so one blackened guajillo taints the batch. The soak then rehydrates the flesh so a blender can break it down, and the vinegar keeps the finished chileajo a week.

ingredients.text: 4 dense dry river stones, fist sized, granite or basalt
600 g mojarra or other firm river fish, filleted and cut in 3 cm pieces
1.2 L cold water or light fish broth
2 chiles de agua, or 4 serranos, sliced

steps.text: Build a wood fire and bury the stones in the embers, bringing them up slowly over an hour or more until they glow dull red.
While they heat, divide the raw fish, prawns, tomato, onion, garlic, chilli, epazote and coriander between four deep jícaras or thick clay bowls and season them.
Pour 300 ml of the cold water into each bowl so the solids are just covered.
Lift a stone with tongs, knock the ash off and lower it in: the bowl erupts and boils hard for 30-40 seconds, then falls back to a rolling simmer.
Take the stone out when the boiling stops, check the fish has turned opaque and flakes under a fork, and serve with lime.

note: A kilo of stone at red heat carries enough stored energy to bring a bowl of cold broth to a violent boil in seconds, and because that heat enters at one point the liquid churns and cooks the fish through in under a minute, which is why it stays flaky instead of chalky. Use dense dry river stone and heat it slowly: porous or damp stone traps water that flashes to steam and spalls the rock apart.

flavor.sentence: Leads with a warm current of chile, acid holding everything up to the light, opening aromatic and staying there.

ingredients.text: 6 g chile de árbol or chile piquín, ground
warm tortillas, guacamole and quesillo, to serve

steps.text: Pick the chapulines over for stray legs and grit, and dry them in a low oven at 90C (195F) for 10 minutes if they feel at all soft.
Set a comal or heavy pan over medium heat with the lard, add the garlic and cook until it is pale gold and stops bubbling hard.
Tip in the chapulines and toast, shaking the pan constantly, 4-6 minutes: they turn from dull grey brown to brick red and begin to rattle against the metal like dry rice.
Off the heat, dust with the ground chilli and salt, squeeze the lime over and toss twice, then eat them at once in a warm tortilla with guacamole and quesillo.

note: The colour reads the moisture: as the shell dries it shifts from grey brown to brick red and the sound changes to a dry rattle. That crispness is the whole texture and it is fragile. Lime juice is water, so it goes on off the heat and at the last second; add it while the pan is hot and the shells drink it straight back and go to leather within a minute.

ingredients.text: 300 g fresh nixtamal masa, from white corn
120 g fermented cacao beans, lightly toasted and husked
80 g pixtle, the pits of mamey sapote, toasted and cracked
20 g dried rosita de cacao flowers

steps.text: Toast the pixtle on the comal until the pieces are brittle and smell of bitter almond, and give the rosita only a few seconds, until it releases its perfume.
Grind the pixtle, rosita and cacao together on a metate or in a mill, in stages, to a dark stiff paste that smears like oiled putty, then grind the masa into it.
Put the paste in a wide bowl and work in cold water a ladle at a time with the flat of your hand, kneading and folding rather than stirring, until it slackens to a batter with no grain left in it.
Beat in the rest of the cold water the same way, lifting your hand clear on each stroke to drag air down; after 10-15 minutes a thick pale foam builds and rises to the top.
Ladle the liquid into cups, spoon the foam over, and let each drinker sweeten with syrup at the table.

note: The cap is not froth. It is cocoa butter and pixtle fat, ground fine, kept solid by the cold water and coated in masa starch so it traps the air your hand drags down. That is why tejate is beaten cold and never warmed: warm water melts the fat, the bubbles collapse, and what rises is a grey slick instead of a cap you could stand a spoon in.
techniques: Dry-pan toasting: spices, seeds and nuts

ingredients.text: 250 g fresh nixtamal masa, from white corn

steps.text: Simmer the canela in 400 ml of the water for 10 minutes, until the liquid is fragrant and faintly amber, then lift the stick out.
Slake the masa in the remaining 800 ml of cold water, rubbing it between your fingers until the liquid is uniformly milky, then press it through a fine sieve and discard the bran left in the mesh.
Combine both liquids with the sugar and salt in a heavy pan and bring to the boil over medium heat, dragging a wooden spoon across the bottom the whole time.
Hold it at a lazy boil 8-10 minutes: it thickens abruptly, the spoon leaves a channel that holds for a second, and the surface turns glossy and stops tasting chalky.
Pour it hot into a wetted shallow mould and leave it uncovered at room temperature for about 2 hours, until it is set firm enough to cut into clean squares.

note: Nicuatole sets on maize starch alone. The grains have to reach a full boil and stay there several minutes to swell and burst, or the gel is weak and the block weeps; it firms as it cools and the loose starch chains re-link. Slake the masa cold and sieve it, because tipped into hot water it lumps on contact. Do not chill it hard or freeze it: the gel goes grainy and pushes its water out.

ingredients.text: 250 g sabut urad (whole black gram), picked over for stones
2.5 litres water, plus 2 litres for soaking
30 g ginger, half pounded to a paste and half cut in fine julienne
20 g garlic, pounded to a paste
500 g ripe tomatoes, blended smooth and passed through a sieve
5 g deghi mirch, for colour rather than heat
150 g unsalted butter, cubed and kept cold
3 g garam masala, ground within the week
2 g kasoori methi, crushed between the palms

steps.text: Rinse the urad and rajma until the water runs clear, then soak both in 2 litres of cold water for at least 8 hours: the urad is ready when a bean crushes to a smooth paste between finger and thumb.

Drain, cover with the fresh water, add the ginger paste, garlic, chillies and 8 g of the salt, boil hard for 10 minutes, then drop the flame until the surface only trembles and hold it there 4 to 5 hours, topping up, until the skins have collapsed and the liquid turns glossy and clings to the spoon.

Stir in the sieved tomato and the deghi mirch and cook uncovered another 45 minutes, dragging a spoon across the base every few minutes, until the raw tomato smell is gone and the colour has dulled from orange to a deep maroon.

Take the pot off the heat and beat in the cold butter one cube at a time, waiting until each disappears before the next goes in so it never pools, then the cream: the dal should be the colour of milky coffee and fall from the spoon in one thick sheet.
Crush the kasoori methi over the surface, add the garam masala, the ginger julienne and the remaining salt to taste, and rest it 20 minutes off the heat before serving.

note: Urad starch has to leach out and gelatinise before the dal will body up, and that only happens under a simmer, over hours. Boil it hard and the beans burst before the starch disperses, leaving grit suspended in thin water. The butter goes in cold and off the heat: dropped into a boiling dal it melts faster than it can emulsify and the fat floats off as a slick.

flavor.sentence: Leads with richness that coats and comforts, aromatics blooming from the first bite, on a slow, honest burn.

ingredients.text: 300 g rajma, Jammu chitra if you can get them
1.2 litres water, plus 1.5 litres for soaking
25 g ginger and 20 g garlic, pounded together to a paste
300 g aged basmati, rinsed until the water runs clear
15 g coriander leaves, chopped with their stems

steps.text: Soak the rajma 8 hours in cold water, then pressure cook them in the fresh water with the black cardamom and 5 g salt for 25 minutes, until a bean smears against the pan side rather than splitting.
Heat the mustard oil until it smokes and its sharpness burns off, drop the flame, and fry the cumin until the seeds darken one shade and stop sputtering.
Add the onions and cook 18 minutes over medium heat, stirring only when they catch, until they collapse, release the pan and go the colour of an old penny.
Stir in the ginger garlic paste until the raw smell turns sweet, then pull the pan off the flame, add the coriander, deghi mirch and turmeric with a spoonful of water, and set it back on.

Add the tomato and bhuna for 15 minutes without hurrying it, stirring, until the mass draws away from the sides in one piece and a rim of red oil stands clear at the edge: everything else depends on reaching this point.

Tip in the beans with their liquor, mash a ladleful against the pan side, simmer 20 minutes until the gravy coats a spoon, then finish with the garam masala, amchur and coriander and serve over the drained basmati.

note: Bhuna is dehydration, not browning. The water in the onion and tomato must leave before the pan can push past 100C (212F), and only then does the fat separate out carrying the spice with it. That rim of oil is the signal; the clock is not. Add the beans before it happens and the pan never gets hot enough again, so the masala stays raw and sour and the gravy thin and pink.

ingredients.text: 8 g loose Assam tea, tied in muslin
2 black cardamom, a 5 cm piece of cassia, 4 cloves and 2 bay leaves
25 g ginger, half pounded to a paste and half in julienne
20 g garlic, pounded to a paste
3 g cumin seeds, dry roasted and coarsely ground

steps.text: Soak the chana 8 hours in 1.5 litres of cold water with the bicarbonate: they are ready when each has doubled and splits cleanly instead of snapping.

Boil them in fresh water with the muslin bag of tea, the whole spices and 6 g salt for 45 minutes, until a chana crushes to a smooth paste against the roof of the mouth and the skins have stained near black; lift out the bag and the whole spices.

Brown the onions in the ghee over medium heat for 15 minutes, until they slump, lose their edges and go the colour of an old penny, then add the ginger and garlic paste and cook until the raw garlic smell turns sweet.
Take the pan off the flame before you add the ground coriander, deghi mirch, anardana and amchur, slacken them with a spoonful of the black cooking liquor, and set the pan back on.

Add the tomatoes and bhuna 12 minutes until the mass pulls from the sides in one piece and dark oil stands at the rim, then fold in the chana with 300 ml of their liquor and simmer 15 minutes until the gravy clings.
Mash a ladleful of chana against the side to thicken it, then finish with the kala namak, roasted cumin, ginger julienne, slit chillies and lemon.

note: Bicarbonate raises the water's pH, weakening the pectin between cell walls so the chana turns creamy rather than mealy; go much past 2 g per 300 g and it saponifies the skins into slime with a soapy taste. Whole spices can sit in the boil for 45 minutes and only sweeten. Ground spice has far more surface area and scorches bitter in hot fat, so it goes in off the flame, wetted.

ingredients.text: 800 g sarson (mustard greens), thick stems pulled off
150 g bathua (goosefoot greens), or more spinach
40 g ginger, half chopped and half julienned

steps.text: Boil the sarson, palak and bathua uncovered in a heavy pot with the chopped ginger, chillies, salt and water for 45 minutes: they are done when a mustard stem crushes to nothing between thumb and finger and the steam smells sweet rather than sharp.
Mash the greens in the pot with a wooden churner, pounding and turning for 10 minutes, until the leaves have broken down but you can still feel fibre against the tongue.
Rain in the makki da atta a little at a time, stirring hard so it cannot clump, and cook 20 minutes more until the saag pulls away from the side of the pot and holds the mark of the spoon.
In a separate pan brown the onion in the ghee, add the garlic, tomato and deghi mirch, and cook until the oil runs red and separates at the edge, then stir two thirds of the tadka through the saag.
Spoon the rest of the tadka over the top with the ginger julienne and let the white butter melt into it at the table.

note: Mustard leaf carries sinigrin, which is what makes it bitter and sharp, and only a long uncovered boil drives that off; there is no shortcut and no lid. A blender shears the cells instead of tearing them and whips in air, so the saag goes grey and slimy: use a wooden churner. The makki da atta thickens, but give it 20 minutes or it tastes of raw grain.

ingredients.text: 300 g makki da atta (fine maize flour)
100 g mooli (white radish), grated and squeezed dry, optional
60 g white butter or ghee, to finish

steps.text: Mix the salt through the flour, then pour in the hot water in three goes, working it with the back of a spoon until the dough is cool enough to touch.

Knead 5 minutes with the heel of the palm, folding in the mooli if using, until the dough is smooth and warm and takes a thumbprint without cracking at the rim; if it cracks, wet the palm and keep going.
Take a ball the size of a lime and pat it flat between wet palms, turning it a quarter after every pat, until it is 12 cm across and 5 mm thick with an unbroken edge.
Lay it on a tawa hot enough to make a water drop skitter, cook 2 minutes until the underside is freckled brown, turn it, then press the edges down with a folded cloth until it puffs.
Finish it straight on the flame or coals for 20 seconds a side, until it blisters and smells toasted, then tear it open and load it with white butter.

note: Maize has no gluten, so the only thing holding this roti together is starch swollen in water hot enough to gelatinise it, around 70C (160F). Mixed with cold water the dough crumbles at every edge and falls apart on the tawa. Shape one at a time and pat it between wet palms: a rolling pin shears the sheet, and the dough stiffens as it cools.

ingredients.text: 15 g ghee for the dough, plus 60 g for cooking
500 g floury potatoes, boiled in their skins and cooled completely
3 g cumin seeds, dry roasted and coarsely ground

steps.text: Work the water into the atta with the salt and 15 g ghee for 6 minutes, until the dough takes a finger with no resistance and springs back slowly, then cover and rest it 30 minutes.
Peel the cold potatoes and grate them on the coarse side of a box grater into a wide bowl: they should fall in loose threads, never in clods.
Toss through the ginger, chillies, ajwain, amchur, roasted cumin, deghi mirch and coriander with fingertips so the threads stay separate, and add the filling salt only when you are ready to stuff.
Cup a ball of dough in the palm, load it with its own weight of filling, gather the edges over the top, pinch off the knot and press it flat; roll from the centre outward, turning often, to 18 cm.
Cook it dry on a medium tawa for 1 minute a side until brown freckles appear, then smear ghee on both faces and press with a cloth until it swells and crisps in patches.

note: The filling has to be dry and cold before it meets the dough. Boil the potatoes in their skins so they take on less water, cool them fully, then grate rather than mash: mashing ruptures the starch cells into a wet glue that steams the seam open. Salt pulls more water out, so season at the moment of stuffing. A tear means warm filling, not thin dough.

ingredients.text: 500 g fresh paneer, cut in 3 cm cubes
500 g full fat dahi, hung in muslin 4 hours to give about 250 g
20 g ginger and garlic, pounded together to a paste
8 g salt, plus 20 g for the soaking water
1 green capsicum and 1 onion, cut into petals
3 g chaat masala and 1 lemon, to finish

steps.text: Soak the paneer 15 minutes in water held at 60C (140F) with the 20 g salt dissolved in it, then lift it out and pat dry: the cubes should now yield slightly under a finger.

Dry roast the besan over a low flame for 3 minutes until it smells of toasted biscuit and loses its raw chalkiness, then whisk it into the hung curd with the ginger garlic, mustard oil, deghi mirch, turmeric, garam masala, kasoori methi, ajwain and salt.
Fold the paneer and the capsicum and onion petals through the marinade, which should hold a soft peak and cloak the cubes without sliding off, and leave it 1 hour and no longer.

Thread them on skewers with a petal between each cube and cook over hot coals, or under a grill at its highest setting, for 8 to 10 minutes, turning, until the marinade sets dry and the edges blacken in spots.
Baste with the melted butter, dust with chaat masala and squeeze the lemon over while they are still hissing.

note: Paneer squeaks when its casein network tightens and wrings out whey, which begins above roughly 70C (160F) and does not reverse. Soak the cubes in salted water at 60C (140F) to relax and rehydrate them, then cook fast and fierce so the outside chars before the centre climbs there. The roasted besan thickens the curd so the marinade grips instead of sliding into the fire.

ingredients.text: 700 g mutton shoulder, trimmed and passed twice through the coarse plate
150 g mutton or lamb fat, minced with the second pass
100 g onion, chopped very fine and squeezed dry in muslin
25 g ginger and garlic, pounded to a paste and squeezed of excess water
20 g roasted chana dal, ground to a flour
3 g cumin seeds, dry roasted and ground

steps.text: Chill the meat and fat to just above freezing, then pass both through the coarse plate a second time so the fat runs evenly through the mince instead of sitting in lumps.

Set the bowl over ice and knead the mince with the salt, onion, ginger garlic, chillies, chana dal flour and spices for 8 minutes, until the mass turns pale and tacky and lifts out in one piece that clings to an upturned palm.
Rest it covered in the fridge 1 hour, then take a handful, press it onto a flat skewer from the middle outward with a wet hand and run a thumb down its length to leave ridges.
Hang the skewers over hot coals without letting the meat touch them and leave them still for 4 minutes, until the surface sets matt and the kebab releases when you turn it.
Rotate and baste with ghee for 6 minutes more, until the fat drips and hisses in the coals and juices run clear from a ridge.

note: Salt plus hard kneading pulls myosin out of the meat, and that dissolved protein is the only glue holding a seekh to its skewer. It sets only while cold: much above 12C (54F) the fat smears and coats the protein, the gel never forms and the kebab slumps into the fire. Squeeze the onion dry, keep the bowl over ice, and rest the mix before moulding.

ingredients.text: 500 g sour dahi, three days old, whisked smooth
60 g ghee, split between the two tadkas
6 sabut lal mirch (whole dried red chillies)
150 g onion, sliced, for the first tadka
20 g ginger and 15 g garlic, minced
250 g onion, sliced paper thin, for the pakoras
2 g ajwain and a pinch of bicarbonate of soda
4 g deghi mirch for the second tadka

steps.text: Whisk the dahi, the 120 g besan, turmeric, salt and water together cold until no grit is left on the whisk and it pours like single cream.

For the first tadka heat 40 g of the ghee, add the methi dana and let them darken one shade only, about 15 seconds, then the cumin, hing, three of the chillies, the sliced onion, ginger and garlic, and cook until the onion is soft and gold.

Pour in the yogurt mixture and stir without once stopping until it reaches a full rolling boil, then leave it uncovered at a lazy simmer for 50 minutes, until it has reduced by a third, gone the colour of old ivory and coats the back of a spoon.

Beat the pakora besan with just enough water to hold a peak, fold in the thin onion, ajwain and bicarbonate, and fry spoonfuls at 170C (340F) for 4 minutes until they are amber and sound hollow when tapped.
Slide the pakoras into the kadhi 10 minutes before serving so they drink it in and go soft through the middle.
Heat the remaining ghee, pull it off the flame, drop in the last chillies and the deghi mirch so they sizzle in the residual heat alone, and pour it over the surface at the table.

note: Yogurt curdles because heat makes its casein clump. Besan is the stabiliser, its starch swelling around the micelles to hold them apart, but only once hydrated, so whisk every lump out cold and stir without pause to the first boil: stop early and the base overheats into grains no whisking recovers. Two tadkas because methi needs the hour to mellow and the second must stay loud.

ingredients.text: 60 g basmati rice, soaked 30 minutes then drained
0.2 g saffron, bloomed in 1 tbsp warm milk

steps.text: Drain the rice and pound or pulse it to the feel of fine sand: pinch some between the fingers and you should still make out separate grains, not flour.
Reduce the milk over medium heat for 20 minutes, scraping the skin off the sides back in, until it has lost a quarter of its volume and faintly coats the spoon.

Slacken the ground rice with 100 ml of the hot milk, rain it in while whisking, and cook on low for 18 minutes, dragging a spoon across the base without pause, until the grains are soft and a spoon drawn through leaves a clean line.
Only now stir in the sugar, then take the pan off the heat and add the cardamom, saffron milk and kewra water.
Pour it hot into shallow earthenware bowls, scatter the nuts over, and chill at least 4 hours until the top sets firm enough to hold a spoon mark.

note: Grind the rice coarse, to the feel of sand: milled to flour it sets as paste with nothing to chew. Sugar goes in last because it competes with the starch for water and lifts the temperature at which the grains swell, so added early it leaves the rice gritty however long you cook it. Unglazed earthenware wicks moisture out as it chills and tightens the surface.

ingredients.text: 70 g dried erjingtiao chillies, stems removed
30 g dried zidantou chillies, stems removed
1 star anise, 4 cm cassia bark, 2 bay leaves and 1 cracked caoguo

steps.text: Toast both chillies in a dry wok over low heat, turning constantly, until they smell of tobacco and snap rather than bend, about 4 minutes; stop while they are still deep red, because past that the oil tastes of ash.
Cool, then pound coarse: flakes the size of coffee grounds with visible seed, not powder. Mix with the sesame, salt and hot water until the flakes look damp and clump slightly.

Heat the rapeseed oil to 190C (375F), until its raw green smell burns off and the surface goes flat and shimmering, then fry the ginger, spring onion, shallot and whole spices until the ginger curls and turns biscuit brown; lift them all out.

Let the oil fall to 150C (300F) and pour one third over the flakes: they should roar and foam up the bowl. At 130C (265F) pour the second third. At 110C (230F) drop the huajiao into the pan, swirl 20 seconds, and pour the last third through a strainer.
Cover and leave a full day before using; colour keeps bleeding out of the flakes overnight and the raw edge goes with it.

note: Chilli colour and chilli aroma live at different temperatures. The red pigment only bleeds out around 150C (300F), while the volatile aromatics scorch above roughly 170C (340F), and once they do the oil is bitter and resting will not fix it. Hence three pours down a temperature ladder. Huajiao goes in last and coolest: its numbing sanshools are fragile and one hot minute boils them off.

ingredients.text: 500 g beef topside or flank, sliced 3 mm thick against the grain
60 ml rapeseed oil, plus 120 ml for the final pour
15 g dried erjingtiao chillies, snipped in 2 cm lengths
700 ml unsalted beef or chicken stock
300 g celery, cut in 6 cm batons
2 g ground roasted huajiao, to finish

steps.text: Rub the beef with salt, wine and the 15 ml water until every drop is drawn in and the slices feel tacky, then work in egg white and starch and leave 15 minutes; they should look glossed, not gluey.
Fry the erjingtiao and whole huajiao in the 60 ml oil over low heat until the chilli turns dark garnet and smells toasted, about 90 seconds; lift out, chop coarse and reserve for the top.
In that same oil fry the doubanjiang over medium low heat until the paste loosens, the oil separates and runs bright red at the edge of the pan, about 3 minutes. There is no shortcut past this point.
Add ginger and garlic, then the stock and soy; simmer 5 minutes, blanch the celery and sprouts in it until just limp, and lift them into a deep bowl.
Take the pan off any hard boil and slide the beef into barely trembling stock, poaching 60 to 90 seconds until the slices turn opaque at the edges and curl; pour beef and stock over the vegetables.
Pile the chopped chilli, ground huajiao and raw garlic on top, heat the remaining 120 ml oil to 200C (390F) and pour it over so it crackles and lifts the garlic in one wave.

note: Shuizhu does not mean boiled. It means the beef finishes in liquid rather than oil, and above a lazy simmer the velveting starch sloughs off and the slices go grey and stringy, so the stock must stop bubbling before the meat goes in. The doubanjiang is fried until the oil separates and runs red because both the colour and the fermented depth sit in the paste's oil phase; stir it straight into liquid and you get muddy brown soup.

ingredients.text: 500 g pork belly, skin on, in one piece
5 g huajiao, whole, for the poaching water
200 g suan miao (green garlic shoots), cut on the bias in 4 cm lengths

steps.text: Poach the belly whole with ginger, spring onion, wine and huajiao at a bare simmer until a chopstick enters the lean against slight resistance, about 30 minutes; cool it in its liquid, then chill hard.
Slice the cold belly across into pieces 2 mm thick and about the size of a large stamp, skin, fat and lean in every slice.

Fry the slices in the oil over medium heat without crowding until the fat runs out and each piece curls into a small cup with a browned rim: this is the deng zhan wo, the lantern shape, and it is the whole point.
Push the pork aside, drop the doubanjiang into the rendered fat and fry until the oil runs red, then add tianmianjiang and douchi for 30 seconds, until they smell toasted and sweet.
Add soy, sugar and the garlic shoots and toss about 40 seconds, only until the white stems turn translucent and the green tops slump; they must stay squeaky.
