Slice it warm and it tears, slice it thick and it never curls, and the curl is what matters: a flat slice sits in its own fat and stews, while a cupped slice presents a browned rim and gives up its fat for the doubanjiang to fry in. Garlic shoots go in at the very end or they turn to grey rag.

ingredients.text: 600 g Chinese aubergine, cut in batons 8 cm by 2 cm
40 g pao la jiao (brine pickled Sichuan chillies), chopped fine
40 g spring onion, white and green, sliced fine

steps.text: Salt the aubergine and leave 15 minutes, then blot dry; the salt collapses the sponge so it drinks far less oil.
Whisk sugar, vinegar, soy, the second salt, starch and water into one sauce and stand it beside the wok. Yuxiang is mixed before it is cooked, never corrected in the pan.
Fry the aubergine at 180C (355F) for about 2 minutes, until the skin blisters and the flesh goes translucent and slumps; drain on a rack, not paper, so it stays loose.

Pour off all but 30 ml of oil, add pao la jiao and doubanjiang over medium low heat and fry about 2 minutes, until the fat turns clear orange red and the sourness turns fragrant; add ginger and garlic for 20 seconds.

Return the aubergine, stir the sauce to lift the settled starch, pour it round the rim of the wok and toss 30 seconds until it goes glossy and clings in a thin coat; kill the heat and fold in the spring onion.

The sauce is premixed because the starch sets in seconds; add sugar and vinegar separately over live heat and the vinegar boils off, leaving a flat sweet gloss.

ingredients.text: 500 g green beans, topped and tailed, left whole

steps.text: Dry the beans absolutely; any surface water turns the oil violent and steams the bean instead of blistering it.

Fry at 170C (340F) for 3 to 4 minutes, until the skins pucker into fine wrinkles all over and the bright green dulls to olive. A bean that still squeaks is not done: you want it limp and faintly leathery.
In 20 ml of the drained oil, fry the pork over medium heat about 3 minutes, until it stops clumping and the grains turn sandy and dry, then add the yacai and fry until it smells sweet and smoky.
Add chilli, huajiao, garlic and ginger and stir just 20 seconds, only until the chilli darkens and the huajiao smells of citrus peel.
Return the beans with wine, soy, sugar and salt and toss over high heat until the pan is dry and nothing pools at the bottom.

ingredients.text: 2 star anise, 5 cm cassia bark, 2 bay leaves and 1 cracked caoguo

steps.text: Bring shin, tripe, tongue and heart up from cold water, skimming the grey scum until the surface runs clear, then rinse each piece and rub the skin off the tongue while it is still too hot to hold comfortably.

Build a brine from fresh water, ginger, spring onion, whole huajiao, the spices and salt; simmer the offal 60 to 90 minutes and the shin about 90, pulling each piece the moment a skewer meets no resistance.
Turn off the heat and let everything cool in the brine to room temperature, then chill. This is the step people skip and the one that decides the texture.
Slice every piece cold and across the grain, thin enough to read light through: about 2 mm for shin and tongue, wider ribbons for tripe.
Dress with hongyou and its sediment, soy, sugar and ground huajiao, turning until every slice is lacquered, and scatter peanuts, sesame and celery leaf only as it goes to the table.

ingredients.text: 600 g free range chicken, leg and breast on the bone

steps.text: Poach the chicken with ginger, spring onion and wine at 80C (175F), never letting it boil, for about 20 minutes, then drop it straight into iced water until cold through; the skin tightens and the flesh stays juicy.
Let the sesame paste down with the soy and vinegar a spoonful at a time, stirring smooth after each addition. Add the liquid all at once and the paste seizes into grit that never comes back.

Tear the cold chicken along the grain into shreds about the thickness of a pencil lead, discarding bone and keeping the skin.
Bed the cucumber, pile the shreds on it and spoon the sauce over only as it goes out; dressed early, the shreds go slack and the sauce splits.

ingredients.text: 400 g minced pork, about 30 percent fat
60 ml ginger and spring onion water, cooled
200 ml light soy sauce, for the fuzhi jiangyou
80 g Chinese slab sugar or brown sugar
1 star anise, 5 cm cassia bark, 2 bay leaves, 5 g huajiao and 1 cracked caoguo
30 g ginger, sliced, for the soy
40 g garlic, crushed to a paste with 20 ml cold water

steps.text: Simmer the soy with sugar, spices and sliced ginger at the lowest possible heat for 20 minutes, until it coats a spoon and reads sweet and liquorice rather than salty, then strain. This is fuzhi jiangyou and it keeps for weeks.

Work flour, salt and water into a firm dough, knead 8 minutes until it gives like an earlobe, rest it covered 30 minutes, then roll and cut 8 cm rounds, thin at the rim and a shade thicker at the centre.

Beat the ginger and spring onion water into the pork 20 ml at a time until each addition disappears and the mince turns pale and sticky, then season with wine, salt and white pepper; it should hold a peak on the spoon.
Fold each round into a plain half moon with no pleats, pressing every bubble out as you seal: trapped air bursts the skin in the pot.
Boil in plenty of water, adding a cup of cold water each time it returns to a rolling boil, three times over, until the dumplings float and the skin goes translucent over the filling.
Spoon fuzhi jiangyou into warm bowls, add garlic water and hongyou, lift the drained dumplings in and scatter sesame. The sauce sits underneath, never poured over.

note: These are dressed, not souped, and the dressing carries no vinegar at all: that absence is what makes them Sichuanese rather than northern. Sweetness comes from fuzhi jiangyou, soy reduced with sugar and spice to a syrup, and it must reduce slowly or the sugar carries past caramel into bitter. Let the raw garlic down in cold water, because hot liquid cooks off the allicin and the sauce loses its edge.
techniques: Resting dough: the pause that does the work

ingredients.text: 30 g garlic, crushed to a paste with 30 ml cold water
20 g spring onion greens, sliced fine

steps.text: Whisk the starch and salt into 300 ml of the cold water until no lump survives and the slurry pours like single cream; a lump here becomes a hard nugget in the finished block.
Bring the remaining 600 ml to a boil, then pour the slurry in a thin stream, stirring hard and always in one direction. It thickens almost at once.

Drop to the lowest heat and keep stirring 6 to 8 minutes, until the paste turns from milky to glassy and pulls away from the pan in a single sheet. Stop before that and the centre stays chalky and tastes of raw starch.
Scrape into an oiled tray, level the top, cool uncovered to room temperature and then chill about 2 hours, until it cuts without sagging.
Cut into thick ribbons and dress at the table with garlic water, soy, vinegar, sugar, ground huajiao and a generous flood of hongyou.

note: The block is a starch gel and it needs two things: enough starch to water, roughly one to six by weight, and long enough cooking to burst every granule. Undercook it and it never fully gelatinises, so it sets soft and weeps on the plate. Dress it only at the table, because salt and vinegar draw water straight back out of the gel; let it sit ten minutes and you get diluted sauce and a slippery, flavourless block.

ingredients.text: 400 g thin fresh alkaline wheat noodles
60 g Yibin yacai, rinsed and chopped fine
30 g spring onion greens, sliced fine
20 g garlic, crushed to a paste with 20 ml cold water

steps.text: Fry the pork in the rapeseed oil over medium heat until the grains separate and crisp at the edges, add the wine and yacai, and keep going until the pan is dry and the yacai smells sweet and smoky.
Boil the noodles in a lot of water for 60 to 90 seconds, until they bend without snapping but still show a thin white line at the core.
Drain hard, spread them on a tray and toss with the sesame oil until every strand is separate and no water beads on the surface. This step is what the name is about.
Tip into a warm bowl with soy, garlic water, hongyou, ground huajiao and salt, and turn from the bottom until the strands go glossy red and nothing pools.
Top with the pork and yacai, peanuts, walnuts and spring onion, and eat at once, while the noodles are still hot enough to carry the aroma.

note: Ran mian means burning noodles: burning because a strand this dry and this oily will take a flame, not because it is hot. Everything depends on drying the noodle. A wet strand dilutes the dressing, which then runs to the bottom of the bowl and leaves the top half naked. Drain, spread and coat with sesame oil before any seasoning goes near it.

ingredients.text: 500g fresh sardines, scaled and filleted (about 300g clean fillet)
60g sultanas (uva passa), soaked 20 minutes in warm water
6 salted anchovy fillets, rinsed and chopped
60g coarse dry breadcrumbs, for the muddica atturrata
1 tbsp olive oil, for the muddica

steps.text: Boil the wild fennel in 3 litres of heavily salted water for 10 minutes, until the stems collapse under the back of a spoon; lift it out, squeeze it, chop it, and keep every drop of the green water.
Sweat the onion in the olive oil over low heat for 12 minutes until it is translucent and slumped with no colour at the edges, then melt in the anchovy until the oil smells of the sea.

Add the pine nuts, drained sultanas, chopped fennel and the saffron loosened in a ladle of the fennel water, lay the sardine fillets on top and cook 6 minutes without stirring, until they turn from glassy to opaque and fall apart when nudged.
Toast the breadcrumbs in a dry pan with the spoon of oil, tossing until they are the colour of dark honey and rattle loose, then tip them straight onto a cold plate.

Cook the bucatini in the fennel water, drain it two minutes short and finish it in the pan with a ladle of that water until the strands are lacquered and no liquid pools underneath; scatter the muddica at the table, not before.

note: Wild fennel is blanched first and that green water becomes the pasta water: the anethole and sugars leach into it, so tipping it away throws out half the dish. Lay the sardines on the onion and leave them alone; stirring shreds them into grey paste. Muddica goes on at the table because toasted crumb wicks sauce and turns to sludge within a minute.

steps.text: Salt the aubergine in a colander for 45 minutes, until brown beads stand on the cut faces, then rinse and press dry in a cloth until the cubes squeak.

In the olive oil, cook the celery 5 minutes until it turns from raw green to olive but still snaps, add the onion until translucent, then the tomatoes, olives, capers, pine nuts and sultanas and simmer 10 minutes until no water runs at the pan edge.
Raise the heat until the pan hisses, pour the vinegar and sugar in together and boil hard for 60 seconds, until the sharp smell drops away and the surface turns glossy.
Fold the aubergine back in off the heat, tear in the basil, and leave it at room temperature for at least 4 hours; it is not finished until it is cool.

note: Agrodolce is a ratio, not a splash: 60ml white wine vinegar to 30g sugar, poured into a pan hot enough to hiss so the acetic acid flashes off and leaves sweetness with a spine. ingredients.text: 800g ripe plum tomatoes, peeled and chopped

steps.text: Salt the aubergine slices in a colander for 40 minutes, until water beads on the surface, then rinse and press hard in a cloth until they feel dense and dry.

Cook the garlic in the olive oil until it just turns blond, lift it out, add the tomatoes and simmer 20 minutes until the sauce pulls away from the pan and no water separates at the edge.
Boil the pasta in heavily salted water, drain it a minute short and toss it through the sauce with a splash of cooking water until every tube is coated and the pan is dry.
Fold in half the aubergine and the torn basil, then grate the ricotta salata over each plate in a snowfall so it stays dry instead of melting into the sauce.

ingredients.text: 800g fresh sardines, scaled, boned and butterflied, tails left on
4 salted anchovy fillets, rinsed and chopped
a handful of flat parsley, chopped

steps.text: Toast the breadcrumbs in 50ml of the oil over medium heat, stirring until they are the colour of toffee and smell nutty, then spread them out and cool them completely.
Mix the cold crumb with the pine nuts, sultanas, anchovy, parsley, orange zest and pepper until it holds when squeezed in the fist but crumbles when dropped.

Lay each sardine skin down, set a heaped teaspoon of stuffing at the head end and roll towards the tail so the tail stands up, then pack the rolls into an oiled dish with a bay leaf standing between each one.
Whisk the orange juice, lemon juice, sugar and remaining oil until cloudy and pour it around the rolls, not over them.
Bake at 200C (400F) for 12 minutes, until the skins are taut and bronzed and a roll gives no resistance at the centre, then serve just warm.

note: Toast the crumb before it ever meets the fish. Raw breadcrumb soaks up the sardine fat as it renders and the roll ends up wet and pasty; toasted crumb has already lost its free water and stays granular. Bay leaves stand between the rolls to hold them apart so the sides colour. Twelve minutes at 200C (400F) is the ceiling: past about 63C the muscle squeezes out its moisture and goes chalky.

steps.text: Cut the chilled loin into 3mm slices, lay each between two sheets of film and beat gently with a flat mallet until it is translucent at the edges and about 2mm thick.

Put a teaspoon of filling on each slice, roll it tight and thread the rolls onto skewers alternating with bay leaves so no two rolls touch.
Grill over fierce heat for about 90 seconds a side, until the surface is marked and opaque and the rolls still spring back under a finger.
Whisk the lemon juice with the warm water, beat in the remaining oil and the oregano until it thickens and turns pale, and spoon this salmoriglio over the skewers while they are hot.

note: Swordfish is lean and almost free of collagen, so there is no gelatine to hide overcooking: it goes from silky to cotton wool inside a minute. Whisk the salmoriglio with warm water first; without that emulsion the lemon and oil separate and slide straight off the fish.

ingredients.text: 3 tbsp olive oil, for the topping

steps.text: Mix the flours with 350ml of the water and rest 30 minutes until no dry flour remains, then work in the yeast, salt, oil and the last of the water until the dough is slack, sticky and peels off the bowl in sheets.
Fold it in the bowl four times at 30 minute intervals, until it holds a low dome, then refrigerate overnight.

Cook the onions in the topping oil over low heat for 40 minutes until jammy, pale gold and sweet with no bite left, melt in the anchovies, then add the tomato and reduce until the mix mounds on the spoon.
Press the dough into an oiled 30x40cm tray and prove 2 hours at room temperature, until it reaches the corners and a poked dent fills back only halfway.

Scatter the cheese, lay the onion on in spoonfuls without pressing, then the breadcrumbs and oregano, and bake on the lowest shelf at 220C (430F) for 25 minutes, until the base is crisp when lifted with a palette knife and the crumb topping is dark gold.

ingredients.text: 250ml salted water at room temperature, for the incocciatura
3 tbsp extra virgin olive oil, for the grain
1.5kg mixed rock fish, scaled and gutted (scorfano, gallinella, tracina)
a large bunch of flat parsley
200g plain flour mixed to a paste with water, for the sealing rope

steps.text: Spread the semolina in a wide bowl, flick on the salted water a few drops at a time and work it in one direction with spread fingertips for 20 minutes, until every grain wears a skin and nothing is larger than a peppercorn.
Rub the 3 tbsp of oil through the grain, then rake it with your fingers until it feels dry and separate again.

Simmer the fish heads and bones with half the rock fish, the onion, garlic, tomato, almonds, saffron, bay, peperoncino and parsley in 2 litres of water for 40 minutes, until the broth runs orange and coats a spoon, then press it through a sieve.
Load the grain loosely into the couscoussier basket, set it over the simmering broth, seal the joint with a rope of flour paste and steam 60 minutes, until steam breaks through the top of the grain.
Poach the remaining fish in the strained broth for 8 minutes, until the flesh parts from the bone at the touch of a fork.
Tip the grain into a warm bowl and add hot broth a ladle at a time until it drinks its fill and stands in soft peaks, cover with a cloth and leave 30 minutes before serving the fish alongside.

note: Incocciatura is the whole technique: salted water is flicked onto the semolina a few drops at a time and worked with fingertips until each grain wears a skin. Pour the water in and the grains cement into lumps that steam through as paste. Seal the pot rim with a flour rope so steam has one exit, then rest the cooked grain under hot broth so it swells evenly.

steps.text: Whisk the chickpea flour into the cold water with the salt until there is not one lump left, rest it 10 minutes and whisk again.
Set it over medium heat and stir without stopping for about 12 minutes, until it thickens past custard and comes away from the pan wall as a single mass that holds the mark of the spoon.
Beat in the parsley and pepper, then spread the paste 3mm thin on oiled trays while it is still hot, working fast before it sets.
Cool 20 minutes until firm and matt, then cut into rectangles or triangles.
Fry at 180C (355F) in small batches for about 2 minutes, until the surfaces blister into blond bubbles and the panelle float, drain, salt, and eat within five minutes in a sesame roll with lemon.

note: Chickpea starch gelatinises around 75C (165F), so whisk the flour into cold water and bring it up slowly; hot water sets the outside of each lump and seals raw flour inside. Stir until the mass pulls cleanly from the pan wall, then spread it 3mm while hot. Fry at 180C (355F): cooler and the panella turns leathery, hotter and the crust sets before trapped water can blister it.

ingredients.text: 400g marzipan (pasta reale), tinted green with pistachio
300g pan di Spagna, cut in 1cm sheets
candied orange, citron and cherries, to decorate

steps.text: Drain the ricotta in a cloth in the fridge for 12 hours, then push it through a fine sieve twice until it is smooth with no grain to it.
Beat in the caster sugar and leave it 1 hour, then rub a little between finger and thumb: if you feel any grit, wait longer.
Fold in the chocolate and zuccata, keeping the cream stiff enough to hold a soft peak.
Line a sloping 24cm tin with film, press cold marzipan strips 8mm thick around the sides and line the base with pan di Spagna brushed with the diluted maraschino.
Fill with the ricotta cream, level it, cap with more sponge and chill at least 6 hours, until the surface is firm under a fingertip.
Turn it out, warm the icing sugar with the water to 40C (105F) until it pours like thick cream, coat the cassata in one unbroken pass and decorate before the glaze skins over.

note: Drain the ricotta 12 hours, sieve it, then beat with the sugar and rest it an hour so the crystals fully dissolve. Undissolved sugar keeps pulling whey by osmosis and the finished cassata weeps inside its marzipan wall. Work the pasta reale cold: almond oil sweats out of warm marzipan and the glaze will not key to a greasy surface. Pour the fondant at 40C (105F) for a glossy set.

ingredients.text: 250g raw almonds, Avola if you can get them
1 litre cold water, for the almond milk
1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tbsp milk, to glaze

steps.text: Soak the almonds 8 hours, slip off the skins, blitz them with the litre of cold water and press through a cloth until the pulp is dry; never warm it.
Stir the sugar and salt into the cold almond milk until dissolved, pour it into a shallow metal tray and freeze.
Scrape the whole surface with a fork every 30 minutes for about 3 hours, until it is a bank of loose crystals that collapse under a spoon.

For the brioche, mix the flour, warm milk, sugar, yeast, eggs, salt and orange zest to a smooth dough, then work in the butter a piece at a time until the dough is glossy and stretches to a windowpane.

Prove until doubled, divide into 100g balls, pinch a small ball on top of each as the tuzzu, prove again until pillowy and slow to spring back, glaze and bake at 180C (355F) for 15 minutes, until deep amber.
Split a warm brioche, load it with granita until it overflows and eat it standing up.

note: Sugar is what makes granita scrapeable: about 160g per litre, near 15 percent, keeps enough water unfrozen to shear into crystals. Less and you get a solid block, more and it never sets at all. ingredients.text: 400 g idli rice (parboiled short grain puzhungal arisi)
Ice water for grinding, roughly 350 ml in total
Gingelly (raw sesame) oil, for the moulds

steps.text: Rinse the idli rice until the water runs clear and soak it in cold water; soak the urad dal and fenugreek in a separate bowl for 5 hours, until a grain crushes to paste between finger and thumb.
Grind the urad dal first, feeding in ice water 30 ml at a time, until the batter has trebled, is bright white and glossy, and a spoonful dropped into a glass of water floats instead of sinking.
Grind the drained rice to the grit of fine semolina, then fold it into the urad batter with your bare hand for two minutes, lifting and turning so you do not knock the foam out.
Cover and hold at 26 to 30C (79 to 86F) for 8 to 12 hours, until the batter has domed, is honeycombed against the side of the bowl and smells sharply sour.
Fold in the salt with a light hand, ladle into oiled moulds and steam 10 to 12 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean and the surface has lost its wet shine.

note: Urad dal brings the two things rice cannot: globulin protein and a slippery arabinogalactan mucilage that together spin a film strong enough to hold the CO2 the Leuconostoc gives off. That film shears apart if the grinder heats the batter past about 30C (86F), so grind the urad with ice water and stop when it holds a peak. Past roughly 14 hours the foam collapses and the idli steams flat and sour.

ingredients.text: Ice water for grinding, about 350 ml
60 ml gingelly oil, for the griddle
1 onion, halved, for wiping the iron

steps.text: Soak both rices with the poha in one bowl and the urad dal with the fenugreek in another, 5 hours, until the dal crushes clean.

Ferment at 26 to 30C (79 to 86F) for 8 to 12 hours, until doubled and ringed with bubbles at the edge of the bowl.
Stir the batter down, salt it, and thin with water until it falls off the ladle in a ribbon like thin cream.

Heat a cast iron griddle until a flicked drop of water skitters and vanishes in two seconds. Splash a palmful of water on, wipe it dry with the cut onion, and pour a ladle at the centre, spreading outward in one tightening spiral.

ingredients.text: 30 g tamarind, soaked in 300 ml hot water
150 g small onions (chinna vengayam), peeled whole
150 g brinjal and ash gourd, in large chunks

steps.text: Cook the toor dal with the turmeric until it collapses under the back of a spoon into a smooth puree, then whisk it loose with a little hot water.

In 2 tsp of the gingelly oil, roast the coriander seeds and chana dal until deep gold, then the chillies, pepper and fenugreek for 30 seconds; kill the heat and stir the coconut through the residual warmth until it is fawn and smells toasted. Grind to a fine paste.
Simmer the small onions, drumstick and vegetables in 300 ml plain salted water until the drumstick gives to a fingernail, about 10 minutes.
Pour in the strained tamarind extract with the jaggery and boil hard for 5 minutes, until the raw metallic smell has gone and the liquid smells rounded.
Stir in the dal and the ground paste and hold at a bare tremble for 5 minutes only, until the surface turns glossy and the sambar coats a spoon.
Heat the remaining oil until it shimmers, crackle the mustard until it pops and greys, throw in the curry leaves and asafoetida for three seconds until the leaves go translucent, and pour it over.

Tamarind's acid keeps the vegetables' pectin cross-linked, so anything simmered in the sour liquid from the start stays hard: soften the drumstick and the small onions in plain water first, then pour the tamarind over. steps.text: Pound the pepper, cumin, garlic and one sprig of curry leaves coarsely in a stone mortar, until the mix smells sharp and you can still see broken pepper.

ingredients.text: 80 ml gingelly oil, the unrefined dark sesame oil, not the toasted Chinese kind
30 g sundakkai vathal or manathakkali vathal, the sun-dried salted berries
60 g shallots, peeled and left whole
40 g tamarind, soaked in 400 ml hot water and squeezed
1 tsp rice flour slaked in 2 tbsp water

steps.text: Heat the gingelly oil until a mustard seed sent in cracks at once, then splutter the mustard, urad dal and fenugreek in that order, 20 seconds apart, so the fenugreek goes gold and not brown.
Add the curry leaves, asafoetida, chillies and vathal and fry 2 min: the dried berries should darken and puff slightly, which is the only chance they get to take on fat.
Add the shallots whole and fry 3 min until their edges catch, then pour in the strained tamarind water with the sambar powder, turmeric and salt.
Simmer uncovered 20 to 25 min. It is done when the raw green edge of the tamarind is gone, the volume has dropped by a third, and a clear layer of oil has risen and stays risen.
Stir in the jaggery and the slaked rice flour and give it 2 min more to thicken to a pouring gravy.

note: The oil is not a cooking medium here, it is the preservative, which is why the quantity looks alarming and why the dish is finished only when it floats clear on top. That layer plus the tamarind's acid and a firm hand with salt is what let this keep a week on a Tamil counter with no refrigeration, and it is the reason vathal exists at all: vegetables salted and dried in the sun so a household has something to cook in the months when nothing grows. Two failures to watch. Fenugreek taken past gold turns the whole pot bitter and cannot be corrected. And tamarind pulled off early tastes raw and green rather than sour, so judge the reduction by the oil separating, not by the clock.

flavor.sentence: Leads with acid holding everything up to the light, aromatics blooming from the first bite, trailing gentle sweetness.

steps.text: Heat the gingelly oil, add the mustard and wait until it pops and greys, then the urad and chana dal, stirring until they are the colour of clear honey and smell like toasted nuts.
Add the chillies, curry leaves and asafoetida for 5 seconds until the leaves blister and go translucent, then the small onions until soft and sweet at the edges.
Tip the cabbage in over high heat, uncovered, and toss 5 to 6 minutes until it loses its raw squeak, wilts by half and picks up a few brown edges. No lid and no water at any point.
Off the heat, salt it and stir the fresh coconut through so it stays white and sweet.

note: Here the tadka starts the dish instead of finishing it, because the urad and chana dal need real time in oil to toast nutty and then stay crunchy inside the cabbage. Everything after is a race against water: salt at the start pulls it out by osmosis and a lid traps it, and either one steams the cabbage limp and grey. Cook uncovered on high, salt at the end, coconut off the heat.

ingredients.text: 1 kg chicken on the bone, cut into small pieces
1 star anise, 3 cm cassia, 4 cloves, 3 green cardamom
25 g ginger and 25 g garlic, pounded to a paste

steps.text: Dry roast on low heat: coriander seeds until they crack and darken a shade, then fennel, pepper, cumin, cassia, cloves, cardamom and star anise for a minute until fragrant. Kill the heat and drop the kalpasi into the residual warmth for 10 seconds only, until it smells of woodsmoke.
Roast the coconut separately, stirring without pause, until it is the colour of dark toast and smells nutty. Grind everything with a splash of water to a fine paste.
Heat the gingelly oil and brown the small onions until collapsed and sweet, add the ginger garlic until the raw edge lifts, then the tomatoes until they break to a jam that pulls away from the pan.
Fry the ground masala in that oil for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until the paste darkens and a rim of red oil pulls away at the sides of the pan.
Add the chicken and turmeric, coat and sear 5 minutes until every piece is lacquered and no pink shows, then 100 ml water, lid on, 20 minutes until the meat pulls from the bone.
Tear in the curry leaves and simmer uncovered until the gravy clings to the chicken instead of pooling under it.

note: Kalpasi is the signature and the trap. It is a lichen, so its aroma sits in a resin that dissolves into fat but scorches to flat bitterness within seconds of dry heat: roast the coriander first, the fennel and pepper after, and give the kalpasi only the last few seconds off the flame. Roast the coconut to the colour of dark toast as well, because pale coconut grinds into a sweet thin gravy that never thickens.

ingredients.text: 700 ml water, for cooking the rice
300 g thick fresh curd, not sour, beaten smooth

steps.text: Cook the rice in the full 700 ml until the grains have burst and collapsed, well past al dente. There should be no bite left at all.
Mash it hot with the back of a ladle into a coarse sticky paste, then stir the warm milk in while it is still hot so the starch drinks it.
Let it cool until the bowl is only just warm against the back of your hand, below 40C (105F), then fold in the beaten curd and the salt.

Heat the ghee, pop the mustard, add the urad dal until golden, then the ginger, green chilli, dried chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida for 10 seconds until the leaves go crisp and translucent. Pour it over.
Scatter the pomegranate and rest 20 minutes before serving, so the rice and curd come together.

note: Cook the rice past done and mash it hot: fully burst starch granules cannot retrograde, which is why proper thayir sadam stays creamy in the fridge while al dente rice turns chalky and weeps. Then let it fall below 40C (105F) before the curd goes in, or the casein curdles into grains and the warmed lactic bacteria sour the whole bowl by evening. The milk goes in first because the rice keeps drinking.

ingredients.text: 60 ml ice water, and not a drop more
1 litre groundnut or gingelly oil, for frying

steps.text: Soak the urad dal 3 hours until a grain crushes clean, then drain it bone dry in a colander for 10 minutes.
Grind it, feeding the ice water in 15 ml at a time, until the batter is white, fluffy and stiff enough to stand in a peak, and a pea of it dropped into water rises to the surface within seconds.
Bring the oil to 170 to 175C (340 to 350F) first, and only then fold the ginger, chilli, pepper, curry leaves and salt through the batter by hand.
Wet your palm, flatten a lime sized ball on it, punch a hole through the middle with a wet thumb, and slide the ring off your fingers into the oil.
Fry, turning once, for 5 to 6 minutes until the hissing dies down and they are an even deep gold; a finished vadai feels light and sounds hollow when tapped with the slotted spoon.

note: The whole dish is air ground into urad dal, so add the ice water by the spoon and stop the moment a pea of batter floats. Slack batter will not hold a hole and drinks oil. Fry at 170 to 175C (340 to 350F): under 160C (320F) the crust never sets and the vadai comes out grease logged, over 190C (375F) it browns while the centre is still raw batter. Salt only just before frying, because it slackens the batter within minutes.

ingredients.text: 400 ml water, for cooking the dal

steps.text: Dry roast the moong dal in 10 g of the ghee over low heat, stirring, until it turns a shade darker and smells like roasted nuts.
Cook it in the 400 ml water until soft and about a third of the grains have collapsed, so the payasam carries both body and texture.
Melt the jaggery in its own 100 ml water and strain out the grit, then stir it into the dal off the boil and cook 3 minutes until it smells caramelly.
Pour in the thin coconut milk and bring it only to a tremble, 3 to 4 minutes, until it thickens enough to coat the back of a ladle.
Kill the heat, wait until the pot stops steaming, then stir in the thick coconut milk, cardamom, dry ginger and salt.
Fry the cashews and coconut slivers in the last of the ghee until golden and pour them over.

note: Coconut milk is an emulsion held by coconut protein, and jaggery's acid and minerals are exactly what breaks it. Melt the jaggery separately and strain it, for grit and so it never meets a hard boil; stir the thin milk in at a tremble and the thick first extract in off the heat entirely. Boil after that and you get sweet water with an oil slick riding on top.

ingredients.text: 60 g whole annatto seed (achiote), brick red and not faded brown
6 g Mexican oregano, the large brittle leaf kind
80 ml sour orange juice (naranja agria), or 40 ml orange with 20 ml grapefruit and 20 ml lime

steps.text: Char the unpeeled garlic on a dry comal over medium heat, turning, until the skins are blackened in patches and the cloves collapse under a thumb, about 12 minutes, then peel.

Toast the oregano, allspice, cumin, cloves and cinnamon in the dry pan for about 40 seconds, only until the cumin smells nutty and the first wisp of smoke lifts, then tip them straight out of the hot pan.
Grind the annatto seed on its own in a spice mill until it is a fine rust powder with nothing rattling, grind the toasted spices with the peppercorns, and sift both through a fine sieve.
Mash in the garlic and salt, then work in the sour orange juice and vinegar a spoonful at a time until you have a stiff clay brick that holds a clean thumbprint.
Wrap tightly and rest at least 12 hours before use so the colour bleeds through evenly. It keeps a month refrigerated.

note: The colour is bixin, a resinous carotenoid sitting on the outside of a seed whose kernel is as hard as gravel. A blender jar just polishes the seeds and hands you orange water, so grind them dry in a spice mill or the paste stays gritty forever. Keep the annatto off the heat as well: toasted past warm, the red goes brown and the flavour goes bitter.

ingredients.text: 1.8 kg boneless pork shoulder, cut into 6 cm chunks with the fat left on
300 ml sour orange juice (naranja agria), or 150 ml orange with 75 ml grapefruit and 75 ml lime
6 garlic cloves, charred on a comal and peeled
5 g Mexican oregano, toasted and crumbled
2 large banana leaves, thick spine trimmed away
300 g pickled red onion, to serve

steps.text: Slake the recado rojo into the sour orange juice with the salt, garlic and oregano until it is a smooth loose paint with no gritty specks, turn the pork through it and refrigerate 6 to 12 hours.

Pass each banana leaf over a flame or hot comal for a few seconds a side, until it flips from matte olive to glossy deep green and hangs limp; unwilted leaf cracks along its ribs and the parcel leaks.

Line a deep dish with crossed leaves, pile in the pork with every drop of marinade and the lard, fold the leaves over into a sealed parcel, then cover the whole dish with foil and crimp it hard to the rim.
Cook at 150 C (300 F) for 4 hours without opening it once. It is ready when a chunk collapses under sideways pressure from a spoon and the juices run clear orange under a finger of red fat.
Shred coarsely in its own juices, never squeezed dry, and serve with pickled red onion and habanero.

note: The pib is a steam oven, not a roaster. Wet leaves and buried heat hold the meat near 100 C (212 F) for hours, so collagen melts to gelatin while the surface never dries out. A domestic oven will roast instead unless you rebuild that seal. Let steam escape and the marinade boils away, the pork surface reaches oven temperature and it shreds into dry string, so crimp the foil over the leaf and do not peek.

ingredients.text: 500 g fresh nixtamal masa, or 300 g masa harina hydrated with 380 ml warm water
400 ml neutral oil, for shallow frying
300 g shredded cochinita pibil, or poached turkey breast

steps.text: Simmer the beans with the onion, epazote and whole habanero until they collapse, about 90 minutes, then lift out the aromatics and blend the beans with just enough of their own liquor to pour.
Push the puree through a sieve, then dry it in a pan with the lard over medium heat, stirring, until it pulls away from the base in one mass and a spoon track holds open for three seconds.
Press 30 g balls of masa into 12 cm rounds and cook on a hot comal, 30 seconds, flip, 45 seconds, flip again and press the centre gently with a cloth until the tortilla balloons.
While it is still hot, slit the puffed upper skin along a third of the rim with a knife tip, spoon in a tablespoon of bean paste, and press the pocket flat and shut.
Shallow fry at 180 C (355 F) for about 40 seconds a side, until the surface blisters and stiffens to biscuit colour, drain, then top with the meat, cabbage, pickled onion and avocado.

note: The pocket is not cut into the tortilla, it is steam. On a hot comal both faces set into skins before the interior water flashes, and the trapped steam lifts them apart. Dry masa never seals, so it never puffs: the dough should feel like fresh putty and show no cracked edges when pressed. Fry hot and brief, because a slow fry heats the bean paste through, it swells, and the seam splits.

ingredients.text: 1.2 kg turkey thigh, or chicken legs
1 head garlic, charred whole on a comal
1 habanero, pricked once with a knife tip
2 lima agria (Yucatecan sour lime), or 3 limes plus a wide strip of grapefruit peel
6 corn tortillas, cut into 5 mm strips

steps.text: Simmer the turkey in the water with half the onion, the charred garlic, oregano, allspice and cloves at a bare tremble for 1 hour, skimming, until the meat pulls away from the bone. Strain and keep 2 litres of broth.

Sweat the remaining onion with the bell pepper and tomato in a spoonful of oil until the tomato has gone jammy and the pan smells sweet rather than green, then add the broth, the shredded meat and the pricked habanero and simmer 10 minutes.
Fry the tortilla strips at 180 C (355 F) until they stop bubbling and turn pale gold, then drain on paper. Baked strips dissolve in the bowl.
Pull the pot off the heat, drop in a thin coin of lima peel with no white pith attached, cover and steep 3 minutes, then fish the peel out and stir the juice in.
Ladle over the strips and carry it to the table at once, before they soften.

note: Lima agria is grown for its rind, not its juice: the perfume is peel oil and the acid is mild. Hold the peel in simmering broth and you extract bitter limonin from the pith instead, which sours the whole pot within minutes, so the coin of zest goes in off the heat and comes straight back out. Add the juice off the heat too, since its aroma is volatile and a simmer strips it.

ingredients.text: 300 g hulled green pumpkin seeds (pepita menuda)

steps.text: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking without pause, until they swell, pop and smell of green tea but stay pale. Any browning turns the sauce khaki and bitter. Cool fully, then grind to a fine flour.
Boil the water with the epazote and salt, take it off the heat and let it fall to about 75 C (167 F), then pour it slowly onto the seed flour, kneading with your hand to a thick green cream.
Tilt the bowl and press the paste with your palm until a slick of dark green oil pools at the low edge. Spoon that oil off and keep it for the top.
Char the tomatoes, onion, garlic and habanero on a comal until blistered black in patches, blend, then fry the sauce in the oil until it darkens and holds a line behind a spoon.

Boil the eggs 9 minutes and chop them, dip each warm tortilla into the seed sauce, roll it around the egg, then flood the plate with the remaining seed sauce, the tomato sauce and the reserved green oil.

note: The seed sauce is an emulsion held together by ground pepita solids, and it breaks like any other. Take it much above 80 C (176 F) and the solids clump, the oil floods out and the sauce turns gritty and greasy. So the epazote water is cooled before it meets the flour, the bowl never goes back over a flame, and the green oil you press out deliberately becomes the garnish instead of the failure.

ingredients.text: 800 g pork leg, cut across the grain into 6 mm steaks
180 ml sour orange juice, or 90 ml orange with 45 ml grapefruit and 45 ml lime
2 white onions, cut into thick rounds

steps.text: Turn the pork through the sour orange, garlic, salt and pepper and leave it exactly 20 minutes, no longer.
Char the tomatoes and habanero on the comal until the skins are black and slipping, then crush them with salt into a coarse chiltomate.
Lift the pork out and blot both faces bone dry on cloth, because a wet surface steams itself grey instead of browning.

Grill over a hot charcoal bed for about 90 seconds a side, until the edges curl up and the surface is mottled deep brown with a few black freckles, and lay the onion rounds alongside until limp and singed.
Rest 3 minutes, chop coarsely on the board, and serve with the chiltomate, the grilled onion and xnipec.

note: Sour orange does two jobs and only the first is wanted. In twenty minutes its acid opens the surface to flavour; past that it denatures protein right through a 6 mm steak, which then wrings out its water on the fire and eats like chalk. Dry the meat before it meets the coals: the juice carries sugar and browns fast, but only once the surface water has gone.

ingredients.text: 1.6 kg turkey legs and thighs, jointed
600 g white onion, sliced 5 mm thick
1 head garlic, charred whole on a comal
6 chile xcatic (pale yellow chilli), or banana peppers
10 g Mexican oregano, toasted until brittle

steps.text: Grind the toasted oregano, peppercorns, allspice, cloves, cinnamon and cumin with the peeled charred garlic and a splash of the vinegar into a stiff pale recado.
Simmer the turkey in the water with half the recado and a heavy hand of salt until the meat is loose on the bone, about 70 minutes, then lift the pieces out and keep the broth.
Blister the xcatic chillies over a flame until the skin lifts away in blackened sheets, then peel, seed and slit them lengthways.
Drop the onion into the broth for 2 minutes only, then pour in the vinegar and sour orange with the chillies and the rest of the recado and take the pot off the heat; the onion should still snap.
Char the turkey over coals or under a fierce grill until the skin crisps and blackens at the edges, then return it to the hot escabeche and serve in deep bowls with the broth.

note: Onion stays crunchy in acid for a reason. The reaction that softens vegetable pectin only runs above roughly pH 5, and vinegar shuts it down, so onion added after the acid is still raw-crisp an hour later. That is why the slices get their two minutes in plain broth first and the vinegar goes in last, and why the pot is never boiled once soured.

ingredients.text: 4 habaneros, ideally the orange Yucatecan kind
1 red onion, about 180 g, diced 3 mm
200 g firm ripe tomato, seeded and diced 5 mm
90 ml sour orange juice, or 45 ml orange with 25 ml grapefruit and 20 ml lime

steps.text: Toss the diced onion with the salt and half the juice and leave 10 minutes, until the pieces go translucent pink at the edges and lose their raw bite.
Slit the habaneros and scrape out the pale ribs to bring the heat down, or mince them whole for the full thing; the seeds themselves carry almost nothing.
Fold the chilli, tomato and coriander through the onion with the rest of the juice, then let it stand 15 minutes, until the liquid turns rosy and lifts a sharp chilli smell as you lean over the bowl.
Serve within the hour, while the tomato still has edges.

note: Capsaicin is made in the pale placental ribs, not the seeds, so seeding a habanero barely moves the heat; strip the ribs instead. Salt is the second dial. It pulls water out of onion and tomato by osmosis, which is what you want briefly, to cure the onion's raw sulfur bite. Leave the whole salsa salted an hour and it slumps into pink soup with no crunch left in it.

ingredients.text: 200 g refried black beans, thick enough to hold a line

steps.text: Char the tomato, onion, garlic and habanero on a comal until blackened in patches, blend to a rough sauce, then fry it in a spoonful of oil until it darkens and stops smelling raw.
Fry the plantain in shallow oil until the cut faces are deep amber and the flesh gives like custard, then drain on paper.
Fry the tortillas one at a time at 180 C (355 F), about 30 seconds a side, until they stiffen and stop bubbling but before they take much colour.
Spread each hot tortilla with warm beans, slide a fried egg on top with the white set and the yolk still liquid, then spoon the tomato sauce over and scatter with peas, ham and cheese.
Ring the plate with plantain and eat immediately, before the beans wet the tortilla through.

ingredients.text: 200 g aged Edam or queso de bola, grated fine
150 g cajeta or thick dulce de leche

steps.text: Whisk the flour, sugar and salt into the eggs, let down with the milk, melted butter and vanilla to the thickness of single cream, and rest 20 minutes so the flour hydrates.
Heat a heavy nonstick pan or a wafer iron over medium and spread 60 ml of batter as thin as it will go, roughly 20 cm across.
Cook without moving it until the steam coming off the surface stops and the whole disc goes evenly pale gold and stiff at the rim, 2 to 3 minutes, then flip for 30 seconds more.
Scatter the grated cheese and a ribbon of cajeta across the hot wafer and roll it tight into a tube within about ten seconds, while it still bends.
Stand the roll upright for a minute; it should crack audibly at the first bite.

note: Crispness here is a glass, not a bake. The wafer bends only while hot, with its last water still mobile; falling through about 60 C (140 F) the sugar and starch set rigid, so you have seconds to roll. Roll it while it is still visibly steaming and the trapped moisture softens it from inside. Use a dry aged cheese too: a young melting cheese weeps water and the tube goes limp before it reaches the table.

ingredients.text: 40 g fresh or frozen grated coconut

steps.text: Rub the water and salt into the polvilho doce with your fingertips until the starch feels like damp sand: no dry pockets, no wet lumps.
Press the damp starch through a fine sieve onto a tray. What falls through should be loose and powdery; discard the hard grains left behind.
Scatter a 4 mm even layer of sieved starch across a dry non-stick pan over medium heat and press it flat. The grains turn glassy and knit into one sheet in about 90 seconds.
Flip when the disc lifts free in a single piece and the top has lost its chalky look; give it 30 seconds more, with no colour.
Butter the hot disc, scatter the coconut over half, fold and eat at once.

note: Nothing binds this but the starch itself: cassava granules gelatinise on dry contact heat and fuse into a sheet, so water content is the whole recipe. Too wet and the layer cements into a rubbery pancake; too dry and it stays powder and never knits. Sieving is the calibration step, and the disc must come off pale, because browning makes it brittle.

ingredients.text: 300 g dried black-eyed peas (feijão fradinho), soaked 8 hours
1 litre dendê (unrefined red palm oil) for frying
150 g vatapá (bread, cashew and coconut milk purée)

steps.text: Rub the soaked peas hard between your palms under water until the skins float off; the peas should look bare and pale yellow with no grey flecks.
Grind the drained peas with the grated onion and salt to a thick paste with no whole pieces left in it.
Beat the paste with a wooden spoon until it lightens in colour and a test spoonful floats in cold water, about 5 minutes of hard work.
Heat the dendê to 170C (340F), slide in oval spoonfuls and fry until the crust is set and deep orange and the fritter rolls over on its own, about 4 minutes.
Split each fritter while hot, spread with vatapá and top with dried shrimp, tomato, sliced onion and malagueta.

note: Soak the peas eight hours first. The skins carry the fibre that stops the paste holding air, so the beating that makes acarajé light only works once they are rubbed off. Beat until a spoonful floats: unaerated paste sinks and fries into a dense, greasy lump. Dendê is not interchangeable with neutral oil here; its carotenes give the colour and the flavour, and they degrade past about 180C (355F) into a dull, harsh fat.

ingredients.text: 800 g mandioca mansa (aipim or macaxeira), peeled, in 5 cm lengths

steps.text: Simmer the cassava in salted water until a knife slides through with no resistance and the pieces begin to split, 20 to 25 minutes; lift out and pull the woody cord from the centre of each piece.
Blend the hot cassava with 200 ml of the coconut milk to a purée thick enough to fall from the spoon in a sheet.
Sweat onion, garlic, pepper and tomato in the olive oil until the tomato has collapsed and no raw garlic smell is left.
Stir in the purée and the remaining coconut milk, loosen with cassava cooking water to a soft dropping consistency, then add the prawns and cook only until they turn opaque and curl into a loose C.
Off the heat, stir in the dendê, coriander, spring onion and lime juice, and serve at once.

note: Sweet cassava is the only kind you can simply boil and eat; bitter cassava carries far more cyanogenic glycoside and has to be grated, pressed and toasted into flour before it is safe. The purée thickens by starch alone and sets to a paste as it cools, so keep it looser than you want it. Dendê goes in off the heat: simmered, it turns from fruity and orange to flat and greasy.

ingredients.text: 1.5 kg beef short rib, cut into single bones
1 kg mandioca mansa, peeled, in 6 cm lengths
20 g cheiro-verde (spring onion and parsley), chopped

steps.text: Brown the ribs in the oil in batches until every face is crusted and the pan base is dark brown; a crowded pan steams and the meat stays grey.
Sweat the onion and garlic in the same fat, scraping until the crust dissolves into the onions.
Return the ribs with tomato, bay, chilli, salt and water and simmer covered at a bare tremble until the meat pulls off the bone with no spring, 2 to 3 hours unattended.
Add the cassava, cutting the woody cord out of each piece as you go, and cook uncovered until half the pieces have collapsed and the liquid has thickened around the rest.
Fold in the cheiro-verde and check the salt; the sauce should coat the bones rather than pool around them.

note: The name means the cow got stuck in the mud, and the mud is cassava starch. Half the root should disintegrate to thicken the braise while half stays in pieces, which only happens if the cassava goes in after the meat is already tender. Add it early and it dissolves to glue while the ribs are still tough. Old roots never soften at all, so buy cassava that snaps white and wet.

ingredients.text: 400 g dried carioca beans, simmered until tender and drained hard
200 g farinha de mandioca torrada (toasted cassava meal)

steps.text: Render the bacon from a cold pan until the fat runs clear and the pieces are crisp; lift it out and brown the linguiça in the same fat.
Fry the onion and garlic in that fat until the garlic is pale gold, then scramble the eggs straight into the pan in loose curds.
Fold in the drained beans and the meats and warm through, stirring gently enough to leave the bean skins intact.
Kill the heat, rain in the farinha while tossing, and stop the moment every grain is coated and the mixture is loose and sandy.
Fold through the couve and spring onion off the heat so they stay bright green, then season.

note: Farinha de mandioca is already grated, pressed and toasted, which is exactly how bitter cassava is made safe to eat. Here it is a dry ingredient soaking up rendered fat, not a thickener to be simmered. Add it to a wet pan or over live heat and it swells into a paste that sets like plaster on the plate. Drain the beans hard for the same reason: tropeiro is loose and sandy, never saucy.

ingredients.text: 200 g coarse farinha de mandioca torrada

steps.text: Melt the butter with the dendê over low heat until the fat is uniformly orange and just fluid; never let it smoke.
Sweat the onion and garlic in it until translucent and sweet, with no colour on the garlic.
Beat in the eggs and scramble them into small curds, then rain in the farinha from a height while stirring.
Toast, stirring constantly, until every grain is orange and dry and the pan smells nutty; it should pour rather than clump.
Season, fold in the parsley and take it off the heat while still loose, since it tightens as it cools.

note: Farofa is a fat delivery system: toasted cassava meal is dry and thirsty, and its job is to soak up whatever the rest of the plate leaves behind. The ratio is the whole trick, roughly one part fat to three parts meal by volume. Wetter and it clumps into pellets; drier and it is dusty and catches in the throat. Dendê gives a savoury, almost sweet weight no other fat has, but it turns bitter if it smokes.

flavor.sentence: Leads with aromatics blooming from the first bite, wood-smoke running underneath, lifted green at the very end.

ingredients.text: 400 g couve manteiga or collard greens, thick stems stripped out

steps.text: Stack the leaves ten at a time, roll them into a tight cigar and slice across into 2 mm ribbons; shake them loose and dry them completely.
Warm the oil, butter and garlic together from cold over medium heat until the garlic is pale gold and smells sweet, then lift it out if it threatens to brown.
Raise the heat to maximum, add the couve all at once and toss constantly for 60 to 90 seconds.
Stop while the ribbons are glossy, bright green and still springy, return the garlic and salt off the heat.

note: Two things ruin couve: water and time. Wet leaves drop the pan temperature and steam instead of frying, which turns the chlorophyll olive and washes out the pepperiness; long cooking does the same. So cut the ribbons fine enough to be done in a minute and dry them before they meet the fat. Garlic starts in cold oil and comes out gold, because at full heat it burns before the greens even wilt.

ingredients.text: 600 g chicken thigh on the bone
500 ml of the chicken poaching broth

steps.text: Poach the chicken with the onion and bay until it shreds under a fork; keep the broth and pull the meat into fine threads.
Bring 500 ml of that broth, the milk and the butter to a rolling boil, tip in all the flour at once and beat over the heat until the dough leaves the sides clean and a film sets on the pan base.
Turn the dough out and knead it while it is almost too hot to hold, until it is smooth and elastic with no cracks when you fold it.
Flatten walnut-sized pieces, fill with the shredded chicken bound with cream cheese, garlic and parsley, and pinch each into a teardrop with no open seam and no trapped air.
Roll through beaten egg then breadcrumbs and fry at 175C (350F) until deep gold and audibly crisp, about 4 minutes; drain standing point upwards.

note: This is a scalded dough: boiling broth gelatinises the flour starch before any frying happens, so the shell holds its teardrop and stays tender rather than reading as raw paste. The failures are seams and heat. An open pinch or a trapped air pocket bursts in the fryer and the filling escapes; below 170C (340F) the crumb drinks oil, above 185C (365F) it colours before the middle is hot.

ingredients.text: 40 g pimenta malagueta chillies, stems removed

steps.text: Split the malaguetas lengthways and scrape out as much pith as you want heat removed; the pith holds more of it than the seeds do.
Pound the chillies with the garlic and salt to a rough paste, coarse enough that you can still see flecks of skin.
Stir in the onion, lime juice, vinegar and oil until the salt has dissolved.
Fold in the coriander last and taste: it should be aggressively sour on its own, because it will be met by beans, pork fat and farofa.

note: This is not heat for its own sake; it is the acid that cuts dendê, pork fat and bean starch, which is why the lime is measured and the chilli is not. Malagueta is thin walled and fierce, and most of that lives in the pith, so scrape it if you want the fruit without the burn. Rest it 30 minutes so the raw onion loses its edge, and use it within a day before the coriander blackens.

ingredients.text: 100 g fresh or frozen grated coconut
butter and sugar for the moulds

steps.text: Stir the yolks into the sugar with a spatula until the sugar has dissolved and the mix is smooth; do not whisk, and let no foam build on the surface.
Stir in the melted butter, coconut milk, salt and grated coconut, then rest the mixture until the coconut has hydrated and any bubbles have risen so you can skim them off.
Butter and sugar the moulds heavily, fill to 5 mm below the rim and stand them in a roasting tin; pour boiling water halfway up their sides.
Bake at 160C (320F) until the surface is set and glossy amber and a skewer comes out clean while the centre still trembles, 35 to 45 minutes.
Cool completely in the moulds, run a knife around each one and invert in a single movement.

note: Quindim builds itself in layers as it bakes: the coconut floats, the yolk custard sinks, and the sweet comes out of the mould upside down with a clear golden top over a coconut base. That only happens in a water bath held below about 165C (330F). Direct heat curdles the yolk protein into grains and pushes bubbles through the surface, and any air whisked in on purpose stays as holes in the glass.

steps.text: Slice the shallots across the grain at an even 2 mm; a thick slice is still wet when a thin one has burnt.
Put shallots and cold oil into a wok together and set it over medium heat; bring it only to a lazy, even fizz, never a roar.
Stir every minute or two for 20 to 25 minutes; the loud bubbling of escaping water quietens to a whisper as the shallots go from white to straw.
Lift them out with a spider while they are still pale gold and spread them on a rack in one layer; they darken a full shade off the heat.
Salt the shallots only once they are cold and crisp, and bottle the cooled oil on its own.

note: This is the base of the whole table, and it yields two things that must be kept apart. The oil holds the shallot's soluble aroma; the slices hold the crunch, and crunch only survives dry storage. Left sitting in their own oil they go limp overnight. The other failure is colour: sugars keep browning on residual heat, so shallots pulled at brown finish bitter.

ingredients.text: 800 g pork belly, skin on, in 4 cm pieces
12 g mild dried red chilli powder

steps.text: Blend shallots, garlic and ginger with 50 ml water to a smooth paste with no visible shreds.
Heat the oil until a drop of paste sizzles at once, take the pot off the flame, stir in turmeric and chilli for five seconds so they bloom without scorching, then add the paste.
Fry on medium for 20 to 25 minutes, scraping the base: the paste goes from pale and loose to brick red and thick, pulls away in one mass, and oil weeps out at the edges.
Add pork, ngapi, fish sauce and salt, turn to coat every piece, then pour in water to sit just below the meat and simmer covered until a skewer meets no resistance.
Take the lid off, raise the heat and cook down until the water has gone and a clear red oil floats a finger deep over the meat.

note: See byan means the oil returns, and that is the doneness test, not a clock. While water remains the fat stays dispersed through the sauce; once it boils away the fat separates and rises, carrying the chilli and turmeric with it. Stopping while the sauce is still creamy leaves raw shallot in the mouth, and splashing water back in at the end simply re-emulsifies it and undoes the work. The covered simmer runs about 70 minutes and is not active time.

ingredients.text: 700 g catfish, whole or thick fillet
120 g chickpea flour, toasted in a dry pan
60 g raw rice, toasted dark and ground
300 g banana stem, outer sheaths removed

steps.text: Simmer the catfish with lemongrass, half the ginger and the water for 15 minutes until the flesh flakes off the bone; lift it out, flake it, and keep every drop of the broth.
Slice the banana stem 3 mm thick straight into water sharpened with lime, winding the long threads off your knife as you go, then rub with salt and rinse.
Blend shallots, garlic and the remaining ginger, fry in the oil with turmeric until the paste is brick red and the oil separates, then stir in the ngapi until it smells toasted rather than sharp.
Whisk the chickpea flour and rice powder into 400 ml of cool broth until slack and lump free, then pour it into the simmering pot with the paste, fish and banana stem.
Stir at the base and simmer 25 minutes, until the soup coats a spoon and the chalky taste of raw flour is gone; season with fish sauce.
Ladle over rinsed rice noodles and hand round egg, coriander, lime and chilli at the table.

note: The body is chickpea flour, and it disperses only in cool liquid: tipped into a hot pot the outer starch gelatinises on contact and seals lumps that never break down. Toasted ground rice adds grip without the gluey pull of more flour. Banana stem goes into acidulated water because its cut faces brown within a minute, and the threads must be wound off or they hang together in the bowl. The soup keeps thickening as it stands, so leave it looser than you want it.

ingredients.text: 8 g mild dried red chilli powder

steps.text: Blend shallots, garlic and ginger, then fry in the peanut oil with turmeric and chilli until the paste is brick coloured and oil pools at the sides.
Add the chicken and turn it in the paste until the outsides tighten and go opaque.
Whisk the chickpea flour into the cold stock, pour it in with the fish sauce, and simmer 15 minutes, stirring, until it lightly coats a spoon.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring it back only to a tremble, where a bubble breaks the surface every few seconds; hold it there five minutes and no hotter.
Boil the noodles, drain them hard, ladle the soup over, and finish each bowl with egg, lime, chilli, then the fried shallots and a spoon of their oil last.

note: The thickener is chickpea flour, not the coconut: the starch is what holds the fat in suspension. Boiling after the coconut goes in breaks that suspension and gives a greasy slick over grainy curds, so the pot never rises past a tremble again. Fried shallots and their oil arrive at the table separately for the reason they are made separately: the oil perfumes the broth, the shallots give crunch, and crunch is gone a minute after it meets hot liquid.

ingredients.text: 20 g garlic, sliced paper thin and fried crisp
60 g yellow split peas, soaked and fried crisp
40 g dried broad beans, fried crisp
150 g firm tomato, in thin wedges

steps.text: Taste the laphet first; rinse it briefly in cold water and squeeze it dry only if it is harshly astringent, because rinsing takes the ferment with it.
Loosen the leaves with half the garlic oil and a squeeze of lime until they sit as a glossy dark mound rather than a dry clump.
Heap the crisp peas, beans, peanuts, sesame, fried garlic, dried shrimp, tomato, cabbage and chilli in separate piles around the leaves on a wide plate.
Toss it at the table with the fish sauce and the rest of the oil and lime, and eat it straight away.

note: Laphet is steamed tea leaf pressed under weight and left to sour, and it is eaten as food, caffeine and all, not brewed. Its own acid and tannin are most of the dressing, which is why so little else goes on. Everything around it is texture, and all of it is thirsty: mixed in the kitchen, the fried peas and beans pull moisture out of the leaves and tomato and are soft before the plate lands. Build it in piles, mix it in front of the eater.

ingredients.text: 300 g roselle leaves, stripped from the stems

steps.text: Pull every leaf off its stem; the stems stay woody however long you cook them.
Fry the shallots and garlic in the oil over medium high heat until the edges are gold, then add the chillies and turmeric.
Add the leaves in handfuls with the pan uncovered, tossing as each lot collapses; they drop to a fifth of their volume and turn from red green to deep olive.
Stir in the bamboo shoot, two tablespoons of water and the salt, and cook five minutes more until the liquid has gone and the oil runs clear at the edge of the pan.

note: Roselle brings its own sourness, sharp and clean, straight out of the acid in the leaf, so the dish needs no lime or tamarind; either one makes it taste tinny. Keep the pan uncovered, because a lid traps acidic steam over the leaves and turns them grey brown and slippery inside a minute. Salt goes in at the end for the same reason: early salt draws water out and the leaves stew in it instead of frying.

ingredients.text: 20 g mild dried red chilli powder

steps.text: Grind the dried shrimp in a dry blender to a light floss; stop while it is still fluffy, before it packs into oily pellets.
Fry the garlic in the oil until pale gold and lift it out, then do the shallots the same way; keep the oil in the pan.
Slacken the ngapi in the tamarind water and fry it in that oil for two minutes, until the ammoniac edge is gone and it smells like toasted anchovy.
Add the shrimp floss, chilli and salt and fry, stirring, for 10 to 15 minutes until the floss is rust coloured, dry, and rustles against the spoon instead of clinging to it.
Fold the garlic and shallots back in off the heat, cool it completely, and jar it with the oil standing over the top.

note: It keeps for weeks only because the water has been driven out and the oil seals the surface; leave any damp in the shrimp floss and it moulds within the week. Garlic and shrimp are fried apart and reunited because garlic browns in three minutes and the floss needs fifteen, so cooked together the garlic is bitter carbon long before the shrimp is dry. ingredients.text: 400 g bottle gourd, peeled and cut in 5 mm batons

steps.text: Salt the gourd batons, leave them 10 minutes, then squeeze them firmly; the water they give up would otherwise thin the batter on contact.
Whisk both flours, the turmeric and salt into the ice cold water to the thickness of pouring cream; it should sheet off a spoon leaving a thin, even film.
Heat the oil to 175 C (350 F), the point where a drop of batter sinks, rises within two seconds and fizzes hard.
Coat the gourd and lift out loose tangled clusters rather than single sticks; fry about four minutes, until the loud hiss falls away and they are deep gold.
Drain on a rack, never on paper on a plate, and serve with the tamarind, palm sugar, garlic and chilli stirred together.

note: Rice flour has no gluten, so the crust sets brittle and stays brittle; a wheat batter goes leathery within minutes as trapped steam softens the gluten network. Ice cold batter into 175 C oil sets the shell before the gourd's water can escape into it. The two usual failures are batter left standing until it warms and slackens, and oil below 165 C, which lets the coating drink oil instead of sealing against it.

steps.text: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt, add the yoghurt, water and oil, and knead 8 minutes until the dough is slack and tacky yet leaves the bowl wall clean.
Prove it covered until doubled and domed, then divide into eight balls of about 110 g and rest them until a pressed dent no longer springs back.
Heat a heavy iron pan or an upturned wok, dry, until a flick of water skitters and vanishes rather than sitting and steaming.
Press each ball out to 20 cm with oiled palms, working from the middle outwards and leaving the rim thick; do not reach for a rolling pin.
Slap it onto the dry pan; when the top domes up in big blisters and the underside is spotted brown, turn it for 40 seconds, brush with ghee and stack under a cloth.

note: The blister is steam caught between two skins of gluten, and a rolling pin presses out the gas pockets that let it form, which is why teashop bread is hand pressed and a rolled one bakes flat and hard. The pan has to be hot enough to set the outside before the crumb dries, or you get a pale cracker. Proving is waiting, roughly 90 minutes plus 20 to rest. Eat it with boiled yellow peas, pe byouk, and a scrape of ghee.

steps.text: Dry toast the semolina in a wide pan over medium heat for about 8 minutes, until it smells of biscuit and has gone straw coloured; do not let it brown.
Melt the palm sugar into the coconut milk, water and salt, then pour that onto the semolina off the heat, whisking as you go so no lumps set.
Return it to medium heat and stir without stopping for about 15 minutes, until the mass pulls away from the pan in one lump and a spoon stands up in it.
Slide the pan off the heat, beat in the ghee, and wait until the mixture has stopped steaming before working in the eggs a third at a time.
Spread it 3 cm deep in a greased tin, scatter the poppy seeds, and bake at 190 C (375 F) until the top is mahogany, blistered and firm to a fingertip.

note: Toasting the semolina first breaks its starch down enough that the grains swell less, which is the difference between a cake you can cut in squares and wallpaper paste. The eggs are the risk: beaten into a mass still above about 70 C they set on contact into visible yellow threads, so take the pan off and let it stop steaming first. ingredients.text: 150 g whole brown teff flour, stone milled and unbleached
50 g whole brown teff flour per daily feed
100 g unchlorinated water per daily feed

steps.text: Whisk the teff flour into the warm water in a glass jar until no dry pockets remain; the batter should pour like single cream. Cover loosely and hold at 22 to 26C (72 to 79 F).
Leave it undisturbed until a thin grey liquid stands on the surface and the smell has turned from wet grass to sharp sour, roughly three days.
Pour off the grey liquid and keep it; discard half the batter, stir in 50 g flour and 100 g water, and repeat this every day.
Judge it ready when a fine even foam covers the surface within eight hours of a feed and the sourness has a green apple edge rather than a vinegar sting.
From then on, the clear liquid poured off a finished injera batter is the ersho for the next batch; keep it cold and it stays live for two weeks.

note: Teff bran carries its own lactobacilli and wild yeast, so the culture builds itself; ersho is only the sour liquid saved off a finished batter. Below 20C (68 F) the yeast stalls while acid bacteria keep working and the starter turns vinegary and dead, with no gas left to open the eyes in injera. Hold it at 22 to 26C (72 to 79 F) and feed the day it separates, not later.

ingredients.text: 250 g plain wheat flour, or barley flour for the highland version

steps.text: Work the salt into the flour, add the water in a stream, and knead until the dough stops sticking to the bowl and springs back slowly when pressed.
Roll into two rounds 3 mm thick and cook on a dry ungreased pan over medium heat until the surface dulls and blisters and the underside shows brown freckles, about two minutes a side.
Tear the hot kita into thumbnail pieces while it is still soft; cold bread shatters instead of tearing.
Wipe the pan, melt the niter kibbeh over low heat, and stir in the berbere until it darkens by a shade and smells toasted rather than raw and dusty, around 40 seconds.
Fold the torn bread through the spiced butter until every piece is coated and glossy, then serve at once with honey spooned over and cold ayib alongside.

note: The kita is cooked on a dry pan because fat on the surface stops the crumb drying, and damp bread turns to paste when it hits the butter later. Berbere is mostly chilli flesh, heavy in sugar, and it scorches to bitterness in seconds over a high flame. Bloom it in warm niter kibbeh on the lowest heat: the fat pulls out capsaicin and colour, and the moment it darkens you stop.

ingredients.text: 120 g dried mild red chillies, stems pulled and most seeds shaken out

steps.text: Dry the chillies further in an oven at 60C (140 F) with the door ajar until they snap cleanly rather than bend, about 30 minutes.

Toast the whole spices separately in a dry pan over low heat until each smells nutty and the coriander begins to pop; pull the fenugreek at the first waft of burnt sugar, because it turns bitter two seconds after it turns fragrant.
Grind the toasted spices to a fine powder, then grind the chillies alone and sieve out the coarse skin.
Fold in the ginger, garlic, besobela and salt, then pass the whole blend through the sieve twice so no pocket of one spice survives.
Seal in a jar away from light and leave it to settle before use; it tastes flat on day one and rounded by day three.

note: Berbere is a bulk ingredient, not a seasoning: eight parts chilli flesh to one part aromatic, which is why a wat takes it by the spoonful. That flesh is hygroscopic, so any chilli that still bends holds enough moisture to cake the blend and grow mould within a month. Dry them to a snap first. Fenugreek is the other trap; toast it a shade too far and the bitterness never leaves.

steps.text: Melt the butter over the lowest heat without stirring until it is fully liquid under a raft of white foam, then skim the foam away with a spoon.
Slide in the onion, ginger, garlic and all the spices; they should sink and sit, not sizzle.

Hold the pan at a bare shiver with no bubbles breaking the surface until the milk solids on the base go the colour of hazelnut skin and the fat above turns clear enough to read print through, roughly an hour.
Strain while hot through doubled muslin and do not press the solids; squeezing forces water and sediment back into the fat.
Leave uncovered until set to a grainy pale gold; it keeps three months cold and a month in a cupboard.

note: Butter is roughly 16 percent water and milk protein, and both cap it: it spits, it browns unevenly, and it burns near 150C (300 F). Clarified and spiced, niter kibbeh runs to about 250C (480 F), so it survives the long dry onion cook and a berbere bloom that would blacken butter. It also does work seasoning cannot: korarima, koseret and besobela are fat soluble, so the fat itself carries them into every dish. Let it boil and the solids scorch; the fat goes acrid and no straining fixes it.

ingredients.text: 900 g red onion, chopped fine and even
800 g beef chuck, in 3 cm cubes
30 g garlic, pounded to a paste
20 g ginger, pounded to a paste
300 ml water, plus more as needed
30 ml tej or dry red wine

steps.text: Put the onions alone in a heavy dry pot over medium low heat, no fat and no water, and stir every few minutes as they weep and the liquid steams off.
Keep going until the pile has sunk to a third of its volume, gone tan, and a spoon dragged across the base leaves a dry track that does not fill in; expect 45 minutes and do not rush it.
Only now stir in half the niter kibbeh, then the garlic and ginger, and cook until the raw garlic smell turns sweet.
Add the berbere and the remaining kibbeh and stir constantly over low heat until the paste darkens to brick red and beads of clear red oil rise at the edge, about eight minutes.
Add the beef, the salt and 300 ml water, cover, and hold at the barest simmer, adding water in splashes whenever the surface tightens, until the meat parts under a spoon and the sauce holds a furrow.
Off the heat, stir through the tej and korarima and let it sit 15 minutes before it goes to the mesob.

note: The dry onion cook is the whole technique. With no fat in the pot the onion's own water boils off and its sugars caramelise against the metal instead of frying in oil, and the cell walls collapse into a pulp that becomes the body of the sauce. A wat is thickened by onion, nothing else. Add butter at the start and the onion fries: the shreds stay intact, they never break down, and you finish with thin greasy gravy and floating strings. Total braise runs about 90 minutes beyond the active work.
techniques: Frying the paste until the oil splits
The bare simmer: holding liquid below the boil

ingredients.text: 400 g yellow split peas, rinsed until the water runs clear
80 g niter kibbeh, or 80 ml sunflower oil on fasting days

steps.text: Simmer the split peas in the water, skimming the grey foam for the first ten minutes, until they slump into mush under the back of a spoon, about 45 minutes.
Meanwhile cook the onion dry in a wide pot over low heat, stirring, until it is limp, translucent and halved in volume with no colour anywhere; the moment an edge goes gold you have gone too far.
Stir in the niter kibbeh, garlic, ginger and turmeric and cook until the fat runs clear gold and the turmeric loses its chalky raw smell.
Tip in the peas with their liquid and simmer, stirring up from the base, until the wat mounds on a spoon and then slumps slowly, around 20 minutes.
Salt now, drop in the slit chillies and korarima, and pull it off the heat while it is still loose enough to pour, since it sets firm as it cools.

note: Alicha is the wat with the berbere taken out, so there is no chilli to hide behind. The onions are still cooked dry, but here you are only driving off water: take them past pale gold and the caramel reads as scorch in a dish meant to taste of ginger and turmeric. Curcumin is fat soluble and almost insoluble in water, so the turmeric must go into the hot niter kibbeh, never straight into the pot liquid, or it stays dusty and chalky on the tongue.

ingredients.text: 700 g white cabbage, cut into 3 cm pieces
400 g waxy potato, in 3 cm chunks
300 g carrot, cut on a steep angle
60 g niter kibbeh, or 60 ml sunflower oil on fasting days

steps.text: Cook the onion dry in a wide pot over medium low heat until limp and translucent with no browning at all, about 15 minutes.
Add the niter kibbeh, garlic, ginger and turmeric and stir until the fat runs bright yellow and smells of ginger rather than raw spice.
Turn the carrot and potato through the fat, add the water, cover, and cook until a knife enters the potato with slight resistance still at the centre.
Pile the cabbage on top without stirring, cover again, and let it steam down until it has collapsed and gone translucent at the cut edges.
Only now fold everything together, salt, add the chilli, and cook uncovered until the base is nearly dry and the vegetables wear a yellow glaze instead of sitting in liquid.

note: Cabbage is over 90 percent water and gives all of it up at once. Put it in with the roots and the pot floods, the potato boils and breaks, and you serve grey soup. Stacking it on top instead turns it into the steam source for the carrot and potato beneath, and the delayed fold keeps the potato edges square. The uncovered finish is not optional: as the water leaves, the turmeric fat comes out of suspension and coats the vegetables.
