ingredients.text: 700 g beef rump or sirloin, cut with the grain into strips 1 cm thick and a finger long
200 g red onion, in thick wedges
30 ml tej or dry red wine

steps.text: Pat the strips bone dry and spread them on a rack, uncovered, while the pan heats; surface water is the whole difference between searing and stewing.
Heat a heavy pan or clay dish until a flicked drop of water skitters and vanishes, add half the niter kibbeh, then lay in the beef in one uncrowded layer, working in two batches if you must.
Leave it untouched until the underside releases from the metal by itself and is crusted deep brown, about 90 seconds, turn once, then lift the meat out to a warm plate.
Drop the onion, chillies, garlic, rosemary and tomato into the hot fat and toss until the onion edges char and the wedges soften at the surface but still snap at the core.
Return the beef with the rest of the kibbeh and the tej, toss for 30 seconds off the heat until the fat glosses every strip, then salt and dust with mitmita.

note: Cutting with the grain, not across it, is what makes zilzil: thick strips whose fibres run the length, so the outside can crust while the middle stays pink. Browning needs the surface above about 150C (300 F), and a crowded pan drops below 100C the moment the meat sweats. It then boils in its own juice and comes out grey and tough. Two batches, dry meat, and a pan hot enough to hurt.

flavor.sentence: Leads with a floral thread lifting the aroma, aromatics blooming from the first bite, on a slow, honest burn.

ingredients.text: 2 litres whole milk, not ultra pasteurised

steps.text: Warm the milk to 40C (104 F), whisk in the yoghurt, cover, and hold somewhere warm until it sets into a thick sour clabber that shears cleanly off a spoon, about 24 hours.
Pour the soured milk into a wide pan and bring it up over the lowest heat without stirring; at 50 to 55C (122 to 131 F) soft white flakes will lift away and the whey will go clear and yellow green.
Hold it there, nudging gently, until the curds gather into a single loose mass, then ladle them into a muslin lined sieve and drain until dripping stops.
Rinse briefly under cold water to halt the acid, press lightly, and crumble; fork through the koseret and salt if using.

note: Ayib is heat set, not rennet set. Souring has already pulled the milk down near casein's isoelectric point around pH 4.6, where the protein loses its charge and stops repelling itself; warmth then only nudges those destabilised micelles together. Push past 60C (140 F) or stir hard and the curd contracts, squeezes out water and turns to rubbery grains with half the yield. Kept low and slow it stays in moist flakes, which is what cools a wat loaded with berbere.

ingredients.text: 5 g berbere, for the savoury version

steps.text: Rub the melted niter kibbeh into the flour, salt, sesame and berbere until the mixture looks like damp sand and holds a shape when squeezed.
Stir the honey into the warm water, pour it in, and knead to a dough far stiffer than bread; it should feel like modelling clay and barely tack to the hand.
Rest it covered for 20 minutes, then roll walnut sized lumps into ropes the thickness of a pencil and cut across into pieces the size of a lentil.
Toast in a dry heavy pan over medium low heat, shaking every minute, until they rattle like gravel, are freckled dark brown, and no soft give remains when you crush one, 20 to 25 minutes.
Tip onto a cold tray in a single layer and leave them alone; they finish hardening as they cool, not in the pan.

note: This is a biscuit baked in a frying pan, and the dough is deliberately dry so the pieces dehydrate through rather than steam. Honey is mostly fructose, which browns at a far lower temperature than the flour needs to dry out, so a hot pan lacquers them black outside while the centres stay raw and bendy. Keep it under medium and let colour arrive late. They always feel soft while hot; judge them cold.

Resting dough: the pause that does the work

ingredients.text: 250 g matsoni or full fat natural yoghurt, at room temperature
30 g soft butter, plus 30 g for finishing
600 g imeruli cheese, or 400 g low moisture mozzarella with 200 g feta

steps.text: Whisk the yeast and sugar into the warm water until it loosens and foams, then work it into the flour with the matsoni, egg, salt and soft butter and knead 8 minutes, to a smooth ball that is still slightly tacky at the palm.
Cover and leave until doubled; meanwhile grate the cheese, taste it, and if it stings with salt cover it in cold water for 20 minutes, then wring it in a cloth until no more liquid runs.
Divide dough and cheese in three, flatten each piece of dough to a 22 cm disc, mound the cheese in the centre, gather the edges over it like a purse and pinch the seam shut with no gaps.
Turn seam down, press out with your palms, then roll gently from the middle to a 25 cm round about 1 cm thick, stopping the moment the dough starts to go translucent over the seam.
Bake on a stone or steel preheated to 250C (480F) for 12 to 14 minutes, until the top is blistered brown and the base sounds hollow and dry, then brush with butter and rest 5 minutes before cutting.

note: The dough wants an hour at 24C (75F) to double. Imeruli is a young brined curd, close to half water and aggressively salted, so it weeps and oversalts at the same time. Grate and wring it, or the steam it throws lifts the top crust clear of a raw grey base. Bake on a preheated stone so the base sets before the filling goes fully liquid and finds the seam.
techniques: Proofing: the rise before the oven

ingredients.text: 500 g sulguni cheese, torn into small pieces

steps.text: Bring the salted water to the boil, rain in the coarse grits while stirring, and cook at a bare bubble for 25 minutes, stirring often, until no grain crunches between your teeth.
Rain in the fine maize flour and beat hard for 5 minutes, until the porridge pulls away from the sides of the pan as one mass.
Drop the heat to its lowest setting and add the sulguni in three lots, beating with a flat wooden spoon and folding the mass over on itself.
Keep beating until no lumps of curd remain and the mass stretches into thick ropes when you lift the spoon 30 cm clear of the pan; serve straight away, from the pan.

note: Sulguni is a pasta filata curd, its protein already stretched into aligned strands, so around 60C (140F) it flows into ropes rather than pooling as fat. The maize must be fully cooked before the cheese goes in, because once it is in you cannot raise the heat again: push it and the curd tightens into rubbery knots and weeps oil. Beat without stopping. Elarji sets hard within minutes of leaving the stove.

ingredients.text: 1 chicken, about 1.6 kg, or the same weight of turkey legs

steps.text: Simmer the chicken with the bay in water just to cover, the surface barely trembling, until a leg joint moves freely, about 50 minutes; lift the bird out and keep 1 litre of the broth.
Sweat the onions in the butter over low heat with a little salt until translucent and completely soft with no bite left, then add half the broth and simmer 10 minutes.
Grind the walnuts to a damp paste that beads oil when you squeeze a handful, pound in the garlic, spices and salt, and let it down with the rest of the broth, cool, to the thickness of pouring cream.

Take the onion pan off the heat, wait until it stops bubbling, stir in the walnut cream, then set it over the lowest flame at 80C (175F) for 10 minutes, stirring, never letting a bubble break the surface.
Stir in the vinegar, joint the bird, submerge the pieces in the sauce and cool to room temperature before chilling; serve cold, with the sauce thick enough to sit on the meat.

note: Walnuts are about two thirds oil, locked in cell walls; grinding frees it and the nut's own protein and fibre hold it in the broth as an emulsion. That emulsion carries half this cuisine. It breaks at a boil: the oil rises as a yellow slick and the sauce goes grainy underneath. Hold it below 85C (185F). If it does split, whisk in a ladle of cold broth off the heat.

ingredients.text: 1.4 kg chicken, jointed into 10 pieces, skin on
700 g ripe tomatoes, skinned and chopped

steps.text: Lay the chicken skin down in a dry, wide, heavy pan over medium heat and leave it alone until it sits in a pool of its own fat and the skin is deep brown, about 12 minutes, then turn and colour the second side.

Add the onions and salt to that rendered fat, lower the heat, cover, and cook until they collapse to pale gold with no crunch anywhere, about 15 minutes, scraping the brown film off the base as they give up water.
Only now add the tomatoes, and simmer uncovered until they no longer taste raw and a spoon dragged across the base leaves a track that fills back slowly.
Stir in the garlic, chilli and dried spices, cook 2 minutes, then kill the heat, fold in every herb and cover for 5 minutes so they wilt without going khaki.

note: No oil goes in: the skin renders enough fat to cook 600 g of onion, and that fat is the flavour. The order is the entire dish. Tomato acid locks onion pectin in place, so onions that are still firm when the tomatoes land will stay firm for an hour. Collapse them first. Blue fenugreek and marigold go in near the end; both are heat labile and long boiling reduces them to hay.
techniques: Rendering fat: and cooking in what runs out

ingredients.text: 1.5 kg pork neck, in 5 cm cubes
2 onions, sliced into rings, to serve
100 ml tkemali, or the seeds of 1 pomegranate
dried grapevine prunings, or lump hardwood charcoal

steps.text: Squeeze the sliced onions hard in your fists until they run with juice, then toss them through the pork with the salt and pepper and leave it cold and covered.
Burn the vine wood right down until no flame is left, the embers are coated in grey ash and glow orange when you fan them.
Wipe every scrap of onion off the meat, thread it onto flat skewers with the fat edges all facing the same way, and set them 12 cm above the coals.
Turn every 2 minutes for about 15 minutes, until the outside is mahogany and crusted and juice beading at a cut runs clear rather than pink.
Pile the hot skewers into a covered dish with the raw onion rings for 5 minutes, then strip the meat off and serve with tkemali or pomegranate.

note: Pork neck is the cut because its fat runs through the muscle and bastes from inside; loin dries out long before a crust forms. Onion juice and salt only, no oil and no vinegar: acid denatures the surface protein and the meat cooks mealy. Marinate 3 hours in the cold. Wait for grey embers, because any live flame catches the dripping fat and lacquers the meat in soot.

ingredients.text: 3 large aubergines, about 900 g, sliced lengthways 8 mm thick
15 g salt, for drawing the slices
1 g cayenne or dried red chilli

steps.text: Salt the slices on both sides, stand them in a colander for 30 minutes, then press each one between cloths until it feels limp and the surface is dry.
Fry in 1 cm of oil held at 180C (355F), a few at a time, until deep gold on both faces and slack enough to roll, and drain them on a rack rather than paper so they do not steam soft.

Pound the walnuts with the garlic, salt and dried spices to a coarse damp paste, or pulse them cold in short bursts, then beat in the vinegar and just enough cold water to make it spreadable and glossy.
Fold the chopped coriander through, spread a thick finger of paste down each slice, roll from the narrow end and stand the rolls seam down.
Leave 30 minutes at room temperature for the paste to firm, then scatter with pomegranate seeds.

note: Aubergine flesh is a foam: its air pockets drink oil until the cell walls collapse, and only then does it stop. Fry hot at 180C (355F) and the collapse is quick and the slice takes little; fry cool and it empties the pan and turns to grease. Grind the walnuts cold and briefly. A hot blade shears the oil straight out and leaves a stiff dull putty that water and vinegar will not bring back.

Salting to draw the water out

ingredients.text: 1 kg hard unripe tkemali plums, or underripe greengages or damsons
5 g dried ombalo (pennyroyal), or dried mint
2 to 4 g dried red chilli flakes

steps.text: Simmer the whole plums with the water, covered, until the skins split and the flesh slides off the stones, about 20 minutes; add no sugar at any point.
Push everything through a sieve or food mill, leaving stones and skins behind, and return the puree to the pan.
Reduce over low heat, stirring, until a spoon drawn across the base leaves a channel that closes slowly and the puree mounds rather than runs.
Pound the garlic, herbs, ombalo, ground coriander, chilli and salt to a wet green paste, stir it into the hot puree and take the pan straight off the heat.
Cool completely before judging it: the first taste should make you wince, then settle. Bottle and keep cold.

note: Everything rests on the fruit being hard and green. Unripe plums carry both the malic acid and the pectin; ripening converts them to sugar, so ripe fruit gives a thin sauce that tastes like jam. Never sweeten it. That acidity is also what preserves it, with ombalo, a pennyroyal, as the second preservative. Herbs go in off the heat, or the green turns grey and the scent flattens.

ingredients.text: 800 g beef shin, in 3 cm pieces
60 g tklapi (sour plum leather), or 80 ml tkemali

steps.text: Cover the beef with cold water, bring it up slowly to a bare simmer and skim the grey foam until the surface runs clear, then add the bay and cook until a piece crushes against the side of the pan, about 90 minutes.
Add the onions and rice and simmer 15 minutes, until the grains are soft and starting to blur at the edges.
Tear the tklapi into a ladle of hot broth on its own and whisk until it has completely dissolved, then stir it back into the pan and add more until the soup makes you blink.
Grind the walnuts with the garlic, salt and dried spices to a paste and let it down with another ladle of hot broth to a smooth cream.

Drop the heat until the surface is still, stir the walnut cream in and hold it there 10 minutes without a single bubble, then kill the heat, add the whole handful of coriander and cover for 5 minutes.

note: Kharcho is sour first and thick second. The sour is tklapi, plum puree dried in sheets on a board; whisk it into a ladle of broth by itself, because dropped into the pan it sets into rubbery lumps that never come apart. Add it after the rice has softened, since acid slows starch swelling and rice cooked in a sour broth stays chalky. Walnut cream last, off the boil, or it splits.

ingredients.text: 400 g waxy potatoes, in 3 cm chunks
400 g red and green peppers, in wide strips

steps.text: Fry the potato in the oil over medium heat until the edges are gold and a knife still meets slight resistance in the middle, then lift it out.
Fry the aubergine in the same oil, hot and in one layer, until browned and slumped, then the peppers until their skins blister and go slack.
Return everything to the pan with the onions, add the tomatoes and salt, cover and cook until the tomatoes have collapsed into a sauce and the potato gives completely, about 15 minutes.
Pound the garlic, chilli, blue fenugreek and marigold with a pinch of salt, stir it in with the vinegar and lift the pan off the heat at once.
Fold in the herbs, put the lid back on for 10 minutes, and serve warm or at room temperature rather than straight from the stove.

note: Blue fenugreek and dried marigold are the two spices that make this cuisine sound like itself, and heat wrecks both. Their aroma sits in volatile compounds, and marigold shifts from saffron gold to brown within minutes of boiling, its scent going to old hay. Pound them raw with the garlic and stir them in as the pan leaves the flame. The rule holds across the table: fenugreek, marigold and coriander leaf go in last.

ingredients.text: 2 litres fresh unfermented red grape must, from Saperavi or another dark grape
strong linen thread and a long needle

steps.text: Thread the walnut halves flat face to flat face into strings 25 cm long, knotted at the bottom and with 10 cm of bare thread left at the top.
Boil the must down by about a third, skimming, until it tastes concentrated rather than fresh; this is the badagi.
Slake the flour into 500 ml of cooled badagi until there is not a single lump, then pour it back into the hot pan through a sieve, whisking hard.
Cook this tatara at a low bubble, stirring constantly, for 15 minutes, until it turns glossy, coats the spoon like thin custard and no longer tastes of raw flour.
Dip each string, hang it to drip, and once the surface is dry to a light touch dip again; three or four coats build the sheath.
Hang the strings in a dry, shaded, airy place until the outside is leathery and no longer tacky anywhere.

note: Tatara is grape must thickened with wheat flour, and it fails two ways. Lumps: slake the flour into cool must before it meets the hot pan, never the reverse. Raw flour: it needs a full 15 minutes past thickening or the coating tastes of paste and will not keep. Each coat must dry to the touch before the next, or trapped moisture sours between the layers. Hanging takes two to four weeks, and the white bloom on a finished string is sugar, not mould.
techniques: Skimming: foam, fat and a clear broth

ingredients.text: 250 g floury potato, boiled, riced and cooled
4 garlic cloves, crushed into 100 ml warm salted water
200 g mild semi-hard cheese, coarsely grated

steps.text: Whisk the yeast and sugar into the lukewarm milk and leave until the surface domes and foams.
Work in the riced potato, flour and salt to a soft tacky dough that slaps the bowl but pulls away clean, then cover and leave until doubled and slack.
Divide into eight, flatten each on an oiled palm and stretch from the centre outward until the middle is almost translucent and the rim stays thick.
Slide into 180C (355F) oil and fry until the underside is blistered deep gold, then turn once.
Brush the hot surface with the garlic water, spread with sour cream and cover with cheese.

note: Fried dough drinks oil below about 170C (340F): the crust sets too slowly and the crumb soaks, giving a heavy grey lángos. Above 190C (375F) the outside colours before the middle cooks. The riced potato holds water that flashes to steam and lifts the dough, but only where it is stretched thin; a thick centre steams into a raw core. The rise takes ninety minutes.

ingredients.text: 1.2 kg beef shin or chuck, in 4 cm cubes
200 g ripe tomatoes, peeled and chopped
1 TV paprika (Hungarian white wax pepper), sliced

steps.text: Melt the lard and cook the onion over a low flame, stirring, until it collapses to a soft gold mass with no white edges left.
Pull the pan off the heat, wait until the fat stops sizzling, then stir in the paprika and caraway until the fat runs deep red.
Return it to the heat with the water at once, add the beef, tomato, sliced wax pepper, whole hot peppers and salt.
Cover and hold at a bare shiver, adding water only when the pan threatens to catch, until a cube gives to a fork but still holds its shape.
Uncover and reduce until the sauce is glossy and clinging, thickened by onion alone, then stir in the garlic off the heat.

note: Pörkölt, gulyás and paprikás are three dishes that the rest of the world runs together. Pörkölt is meat braised in onion with almost no added liquid; gulyás is a soup with potato and pinched pasta; paprikás is finished with soured cream. Paprika is about a tenth sugar, and past roughly 140C (285F) those sugars scorch bitter in seconds, so the pan leaves the heat first and the liquid follows at once. Two unhurried hours of simmering follow.

ingredients.text: 1 TV paprika (Hungarian white wax pepper), diced
20 g plain flour, for the tempering
300 g plain flour, for the nokedli

steps.text: Cook the onion in the butter over a low flame until slack and pale gold, add the mushrooms and diced wax pepper, and cook hard until their water has boiled away and the pan squeaks.
Off the heat and off the boil, stir the paprika into the fat, pour in the water at once, season and simmer for ten minutes.
Beat the nokedli flour, eggs, water and salt to a thick sticky batter, rest it, then scrape thin ribbons off a wet board into rolling water and lift them out as they bob up.
Whisk the tempering flour into the sour cream, then beat in three ladles of the hot mushroom liquid one at a time until the mixture is loose and hot to the finger.
Pour the tempered cream back into the pan off the heat, bring it only to a tremble to cook out the flour, and never let it boil.
Toss the drained nokedli in butter and spoon the paprikás over.

note: Sour cream at 20 percent fat curdles when acid and heat reach its casein together: tipped cold into a boiling pan it seizes into white grains floating in thin orange liquid. Two defences work together. Flour whisked into the cream swells and shields the protein, and warming it ladle by ladle means the cream never faces more than a few degrees of change at once. After that, keep the pan below a boil.

flavor.sentence: Leads with richness that coats and comforts, savory depth stacked from the pantry’s bass notes, melting away silken.

ingredients.text: 2 kg whole carp, scaled and gutted, filleted with head, bones and fins kept
carp roe and milt, if present

steps.text: Cut the fillets into thick pieces, salt them and leave them in the cold while the broth is built.
Simmer the head, bones and fins with the onion and water, uncovered, until the onion has gone to pulp and the liquid tastes strongly of fish.
Push the whole lot through a sieve, pressing hard on the solids, then return the red brown broth to the pot and take it just off the boil.
Stir both paprikas and the cherry peppers into the still broth, salt it, and bring it back only to a lazy simmer.
Lower in the fish and the roe and cook without a spoon touching the pot, swirling it by the handles, until the flesh parts from the bone.

note: Two rules govern this kettle. Paprika stirred into liquid at a rolling boil goes dull and bitter, because the pigment oxidises and the sugars catch on the pot floor, so it always goes in off the boil. And once the fish is in, a spoon destroys it: the collagen has only just let go and the flakes hold together by almost nothing, so the pot is swirled by its handles instead of stirred.

flavor.sentence: A quiet dish that lets its main ingredient speak: season well and stand aside.

ingredients.text: 800 g TV paprika (Hungarian white wax peppers), seeded and cut in wide strips
500 g ripe tomatoes, peeled and roughly chopped

steps.text: Cook the onion in the oil over a low flame until glassy and yielding but not coloured.
Take the pan off the heat, stir in the ground paprika until the oil runs red, then set it back and tip in the pepper strips.
Cover and let the peppers sweat in their own moisture, stirring now and then, until they are limp and their skins have gone slack.
Add the tomatoes and salt and cook uncovered until the liquid has reduced to a thick red syrup that clings to the strips rather than pooling.

note: TV paprika is a pale thin-walled wax pepper with little heat and a great deal of water, and it collapses rather than roasts, which is the entire point. Salt it at the start and that water leaves early, so the strips boil to mush long before the tomato reduces; salt goes in with the tomatoes instead. Bell peppers give a flabby sweeter dish and skins that curl off in sheets.

flavor.sentence: A quiet dish that lets its main ingredient speak: season well and stand aside.

ingredients.text: 1 kg pale marrow squash, peeled, seeded and cut in long shreds

steps.text: Toss the shredded marrow with the salt and leave it in a colander until it weeps and slumps to half its bulk, then squeeze it dry by the handful.
Cook the butter and flour together, whisking, until the paste smells of biscuit and is the colour of straw, then take it off the heat and stir the paprika into the hot fat before any liquid.
Whisk the cold water into the off-heat roux, then the sour cream, until the sauce is smooth and free of lumps.
Fold in the squeezed marrow and the dill and simmer until the strands turn translucent and the sauce holds a spoon track.
Finish with the vinegar and sugar, tasting until the sourness sits clearly ahead of the sweetness.

note: Rántás is the Hungarian roux: fat and flour cooked to blond, then paprika stirred in off the heat, while the fat is still hot enough to dissolve its pigment but no longer hot enough to burn its sugars. Pour liquid into a roux still over the flame and the starch gelatinises on contact and seizes into lumps. Off the heat, with cold liquid, the granules scatter before they swell.

ingredients.text: 250 g juhtúró (soft sheep's milk curd), at room temperature
60 g onion, grated to a pulp
5 g caraway seed, toasted and ground

steps.text: Beat the butter on its own until it is pale, light and holds a soft peak.
Rub the paprika and ground caraway into the butter and let it stand until the butter has gone apricot and smells of spice rather than of dust.
Work in the curd a spoonful at a time, then the grated onion, mustard and chives, and salt harder than feels right.
Press into a bowl, cover and hold in the cold for an hour, then bring it back to cool room temperature before serving.

note: Paprika's colour and most of its aroma sit in a fat-soluble oleoresin. Stirred into cheese alone it stays gritty and pale and the spread tastes of raw dust; creamed into soft butter first, the pigment dissolves and the whole bowl turns apricot. Butter below about 18C (65F) will not accept the curd, and the mixture breaks into wet grains that no amount of beating brings back.

ingredients.text: 1.2 kg small ridge cucumbers, firm and unwaxed
2 thick slices of sourdough rye bread

steps.text: Trim both ends of each cucumber and split them lengthways from tip to almost the base, so brine can reach the seed core.
Dissolve the salt in the water, warming it if it will not go, and let it fall to blood heat.
Pack the jar with dill, garlic and cucumbers standing upright, tuck the bread down the sides below the surface and pour the brine over so nothing floats.
Cover the mouth with a plate rather than a lid and stand the jar in full sun until the brine turns cloudy and the cucumbers go from opaque green to olive and translucent.
Lift out the bread, strain the brine and store cucumbers and brine together in the cold.

note: The bread is a starter culture, not a flavouring: its lactobacilli seed the brine and outrun the spoilage yeasts, so two to four days in high summer sun taste clean rather than fizzy and slack. Salt at 3 percent selects for those bacteria. Anything sitting above the brine, bread included, grows white kahm yeast and softens the whole jar, so weight everything under the surface.

flavor.sentence: Leads with fresh herbs arguing happily on top, aromatics blooming from the first bite, fading in warm spice.

ingredients.text: 1.5 kg whole soured cabbage head, leaves separated
700 g coarsely minced pork shoulder, about a quarter fat
200 g tejföl (20 percent sour cream), to serve

steps.text: Sweat half the onion in half the lard until soft, take it off the heat, stir in a third of the paprika and let it go completely cold.
Mix that cold paprika onion into the pork with the raw rice, egg, garlic, caraway, salt and pepper and beat until the mass turns tacky and holds together.
Pare the thick rib from each soured leaf, roll a heaped spoonful of filling into a loose parcel and tuck the ends in so the rice has room to swell.
Spread half the sauerkraut in a heavy pot, lay the parcels and the smoked ribs on it, cover with the rest of the kraut and pour in water until it just shows at the sides.
Cook the remaining onion in the rest of the lard, stir the last paprika in off the heat, pour it over the pot and hold everything at a whisper for two hours without stirring.
Spoon cold sour cream over each portion at the table rather than into the pot.

note: Raw rice is the point: it drinks the sour cabbage liquor as it swells, which is why the parcels are rolled loose. Packed tight they split, and pre-cooked rice gives a pasty filling in a watery pot. Acid slows starch gelatinisation, so kraut-braised rice needs the full two hours at a whisper. The sour cream goes on cold at the table because the pot's acidity would break it on contact.
techniques: The bare simmer: holding liquid below the boil

flavor.sentence: Leads with richness that coats and comforts, wood-smoke running underneath, opening aromatic and staying there.

ingredients.text: 180 g caster sugar, for the sponge
30 g unsalted butter, melted and cooled
180 g caster sugar, for the buttercream
150 g dark chocolate at 60 to 70 percent, melted and cooled
150 g caster sugar, for the caramel
sunflower oil, for the knife and paper

steps.text: Whip the whites to a firm meringue with half the sponge sugar, beat the yolks with the rest until pale and ribboning, then fold the two together with the sifted flour and melted butter without knocking the air out.
Spread the batter as six thin 22 cm discs on lined trays and bake at 200C (390F) until the edges are dry and just tan, then peel each one off hot and cool it flat under a board.

Cook the buttercream sugar and water to 118C (245F), pour it in a thread onto the beating yolks and keep beating until the bowl is no warmer than your hand before working in the soft butter, the chocolate and the salt.
Set the flattest layer on oiled paper, cook the caramel sugar with the lemon juice to a clear mid amber, and pour it over, tilting to a thin even sheet.
The moment the caramel stops running, mark it into twelve wedges with an oiled knife and cut clean through while it still yields.
Stack and fill the other five layers with buttercream, mask the sides and press on the ground walnuts, then prop each caramel wedge on a ridge of buttercream.

note: The caramel lid is the whole difficulty. Sugar much past 180C (355F) turns acrid, and once it cools below roughly 100C (210F) it is glass: a knife then shatters it into shards. So it is scored and cut in the few seconds while it is still plastic, on oiled paper with an oiled blade. The lemon juice inverts some of the sugar and stops the sheet crystallising to a dull opaque slab.

flavor.sentence: Leads with richness that coats and comforts, a sweet edge rounding the corners, settling low and earthy.

ingredients.text: za'atar and boiled eggs, to serve

steps.text: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt, pour in the warm milk and oil, then knead 10 minutes until the dough pulls clean off the bowl and a stretched piece goes translucent before it tears.
Divide into six, roll each to a rope about 40 cm long, join the ends and stretch the ring into a long oval with a hole you can put a fist through.
Whisk the dibs into the warm water, dip each ring so both faces are wet, then press it into the sesame until no dough shows through.
Prove the rings on lined trays until a fingertip dent springs back only halfway and the hole has closed to a slot.
Bake at 230C (450F) for 12 to 14 minutes, until the sesame is toasted brown and the base sounds hollow when tapped.

note: The sesame sticks because dibs is a sugar syrup, not because the dough is wet: the sugar sets tacky at the surface and glues the seeds while they toast. Dip in plain water and the seeds slide off in the oven and scorch on the tray. Open the ring wider than looks right, because proving closes it, and a sealed ka'ak steams from the inside instead of crisping.

flavor.sentence: Leads with toasted, nutty warmth throughout, a sweet edge rounding the corners, ending saline and clean.

ingredients.text: 1 kg full-fat live yoghurt, with no added gum or starch
20 g dried wild thyme leaf (za'atar baladi)
3 g fine salt, for the blend
80 ml green extra virgin olive oil

steps.text: Whisk the sea salt through the yoghurt, tip it into doubled muslin, tie the corners and hang it over a bowl in the fridge until it stops dripping and holds a peak, 12 to 24 hours.
Toast the sesame in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking, until the seeds turn straw gold and begin to skip, then tip them out to cool completely.
Rub the dried thyme between your palms to break the leaf, then stir through the cooled sesame, the sumac and the blend salt; it should smell resinous and sour, not dusty.
Spread the labneh in a shallow bowl, hollow the surface with the back of a spoon, flood the hollow with olive oil and scatter the za'atar over only as it goes to the table.

note: Salt drives the drain: it collapses the casein gel so whey runs, and about 1.2 percent sets labneh firm without tasting seasoned. Yoghurt thickened with gum or starch holds its water and will never drain, so read the tub. Dress at the last moment, because sumac is powdered malic acid; once it meets the oil it wets, dulls and stops tasting sour within minutes.
techniques: Dry-pan toasting: spices, seeds and nuts

ingredients.text: a handful of flat leaf parsley, chopped

steps.text: Drain the soaked chickpeas, rub them with the bicarbonate in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes until they squeak and smell toasted, then cover well with water and bring to a simmer.
Cook, skimming off the loose skins and grey foam, until a chickpea crushes to paste between finger and thumb with no chalky core, 45 to 70 minutes; keep 200 ml of the cooking liquor.
Pound the garlic to a paste with the salt, stir in the lemon juice and leave it 10 minutes, then whisk in the tahini: it will tighten into stiff putty.
Add the iced water a spoonful at a time, whisking hard, until the paste loosens, pales to ivory and falls from the whisk in ribbons; season with the cumin.
Fold two thirds of the warm chickpeas through the sauce, slacken with cooking liquor to a spoonable cream, then spread it out and top with the rest, the olive oil, Aleppo pepper and parsley.

note: Tahini is a fat continuous paste. Adding acid or a trickle of water flips it to a water continuous emulsion, and at the crossover it seizes to putty. That stage is correct, not a failure, so keep whisking and keep adding water until it thins and pales; stop early and you serve cement. The bicarbonate raises the cooking pH so the skins dissolve and the pulses collapse; without it they stay chalky and the dish reads gritty.

steps.text: Simmer the lentils in the water until tender but still holding their shape, about 25 minutes, and leave them sitting in their liquid.

Fry the onions in the olive oil over medium heat, stirring often, through translucent, through gold, and on for another 10 to 15 minutes until they are dark mahogany and smell of caramel rather than raw sugar.
Lift a third of the onions onto paper to drain and crisp, then scrape the rest into the lentils, oil and all, with the salt, cumin and pepper.
Stir in the bulgur, bring back to a simmer, cover and cook on the lowest heat until the grain has drunk the liquid and a spoon dragged across the base leaves a clean channel, about 15 minutes.
Rest off the heat, still covered, for 10 minutes, then fork it loose and pile the reserved onions on top; serve warm or at room temperature.

note: Colour and flavour here are onion, not spice, so the pan has to run past golden into mahogany. Golden onions are only sweet and thin; the darker stage builds the faintly bitter edge that stops the lentils tasting flat. Push on to black and it turns acrid with no way back, so pull the pan the moment the smell shifts from caramel towards coffee. Coarse bulgur, not rice, and it goes in after the lentils are soft because it only needs to swell.

flavor.sentence: Leads with an earthy, grounding base, a sweet edge rounding the corners, ending saline and clean.

ingredients.text: 1 chicken, about 1.6 kg, jointed into six
4 loaves khubz taboon or other thick flatbread

steps.text: Rub the chicken with half the sumac, the allspice, cardamom, salt and 60 ml of the oil, and leave it on the side while the oven comes up to 200C (400F).
Sweat the onions in the remaining oil over low heat with a pinch of salt, covered, until they collapse into a soft pale sludge with no bite left, about 25 minutes; do not let them take colour.
Pull the pan off the heat and stir in the rest of the sumac, so the onions turn purple brown and smell sharp.

Roast the chicken skin side up on a rack for 35 to 40 minutes, until the skin is crisp and the juices at the thigh joint run clear; fry the pine nuts in a little oil to pale gold and lift them out at once.
Spread the sumac onions thickly over the bread, sit the chicken and its roasting juices on top, scatter the pine nuts and squeeze over the lemon.

note: Sumac is the acid in this dish, not a dusting: 40 g sours a kilo of onions the way a lemon would, and the bread underneath exists to drink the oil and the juice. Stir it in off the heat, because prolonged frying turns its tannins bitter and drives off the fruit. The onions are sweated pale and never browned; caramel sweetness fights the sourness instead of carrying it.

flavor.sentence: Leads with acid holding everything up to the light, warm spice humming through the middle, ending saline and clean.

steps.text: Cut the stalk ends flat and core each courgette with a narrow corer, turning and drawing out flesh until the wall is about 5 mm thick and the tube runs almost to the base.
Mix the lamb, rice, allspice, cinnamon and half the salt, then fill each shell two thirds full and no more, because the rice swells and a packed courgette splits along its side.
Stand them upright and snug in a wide pan, cover with water, weight with a plate and simmer 25 minutes until a skewer meets no resistance; save 200 ml of the liquid and drain the rest.

Whisk the yoghurt with the cornflour, egg white and remaining salt in a cold pan, then bring it to a full boil over medium heat, stirring without pause so the surface never stops moving, until it thickens and turns glossy.
Slide in the courgettes with the reserved liquid, simmer 10 minutes uncovered, then pound the garlic with salt, fry it in the samneh with the dried mint until it smells sweet, and pour it over.

note: Yoghurt splits on the stove because its casein has already been acid set and has nothing left holding it in suspension. Cornflour and egg white rebuild that scaffold, but only if the sauce reaches a genuine boil once, stirred without stopping; short of that it grains the moment the cold courgettes go in. Keep the pan uncovered, because condensation dripping back chills the surface locally and curdles it in patches.

ingredients.text: 400 g lean lamb leg, well chilled and twice minced
250 g minced lamb shoulder, for the filling
5 g ground allspice, for the filling

steps.text: Rinse the fine bulgur, squeeze it dry in your fist and leave it to swell for 10 minutes while you make the filling.

Fry the diced onion in the samneh until soft, add the shoulder mince and cook until it loses its raw colour and the fat runs, then stir in the pine nuts, allspice and pomegranate molasses and cool it completely.

Work the lean lamb, grated onion and spices to a smooth paste, blend in the bulgur, then knead with iced water a splash at a time until the dough is tacky, cold and takes a fingerprint without cracking.
With wet hands, open a walnut of dough around one finger into a shell no thicker than a coin, fill it, seal the mouth and taper both ends to a torpedo, smoothing the seam under a wet thumb.
Fry a few at a time at 180C (355F) until deep brown and floating, 4 to 5 minutes, then drain them standing on end so the seams stay dry.

note: Fine bulgur is the binder, not a filler: it hydrates on the meat's own moisture and its starch glues the shell together. That is why the shell meat must be lean and twice minced. Fat in the dough renders in the fryer, steams, and blows the seam open. Iced water keeps the paste below the temperature at which fat smears and turns it greasy and short. Any shell thicker than a coin burns outside before the middle is hot.

flavor.sentence: Leads with warm spice humming through the middle, a sweet edge rounding the corners, closing toasted and warm.

ingredients.text: 800 g flat romano green beans, topped and tailed

steps.text: Sweat the onions in the olive oil over low heat until soft and just colouring at the edges, then add the garlic and cook one minute more, until it smells sweet rather than raw.
Add the beans and turn them in the oil for about 8 minutes, until they lose their squeak and the raw green dulls to olive.

Only now stir in the grated tomato, the paste, the salt, pepper and water, and simmer uncovered until the beans slump when lifted on a spoon and the oil pools clear and red at the edge of the pan, 25 to 35 minutes.
Take off the heat, sharpen with lemon to taste, and let it come down to room temperature before serving; fridge cold flattens both the oil and the tomato.

note: Beans first, tomato second. Acid keeps pectin cross linked, so beans dropped into tomato at the start can simmer an hour and still chew like leather. Soften them in oil until they are already yielding, then acidify. The oil is the cooking medium rather than a dressing, and the dish is done when it splits and the beans sit in a clear pool. Squeaky and bright green is the failure here, not the goal.

flavor.sentence: Leads with a briny, maritime salinity, acid holding everything up to the light, finishing long and savory.

steps.text: Blacken the peppers whole over a flame or under a hot grill until the skin is loose and papery all over, close them in a bowl for 10 minutes, then rub the skin away without rinsing, or the smoke goes down the sink.
Toast the walnuts in a low oven for about 8 minutes, until they smell of butter and the skins craze, then cool them fully; warm walnuts grind to a bitter oily sludge.
Pound or briefly pulse the walnuts, breadcrumbs, garlic, Aleppo pepper, cumin and salt to a coarse rubble, stopping well short of powder.
Add the peppers and pomegranate molasses, work to a paste that still has grain in it, then beat in the olive oil in a slow stream until it turns glossy and holds a ridge.
Rest an hour and taste: it should read sweet, then sour, then a slow warm heat. Correct with molasses or lemon.

note: The breadcrumbs are structural. Peppers are mostly water, and without a starch to hold it the walnut oil and pepper juice separate into a puddle inside the hour. Aleppo pepper is sun dried and salted, so it brings raisin sweetness and a slow heat; cayenne in its place makes the dish sharp and one dimensional. Pomegranate molasses is the acid and also the sugar, so add it last and in stages or it slides into jam.
techniques: Dry-pan toasting: spices, seeds and nuts

ingredients.text: 400 g akkawi cheese, or low-moisture mozzarella
250 g ashta or thick clotted cream

steps.text: If you are using akkawi, cube it and soak in several changes of cold water over about 8 hours, tasting until only a whisper of salt is left, then drain and pat it dry.
Boil the sugar, water and lemon juice until the syrup runs off a spoon in a thread rather than drops, take it off the heat and stir in the orange blossom water; set half aside for serving.

Warm the other half of the syrup in a wide pan over low heat, add the cheese and stir until it melts into long strings, then rain in the semolina and keep stirring until the mass leaves the sides in one glossy sheet.
Tip it onto a syrup wetted surface and knead with a wet palm until smooth and elastic, then press or roll it out to about 3 mm and cut into strips a hand wide.
Pipe a line of ashta down each strip, roll it up, chill briefly, then dress with the reserved syrup, the ground pistachio and the rose water.

note: Cheese is the dough here: heat melts casein into stretchable strands and the semolina starch fixes them into a pliable sheet. Both failures are temperature. Too hot and the curd tightens and squeezes out its fat, leaving greasy rubber that tears instead of rolling; too cool and the semolina stays raw and grits the teeth. Hold the pan low and stop the second it comes together. Akkawi is brined, so desalt it or the sweet turns savoury.

flavor.sentence: Leads with richness that coats and comforts, a floral thread lifting the aroma, closing toasted and warm.

ingredients.text: 15 g plain flour, for the roomal glaze
200 g water, for the roomal glaze

steps.text: Mix the bread flour, 350 g water, yeast, salt and oil to a shaggy mass, rest 20 minutes, then stretch and fold in the bowl every 20 minutes until the dough peels off the sides in one smooth sheet.
Whisk the 15 g plain flour, 200 g water, bicarbonate of soda and sugar in a small pan and simmer, stirring, to the thickness of single cream; cool it completely.
Bulk ferment until the dough is domed and doubled, then tip it out and shape one long oval on parchment without knocking the gas from the edges.
Brush the cooled roomal on thickly, then drag four fingers the length of the loaf to plough deep furrows, and scatter the sesame and nigella into them.
Bake on a stone at 260C (500F) until the furrow ridges are dark amber and the base sounds hollow, 12 to 14 minutes.

note: The roomal is the whole trick. Its gelatinised starch seals the surface so the crust stays glossy and pliable rather than crisping shut, and the bicarbonate raises surface pH so browning runs hard and fast before the crumb dries. Skip it, or brush it on thin and watery, and you get a pale papery loaf whose furrows close up in the oven instead of holding their shape.

flavor.sentence: Leads with toasted, nutty warmth throughout, richness that coats and comforts.

ingredients.text: 60 g fine salt, for the par-boil water
5 g caster sugar, for grinding with the saffron

steps.text: Grind the saffron with the 5 g sugar to a powder and steep it in 60 ml water just off the boil until the liquid is deep orange, about 20 minutes.
Fry the onions in 45 ml of the oil until deep gold, add the turmeric, pepper, chicken, 8 g salt and half the saffron water, cover and cook low until the thigh meat slides off the bone under a spoon.

Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, then boil it in the 3 L of water with the 60 g salt until a grain bends without snapping and a bitten one still shows a chalky core, 5 to 7 minutes; drain at once.
Fold two ladles of drained rice with the yoghurt and a spoonful of saffron water, spread it over the remaining 45 ml oil and half the butter in the pot and press it flat.

Mound the rest of the rice in a cone, drive five holes to the base with a spoon handle, drizzle over 60 ml water, wrap the lid in a tea towel and steam on the lowest heat until the pot smells of toasted crust, 45 to 50 minutes.

Swirl the rinsed barberries with the 20 g sugar in the last of the butter off the heat for under a minute, just until they plump and go glossy red, then scatter them over the rice with the rest of the saffron.

note: Rice takes salt only while it boils, so that water is brined like pasta water; once drained it steams in its own moisture and absorbs nothing further. Drain while the core is still chalky. A grain boiled through has no dry starch left to set into a separate strand and the 45 minute steam turns it to porridge. Bloom the saffron ground, warm and wet: the colour is water soluble and needs twenty minutes to leave the thread.

ingredients.text: 700 g lamb shoulder, cut in 3 cm dice
200 g garlic chives or leek greens
180 g dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight

steps.text: Fry the onions in 45 ml of the oil until deep gold, add the turmeric and the lamb and brown the meat on all faces.

Chop the parsley, coriander and chives very fine and fry them in the remaining oil over medium heat, stirring, until the volume collapses by two thirds and the smell turns dark and nutty, 15 to 20 minutes; stir the fenugreek in only for the final 2 minutes.
Tip the herbs onto the meat, add the drained beans and the water, and pierce each dried lime twice with a skewer before dropping it in.
Simmer with the lid ajar until the lamb yields to a spoon, the beans are creamy and a slick of dark green oil stands on the surface, about 2.5 hours.
Press the limes against the side of the pot to release their juice, then taste and correct salt and sourness.

note: Frying the herbs down is what makes the stew dark and oily rather than grassy; raw herbs give a soup the colour of pond water. ingredients.text: 800 g lamb shoulder, twice minced, about 20 percent fat
0.3 g saffron threads, ground and steeped in 20 ml hot water

steps.text: Grate the onion on the coarse side of a box grater, then wring it in a cloth until no more juice runs and discard every drop of that juice.
Knead the mince with the onion pulp, salt, pepper and turmeric for a full 8 to 10 minutes, until the mass turns tacky and hangs from an upturned palm without falling.
Chill the mixture for an hour, then with wet hands press it onto flat 2.5 cm skewers in an even 2 cm ribbon, pinching ridges every 3 cm.

Grill over hot coals with the skewers raised off the bars, turning every 30 seconds and never letting the kebab hang still, until juice beads on the surface and the ridges are browned, 5 to 6 minutes.
Baste with the saffron melted into the butter in the last turn, grill the tomatoes alongside until their skins split, and dust with sumac.

note: Salt plus hard kneading pulls myosin out of the mince into a sticky sol, and that sol is the only thing gluing meat to metal. Knead until it clings to an upturned palm. Onion juice wrecks the bond, hence the wringing, and below roughly 20 percent fat the ribbon cracks as it sets. Turn every half minute: the protein must firm all the way round before the underside softens and drops the lot into the coals.

ingredients.text: 150 g dried red kidney beans, soaked overnight
150 g garlic chives or spring onion greens, chopped

steps.text: Simmer the drained chickpeas and kidney beans in the water until they crush easily between finger and thumb, adding the lentils for the last 25 minutes.
Fry the onions in half the oil until deep brown and reserve half of them; soften the garlic in the same pan, stir in the turmeric and tip pan and all into the pot.
Add the parsley, spinach, coriander and chives by the bowlful, salt, and simmer until the ash is dark green and a spoon dragged across leaves a track that closes slowly.
Break in the reshteh and cook until soft, stirring often so it cannot settle and catch; its starch is what gives the soup its body.
Lift the remaining oil off the heat, wait fifteen seconds, then stir in the dried mint until it darkens and smells of mint toffee, no longer.
Take the pot off the boil, stir in three quarters of the kashk, then swirl the rest over each bowl with the mint oil and the reserved fried onions.

note: Two things go in off the boil. Kashk is soured, dried whey whose proteins already sit near the point where acid drops them out of suspension, so a rolling boil curdles it into chalky grains and greys the soup. Dried mint has no water in it to buy you time and blackens to something acrid in about five seconds over direct heat, so pull the oil off the flame and let residual heat do the work.

ingredients.text: 400 g ripe tomatoes, skinned and chopped

steps.text: Char the whole aubergines directly on a gas flame or over coals, turning, until the skin is black and blistered everywhere and the body collapses when pressed, 15 to 20 minutes.
Peel them while hot, drain the flesh in a sieve for 10 minutes, then chop it coarsely with a knife.
Soften the garlic in the oil over medium-low heat until pale gold and sweet smelling, never brown, then stir in the turmeric for 20 seconds.

Add the aubergine and fry, pressing and turning, until the water has gone and it sizzles rather than steams; add the tomatoes, salt and pepper and cook until no liquid pools when you draw the spoon through.
Push the mixture aside, break the eggs into the bare pan, let them just set, then fold them through in streaks rather than beating them in.

note: The smoke is the seasoning: charring over a live flame lays phenols onto the flesh through the split skin, which is why an oven-baked aubergine gives you a sweet, flat, entirely different dish. Drain the hot flesh before it hits the pan or its water holds the mixture at boiling point and it stews grey instead of frying. Chop by hand; a blender shears the pectin-rich flesh into glue.

steps.text: Char the aubergines whole over a flame until collapsed, peel them, chop the flesh fine and press it in a colander under a weight until it stops dripping, about an hour.
Bring the vinegar to a boil, then cool it completely before it goes near the herbs.
Chop the mint, tarragon and coriander very fine and mix them with the pressed aubergine, savory, garlic, nigella, golpar, salt and pepper.
Work in enough of the cold vinegar to make a loose, spoonable mash, pack it into a sterilised jar and tap out the air pockets.
Top with a finger of vinegar as a seal, cap, and keep in the dark until the raw vinegar edge has gone and the mash smells of herbs rather than acid.

note: The aubergine must be pressed dry before it meets the vinegar, because its water dilutes the acid and a pickle that drifts above roughly pH 4 grows mould instead of souring. Keep a centimetre of vinegar standing over the surface at all times and push the solids back under after every spoonful; whatever sits proud of the liquid is the part that spoils. It needs six weeks in the dark before it is worth opening.

steps.text: Quarter the tomatoes and scrape out the seed jelly, keeping only the firm walls.
Cut the tomato walls, cucumber and onion into an even 5 mm dice; the uniformity is the dish.

ingredients.text: 1 g saffron threads, ground and steeped in 60 ml hot water

steps.text: Rinse the rice, then simmer it uncovered in the water with the salt, stirring now and then, until the grains have burst and there is no bite left at all, about 50 minutes.
Only now stir in the sugar and butter; the pot will slacken and go soupy before it thickens again over the next 25 minutes.
Add the saffron and its water and cook on until a spoon dragged across the base leaves a track that closes slowly.
Off the heat, stir through the rosewater and the almonds.
Pour into shallow dishes while still loose and leave to cool to room temperature, then pattern the tops with cinnamon and pistachio.

note: Sugar goes in only once the grain has collapsed. In syrup it competes with the starch for water and lifts the temperature at which that starch gelatinises, so rice cooked with sugar from the start stays chalky however long you give it. ingredients.text: 400 g sole or corvina loin, sashimi grade, skinned
120 ml juice of small key limes (limón sutil)
1 ají limo, deveined and cut in fine strips

steps.text: Firm the loin in the freezer for 15 minutes, then read the direction of the muscle fibres and set the knife across them at 45 degrees.
Take each slice in one long pull, 3 mm thick, and lay them flat and just overlapping on a chilled plate; a sawing stroke shreds the fibres and the fish weeps.
Blend the ají amarillo, garlic, kion, salt, ice and half the lime to a loose sauce, then stir in the sillao, the dashi and the rest of the lime; it should sting first and read salty second.
Spoon the cold sauce over the fish at the moment of serving, scatter the ají limo and coriander, and carry it out while the slices are still translucent at the centre.

note: Lime does not marinate, it denatures. Acid unwinds the surface proteins from the outside in, so a 3 mm slice cut across the grain goes opaque in under a minute and stays juicy. Cut with the grain, or let the fish sit in the sauce, and the fibres contract, wring out their water and turn chalky. Sauce it at the pass, never before.

ingredients.text: 800 g yellow waxy potatoes (papa amarilla), unpeeled
4 fresh ají amarillo, halved and deveined

steps.text: Boil the deveined ají for 2 minutes, drain, and repeat twice with fresh water; the flesh should slump and the raw green smell give way to apricot.

Boil the potatoes whole in well salted water until a skewer meets no resistance, about 20 minutes, peel them warm, then cool and slice 1 cm thick.
Blend the cooled ají base with the queso fresco, crackers, evaporated milk and salt in short bursts, to a sauce that ribbons off the spatula and holds its line for a second.
Pour over the potatoes on lettuce, top with egg and olives, and serve at room temperature; fridge cold, the sauce sets stiff and reads only of raw onion.

note: Ají amarillo keeps its heat in the pale placenta and its bitterness in a waxy skin. Devein it and boil it through three changes of water and you keep the fruit and the apricot smell without the burn. The sauce is an oil in water emulsion held by cracker starch and cheese protein: blend it long and friction heat melts the fat out of the cheese, leaving it grainy and greasy. Short bursts, cool ingredients.

Ten minutes in salted ice water leaches out the rest, then drain hard, because carried water dilutes the lime. Dress it within ten minutes of the table: salt pulls water from the shreds and they slump grey and limp.

ingredients.text: 2 cobs choclo, the big kernelled Andean corn
200 g queso fresco, in 1 cm dice
200 g ripe tomato, seeded and diced

steps.text: Boil the choclo in unsalted water until a kernel is chalky tender but still snaps between the teeth, about 25 minutes; salt in the water toughens the skins. Cool, then cut the kernels off.
Blanch the habas 3 minutes, chill them in ice water and pinch each one out of its grey second skin; they should come out bright green and yield with no chalk.
Soak the onion feathers in ice water for 10 minutes, then drain and dry them hard.
Toss everything except the cheese with the vinegar, oil, oregano and salt, then fold the queso fresco through last so the dice stay square.
Rest 5 minutes and taste: the vinegar should sit behind the vegetables, and the rocoto should arrive as heat only after you swallow.

note: Rocoto is Capsicum pubescens, a different species from the ajíes: thick fleshed, apple crisp, with its heat locked in the pale placenta and the black seeds. Strip both and it eats like a sweet pepper. Habas must lose their second skin after blanching or they stay leathery and taste of chalk. Dress it late, because vinegar standing on queso fresco draws it wet and crumbly.

Return the pork with the cumin, cloves, bay and stock, cover, and hold at a bare tremble until the meat gives to the edge of a spoon.
Drain the papa seca, stir it in with the ground peanuts and cook uncovered until the potato is tender and the pot holds the mark of the spoon; loosen with stock if it seizes.

Fry the ají panca in fat over medium heat until the oil runs red: a dry hot pan scorches its sugars and the whole dish turns bitter.

Deglaze with the chicha, scraping the base clean, return the lamb with the grated squash and water to come halfway up, cover, and cook at a shiver for about 90 minutes, until the meat pulls off the bone under a spoon.
Blend the coriander with 150 ml cold water to a bright green puree and keep it cold.

ingredients.text: 600 g cooked long grain rice, a day old and fridge cold
250 g chicken thigh, in 1 cm dice
3 eggs, beaten with a pinch of salt
6 spring onions, whites and greens kept separate
45 ml sillao, light and dark soy mixed
45 ml neutral oil with a high smoke point

steps.text: Break the cold rice apart with wet hands until no grain clings to another; if it smears, it is still too warm to fry.
Take the wok to smoking, oil it and set a thin omelette from the beaten eggs; slide it out, roll it and cut it into ribbons.

Add the rice and toss it against the hot metal until the grains dance loose and a faint scorched smell rises.
Pour the sillao down the hot side of the wok, toss once, then kill the heat and fold in the egg ribbons, the onion greens, the sesame oil and the white pepper.

Pour the sillao down the hot side so it hits bare metal and caramelises rather than pooling into a puddle.

ingredients.text: 1 kg pork belly, skin on, in 3 cm cubes

steps.text: Put the belly, water, salt, garlic, cumin and pepper in a wide heavy pan and simmer uncovered, the meat barely covered.

Turn them once the underside is amber and the skin has blistered glassy, then lift onto a rack; they should sound hollow when knocked together.
Fry the camote slices in a little of the rendered fat until the edges caramelise and the centre gives to a knife.

ingredients.text: 500 g maíz morado, whole purple corn cobs

steps.text: Snap the cobs in half and put them in the pot with the water, pineapple peel, quince, cinnamon and cloves.

steps.text: Cook the two milks together in a heavy pan over medium heat, scraping the whole base with a flat spatula, until the mixture is the colour of wet sand and a track drawn across the pan stays open for a beat.

Off the heat, whisk a ladle of the hot manjar into the yolks with the vanilla, return it all to the pan and stir over low heat for 2 minutes until it coats the spatula thickly; never let it boil or the yolks curdle into threads.
Pour into glasses and chill until cold and set.
Boil the port and sugar without stirring to 118C (244F), the point where a drop pressed in cold water rolls into a soft ball.
Whip the whites with the salt to soft peaks, pour the syrup in a thin thread down the side of the bowl and beat until the meringue is glossy, holds a stiff hook and the bowl is only blood warm.
Spoon it over the cold manjar and dust with cinnamon.

note: Manjar blanco is lactose and milk protein browning in a shrinking amount of water, so the pan base runs far hotter than the bulk and scorches the moment you stop scraping. Use a flat spatula, edge to edge. The port syrup must reach 118C (244F): that concentration cooks the whites and sets the foam. Below 115C (239F) the meringue weeps and slides off the manjar in the glass.

ingredients.text: 400 g short grain white rice, washed until the water runs clear

steps.text: Bring the rice and water to a boil in a heavy pan, cover, and cook on the lowest heat until no free water remains and the grains have burst open.
Pour in the thick coconut milk with the salt and stir steadily over low heat; the mass loosens first, then begins to thicken again.

steps.text: Blend the cooked rice with 150 ml of the warm thin coconut milk to a smooth cream, then whisk it into the rice flour with the sugar, yeast and remaining thin milk until lump free and the consistency of single cream.
Cover and leave in a warm place until the surface domes, carries fine bubbles all over, and smells faintly of beer.
Stir in the thick coconut milk and salt; the batter should now coat a spoon thinly and run off it in a sheet.
Heat a hopper pan or small deep wok over medium heat, wipe with coconut oil, pour in a small ladleful and immediately swirl so batter climbs the walls in a thin film.

note: Yeast gas gives the lace; the swirl gives the shape. Batter at single cream consistency climbs the hot bowl as a film that dries to a crisp rim, while the pool at the base steams soft under the lid. Too thick and it slides back into a pancake. Ferment 8 to 10 hours at warm room temperature; past about twelve it sours and the walls slump.

ingredients.text: 30 ml water, plus 15 ml held back to slacken

steps.text: Set a stainless bowl over a pan of water held at 70C (158F), a bare shiver with no bubbles breaking the surface, and check that the bowl base sits clear of the water.

Whisk the yolks with 30 ml water off the heat until frothy, then set the bowl over the bath and whisk steadily until the sabayon triples in volume, holds a ribbon on the surface for two seconds and reads 65C (149F).
Lift the bowl off the heat and add the clarified butter in a thread no thicker than a pencil lead for the first 50 g, whisking until each addition disappears and the sauce climbs the wires.
Pour the rest faster once the emulsion is set, stopping to slacken with the held 15 ml of water whenever the sauce stiffens to mayonnaise thickness instead of falling off the whisk in a ribbon.
Season with lemon, salt, cayenne and white pepper, then hold covered at 55C (131F) and no hotter; a metal pan left on a warm hob will take it past 70C (158F) unnoticed.

note: Yolk proteins begin to thicken near 65C (149F) and set solid by 72C (162F), so the sabayon lives in a seven degree window. Split one is heat: the protein coagulates into grains and drops the fat it was holding. Split two is crowding: butter poured faster than the water phase can carry it, past roughly four parts fat to one of water, and the droplets merge into a slick. Water is the cure for both.

ingredients.text: 10 g tarragon stalks, plus 8 g leaves chopped

steps.text: Simmer the vinegar, wine, shallot, tarragon stalks and cracked peppercorns until reduced to 45 ml, thick enough that a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a track that fills back slowly.

Whisk the yolks into the cooled reduction over water held at 70C (158F) until the sabayon holds a figure of eight on its own surface and reads 65C (149F).
Off the heat, thread in the clarified butter, drop by drop for the first 50 g and then in a steady stream, until the sauce holds the shape a spoon cuts into it.
Fold in the chopped tarragon and chervil off the heat and hold at 55C (131F); herbs added any earlier lose their anise to the steam.

note: The reduction is not only flavour, it is the water phase. Diluting each yolk with 15 ml of liquid lifts its setting point several degrees, and that margin is what keeps a béarnaise from scrambling where neat yolk would. Reduce past 45 ml and the buffer goes with it; the sauce then grains first at the bowl edge, where the metal runs hottest and the film is thinnest.

ingredients.text: 250 g unsalted butter at 82% fat, cut into 20 g cubes and kept refrigerator cold
30 ml double cream at 48% fat, optional insurance

steps.text: Reduce the wine, vinegar and shallot in a heavy pan until only 30 ml of syrupy liquid is left and the shallot sits in it like wet jam.
Add the cream if you are using it and bring to a bare simmer; casein tolerates more heat than butter's own emulsifiers and buys you a wider working band.

Drop the heat to its lowest setting and whisk in the cold butter two cubes at a time, adding the next pair only when the last has vanished and the sauce reads opaque and glossy rather than yellow and clear.
Keep a probe in the pan and hold the sauce between 55C and 65C (131F and 149F), lifting it off the heat whenever it climbs; by 80C (176F) it will have broken to oil.
Season, strain if you want it smooth, and hold in a water bath at 52C (126F); it cannot be reboiled, so make it inside the hour you plan to serve.

note: Butter is already an emulsion: roughly 82% fat, 16% water, 2% milk solids, and it is those solids and their phospholipids that hold the sauce together. Cold butter enters as part crystalline fat and is sheared into fine droplets before it melts. Warm butter arrives as free oil and coalesces on contact. Boil it and the water phase evaporates, leaving more fat than the solids can coat.

Add the rest cube by cube, never letting the pan exceed 88C (190F) on a probe; past 90C (194F) the water boils away and the fat separates within seconds.
Season and hold between 82C and 88C (180F and 190F) for poaching or for finishing vegetables, whisking once if the edge starts to look clear.

note: The 60 ml of water is the seed of a continuous water phase; without it butter simply melts, its own 16% water flashes off, and fat separates from browning solids. Held between 82C and 88C (180F and 190F) the emulsion is stable enough to poach in. Above 90C (194F) it breaks. Chilled it sets solid, and comes back only if rewarmed slowly with a whisk, never over a fierce flame.

ingredients.text: 400 g chicken thighs or breasts, to build the fond

Pour in the stock and reduce by half to roughly 90 ml, until it coats the spatula and a drip hangs for a moment before falling.

ingredients.text: 500 ml brown veal stock, gelatine rich

ingredients.text: 240 g broken sauce: hollandaise, beurre blanc or mayonnaise
15 ml cold water, plus 15 ml boiling
ice and cold water for a bath

steps.text: Diagnose before you touch it: grainy specks in a thin liquid means the yolk cooked, a clear oil layer over sludge means the emulsion was overloaded, a stiff dull paste means it only got cold.
For a cold seize, stand the pan in water at 45C (113F) and whisk until it flows again; adding anything here just dilutes a sauce that was never broken.

For an overloaded emulsion, put 15 ml of boiling water in a clean warm bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it a teaspoon at a time until it takes, then in a thread; the fresh water phase gives the droplets somewhere to sit.
For a cooked yolk, strain out the specks, beat a fresh yolk with 15 ml of cold water off the heat, and whisk the strained sauce into that drop by drop; the grains themselves never come back.
For a broken butter sauce, drop the pan into the ice bath until it is below 60C (140F), then whisk 30 ml of cream or a 20 g cube of cold butter in a clean pan and rebuild the broken sauce into it.

note: Every rescue is the same move: build a fresh continuous water phase and feed the broken sauce into it slowly enough that the fat redisperses as droplets rather than pooling. Heat damage is the exception, because coagulated protein cannot be uncoagulated; strain the grains out and accept a thinner sauce. Work below 60C (140F) throughout or you will break the rescue too.

Taste the acid before you set the ratio. Mustard is the stabiliser; its mucilage coats the oil droplets and keeps them from touching. Pour the oil in a thread, because oil dumped in cannot be sheared fine enough and the sauce slicks instead of thickening.

ingredients.text: 15 g water, plus more to let the sauce down
300 g neutral oil such as grapeseed, 150 g per yolk

steps.text: Whisk the yolks, mustard, salt and vinegar in a bowl seated on a damp cloth for 30 seconds, until the base is smooth, glossy and pale enough to show clean whisk tracks.
Add the oil drop by drop for the first 50 g, until the base thickens and turns matte; the emulsion has to be seeded before it can be fed.
Pour the rest in a slow thread, whisking each addition out before the next, until the mayonnaise stands in a soft peak and a spoon drawn through leaves a channel that does not close.
Whenever it climbs the whisk and starts to look stiff and greasy, let it down with 5 g of water at a time until it slackens back to a glossy ribbon, then carry on with the oil.
To rescue a split batch, put 15 g of water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl, whisk in one spoonful of the broken sauce until it thickens and grips, then feed the remainder back in a thread.

note: Yolk lecithin and lipoproteins crowd the oil and water boundary; one yolk will hold about 200 g of oil before the surfactant runs out. Splitting is rarely too much oil, it is too much at once: the droplets pack past roughly 74 percent by volume and coalesce back into a slick. That is also why water is the cure. Adding it rebuilds the continuous phase the droplets are suspended in.

ingredients.text: 200 g tender leaves: butterhead, lamb's lettuce, a little frisee for structure
25 g vinaigrette, about 12 g per 100 g of leaves
5 g chervil and chive, torn rather than cut

steps.text: Wash the leaves in a deep sink of cold water, lifting them out of the grit rather than pouring the water off them, then spin dry in three light loads until a leaf pressed to your palm leaves no damp print.
Hold the dry leaves in a covered box at 4C (39F) until service; a cold turgid leaf stays crisp several minutes longer once the dressing is on it.

At the moment of serving, tip the leaves into a bowl twice their volume, spoon the vinaigrette down the inside wall, and turn with open hands 8 to 10 times until every leaf carries a shine and nothing pools at the base.
Finish with flaky salt and pepper on the plate, scatter the herbs and send it; from here you have about three minutes before the leaves slump.

note: Salt and acid pull water out of the leaf cells by osmosis, so a dressed salad loses turgor within about three minutes and ends up sitting in a puddle of its own sap. Dress at the pass, 12 to 15 g of vinaigrette per 100 g of leaves, and no earlier. Dry the leaves first: oil will not wet a film of water, so on damp leaves the dressing beads, slides off and collects in the bottom of the bowl.

ingredients.text: 400 g new potatoes, matched for size
4 eggs, straight from the fridge at 4C (39F)
80 g tender leaves, butterhead or little gem
30 g shallot, sliced into fine rings
10 g salt per litre for the potato water, 1 percent
20 g salt per litre for the bean water, 2 percent

steps.text: Start the potatoes in cold 1 percent salted water, bring to a bare tremble and cook 18 to 22 minutes, until a knife slides to the centre and withdraws with no drag.
Drain, halve, and dress with a third of the vinaigrette while they read about 55C (131F) to the finger; warm swollen starch drinks the dressing, and a cold potato sheds it.
Boil the beans in 2 percent water for 3 minutes, until they bend without snapping, then plunge into iced water and lift them out the instant they are cold, before the green slides toward olive.
Lower the fridge-cold eggs into rolling water for 6 minutes 30 seconds, chill 3 minutes in ice, peel and halve; the yolk should be set at the rim and jammy at the centre.

Season and dress each element on its own, then build from the base up: potatoes, beans, shallot and capers, the leaves turned last in the remaining vinaigrette, eggs on top with flaky salt on the cut yolk.

note: Composed means every element is cooked, seasoned and dressed alone, then assembled, so nothing is diluted or wilted by its neighbour. The one time-critical step is the potato: dress it at about 55C (131F), because the swollen starch matrix is still open and absorbs vinaigrette, while a cooled potato has retrograded and simply sheds it onto the plate.

ingredients.text: 600 g pork shoulder, diced and chilled to 2C (36F)
18 g fine salt, 1.8 percent of the 1 kg forcemeat
2.5 g curing salt at 6.25 percent sodium nitrite, 0.25 percent, optional for colour
10 g garlic, pounded to a paste
60 g shallot, sweated in butter and cooled
150 g caul fat, soaked and rinsed

steps.text: Toss the diced shoulder, back fat and liver with the salts, spices, garlic, shallot, brandy and wine, and cure covered at 2C (36F) for 12 hours, until the surfaces have gone matte and tacky and the meat feels sticky between the fingers.

Grind the shoulder through an 8 mm plate and the fat and liver through 4 mm, holding everything under 4C (39F); if the fat begins to look shiny and smeared on the plate, stop and return the lot to the freezer for 20 minutes.
Beat in the egg by hand for 45 seconds, until the forcemeat pulls together and a spoonful pressed to the bowl holds a standing ridge, then fry a teaspoon and taste for salt before it is committed.
Line the mould with caul fat, pack in three layers, knocking the mould hard on the bench after each so the air pockets close, lay on bay and thyme and fold the caul over the top.
Bake at 150C (302F) in a bain-marie held at 80C (176F) until the core reads 68C (154F), around 75 minutes, when the juices at the edge run clear amber rather than pink.
Press at once under a board and about 1 kg of weight, cool to room temperature, then chill 48 hours; serve at 12C (54F), never fridge-cold, or the fat eats like wax.

note: Fat is the whole argument. Below 25 percent the forcemeat eats dry and grainy; above 40 percent it renders out and the slice is greasy. This mix runs near 35 percent. Keep every part under 4C (39F) through grinding, because warm fat smears and then breaks out as a cap in the oven. Press under about 1 kg while it cools, to close the voids left by shrinkage; heavier than that and you squeeze the fat straight back out.

ingredients.text: 400 g chicken livers, trimmed of sinew and any green stain
13 g fine salt, 1.2 percent of the total mix
1.5 g curing salt at 6.25 percent sodium nitrite, optional for a pink set
100 g clarified butter, for the seal

steps.text: Soak the trimmed livers in the milk at 4C (39F) for 6 hours, then drain and pat dry; the milk draws out blood that otherwise reads metallic and sets a dull grey.
Reduce the port, madeira, shallot, garlic and thyme to 60 g, a loose syrup that leaves a clear trail on the pan base, then strain and cool.
Blend the livers, eggs, reduction and salts to a smooth liquid, pass through a fine chinois pressing with a ladle, and warm the puree over a bain-marie to 50C (122F).
With the blender running, pour in butter melted to 55C (131F) in a steady thread, until the mix is glossy and pours like double cream; stay inside 45C (113F) to 65C (149F) throughout.
Pour into a terrine, cover, and bake at 100C (212F) in a bain-marie of 80C (176F) water to a core of 63C (145F), about 45 minutes, when a tap on the mould no longer sends a ripple across the surface.
Chill overnight, then flood the top with clarified butter at 40C (104F) to a depth of 4 mm and set.

note: This is a butterfat in water emulsion and it lives in a narrow band. Below 45C (113F) the butterfat crystallises and the mix goes grainy; above 65C (149F) the egg sets in the blender jug and the emulsion splits. Bake to a core of 63C (145F): past 70C (158F) the egg proteins contract and squeeze out water, and the parfait weeps in the tray. The butter seal is not decoration; without it the surface oxidises grey inside a day.

ingredients.text: 1 kg salmon fillet, skin on and pin-boned, previously frozen at -20C (-4F) for 7 days
30 g fine sea salt, 3 percent of the fillet weight
2 g coriander seed, toasted and cracked

steps.text: Weigh the pin-boned fillet, then weigh the cure to it: salt at 3 percent, sugar at 2 percent, mixed with the pepper and coriander.
Rub the cure over the flesh side, working the thin tail end last and lightest, then press the dill on in a thick blanket.
Seal tight in a bag or double wrap with no air pocket, sit it in a tray under a 500 g weight, and cure at 3C (37F) for 36 to 48 hours, turning it every 12 hours in the brine it throws.
Unwrap, scrape off the dill and pat dry; the flesh should have darkened to deep coral, feel springy under the thumb and no longer hold a dent.
Slice on a shallow angle almost parallel to the board, in sheets thin enough to read a knife blade through, leaving the grey line against the skin behind.

note: Dosing the cure as a percentage of the fish removes the guesswork. Sealed with 3 percent salt and 2 percent sugar there is nowhere for the salt to go but into the flesh, so it equilibrates at 3 percent and cannot over-salt however long it sits. Burying a side in loose salt is a timing gamble by comparison. The sugar is not there to sweeten; it offsets the salt and holds water, so the slices stay supple rather than leathery.
