ingredients.text: 1 whole sea trout, 1.8 kg, gutted and scaled
28 g fine sea salt, 3.5 percent of the roughly 800 g of trimmed fillet
2 g fennel seed, toasted and ground

steps.text: Wipe the scaled fish dry, cut down behind the pectoral fin to the backbone, then turn the blade flat and run it head to tail along the spine in long strokes, letting the flex of the blade ride the bones, until the fillet lifts away and the frame is left clean and pearl white.
Repeat on the second side, trim the belly line and the thin tail, and weigh what you have: a round fish yields about 45 percent of its whole weight, so expect around 800 g.
Run a fingertip down the centre line to find the pin bones and pull each one toward the head with pliers, following the angle it sits at, so the flesh closes behind it rather than tearing.
Mix the cure, weigh it to the fillet at 3.5 percent salt, and spread it evenly on the flesh side only; leave 40 minutes at 4C (39F), by which time beads of liquid stand on the surface.
Rinse in iced water, pat dry, and rest uncovered on a rack at 4C (39F) for 4 hours, until the surface is tacky to a fingertip and dulled to a matte sheen.

note: Weigh the fillet, never the fish: a round fish gives up only about 45 percent of its whole weight, so cure dosed to the live weight lands roughly twice as salty as intended. At 3.5 percent for 40 minutes the salt only reaches the outer few millimetres, firming surface protein without curing through. The 4 hour dry forms a pellicle of dissolved protein, and that skin is what lets the flesh slice cleanly instead of tearing.

ingredients.text: 200 g rice or white wine vinegar, 5 percent acidity
150 g cucumber, deseeded and cut into 5 mm batons
100 g fennel, sliced 2 mm on a mandoline
2 strips lemon peel, pith scraped away

steps.text: Bring the vinegar, water, sugar, salt, seeds, bay and lemon peel to 90C (194F) and hold 2 minutes, until the brine runs clear and no grit remains on the pan base, then draw it off the heat.
Pack the carrot and fennel into a jar and pour the brine over at 80C (176F); the heat opens the firmer roots and drives diffusion, and the edges will go translucent within a minute.

Cool the remaining brine to 55C (131F) before pouring it over the cucumber and radish, and hold them there for 20 minutes; at that temperature their pectin methylesterase cross-links the cell walls and sets the crunch.
Cool everything uncovered to room temperature, then hold at 4C (39F) for at least 4 hours before service; a baton is ready when it snaps cleanly and tastes seasoned rather than raw.

note: Plate pickles season a dish, they do not preserve it. This brine settles near 1.7 percent acetic acid, well short of the level a shelf-stable jar needs, so it lives in the fridge and is finished within ten days. Texture is decided by pouring temperature: hold cucumber and radish at 55C (131F) and their pectin firms, but pour brine on at a boil and the cell walls collapse to slush in the jar.

ingredients.text: 20 g salt per litre of blanching water, 2 percent

steps.text: Blanch all the greens together in the 2 percent water at a hard rolling boil for 20 seconds, until they go slack and flare to a bright emerald.
Lift them straight into iced water and pull them out the moment they are cold; left to soak, the flavour washes into the bath.
Squeeze the greens in a cloth to a tight dry ball of about 25 g, then blend to a fine puree with the lemon juice, scraping down twice, until no fibre shows on the back of a spoon.
Fold the puree into the mayonnaise a third at a time, checking the body as you go; it should still hold a soft peak. Season with white pepper and serve within two hours.

note: Twenty seconds in boiling water denatures the chlorophyllase that would brown the herbs, and the ice bath stops the clock. Even so, the acid in the mayonnaise slowly strips magnesium from the chlorophyll and turns it olive, so build this within two hours of service. Squeeze the greens hard: more than about 20 g of free water per 250 g of mayonnaise thins a spoonable sauce into a pouring dressing.

ingredients.text: 300 g 00 flour, soft wheat, W180 to W220 (100%)
10 g salt per litre of cooking water

steps.text: Mound the flour, crater it, and break the whole eggs and yolks into the well with the salt; draw flour in from the inner wall with a fork until the paste is too stiff to stir and drags on the tines.
Knead 10 minutes on an unfloured board, pushing with the heel and folding back, until the surface turns from ragged to satin and a pressed thumbprint fills back slowly instead of snapping shut.
Wrap airtight and rest 45 minutes at room temperature; it is ready when a pinched corner pulls to twice its length before it parts.

Roll from the centre outward with a long pin, giving the sheet a quarter turn each pass and wrapping the far edge around the pin to stretch rather than press, until it is 0.6 mm and the grain of the board reads through it.
Cut, then boil 90 seconds in water at 100C (212F) salted at 10 g per litre; this is the only seasoning the pasta itself will ever take.

note: Yolk is roughly half water, half fat and protein, and the fat coats gluten strands and shortens them, which is why a yolk-rich sheet rolls thin and stays tender. But yolks bring little water: 218 g egg to 300 g flour sits near 45% hydration, and below that the sheet cracks at the edges as you roll. Cracking means dry, not underkneaded. Rest the full 45 minutes so water reaches the starch.

ingredients.text: 500 g semola rimacinata di grano duro (100%)

steps.text: Dissolve the salt in the warm water, pour it over the semola while turning with one hand, and keep turning until no dry grain is left and the mass holds as a coarse, pebbled rubble.
Knead 10 minutes, driving the heel forward and folding back, until the surface stops tearing and takes a dull sheen; the ball should feel as firm as stiff modelling clay.
Wrap and rest 30 minutes at room temperature, then cut the ball in half and read the cut face: one even yellow, with no chalky white core.

Roll ropes and drag or press them into cavatelli, trofie or busiate on a board dusted with semola only, dry 30 minutes on a semola tray, and boil 6 to 8 minutes at 100C (212F) salted at 10 g per litre.

For a bronze die extruder drop the water to 150 g (30%), so the mix stays a damp sand that clumps only when squeezed in the fist; anything wetter binds the auger and the strands weld together as they leave the die.

note: Durum is milled hard and coarse, so its particles drink slowly. The dough can look smooth while the granule cores are still dry, and that chalky core dissolves in the pot and the shape falls apart. Warm water at 45C (113F) and a 30 minute rest are the fix, and the test is a cut face of one even colour. No egg here, so all the chew comes from durum protein.

80 g hard aged grating cheese, finely grated
1 egg yolk, 18 g, for the filling

steps.text: Make and rest the egg dough as for sfoglia, then beat the drained ricotta with the cheese, yolk, salt and nutmeg until it is stiff enough to hold a piped ridge without slumping.
Roll one sheet to 0.8 mm and work fast; a sheet dried past tacky will not weld, and the parcels open in the pot.
Pipe 8 g mounds at 4 cm centres, drape the second sheet over, and press outward from each mound with the sides of both hands, chasing every pocket of air to the edge before the border goes shut.
Cut with a wheel, pinch each border once more between finger and thumb, and set the parcels on semola, never on flour.
Cook at a bare simmer, 90C to 95C (194F to 203F), for 3 minutes; a rolling boil batters the seams open.

note: Two things burst a raviolo. Trapped air expands as it heats and splits the weakest seam, and a wet filling steams and does the same. So the ricotta is drained overnight and bound with a yolk that sets near 65C (149F), and the air is chased outward before the border closes. Seal with dry hands on a still tacky sheet: brushed water makes a slippery layer, not a weld.

ingredients.text: 1.4 kg floury baking potatoes, matched in size, unpeeled and unpricked
200 g 00 flour, 20% of the riced flesh

steps.text: Bake the potatoes on the bare oven rack at 200C (392F) for 60 to 75 minutes, until a skewer meets no resistance at the centre and the skins have gone papery.
Split them the moment they come out, rice the steaming flesh in a thin layer onto a cool board, weigh it, and leave 5 minutes until the surface looks dry and floury rather than glossy.
Scatter the flour, salt and nutmeg over, add the yolks, cut everything together with a scraper, then press only until there are no dry patches left; stop there.
Roll finger thick ropes, cut 2 cm pillows, and press each one down a gnocchi board or fork tines with a single light thumb stroke to leave ridges on one face and a hollow on the other.
Test one in water at a bare simmer, 90C (194F), salted at 10 g per litre: it should rise in 60 to 90 seconds and hold its edges. Give the rest 20 seconds past the rise.

note: A boiled potato takes on water, and every extra gram of water demands another gram of flour, and flour is exactly what turns gnocchi rubbery. Baking drives moisture off, so 20% flour is enough. Rice while steaming hot: as potato cools its amylose retrogrades into crystals that will not bind, you compensate with more flour, and you get bullets. Work it only until it coheres.

ingredients.text: 250 g plain wheat flour, 10 to 11% protein (100%)

steps.text: Whisk the eggs, milk, salt and nutmeg, beat in the flour with a wooden spoon, and keep beating hard for 4 to 5 minutes until the batter blisters and falls from the lifted spoon in one slow unbroken ribbon.
Cover and rest 20 minutes so the gluten relaxes and the batter drops off the board cleanly instead of clinging in tails.
Bring a wide pan to 100C (212F) salted at 10 g per litre, hold it at a lazy boil, and press or scrape the batter through in three batches so the water never falls off temperature.
Lift each batch 30 seconds after it surfaces, about 90 seconds in all, into iced water if you are frying them later, or straight into foaming butter if you are not.

note: Spätzle is the one pasta you want at roughly 90% hydration with the gluten fully built, and you cannot knead a batter, so you beat it. The strands have to be strong enough to survive the fall through the press. Underbeaten batter shreds into ragged crumbs. If the ribbon breaks as it leaves the spoon, beat two minutes more; if it will not drop at all, thin with 10 g milk and no more.

ingredients.text: 500 g strong bread flour, 12 to 13% protein (100%)

steps.text: Stir the salt into the water, rub it through the flour with your fingertips until the bowl holds only damp crumbs, squeeze those crumbs into one rough lump, and cover 20 minutes; do not try to force it smooth yet.

Knead 6 minutes. The dough will fight back and stay lumpy, which is correct. Cover and rest 60 minutes, after which the same dough spreads under the heel like putty and its torn edge is smooth rather than shaggy.
Roll to 2 mm on a semola dusted board, dust the sheet itself, fold it loosely in four, and cut 3 mm ribbons with single downward strokes of a long blade.
Lift and shake the ribbons apart at once, toss with more semola, and boil 3 minutes at 100C (212F) salted at 10 g per litre.

note: At 48% hydration there is barely enough water to wet the gluten, so the dough resists from the first minute and will not go smooth by force. steps.text: Mix, knead 10 minutes to a firm smooth ball, and rest 30 minutes wrapped; the dough must be stiff enough that a rolled rope holds its shape without sagging on the board.
Roll one piece into a rope 1.5 cm thick and cut 8 mm discs, keeping the rest covered, since a dried surface skids instead of dragging.
Lay the flat of a round tipped table knife on a disc and drag it 3 cm across unvarnished wood, so the disc smears forward into a curled shell with a torn, matt face.
Flip that shell inside out over the pad of your thumb; the finished ear should be about 1 mm at the dished centre and 3 mm at the rim.

steps.text: Bring the dough together, knead 8 minutes to a firm ball that dents slowly under a thumb, and rest it wrapped for 45 minutes.

ingredients.text: 200 g fine white rice flour, 50% of the blend

12 g psyllium husk powder, 3% of the blend

steps.text: Whisk the three flours, the psyllium and the salt together until the colour is uniform; psyllium that goes in as a lump hydrates as a lump and shows up later as a slimy streak in the sheet.
Beat the eggs, yolks, water and oil, pour them into the dry mix, and work to a dough; it stays sticky for the first minute and then visibly tightens as the psyllium gels.
Wrap and rest 30 minutes at room temperature, then test: a pinch pulled between finger and thumb should stretch 2 cm and part cleanly, with no cracking along the edge.
Roll between two sheets of baking paper to 1 mm, peel the top sheet back and cut; with no gluten the dough will not spring back, but it will not tolerate being stretched by hand either.
Cook at a bare simmer, 90C (194F), for 3 to 4 minutes, salted at 10 g per litre; a rolling boil knocks the strands apart.

note: With no gluten there is no elastic network, so a hydrocolloid stands in: psyllium husk at 3% of the flour blend, or xanthan at 1.5%. It must be fully hydrated before rolling, which takes 30 minutes, and a sheet rolled early cracks along every edge. The starch choice matters too: rice flour alone is sandy and brittle, and it is the tapioca and potato starch that supply chew.

ingredients.text: 140 g plain flour, T55 (flour 100 percent, liquid 179 percent, butter 79 percent, egg 161 percent)

steps.text: Bring water, milk, butter, sugar and salt to a full rolling boil in one movement, with the butter fully melted before the surface breaks, so you do not boil away liquid before the flour goes in.
Off the heat, beat in all the flour at once until no dry patch remains, then return to medium heat and stir 2 to 3 minutes until the paste pulls from the sides and a thin film forms on the pan base.
Spread the paste on a cold tray and let it fall to 60C (140F), warm but not hot to a fingertip, then beat the egg in over four additions.
Stop adding egg when the paste falls from the spatula in a slow V that closes in about three seconds, and a furrow drawn with a finger fills back halfway.
Pipe on to a lined tray and bake at 200C (390F) for 20 minutes without opening the door, then drop to 170C (340F) for 15 to 20 minutes until deep gold and light in the hand.
Pierce each shell at the base and return it to the switched off oven for 10 minutes to dry the inside.

note: The paste is a cooked starch gel carrying a great deal of egg. Water in it flashes to steam and inflates the shell while gelatinised starch and coagulating egg hold the wall until it sets. Add egg above 60C (140F) and it scrambles into lumps. Underbake and the wall is still soft, so the steam condenses and the shell folds.

ingredients.text: 40 g cornflour (8 percent of the milk)
50 g unsalted butter, cold and cubed

steps.text: Heat the milk with the vanilla to 80C (176F) and infuse off the heat for 20 minutes, then bring it back to the boil.
Whisk yolks, sugar and cornflour to a smooth pale paste, then temper with a third of the hot milk, whisking without stopping.
Return everything to the pan over medium heat and whisk hard through the thickening, keeping the whisk moving into the corners.
Once it thickens, hold it at a full boil for a further 60 seconds, until large slow bubbles break the surface and the cream slackens slightly and turns glossy.
Off the heat beat in the cold butter, spread on to a cold tray, film flat against the surface and chill to 4C (39F) within 90 minutes.
Whisk it smooth before use; the chilled gel breaks back to a pipeable cream.

note: Cornflour does two jobs: it gelatinises near 85C (185F) and it shields the yolk protein, which is why this custard can boil where anglaise cannot. Boil it hard for a full minute. Anything less leaves the alpha amylase in the yolks alive, and that enzyme cuts the starch overnight, turning a firm cream into soup by morning.

ingredients.text: 5 g cornflour, optional insurance at 1 percent of the dairy

steps.text: Heat milk, cream and vanilla to 80C (176F) and infuse off the heat for 20 minutes.
Whisk the yolks and sugar only until combined; whipping in air builds a foam that hides the thickening from you.
Temper with a third of the hot dairy, return everything to the pan and stir over low heat with a spatula in a figure of eight, reaching into the corners.
Cook to 82C (180F), the point where the foam on top disappears and the sauce coats the spatula so a finger drawn through leaves a clean channel.
Pour it at once through a fine sieve into a bowl set on ice and stir until it drops below 30C (86F).

note: No starch here, so nothing protects the yolk. Diluted and sweetened, its protein thickens from 78C (172F) and curdles above 85C (185F): a working window of seven degrees. Stop at 82C (180F) and strain straight into a bowl on ice, because carryover heat in a hot pan carries it past the ceiling after you stop stirring.

ingredients.text: For Italian: 100 g egg white at 20C (68F)
For Italian: 60 g water, 30 percent of the sugar
For Italian: 1 g cream of tartar
White wine vinegar, for wiping out the bowl

steps.text: Wipe bowl and whisk with vinegar and dry them; a trace of fat or yolk stops the foam climbing at all.
For Italian, start the whites and cream of tartar at medium speed while the sugar and water cook to 118C (244F), soft ball, brushing crystals off the pan sides with a wet brush.

With the whites at soft peak, pour the syrup in a thin steady thread down the inside of the bowl, never on to the moving whisk, then whip until the bowl is barely warm at 30C (86F) and the peak holds a straight beak.
For Swiss, whisk whites and sugar together in a bowl over barely simmering water, the base clear of the water, to 65C (150F), until no grit is left between finger and thumb.
Move it to the mixer and whip 8 to 10 minutes on high until the bowl is cool and the mass is dense, glossy and holds a sharp ridge.
Use Italian where it must stay light and stable, in mousse, buttercream and torched tops; use Swiss where you want density, for buttercream and for shapes piped to dry at 90C (194F).

note: Both cook the white so the foam holds for days. Italian sets it with 118C (244F) syrup, which brings the whipping mass to about 72C (162F); Swiss sets it in the bowl at 65C (150F). Whip the whites past soft peak before the syrup lands and the bubble walls have no stretch left, so the meringue turns grainy and weeps its syrup out.

ingredients.text: 350 g dark couverture, 64 to 70 percent cocoa solids, in callets or finely chopped
150 g of the same couverture, held back as seed, 30 percent of the total
20 g cocoa butter, optional, for thinning a stiff mass

steps.text: Melt the 350 g over a bain marie or in short bursts to 50C (122F), stirring, keeping every drop of water and every wisp of steam off the bowl.
Off the heat, add the seed in three lots and stir steadily down to 28C (82F); let the seed dissolve rather than forcing the temperature with cold.
Warm back to 31C (88F) for dark chocolate and no higher, then lift out any seed still unmelted.
Test on the tip of a palette knife: at 20C (68F) it should set glossy and firm within 3 to 5 minutes, snapping cleanly with no grey streaks.
Work between 31 and 32C (88 and 90F); if it thickens, thin it with a little melted cocoa butter, never with heat.
Milk chocolate runs the same three points at 45C (113F), 27C (81F) and 29C (84F); white runs 45C (113F), 26C (79F) and 28C (82F).

note: Cocoa butter sets in six crystal forms and only form V is glossy and snaps; it melts at 34C (93F). The three point curve exists to kill the others: 50C (122F) wipes the slate, 28C (82F) with seed grows form V, 31C (88F) melts off the soft form IV without touching V. Hold it above 33C (91F) and temper is lost. One drop of water seizes the mass for good.

ingredients.text: 150 g water, 30 percent of the sugar
50 g liquid glucose, 10 percent of the sugar, or 1 g cream of tartar
1 litre iced water, for the cold water test and for shocking the pan

steps.text: Stir sugar, water and glucose over low heat until every grain has dissolved and the syrup runs clear, then stop stirring for good.
Cover for 2 minutes so the trapped steam washes the pan walls, then uncover, raise the heat and brush any stray crystals down with a wet brush.
Read the stages as water leaves: thread at 110C (230F), soft ball at 115C (239F), firm ball at 120C (248F), hard ball at 125C (257F), soft crack at 140C (284F), hard crack at 150C (302F).
Confirm by hand: a spoonful dropped into iced water rolls into a ball you can flatten between finger and thumb at 115C (239F), and shatters into brittle threads at 150C (302F).
Past 160C (320F) the sugar starts to colour and no thermometer keeps up; pull at pale amber around 170C (338F) and dip the pan base in cold water to stop the run.

note: The thermometer reads water, not sugar: as water boils off the concentration climbs and the boiling point climbs with it, so 115C (239F) means soft ball and 150C (302F) means hard crack. A single stray crystal on the pan wall seeds the whole syrup back to grit, so wash the sides down and never stir once it boils. Glucose or acid blocks the lattice.

ingredients.text: 20 g soft butter, for the moulds
30 g caster sugar, for the moulds
45 g caster sugar, for the whites

steps.text: Butter six 200 ml ramekins in upward strokes only, chill them, butter again, then coat with caster sugar and knock out the excess.
Loosen the pastry cream with the vanilla seeds until it drops from the spatula in a soft ribbon; a cold stiff base will not take the whites.
Whip the whites and cream of tartar to medium peak, adding the 45 g sugar in three lots from the moment they turn opaque; the peak should nod over at its tip.
Beat a third of the whites into the base to slacken it, then fold in the rest in two additions, stopping the instant the last white streak disappears.
Fill to the rim, level with a palette knife and run a thumb round the inside edge so the batter is free of the lip.
Bake on a preheated tray at 190C (375F) for 12 to 14 minutes, until risen 4 to 5 cm with a set collar and a centre that still trembles; serve within two minutes.

note: The rise is gas expanding, not leavening: trapped air grows about a third by volume on the way to 100C (212F) and steam does the rest, while egg and starch set the wall near 80C (176F). Whip the whites only to medium, because stiff whites cannot stretch and tear instead. Butter upward and wipe the rim, or the batter has nothing to climb.

ingredients.text: 250 g cold unsalted butter in 2 cm cubes, 100 percent

steps.text: Toss the butter cubes through the flour and salt, pressing each cube flat once between finger and thumb, and stop while the pieces are still the size of a thumbnail.
Add the iced water and lemon juice and bring it together with a scraper into a shaggy marbled block that looks dry in patches; it should not look like a dough.
Roll to a rectangle three times as long as it is wide, fold in three like a letter, turn 90 degrees, repeat once, then rest at 4C (39F) for 30 minutes.
Give it two more letter folds the same way and rest again; each fold trebles the count, so four folds leave 81 sheets of butter.
Check the dough sits at 12 to 15C (54 to 59F) before every roll, and if butter starts smearing through the surface, chill 20 minutes before going on.
Rest the shaped pastry 30 minutes cold, then bake at 200C (390F) until the layers are set and a cut edge shows open leaves rather than a seam.

note: Lift comes from the water in butter, 16 to 18 percent of it, flashing to steam between the sheets. Butter is only plastic from 15 to 19C (59 to 66F): colder and it shatters, so layers break and leak fat; warmer and it merges into the flour, which gives shortcrust. Rest cold between turns and roll straight, never past the folded edges.

ingredients.text: 150 g cold unsalted butter in 1 cm cubes, 60 percent
50 g whole egg, beaten, about 1 medium

steps.text: Rub the cold butter into the flour, salt and ground almonds with fingertips until it looks like damp sand with no lump bigger than a grain of rice.
Stir through the icing sugar, add the egg and cut it together with a scraper only until it clumps; the moment it forms a ball, stop working it.
Flatten to a 2 cm slab, wrap and rest at 4C (39F) for 2 hours at least, overnight for a shell that will not move.
Roll to 3 mm between two sheets, line the ring without stretching, press into the corner with a ball of offcut, and freeze the lined ring for 20 minutes.
Blind bake at 160C (320F) for 18 minutes with paper and beans, then 8 to 10 minutes uncovered until it is sandy gold right into the corner.
Brush the hot shell with beaten yolk and return it for 2 minutes to seal the inside against a wet filling.

note: Sanding coats the flour in fat before any water arrives, so the grains cannot link into gluten and the baked shell breaks with a clean snap instead of chewing. What shrinks in the oven is gluten you built by kneading and rolling; two hours at 4C (39F) lets it relax, and freezing the lined ring sets the fat so the walls hold their height.

ingredients.text: 150 g caster sugar, for the caramel
80 g caster sugar, for the custard

steps.text: Cook the 150 g sugar and the water without stirring to a dark amber at 175C (347F), then pour at once into six 150 ml moulds and tilt to floor them evenly.
Heat milk, cream and vanilla to 80C (176F), infuse 20 minutes, and whisk the eggs, yolks and 80 g sugar together without raising any foam.
Pour the warm dairy on to the eggs, stir, strain, then skim every bubble from the surface; bubbles left there bake into holes.
Sit the moulds in a deep tray, pour water at 60C (140F) two thirds up their sides and bake at 150C (300F) for 35 to 45 minutes.
Pull them when the centre reads 80C (176F) and the whole custard shivers as one piece; a ripple that travels independently means it is still liquid inside.
Chill at 4C (39F) for at least 4 hours, then run a knife round the rim and invert.

note: Egg alone sets this, with no starch: whole egg coagulates from 62C (144F), but milk and sugar hold it off to between 78 and 82C (172 and 180F). Pull it at 80C (176F) in the centre. Past 85C (185F) the protein network tightens and squeezes water out, so the custard weeps and turns honeycombed. The water bath is the brake; it cannot pass 100C (212F).

ingredients.text: 1 floury potato, about 150 g, peeled and diced
150 g plain flour, for the bug
250 ml warm water, for the dough

steps.text: Simmer the potato in the 250 ml water until it collapses, mash it into its own cooking water and let it cool to blood heat; above 40C (104F) you kill the wild yeast you are trying to catch.
Beat in the bug flour and the sugar, cover loosely and leave in a warm corner for two to four days, stirring once daily, until it domes with bubbles and smells sharply of cider rather than of paste.
Mix the whole bug into the high grade flour, salt and warm water, then knead about ten minutes until the dough is slack, tacky and smooth.
Sprinkle over the baking soda and knead it through until you cannot see a streak of it; streaks bake out as grey soapy patches.
Prove in a buttered tin until a fingertip dent fills back slowly, then bake at 200C (390F) until deep brown and hollow when knuckled underneath, about 40 minutes.

note: The bug is a wild culture: yeast off the potato skin and the flour, fed on sugars the gelatinised potato starch gives up. Mix it into anything above 40C (104F) and it dies. Starved, it turns grey and smells of nail polish; feed it weekly with flour, water and a slice of raw potato. Baking soda is not the lift, it corrects the acid the bug makes, and too much gives a green-grey, soapy crumb.

ingredients.text: 1.5 kg pork neck bones or hock, cut through
250 g plain flour, for the doughboys

steps.text: Cover the bones and onions with the cold water, bring them to a bare tremble and skim the grey scum off until the surface runs clear.
Hold that tremble, never a rolling boil, for about two hours, until the meat slides off the bone at a push.
Rub the pūhā between your palms in a sink of cold water until the water clouds and the leaves go limp, then wring them out; that is where the bitterness goes.
Add the kūmara and potato to the pot and cook until a knife slides out of them clean.

Rub the flour, baking powder and a pinch of salt to a soft dough with the water, drop it in spoonfuls onto the surface, put the lid on and steam until the doughboys are dry at the centre, about 15 minutes.
Push the greens under the broth, give them four minutes until they collapse and darken, and serve straight from the pot.

note: Pork neck bones are collagen and little else; held at a bare tremble for two hours that collagen turns to gelatin and gives the broth its slip. Boil it hard instead and the fat emulsifies into the liquid, leaving it cloudy and greasy. Pūhā carries a bitter white latex, so rub the leaves under water until it clouds before they go near the pot, and give the greens four minutes at the most.

ingredients.text: 3 kg pork shoulder, on the bone
dry mānuka or other hardwood, enough for a four hour fire

steps.text: Dig a pit about a metre square and 60 cm deep, stack the stones through a criss cross of hardwood and burn it down for three to four hours, until the stones glow dull red and knock together with a dead thud.
Rake out the embers and level the stones, then lay wet cabbage leaves and a soaked sack over them until the steam coming off is white rather than smoky.
Set the salted meat baskets straight onto the sacking and the vegetable baskets above them, so fat and juice run down through nothing you want dry.
Throw a bucket of water onto the stones at the edges, cover the lot with the soaked sheets and sacks and shovel the earth back fast, until not one wisp of steam escapes.
Patch any leak the moment you see it and leave the mound shut for three and a half hours.
Open from the downwind side, peel the sacking back away from yourself, and lift the baskets straight up so no soil falls in.

note: The earth is the lid. Hot stones and wet sacking make the steam, and packed soil holds it against the food at a little over 100C (212F) for hours; nothing roasts, everything steams. Two things ruin it. A porous stone still holds water and will burst, so use dense volcanic rock and reject any that rings rather than thuds. And every wisp of steam leaving the mound is heat leaving: shovel more soil on it at once, or the centre comes out raw.

flavor.sentence: A quiet dish that lets its main ingredient speak: season well and stand aside.

ingredients.text: 800 g floury potatoes, in 4 cm chunks
600 g crown pumpkin, in 6 cm wedges
half a green cabbage, plus its outer leaves

steps.text: Blacken the outer cabbage leaves directly over a gas flame or on a dry pan until they blister and smell of smoke; this is the only honest smoke a kitchen can give you.
Line a deep roasting tin with the charred leaves, pack in the kūmara, potato, pumpkin, onion and cabbage quarters, salt through the layers and dot with the butter.
Pour the water down the side of the tin, lay the wet muslin over the vegetables and clamp on a lid or doubled foil so nothing can vent.
Bake at 160C (320F) until a skewer meets no resistance in the kūmara and the cabbage beneath has gone translucent and sweet, about 90 minutes.
Leave it sealed off the heat for ten minutes, then lift the vegetables out on their leaves and spoon the tin juices over.

note: Call this what it is: a steam bake, not a hāngī. No oven makes smoke and hot stone, and charred cabbage leaves are the nearest honest substitute. What an oven can copy is the long wet ramp, which keeps the kūmara below the point where its surface dries and lets its amylase go on turning starch into sugar. Lid off, or above 180C (355F), and you have roast vegetables: a good dish, a different one.

ingredients.text: white bread and butter, to serve

steps.text: Tip the whitebait into a sieve and let it drain until no more water runs; do not rinse it again, the fish bruise and go milky.

Fold the fish through with the salt and pepper until it looks like fish held in a film of egg, not batter with fish in it.
Get the butter foaming in a heavy pan over high heat, ladle in a thin round and cook until the edges turn opaque and the underside is pale gold, about 90 seconds.
Flip once, count thirty seconds and lift it while the centre is only just set; lemon at the table.

Drain the inanga properly first, because water in the mix steams the egg apart. Past about two minutes total the tiny fish wring out their own water, the fritter weeps and the texture goes rubbery. Flour is the usual cheat and it makes a pancake.

ingredients.text: 3 pāua, about 500 g of foot once shucked

steps.text: Run a blunt knife under the foot at the wide end to lift it off the shell, cut away the gut and the hard mouth, then scrub the foot with coarse salt until the slime is gone and the black skirt is clean.
Beat each foot with a mallet until it goes from rubber firm to slack and floppy and the edges frill; you are tearing the sheets of connective tissue that run through the muscle.
Mince the beaten foot coarsely by knife or mincer, stopping well short of paste.
Stir through the egg, flour, milk, onion, salt and pepper to a batter that only just coats the meat.
Fry spoonfuls in a very hot thin film of oil for about 45 seconds a side, until the edges are set and lacquered brown, and lift them out on the early side; lemon over.

note: Pāua foot is dense muscle laced with sheets of connective tissue, and heat gives two outcomes only: seconds, or two hours. Pounding tears those sheets mechanically, which is what makes the seconds route possible at all. In a very hot pan a fritter sets in about 45 seconds a side; past a minute the collagen contracts, wrings out the water and leaves you chewing an eraser. Get the pan hotter than feels right and pull them early.

ingredients.text: 500 ml seawater, or water with 18 g salt dissolved in it

steps.text: Hold each kina mouth side up on a folded cloth and cut a circle out around the mouth with a knife point; the shell is brittle and lifts away as a cap.
Tip the dark gut liquor out and away from the shell before it can run over the roe, then find the five orange tongues lying against the inside wall.

Tip the dark gut liquor away first, or the whole lot tastes of iodine.

ingredients.text: 500 g golden kūmara, in 1.5 cm dice

steps.text: Scrub the mussels and pull each beard down towards the hinge; throw out any that stays open when you tap it.

Sweat the onion and celery in the butter until translucent with no colour, stir in the flour and cook it two minutes, until it smells of biscuit.
Whisk in the mussel liquor, then the milk and bay, add the kūmara and simmer until the dice is tender but still holds its edge, about 15 minutes.

steps.text: Pour boiling water over the tomatoes, count thirty seconds and slip the skins off, then chop them and the onions coarsely.
Layer them with the salt in a bowl and leave overnight, then drain off the brine that has collected and throw it away.
Simmer the drained tomato and onion with the sugar and 300 ml of the vinegar, uncovered and stirred often, until the pieces slump and the syrup sheets off a spoon.

Slake the cornflour, mustard, curry powder, cayenne and pepper in the last 50 ml of cold vinegar, stir it in and cook five minutes more, until dragging a spoon across the pan leaves a channel that closes slowly.
Ladle into hot sterilised jars while the relish is still above 85C (185F) and seal at once.

note: The overnight salt does the work: it pulls water out of tomato and onion by osmosis so the relish thickens by concentration rather than by an hour of hard boiling, which would carry the fresh tomato off in the steam. Cornflour is insurance at the end, and it must be slaked in cold vinegar or it lumps. Jar it above 85C (185F) and seal immediately; potted cool, it grows mould at the surface inside a fortnight.

steps.text: Butter a 20 cm tin and line it with paper before you start; once the soda goes in there is no time for anything else.
Warm the sugar and golden syrup together in a deep heavy pan, stirring only until the sugar has dissolved, then stop stirring altogether.
Boil to 150C (300F), or until a drop in cold water sets hard and snaps between the fingers; the colour will be deep amber.
Take the pan off the heat, tip in the sifted baking soda and beat hard for three seconds only, while it quadruples and climbs the pan.
Pour it into the tin without spreading it, leave it until cold and hard, then break it into shards.

note: Baking soda breaks down in the hot syrup into sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide, and that gas is trapped as the sugar cools through its glass transition. That is the honeycomb. The syrup must reach 150C (300F) hard crack; under it, the candy stays chewy and goes sticky within the hour. Beat three seconds, then pour without spreading, because every stir and scrape knocks the bubbles back out.

ingredients.text: 450 g self-raising flour, plus extra for dusting

steps.text: Heat the oven to 220C (430F) with a heavy tray inside. The leavening starts the second liquid meets the flour, so the oven must be at temperature before you mix.
Rub the cold butter into the flour and salt until it looks like coarse breadcrumbs with a few flatter flakes left; stop while the bowl still feels cool.
Pour in the milk and water and cut it together with a butter knife until no dry flour remains, then bring it into a round with two or three folds only. It should feel tacky, not smooth.
Sit the round on the hot tray, slash a cross 2 cm deep across the top, brush with milk and dust with flour.
Bake 25 to 30 minutes until the crust is deep gold and the base sounds hollow on a knuckle rap; a skewer through the cross comes out dry.

note: Self-raising flour carries bicarbonate and an acid phosphate that start gassing on contact with cold milk and are largely spent inside twenty minutes, so a cold oven means a flat, tight loaf. Knead it like bread and the gluten you build traps nothing and chews like leather: cut it together, fold twice, bake. The deep cross lets the middle set before the crust seals it shut.

ingredients.text: 700 g beef chuck, cut into 1 cm dice
2 tbsp cornflour slaked in 50 ml cold water
1 egg, beaten with a pinch of salt

steps.text: Brown the diced beef hard in the dripping in two batches until each piece is crusted and the pan base is dark; a crowded pan greys the meat and the gravy tastes of nothing.
Soften the onion in the same pan, stir in the flour and cook it out for two minutes, then whisk in the stock, yeast extract, Worcestershire, tomato sauce and pepper and return the beef.

Simmer covered on the lowest heat for about 2 hours until a cube crushes between finger and thumb, then stir in the slaked cornflour and cook until a spoon dragged through leaves a parting that closes slowly.
Cool the filling completely, ideally overnight in the fridge, until it can be spooned out in a solid block.
Line the tins with shortcrust, blind bake at 200C (390F) for 15 minutes until the base looks dry and sandy, fill cold, lid with puff, seal the rim, egg wash and cut a steam vent.
Bake at 200C (390F) for 25 to 30 minutes until the lid is risen and mahogany and gravy just blips at the vent.

note: The base is the whole problem. Hot, loose gravy steams the pastry from inside and you serve raw dough. Two defences, both needed: blind bake the shortcrust so its starch is set and its fat has sealed the crumb, and load the filling fridge cold and thick enough to stand in a spoon so the base bakes before the gravy loosens. Puff goes on top only; it will not carry weight.

ingredients.text: 1 lamb shoulder on the bone, about 2.2 kg
20 g dried old man saltbush leaf
1 head garlic, halved across the equator

steps.text: Score the fat cap in a 2 cm lattice, down to the fat line but not into the meat, so the rub reaches it and the fat has somewhere to run.
Grind the saltbush, salt, coriander and pepper together, work the mix into the scores with the oil, and leave the shoulder uncovered in the fridge overnight to dry the surface.
Sit it on the garlic and rosemary in a deep tray, pour the wine and water around it rather than over it, cover tightly with foil and cook at 150C (300F) for 4 hours.
Pull the foil, raise the oven to 220C (430F) and roast 25 minutes more until the cap is blistered and a skewer slides to the bone with no resistance at all.
Rest 20 minutes, fork the meat into the tray juices, skim the fat, then sharpen with the vinegar until the pan sauce tastes bright rather than only rich.

note: Old man saltbush is a halophyte: it parks sodium in its leaves, so the ground leaf is already seasoning and brings a savoury, faintly mineral edge where you might otherwise reach for anchovy. Taste it, then salt as if half the salt is in. The other rule is temperature, not time. Collagen only melts to gelatine held well above 70C for hours, so a shoulder pulled at 65C is simply tough. Cook to the skewer.

ingredients.text: 4 barramundi fillets, skin on, about 180 g each
1 tsp dried lemon myrtle leaf, finely ground

steps.text: Dry the skin hard with paper, salt it lightly ten minutes ahead, then blot again; any visible moisture steams instead of crisping.
Lay the fillets skin down in a hot oiled pan and press each one flat with a spatula for the first 20 seconds, until it stops trying to dome, then leave them alone.
Cook 4 to 5 minutes over medium heat until the flesh has turned opaque two thirds of the way up the side and the skin releases cleanly, then turn and give the flesh 45 seconds only.

In a small pan bring the lemon juice and water to a bare simmer, take it off the heat and whisk in the cold butter piece by piece to a glossy emulsion, then stir the lemon myrtle in with the pan off the flame.
Spoon the butter over the fish, scatter the finger lime pearls and finish with sea salt flakes.

note: Lemon myrtle is close to pure citral, several times the concentration in lemongrass, and citral is volatile and heat labile. Boil it and the lemon lifts off; hold it hot and what stays behind reads eucalyptus, medicinal and bitter at the back of the throat. So it goes into the butter off the heat, at about a quarter the dose you would use of a dried garden herb. Barramundi skin is thick and gelatinous, so press it flat early or only the edges will crisp.

ingredients.text: 600 g kangaroo loin fillet, silverskin trimmed off
2 tsp dried mountain pepperberry, coarsely ground

steps.text: Bring the loin to room temperature, dry it thoroughly and season with the salt and half the pepperberry; a cold wet fillet needs longer in the pan and there is no fat inside to buy you that time.
Sear in smoking oil for 60 to 90 seconds a side, turning to build an even crust, and lift it out the moment a probe in the thickest part reads 50C (122F).
Rest on a warm plate for 8 minutes, uncovered; it will climb to about 55C (131F), which is rare and correct.
Deglaze the pan with the wine and reduce to a syrup, add the stock, jelly and remaining pepperberry, reduce again, then swirl in the butter and thyme off the heat until glossy.
Carve across the grain in 1 cm slices and read the cut face: even deep ruby throughout, with no grey band under the crust.

note: Kangaroo runs under two percent fat and very high in myoglobin. There is no intramuscular fat to buffer the heat and nothing to lubricate a fibre once it has tightened, so between about 55 and 65C the muscle contracts, wrings out its water and goes from ruby and tender to grey, dry and livery in well under a minute. Probe it, do not guess. Mountain pepperberry is fruity first, then numbing, and it builds for a minute after the mouthful, so season before the rest and taste again.

ingredients.text: 4 raw Moreton Bay bugs, about 250 g each
2 tbsp flat leaf parsley, finely chopped

steps.text: Chill the bugs in the freezer for 20 minutes until they are still, then split each one lengthways through the head with one stroke of a heavy knife and lift out the dark gut thread.
Beat the butter with the garlic, chilli, lemon zest, parsley and a good pinch of salt, and press it into the split tails.
Set the halves shell down on a fiercely hot barbecue plate or grill and leave them there. Do not turn them at any point.
Grill 5 to 6 minutes until the butter is bubbling and the flesh has gone from glassy to chalk white right through the thickest part of the tail, then serve with the lemon cheeks.

note: The shell is the cooking vessel. Bug tail is lean and sweet and sets hard: the proteins are done around 60C, and past that the muscle expels water and turns cottony with a faint ammoniac edge. Cooked shell down, the shell takes the fierce heat and the flesh poaches gently in its own butter from below, so there is no second side to overshoot. Flip them flesh down for even a minute and you grill the sweetness straight out.

ingredients.text: 1 kg Kent pumpkin, unpeeled, in 3 cm wedges
200 g warrigal greens, thick stems pulled off
80 g macadamias, toasted and roughly chopped

steps.text: Toss the pumpkin with 2 tbsp of the oil and the salt and spread it in one layer with space around every wedge; a crowded tray traps steam and nothing will colour.
Roast at 220C (430F) for 30 to 35 minutes, turning once, until the cut faces are burnished and a knife tip meets no resistance at the thickest point.
Meanwhile drop the warrigal greens into a large pot of boiling unsalted water for 45 seconds, lift them into iced water, squeeze dry, and tip the blanching water down the sink.
Whisk the lemon juice, honey and remaining oil with a pinch of salt and dress the squeezed greens in it.
Pile the warm pumpkin and the greens together, dot with ricotta, scatter the macadamias and chilli and crack pepper over.

note: Warrigal greens are not spinach with an accent. The leaves carry soluble oxalates that bind calcium in the mouth and leave a chalky, tongue numbing film, and raw in quantity they are genuinely unpleasant. Forty five seconds in plenty of boiling water leaches most of it out, which is why the water is discarded and why you do not salt it. Macadamia is around 75 percent fat and slides from gold to bitter in seconds, so toast it low and pull it early.

ingredients.text: 1.2 kg ripe roma tomatoes, roughly chopped

steps.text: Sweat the onion with the salt in a wide heavy pan until translucent and sweet, with no raw bite left when you chew a piece.

Add the cornflour paste only if it is still watery, cook two minutes more, then ladle boiling hot into sterilised jars and seal.

note: Akudjura is the dried desert raisin, ground: caramel and tamarillo at a low dose, harsh and tannic much above two percent of the batch, so weigh it rather than eyeball it. It goes in late because its aromatics are fragile and a long boil flattens them to dust. The relish sets on cooling, from pectin and sugar, so judge it a shade looser than you want in the jar. Boiled to the right texture while hot, it will be a brick cold.

steps.text: Mix the oats, flour, coconut, sugar and salt in a wide bowl.
Melt the butter with the golden syrup over low heat until just fluid and pourable, not bubbling.
Dissolve the bicarbonate in the boiling water and stir it into the warm butter; it will foam up pale and roughly double, and that foam is the entire leavening, so use it at once.
Pour the hot mixture into the dry, stir to a stiff, faintly greasy dough, roll walnut sized balls and flatten them lightly on lined trays with 5 cm between each.
Bake at 160C (320F), 12 minutes for chewy or 18 for snap, and pull them while the edges are deep gold and the centres still look underdone; they set on the tray.

note: No egg here, so texture is decided by sugar, syrup and minutes alone. Golden syrup is largely invert sugar, which holds onto water and keeps the middle chewy, while the bicarbonate does two jobs: it gasses against the syrup's acidity and it lifts the pH, which speeds Maillard browning to that deep amber. Bake until the centre firms in the oven and you have made hard tack. Pull them soft and let the tray finish them.

steps.text: Line a 23 cm tart tin with the pastry, chill it hard for 30 minutes, then blind bake at 180C (350F) for 20 minutes with beans and 10 minutes without, until the base is dry and sandy under a fingertip.
Bring the cream to just below a simmer, stir in the ground wattleseed, cover and steep 20 minutes, then strain and press the grounds firmly to recover the liquid.
Whisk the golden syrup, brown sugar, melted butter, salt and vanilla into the wattleseed cream, then whisk in the eggs one at a time, keeping the whisk under the surface so you beat in no air.
Scatter the macadamias across the blind baked shell and pour the filling over; the nuts will float and set as a single layer on top.
Bake at 160C (320F) for 35 to 40 minutes until the edge is set and the centre wobbles as one piece, like a set custard, then cool completely before cutting.

note: Wattleseed is roasted acacia seed: coffee, dark chocolate and hazelnut, with a bitter edge that wants fat and sugar around it. It is a hard seed, so ground and stirred in raw it stays gritty and tastes of dust. Steep it in hot cream and strain, exactly as you would coffee. Then bake gently. Push a syrup and egg filling much past 85C and the proteins tighten, weep and crack, and the tart goes rubbery under the nuts.

ingredients.text: 3 tbsp sunflower oil for the pan

steps.text: Whisk the flour, baking powder, salt and sugar, then rub in the cold butter with your fingertips until the flour looks like coarse meal and no lump is bigger than a pea.
Pour in the water all at once and turn it with a fork only until a shaggy sticky dough gathers; stop while a few dry streaks still show at the side of the bowl.
Tip onto a floured board, fold it over on itself four times and no more, press to a disc 2 cm thick and cut into eight wedges.
Heat the oil in a heavy pan over medium-low until a scrap of dough sizzles lazily rather than fiercely, then fry the wedges 5 to 6 minutes a side until deep gold and hollow-sounding when tapped.
Drain on a rack rather than paper so the underside stays crisp, and split them while still warm.

note: Bannock is chemically leavened, so it rises once: the baking powder starts giving off gas the moment water hits it, and a dough kneaded like bread turns rubbery instead. The other failure is heat. This dough is thick and conducts slowly, so a hot pan gives you a dark crust over a raw wet middle. Keep the oil at a lazy sizzle and give it the full five minutes a side.

ingredients.text: 300 g fresh cheese curds, at room temperature

steps.text: Cut the potatoes into 1 cm batons, rinse until the water runs clear and hold them in cold water while you make the gravy.

Cook the butter and flour together over medium heat, stirring, until the roux smells of toasted biscuit and is the colour of peanut butter, about 6 minutes; stir in the tomato paste, then whisk in both stocks in three additions so no lumps set.
Simmer until a finger drawn through the gravy on the back of a spoon leaves a clean line, season with the vinegar, pepper and salt, and hold it at 80 to 85C (175 to 185F).
Dry the potatoes hard, fry at 150C (300F) for 6 minutes until pale and floppy, lift them out and rest 10 minutes, then fry again at 190C (375F) until they rattle in the basket and are deep gold.
Salt the fries, pile them hot into bowls, scatter the room-temperature curds over them and ladle the gravy on last so it runs down through the pile.

note: The squeak is an intact casein network dragging on tooth enamel. It belongs to curds a day or two old and it goes for two reasons: cold sets the butterfat rigid, and the cheese's own enzymes cut the protein into shorter pieces that no longer grip. So bring them out of the fridge an hour ahead, and buy them fresh. Gravy at 80 to 85C (175 to 185F) softens the curds; boiling gravy melts them into a puddle.

steps.text: Toast the flour dry in a heavy pan over medium heat, stirring without stopping, until it is the colour of milk chocolate and smells of hazelnut, 10 to 12 minutes; tip it straight onto a cold plate so it stops there.
Mix the pork with the onion, breadcrumbs, egg, cinnamon, clove, allspice, mustard, salt and pepper, and roll walnut-sized balls with wet hands.
Brown the boulettes in the butter in batches until they are crusted on two sides and release from the pan on their own, then return them all to the pot with the stock.
Hold at a bare tremble for 45 minutes, until a boulette gives way under light pressure from a spoon.
Whisk the toasted flour into the cold water until there is no lump left, stir it into the pot and simmer 10 minutes more, until the sauce is glossy and clings to the boulettes; taste for salt.

Dry toasting breaks the starch down into dextrins, which is where the nutty flavour comes from, but a dextrinised starch swells far less, so you need roughly twice what you would use raw. Push it past dark chocolate and it turns bitter and stops thickening altogether. Slurry it with cold water; hot liquid gelatinises the outside of every lump and seals the dry flour inside.

ingredients.text: 3 kg beef brisket, point end, fat cap trimmed to 8 mm
7.5 g curing salt, 6.25 percent sodium nitrite
maple or oak wood for smoking

steps.text: Mix the pickling salt, curing salt, sugar, savory, bay, garlic, mustard seed and half the pepper and coriander; rub it into every surface and into the seam between the muscles, then pack the brisket in a non-reactive tub, weight it and refrigerate 8 to 10 days, turning it daily, until a cut into the thickest part shows the same even pink right through.
Rinse hard under cold water and soak 2 hours in fresh cold water, changing it once; fry a coin-sized slice and taste it, and soak longer if it sends you to the tap.
Pat dry, press on the remaining pepper and coriander in a thick even crust, and leave the meat uncovered on a rack in the fridge overnight until the surface is dry and tacky to the finger.
Smoke at 105 to 110C (220 to 230F) over maple until the internal temperature reaches 74C (165F), about 6 hours; the crust will be near black and that is right.

Steam the whole piece over rolling water for about 3 hours, until a skewer slides into the point with no resistance at all and the fat between the muscles has gone translucent; slice by hand across the grain at 5 mm.

note: Smoked meat and pastrami part company at the cure and at the finish. Pastrami is usually wet-brined and carries real sugar; this cure is dry and salt-forward with only a token of sugar, and leans hard on coriander, garlic and cracked pepper, so it reads peppery and sour rather than sweet. The steam is not a reheating step. Collagen in the point only melts under wet heat, and a brisket sliced straight off the smoker at 74C (165F) is tight and dry however good the smoke was.

steps.text: Cover the peas with cold water by 8 cm and leave them overnight, then drain.
Sweat the onion, carrot and celery in the butter until the onion is translucent and smells sweet, with no colour on it.
Add the drained peas, the hock, savory, bay and the water; bring it up and skim the grey foam for the first ten minutes, then drop it to a bare tremble and leave the lid off.
Cook 2.5 to 3 hours, until a pea crushes to nothing against the side of the pot and the hock meat pulls off the bone in strings.

Lift out the hock, shred the meat back into the pot and discard the bone, skin and bay; season with plenty of pepper and only now with salt, and thin with water if it will not hold the track of a spoon.

ingredients.text: 500 g new potatoes, walnut-sized, skins on

Pour in the cream, bring it only to the point where the surface shivers, and take it straight off the heat.
Season with white pepper, check the salt and scatter the chives over.

So do not drain the pot, and use waxy new potatoes, because a floury baker sloughs its outside into the water and gives you glue. Bring the cream just to a shiver. ingredients.text: 80 g raisins, soaked 10 minutes in hot water and drained

steps.text: Cut the cold butter into the flour and salt until the biggest pieces are the size of split almonds, add the ice water, press the dough together without kneading and chill 30 minutes.
Roll 3 mm thick, cut 11 cm rounds, line a 12-cup muffin tin and chill again until the pastry is firm to the fingertip.
Whisk the brown sugar, corn syrup, melted butter, eggs, vinegar, vanilla and salt just until smooth, stopping before it goes pale; beaten-in air makes the filling dome and then crater.
Scatter the plumped raisins into the shells and fill each two-thirds only, since the filling climbs and any overflow glues the tarts into the tin.
Bake at 190C (375F) for 5 minutes to set the bases, drop to 175C (350F) and bake 15 to 18 minutes, until the filling is puffed at the rim and still shivers like loose jelly in the middle.
Cool 10 minutes in the tin, then twist each tart free while the caramel at the edge is still soft.

note: The filling is a custard, not a caramel: egg sets it, and egg curdles. Pull them while the centre shivers and let carryover finish the job; leave them in until the middle is firm and you get a grainy tart that weeps syrup. Runny or firm is two minutes apart. On the raisin question Ontario has argued for a century and will not stop, but the technical point is that dry raisins pull moisture out of the filling around them, so plump them first.

ingredients.text: 500 ml amber maple syrup, rich taste
a tray of clean packed snow, or crushed ice frozen hard

steps.text: Pack the snow into a tray, press it flat and hard, and put it back outside or in the freezer until you need it; loose snow melts under the syrup and gives you sweet slush.
Bring the syrup and butter to a boil in a pan at least four times as deep as the syrup, because it climbs violently near the finish.
Cook to 113 to 115C (235 to 240F), or until a drop into cold water forms a ball that flattens between finger and thumb.
Pour the syrup in long ribbons over the cold snow and count ten seconds, until the surface goes from shiny to dull.
Catch one end with a stick and roll the ribbon up onto it, and eat it before it stiffens.

note: Grades tell you when the sap ran, not how good it is. Golden, delicate, is early and belongs on a plate uncooked; amber, rich, is the middle of the run and the one to boil, since its flavour survives concentration; dark and very dark come late and suit baking and glazes. Then it is all temperature: 113C (235F) ropes onto the stick, two degrees more shatters like glass, two less slides off as syrup. Subtract from the target however far your boiling point sits under 100C.

ingredients.text: 12 large dry-pack sea scallops, about 600 g

steps.text: Pull the small tough side muscle off each scallop, lay them on a towel and leave them uncovered in the fridge 30 minutes, turning once, until the surface reads matte and tacky instead of wet and glossy.
Heat the oil in a heavy pan until it shimmers and a flicked drop of water skitters; salt the scallops as they go in, not before, and lay them down with a finger's gap between each.
Sear undisturbed for about 90 seconds, until a deep even crust has built and each one releases from the pan by itself, then turn them once.
Add the butter, let it foam and go nut-brown, and baste for 30 seconds; lift them at 50 to 52C (122 to 126F), when the sides have just gone opaque and the centre still looks translucent.
Off the heat, sharpen the brown butter with lemon, stir in the parsley and spoon it over the scallops with a grind of pepper.

note: Ask for dry scallops. Wet-pack ones are soaked in phosphate, carry up to a third more water and weep it into the pan on contact, so they steam grey instead of browning and then shrink to rubber. Even dry ones need their surface water gone before they take colour. After that it is a race: the protein sets around 50C and starts squeezing out its own moisture past 55C, which is why the pan has to be hot enough to build the crust inside ninety seconds.

ingredients.text: 250g green cubanelle peppers, seeded and in 5mm dice
10g fine salt, plus more to taste
300g ripe tomato, grated on the coarse side and skins discarded
80ml vino seco (Cuban dry white cooking wine)

steps.text: Warm the oil in a wide pan over low heat, add the onion and pepper with a pinch of the salt and sweat until they slump and turn glassy with no trace of browning, about 15 minutes.
Mash the garlic to a smooth paste in a mortar with a little salt, stir it in with the cumin and oregano and cook only until the raw sting turns nutty and the oil stains gold, roughly 90 seconds.
Add the grated tomato and bay and cook down, stirring less and less often, until the mass pulls back from the pan and a clear rim of red oil pools at the edge.
Pour in the vino seco, scrape the base clean and cook until the alcohol smell has gone and the pan is thick again; season with the remaining salt and the pepper.
Cool completely, pack into a jar and cover the surface with a film of oil; it keeps ten days cold and freezes in ice cube trays.

note: The signal is the oil breaking out. Sofrito is done when the water has gone and the fat re-separates, because only then can the pan get above 100C and the sugars brown. Push the heat early and the onion colours while it is still wet: you get scorched bitterness and no sweetness underneath. Cumin goes into the hot oil, never the watery stage, since its aroma is fat soluble.

ingredients.text: 1 green cubanelle pepper, halved and seeded

steps.text: Soak the beans overnight in the cold water with the halved pepper; do not drain them, that black liquor is the body of the dish.
Bring to a boil, skim the grey foam, then hold at a bare tremble, topping up so the beans stay just covered, until a bean crushes to smooth paste with no chalky point in the middle, about 90 minutes.
Meanwhile sweat the diced onion, pepper and garlic in the olive oil until slumped, stir in the cumin and oregano until fragrant, then mash in a ladle of cooked beans to thicken.
Scrape the sofrito into the pot with the bay and the salt and simmer uncovered until the liquor slides off a spoon in a glossy sheet rather than running clear.
Take off the heat and stir in the vinegar, the vino seco and the sugar; cool, refrigerate overnight and reheat gently to serve over white rice.

note: Acid is what keeps a black bean leathery: vinegar, wine or tomato added early stops the pectin in the cell walls from dissolving, and no amount of boiling will fix it. Hold all three until a bean crushes clean between finger and thumb. The overnight sleep is not superstition either; leached starch sets as the pot cools and thickens the liquor without a spoonful of flour.

ingredients.text: 100g tocino or slab bacon, in 5mm dice

steps.text: Simmer the soaked beans in the water with one bay leaf until tender but still whole, then measure out 800ml of the black cooking liquor and keep the beans separately.

Rinse the rice under cold water until the water runs almost clear, drain it well, then stir it through the sofrito until every grain is filmed in fat and has turned chalky opaque.
Pour in the 800ml of liquor with the vino seco, beans, bay, salt and sugar; taste the liquid and pull it a shade saltier than you want the finished rice.

Boil hard and uncovered until craters open on the surface and the liquid drops level with the rice, then clamp on a lid, drop to the lowest heat for 18 minutes, and rest 10 minutes off the heat before forking it up from the edges.

Rinsing strips loose surface amylose and the coat of fat seals what remains, which is what keeps the grains separate rather than gluing into a cake. ingredients.text: 35g coarse salt, plus 10g for the skin
500ml naranja agria juice, or 350ml orange juice with 150ml lime juice

steps.text: Score the skin in a close diamond lattice, cutting through rind and fat but stopping before the meat, then drive a thin knife deep into the flesh in twenty places to make pockets.

Pound the garlic, coarse salt, cumin, oregano and peppercorns to a wet paste in a mortar, push it into every pocket, whisk the remainder into the sour orange with the oil, onions and bay and pour it over; marinate cold for 24 hours, turning twice.

Lift the meat out, wipe the skin bone dry and rub it with the reserved salt; roast fat side up at 150C (300F), basting the meat but never the rind, until a probe slides in with no resistance and the centre reads 92C (198F), about 5 hours.
Raise the oven to 230C (450F) and roast until the rind has blistered into crackling all over and taps hollow, 20 to 30 minutes; rest 30 minutes, then pull the meat into strands.
Strain the marinade, boil it hard for 3 minutes with a spoonful of the pan fat and pour it over the shredded pork as mojo.

note: Two temperatures doing two opposite jobs. The long 150C stretch is for collagen, which needs hours above 70C to melt into gelatin; the 92C reading tells you it has, not the clock. Crackling needs the reverse, a bone dry surface and fierce heat, which is why the rind is never basted. Any liquid on it steams the skin and it stays leathery however hot you finish. Boil the used marinade before it touches cooked meat.

ingredients.text: 120ml naranja agria juice, or 80ml orange juice with 40ml lime juice

steps.text: Cut the yuca into 8cm lengths, pare away the brown bark and the pink underskin beneath it, split each length and pull out the woody central cord, which never softens.
Boil hard in heavily salted water until a knife meets no grip and the pieces begin to split along their seams, 20 to 30 minutes; drain and keep them hot in the covered pan.
Mash the garlic with the flaky salt to a loose paste in a mortar and scrape it into a heatproof bowl with the cumin, the onion rings and the pepper.
Heat the olive oil until it shimmers and a scrap of garlic fizzes the instant it lands, around 130C (265F), and pour it straight over the paste; it should hiss and foam up.
Whisk the sour orange juice in off the heat, taste for salt, and pour the mojo over the hot yuca so it drinks while the starch is still open.

note: Mojo is scalded garlic, not fried garlic. Oil at roughly 130C hits the raw paste hard enough to knock out the harsh allicin and set its sweetness, but not hot enough to brown it. Cooler and it stays raw and acrid; hotter and it turns bitter in seconds. The juice goes in off the heat, because boiling the sour orange kills the sharp edge that cuts through all that starch.

ingredients.text: 4 green plantains, hard and dark skinned
1 litre water with 20g salt and 4 mashed garlic cloves, for soaking
300g raw shrimp, peeled and roughly chopped

steps.text: Score the plantain skin along its ridges and lever it off in strips, cut the flesh into 4cm barrels and drop them into the garlic salt water while the frying oil comes up to heat.
Drain and dry the barrels, then fry at 150C (300F) until pale straw, floating, and yielding all the way to the centre when you push in a skewer, 5 to 6 minutes; lift out onto paper.
While they are still hot, press each barrel into a tostonera cup or over the base of a small glass to open it into a walled cup; if one cracks apart, the first fry was short.

For the filling, sweat the onion, pepper and garlic in the olive oil, add tomato, cumin, oregano and pimentón and cook until the oil separates, then stir in the shrimp and vino seco and pull the pan off the heat the moment they curl and go opaque.
Raise the frying oil to 190C (375F) and fry the cups until deep gold and audibly rattling, about 2 minutes; drain, salt at once, fill hot and serve with lime.

note: Two fries, two jobs. The first at 150C is really a poach in oil: it gelatinises the plantain's dense starch right through to the middle, which is the only reason you can press the barrel flat instead of shattering it. The second at 190C drives water out of that crushed, opened surface and browns it. One hot fry gives a burnt shell over a raw soapy core, and a cooled barrel breaks under the press every time.

ingredients.text: 700g coarsely ground beef chuck, about 20 percent fat

steps.text: Fry the diced potato in the olive oil until the edges are gold and the centres give, lift onto paper and salt lightly.
Raise the heat, spread the beef in one flat layer in the same pan and leave it completely still until the underside has crusted and releases on its own; only then break it up and salt it.

Add the tomato, vino seco and bay and simmer until the fat rises and shines on the surface, then fold in the olives, capers and raisins and cook 10 minutes more.
Off the heat, stir in the vinegar and return the potatoes; check the salt, aiming for a balance that lands savoury, then sweet, then sour.

ingredients.text: 1.4kg chicken, jointed into 8 pieces, bone in and skin on

steps.text: Salt the chicken and brown it hard in the oil, skin down and unmoved, until the skin is deep gold and lifts away from the pan by itself; set it aside.
Sweat the onion, pepper and garlic in the same fat until slumped, stir in the cumin, oregano and annatto, then the tomato, and cook until an orange rim of oil separates.
Return the chicken with the vino seco, lager, stock and bay and simmer until the thigh reads 74C (165F) against the bone, about 20 minutes.
Rain in the rice, stir once to settle it, then simmer uncovered at a lazy bubble without touching it again until the grains are tender but the pot is still loose and soupy, 18 to 20 minutes.
Scatter the peas and morrones over the surface, cover, cut the heat and let it stand 5 minutes; ladle into bowls with lime.

note: A la chorrera means running wet, and that is the whole point: about three parts liquid to one of rice by volume, where a dry arroz takes two. Medium grain leaks amylose and thickens the broth into sauce around the grains. Stir once the rice is in and you scrub out far more starch than you want, and the pot sets to paste. ingredients.text: 1 white onion, halved, plus 2 more sliced thin for frying

steps.text: Simmer the flank with the halved onion, carrot, bay and peppercorns in barely trembling water until a strand pulls free with no spring left in it, about 90 minutes; let it cool in the broth.
Shred the meat along the grain into thin strands, then squeeze each handful dry over the sink so no broth is left in it.
Toss the strands with the mashed garlic, lime juice, cumin and salt and leave exactly 30 minutes, no longer.
Get a heavy pan or plancha very hot with a film of olive oil, lay in half the beef in a thin layer, press it down flat and do not touch it until the underside is mahogany and crisping at the edges.

Turn once, throw in half the sliced onion and let it char at the edges while staying juicy at the heart, squeeze lime into the pan so it hisses, scrape up and serve at once; repeat with the second batch.

note: Boiled tender then fried dry, and the second half only works if the strands are squeezed, spread thin and left alone. Wet heaped meat steams: its surface never climbs past 100C and no crust can form. Work in two batches even when the pan looks big enough. steps.text: Melt the sugar with the water and lime over medium heat without stirring, swirling the pan only, until it is the colour of dark honey and smells faintly bitter, then pour it at once into a warmed 20cm mould and tilt to coat the base.
Whisk the eggs and yolks just until the ropes of white have broken, stopping well short of foam, then whisk in the condensed milk, evaporated milk, vanilla and salt.
Strain the custard through a fine sieve onto the set caramel and lift off any bubbles from the surface with the back of a spoon.

Cover with foil, set in a roasting tin, pour boiling water halfway up the mould and bake at 160C (325F) until the edge is set and the middle wobbles as one piece, or the centre reads 78C (172F), 55 to 65 minutes.
Chill at least 6 hours, run a thin knife around the rim and invert onto a lipped dish so the loosened caramel floods out with it.

note: Egg proteins set from about 75C and curdle by 85C, so the water bath is structural, not fussy: it caps the mould at 100C and heats evenly, while a dry oven drives the outer custard past 85C and leaves it weeping and pitted with holes. Bake to a single wobble, never to firm, because it keeps setting as it cools. The caramel only turns liquid after a night of drawing water out of the custard; unmould early and half stays in the tin.

ingredients.text: 500 g stoneground wholemeal flour, full extraction
80 g coarse wheat bran, for the boards and the coating

steps.text: Mix both flours, the yeast and all the water to a shaggy mass and leave it 20 minutes, then work in the salt and knead until the dough stops tearing and pulls off the bowl wall in one sheet.
Cover and ferment warm until doubled and domed, roughly 90 minutes, then divide into six pieces of about 165 g and roll each ball through bran until dry to the hand.
Flatten each into an 18 cm disc a good 8 mm thick on a bran dusted board, cover, and prove until a pressed fingerprint fills back slowly, about 30 minutes.
Heat a baking stone or steel at 300C (570F) for a full 45 minutes, then slide two discs straight on.
Bake 2 to 3 minutes: the disc rises like a pillow, the crown pales to gold and the bran freckles. Stack them under a cloth as they come out so they collapse soft rather than crisp.

note: The pocket is steam. At 300C the skin sets in seconds while the interior water flashes and lifts it, so a cool oven is fatal: below about 260C the disc dries out before pressure builds and you get a flat cracker. Bran, not flour, on the boards; flour hydrates into a paste that glues the two faces together and pins the loaf shut.

ingredients.text: 500 g dried split skinless fava beans, soaked 12 hours

steps.text: Drain the soaked fava hard and spread it on a cloth until the beans look matt and feel dry to the fingertips.

Pass the fava through the coarse plate of a mincer with the onion, leek, garlic and all three herbs, then send it through a second time: you want a damp green rubble that takes a fingerprint, never a smooth puree.
Chill the paste covered for an hour, then fold in the salt, spices and bicarbonate only when the oil is already hot.
Shape 45 g patties 2 cm thick, press one face hard into the sesame and slide them sesame down into oil at 175C (350F).

Salt and bicarbonate pull water out fast, so a paste seasoned early goes slack and the patty steams itself hollow and bursts in the oil. ingredients.text: 400 g Egyptian short grain rice, rinsed until the water runs clear

steps.text: Core the cabbage, lower the head into boiling salted water and peel the leaves away as they slacken, lifting each one while it is still bright and bends without cracking; shave the thick rib flat.
Mix the raw rice with the grated tomato, onion, herbs, oil, cumin, coriander and salt. It should taste a shade too salty in the bowl; the rice will take it up.
Roll pencil thick lines of filling in the leaves, seam down, packed loose, leaving a third of the leaf empty at each end for the rice to grow into.
Line the pot with the shaved ribs and the outer leaves, pack the rolls in tight layers, set a plate on top as a weight, then pour in the water slaked with tomato paste and lemon juice to just cover.
Bring to a boil, drop to the faintest simmer for 45 minutes, then pour over the garlic and dried mint fried in the samna, cover and leave off the heat for 5 minutes.

note: Rice roughly triples as it cooks. Fill a leaf tight and the swelling grains have nowhere to go, so they split the wrapper and empty into the broth, which then thickens to porridge and scorches on the base. Pack loose, leave headroom at both ends, and set the plate on before the liquid goes in so the rolls cannot float and unwind. A hard boil undoes all of it.

flavor.sentence: Leads with fresh herbs arguing happily on top, savory depth stacked from the pantry’s bass notes, settling low and earthy.

steps.text: Roast the hazelnuts at 170C (340F) until the skins split and a cut nut is straw coloured to the centre, then rub them in a cloth while hot to shed the skins.
Toast the sesame in a dry pan, moving it without pause, until the seeds hiss, jump and smell oily; tip them out of the pan at once, they keep colouring in the residual heat.
Toast the coriander seed until it smells of orange peel, then the cumin on its own until it darkens one shade; they reach their point minutes apart, so never toast them together.
Cool everything to room temperature, then pound or pulse the nuts, chickpeas and seeds in short bursts to a dry rubble that still rattles; stir in the salt, pepper and mint.

note: Dukkah is a dry crumble, and the thing that ruins it is hazelnut oil. Pounded while warm, or ground a few seconds too long, the nuts weep and the mix packs into a paste that smears on oiled bread instead of clinging in separate grains. Cool completely, work in bursts, and keep it airtight and dark; free oil also turns rancid within a fortnight.

ingredients.text: 300 g samna, melted and kept warm
honey, thick cream or salty white cheese, to serve

steps.text: Work the flour, salt and water to a soft slack dough and knead just 5 minutes, to smoothness and no further; this dough needs to stretch, not to fight back.
Divide into eight, roll each ball through the melted samna until slick, cover and rest 45 minutes, until a poked ball dents with no resistance and does not spring back.
On a heavily greased worktop, push and coax one ball outwards from the centre until it is a sheet you can read newsprint through; holes at the thin edge are of no consequence.
Brush the sheet with samna, fold it in to a small square parcel, and set it aside; repeat with the rest, then stack the parcels, brushing samna between them.
Press and stretch the stack into a greased tray, brush the top, and bake at 220C (430F) until the top leaves lift, blister and go mahogany and the base is crisp, 25 to 30 minutes.

note: Samna is clarified, so it is pure fat: it coats each sheet and keeps it separate, which is why the finished feteer shatters into leaves. Whole butter carries water, and water hydrates the flour where the sheets touch, gluing them into bread. Flour on the bench does the same. If the dough snaps back and tears, it is underrested, not underworked; give it warmth and another 20 minutes.
