steps.text: Make the syrup first: boil the sugar, water and lemon juice to 105C (220F), about 8 minutes, until it runs from the spoon in a thin thread, then cool it completely.
Stir the semolina with the caster sugar, coconut and baking powder, then beat in the yoghurt and warm samna to a thick dropping batter and leave it 30 minutes for the grain to drink.
Smear the tin with tahini, level the batter to 2 cm, score it into diamonds cutting right down to the base and press an almond into each.
Bake at 190C (375F) until the top is an even chestnut brown and the edges have shrunk from the tin, 30 to 35 minutes.

Pour the cold syrup over the cake the second it comes out of the oven, aiming into the score lines; it should hiss and vanish within a couple of minutes. Leave it 2 hours before lifting the pieces out.

note: The soak works on a temperature gap: steam condensing inside a hot crumb pulls cold syrup in fast and evenly. Hot syrup on hot cake sits on the surface and sogs the top while the middle stays dry; cold on cold barely penetrates at all. Score to the base so every diamond can drink from its sides, and never pour more syrup on a cake that has already stopped hissing.

ingredients.text: 600 g fermented white maize dough, three days old

steps.text: Break both doughs into the cold water and squeeze them through your fingers until no lump larger than a grain survives; the slurry should pour like thin cream.
Set over medium heat and stir without pause with a flat wooden spatula, scraping base and corners, until the mixture turns from chalk white to glossy and starts to drag on the spoon.
Drop the heat and keep beating, pressing the paste up the pot wall and folding it back, for 20 minutes; it is ready when it pulls away in one mass and tastes of sour bread rather than raw flour.
Beat in the salt, then wet your hands in cold water and mould the hot paste into smooth balls.
Wrap each ball while it is still hot and eat warm, before the cooling starch sets it rubbery.

note: The sour is lactic acid from three days of wild fermentation in the maize dough; the cassava dough brings the amylopectin that lets banku stretch instead of crumble. Slake both cold: dropped into hot water they skin over and lump for good. Stir without stopping or the base scorches bitter. Then pinch, dip, swallow whole; chewing floods it with salivary amylase and the mouthful goes slack and sweet.

flavor.sentence: Leads with richness that coats and comforts, ferment tang with real depth behind it.

ingredients.text: 200 g ayoyo (jute mallow) leaves, stripped from the stems

steps.text: Dissolve the kanwa in 800 ml of the water, bring to the boil with the onion, then drop in the ayoyo and boil uncovered until the leaves collapse and the liquid strings off the spoon.
Stir in the dawadawa, ground okra, chilli and salt and simmer 10 minutes, until the soup draws in an unbroken thread and smells of fermented bean rather than raw leaf.
In a second pot, whisk 100 g of the maize flour into the remaining cold water and bring to a simmer, whisking, until it thickens to a porridge that coats the whisk.

Beat in the rest of the flour a handful at a time with a flat wooden spatula, crushing each addition against the side of the pot before the next goes in, until the mass is smooth, glossy and just holds a shape.
Cover and leave on the lowest heat 5 minutes to cook out the raw flour, beat once more, then mould with a wet ladle and serve with the ayoyo alongside.

note: Kanwa is the lesson. The alkali lifts the pH, which swells the jute's mucilage into the draw that carries the swallow, and it holds the leaf green rather than olive. Overdo it and the soup turns slippery and soapy and the leaf tastes of ash, so one level teaspoon for the pot. The tuo is cooked in two stages because flour beaten into an already gelatinised porridge cannot lump.

ingredients.text: 300 g dried black-eyed peas, soaked overnight
400 g long grain rice, rinsed until the water runs clear

steps.text: Boil the sorghum leaves with the bicarbonate in the water for 10 minutes, until the liquid runs the colour of dark mahogany, then lift the leaves out and throw them away.
Add the drained peas and simmer with the lid ajar until a bean crushes to paste between finger and thumb while its skin stays whole, topping up with boiling water to keep them covered.
Stir in the rice and salt so the liquid sits two fingers above the grain, then boil hard and uncovered until craters open right across the surface.
Cover, drop to the lowest heat and leave until steam holes have tunnelled through to the base and no water pools when you tilt the pot.
Rest covered off the heat, then fork through so the beans lift and the grains separate, stained rust red. Serve with gari.

note: The colour is anthocyanin leached out of the dried sorghum leaf, and it reads red-brown only away from acid, which is why the pot takes a pinch of bicarbonate; the same alkali softens the bean skins by loosening their pectin. Go past a quarter teaspoon and the rice turns slimy and soapy and the peas slump to mush. Rinse the rice hard first or its surface starch will clag the grains into a block.

steps.text: Season the chicken with salt, half the ginger and one grated onion, then set it over low heat with a splash of water, covered, until it gives up its own juices and the flesh stiffens.
Blend the tomatoes with the second onion, the garlic, the rest of the ginger and the chillies, pour into a wide pot and boil hard, stirring, until it darkens and the raw smell is gone.
Slake the groundnut paste with 500 ml warm water, whisking to a smooth cream with no grain left in it, then stir it into the pot.

Add the chicken with its juices, the garden eggs and the remaining water; simmer uncovered, stirring the base every few minutes, until the soup coats a spoon and a slick of red gold oil rises and holds on the surface.
Lift out the garden eggs, crush them and stir them back for body, then season and serve with rice balls.

note: Groundnut paste is oil suspended in peanut protein. Tip it straight into a hot pot and the protein tightens, the oil floods out and the soup goes grainy, so slake it to a cream in warm water first. After that it has to simmer uncovered and be stirred, because the paste sinks and catches within seconds and a scorched base turns the whole pot bitter. The oil that finally rises is the doneness cue, not a split.

ingredients.text: 2 whole tilapia, about 400 g each, scaled, gutted and cut into thick steaks

steps.text: Boil the tomatoes, one onion, the garden eggs, chillies and ginger in the water until the tomato skins slip and the garden eggs are collapsing soft.
Lift the solids into a blender with a ladle of the liquid, blend smooth and return them to the pot with the hwentia and the salt.
Simmer uncovered 20 minutes, until the raw tomato smell has gone and the soup tastes round and seasoned but stays thin enough to drink from a spoon.
Slice the second onion into the pot, slide in the fish and do not stir; hold the surface at a bare tremble until the flesh at the backbone turns opaque and lifts cleanly from the bone.
Rest off the heat 5 minutes, then lift the fish out with a slotted spoon and serve with fufu or banku.

note: Light soup carries no fat and no thickener. All its body is pulp from blended garden egg and tomato, so it must be simmered down before the fish goes in and never boiled after. A rolling boil shreds tilapia, clouds the broth and drags collagen out of the skin. That thin, sharp, aromatic liquid is the whole point, and the exact opposite of nkatenkwan, where rendered fat is the body.

ingredients.text: 400 g dried black-eyed peas, soaked overnight
2 ripe plantains, skins heavily black spotted

steps.text: Simmer the drained peas with half an onion in unsalted water until the skins loosen and a bean crushes easily while still holding its shape; drain and keep the liquor.
Warm the palm oil over medium heat only until it thins and runs bright orange, well short of any smoke, then add the sliced onion and cook it to translucent.
Stir in the ginger, chilli and tomato paste and fry, stirring, until the paste darkens to brick and oil pools red at the edge of the pan.
Fold in the peas with enough of their liquor to loosen, salt, and simmer until the stew thickens and every bean is stained red.
Fry thick diagonal slices of plantain in hot groundnut oil until the edges go deep amber and the centres yield to a spoon; serve alongside with gari.

note: The red is carotene and carotene is heat fragile. Push palm oil to its smoke point and it pales to straw, the fruity smell turns acrid, and no amount of tomato paste puts the colour back; warm it only until it runs fluid and bright. The plantain has to be black spotted. A yellow one is still starch rather than sugar, so it fries pale and dry instead of caramelising at the edge.

ingredients.text: 600 g beef topside, cut across the grain into 3 mm ribbons
80 g kulikuli (pressed groundnut cake), ground to a powder
1 onion and 2 tomatoes, sliced, to serve

steps.text: Thread the beef ribbons onto soaked skewers in a loose concertina so heat reaches both faces of every fold.
Grind the kulikuli with the chilli, ginger, garlic, onion powder, cloves and salt to a dry sandy dust; keep it dry, with no oil worked in.
Brush the meat with the groundnut oil, press half the dust into it and leave 15 minutes while the coals burn down to grey ash with no flame licking up.
Grill close to the coals, turning every 30 seconds, until the edges frill and char in spots and the meat is only just firm; 4 to 6 minutes.
Off the fire, shower on the remaining dust and serve with raw onion and tomato.

note: Kulikuli is groundnut cake with the oil pressed out, and that is exactly the point: free peanut oil over coals at 250C (480F) goes acrid and bitter within seconds. Half the dust before the fire, so it toasts and grips, half after, so it stays raw and aromatic. Cut the beef thin and turn it constantly; a thick cube only cooks through long after its coating has burnt.

ingredients.text: 500 g kontomire (cocoyam leaves), coarse stalks stripped out
3 kpakpo shito chillies, or 2 scotch bonnet

steps.text: Shred the stripped leaves and wash them through several changes of water until no grit settles in the bottom of the bowl.
Boil hard in salted water, uncovered, for at least 15 minutes, until the leaves are drab army green and completely limp; still bright green means not yet.
Drain and press the leaves against the sieve with the back of a ladle to force out every drop of water.
Grind the onion, chillies and tomato to a rough paste in an asanka, then work the leaves in a handful at a time to a coarse dark mash.
Salt it, pour the palm oil over off the heat and fold it through; eat warm or at room temperature with boiled yam or plantain.

note: Cocoyam leaf is loaded with needle shaped calcium oxalate crystals and a quick blanch leaves them intact, so the dish scratches and itches at the back of the throat for an hour afterwards. They break down only in a long, hard, uncovered boil: judge by colour and give it a full 15 minutes. The palm oil goes in off the heat, where it stays fruity and red instead of frying flat.

ingredients.text: 400 g onions, blended to a paste

steps.text: Fry the onion, ginger and garlic paste in the oil over medium heat, stirring often, until the loud crackle of boiling water dies to a quiet sizzle and the mass is brown and grainy; 35 to 40 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste and fry until it darkens to rust and clear oil separates at the edges.
Add the ground herring and shrimp and fry until they smell toasted rather than raw and the paste tightens around the spoon.
Pull the pot to the lowest heat, stir in the chilli, cloves, hwentia and salt, and cook, stirring constantly, until the whole mass is near black and the oil floats clear on top; about 25 minutes.
Cool completely, then pack into dry jars with the oil covering the solids by a finger's width.

note: Shito keeps because it is a confit: everything in it is fried until its water is gone, then sealed under oil that nothing can grow through. There are two ways to lose a batch. Rush the onion and the moisture left behind blooms mould inside a week. Add the chilli over a lively heat and it scorches in under a minute, leaving the pot grey and bitter instead of black and sweet.

steps.text: Whisk the flour, sugar, yeast, nutmeg and salt together, then beat in the egg and warm water to a thick sticky batter that falls from the spoon in a slow ribbon.
Cover and leave somewhere warm until it has doubled and domed, the surface pocked with bubbles that pop when you knock the side of the bowl.
Heat the oil to 170C (340F); a scrap of batter should surface within three seconds and take a full minute to take colour.

Squeeze the batter up between thumb and forefinger into a ball, scoop it off with a wet spoon straight into the oil, and fry until each one rolls over by itself and is an even deep amber all round; 5 to 6 minutes.
Lift onto a rack rather than paper so the crust stays crisp, and eat within the hour.

note: This is a batter, not a dough: nothing is kneaded, there is no gluten network, and the lift is all yeast gas held in a loose starch matrix. Give it the full rise or the centres stay wet and heavy. Hold the oil at 170C (340F). Hotter and the crust browns while the middle is raw batter; cooler and the ball sits still, drinks oil and comes out greasy. A pale belt round the equator says it turned at the right moment.

steps.text: Blend the tomatoes, tatashe, scotch bonnet and half the onion coarse rather than smooth, so the finished sauce keeps some grain.
Boil the blend in a wide uncovered pot until it has lost half its volume and a spoon dragged across the base leaves a track that fills back slowly.
Heat the oil in a second pot and fry the sliced onion until the edges brown.
Tip in the reduced puree and fry over medium heat, stirring every couple of minutes, until it darkens from orange scarlet to deep brick and clear oil pools at the sides.
Stir in the seasoning cubes, thyme and salt, cook two minutes more, then leave off the heat to settle so the oil rises in a sheet.

Reduce the puree hard first, then fry it in the fat: the oil strips the carotenoids out of the pulp and the colour deepens to brick. Oil rising clear at the edges is the only reliable signal it is done. Stop before that and every stew you build on this base tastes thin and raw.

steps.text: Bring 500 ml of the water to a rolling boil in a heavy pot and keep the rest hot in a jug.
Rain the elubo in through your fingers in a thin veil, stirring hard with a flat wooden turner the whole time so nothing settles in a heap.
Work the paste against the side of the pot, crushing every lump you find, until it pulls away from the base in one mass and turns from beige to dark chocolate.
Splash in a little of the reserved hot water, cover, and stand it off the heat for two minutes.
Beat again until smooth and elastic, then turn it into a bowl and swirl it round to give a domed, glossy surface.

note: Elubo is already cooked yam, so the job is only rehydrating starch. Dumped in, the outside of each clump gelatinises on contact and seals dry flour inside; that is a lump, and no amount of beating opens it later. Rain it in as a veil, crush anything that forms against the pot wall, then cover off the heat so the middle steams through. It darkens as it hydrates, so pale amala is underworked.

steps.text: Warm the palm oil until it thins and loosens but well short of smoking, then soften the onion in it with the iru.
Stir in the pepper base and fry until it tightens and the oil separates back out, about eight minutes.
Add the crayfish, panla, ponmo and beef with a ladle of the beef stock, and simmer until the meats take the colour of the stew.

ingredients.text: 200 g onion for blending, plus 150 g sliced

steps.text: Blend the green peppers, scotch bonnet and the 200 g onion coarse, then boil the blend down in a wide pot until it is almost dry and jammy.

Cut the heat, let the oil settle for a minute, then fry the sliced onion and iru in it until fragrant.

ingredients.text: 80 g ogbono, ground fine that day

steps.text: Warm the palm oil off the heat and stir the ground ogbono into it until you have a loose, smooth paste with no dry specks left.
Bring the stock to a simmer and thread the ogbono paste in slowly while stirring, so it disperses instead of seizing.
Hold it at a low uncovered simmer, stirring now and then, until a spoon lifted from the pot pulls a thread that stretches without snapping.
Add the meats, stockfish, crayfish, chilli, ogiri and seasoning, and bring it back to the barest simmer.
Scatter the ugu over the surface, stir once, and take the pot off the heat while the leaves are still bright.

note: The draw is polysaccharide from the ground seed, and it needs fat to disperse: stirred straight into water the powder seizes into dry pellets that never hydrate. ingredients.text: 800 g fresh catfish, cut into thick steaks

steps.text: Rinse the catfish in very hot salted water, rubbing each steak until the skin squeaks and no slime is left, then drain.

Simmer the blended onion, scotch bonnet, crayfish, ogiri and seasoning in the water for five minutes to build the broth.

note: There is no palm oil here, so the body is pure yam starch and the fish has nowhere to hide. Rinse the catfish in hot salted water until the skin squeaks or the slime will cloud the broth. Drop the pounded yam in small pellets so each gelatinises separately; one big lump skins over and stays raw inside. Ehuru is resinous and volatile, so toast and grind it fresh and add it at the end.

ingredients.text: 1 kg goat leg with the skin on, in large pieces
150 g onion, half quartered and half sliced thin
80 g red scotch bonnet, deseeded and slivered
100 g red bell pepper, cut small
3 tbsp of the goat fat skimmed from the pot, or groundnut oil

steps.text: Simmer the goat with the quartered onion, thyme, bay, seasoning and salt in water barely to cover, skimming, until a skewer slides through with no resistance.
Lift the meat out, dry it well on a rack, and keep the stock and the fat that rises on it.
Char the pieces over hot coals or under the fiercest grill, turning, until the skin blisters and the edges go almost black.
Chop into rough 2 cm cubes while still hot and tip them into a warmed bowl.
Toss off the fire with the hot fat, sliced onion, scotch bonnet, bell pepper, a spoon of stock and a squeeze of lime, and serve at once.

note: Goat leg is collagen, and collagen wants wet heat and time before dry heat will do anything but leather it. Simmer until the skewer slides, then char fast and hard so the outside crusts before the inside dries. The peppers and onion go in off the fire so their heat stays raw and sharp against the smoke; cook them into the meat and you have made a stew, not asun. The simmer runs about an hour.

steps.text: Soak the beans in warm water, then rub them between your palms and float the skins off, changing the water until what is left is clean and white.
Blend the beans with the onion and scotch bonnet using as little water as you dare, stopping at a thick paste that holds a ridge from the spoon.
Beat the paste hard with a wooden spoon until it lightens in colour and a small spoonful floats when dropped into cold water; salt it only now.
Heat the oil to 175C (350F) and drop in spoonfuls well apart, frying until the undersides are deep gold before turning.
Lift them out once both faces are crisp and the middle springs back, and drain standing on a rack so the bottoms stay dry.

note: There is no raising agent. The lift is air you beat into the paste, so blend with barely any water, keep it stiff enough to hold a ridge, and whip until a spoonful floats in cold water. Salt late: salt early slackens the paste and the foam falls. Loose batter spreads flat in the oil and drinks it, giving heavy grey akara instead of a crisp shell over an open crumb. Soak the beans two hours first.

steps.text: Dry the kuli kuli in a low oven or a dry pan until a piece snaps cleanly instead of bending.
Grind it in short bursts so friction does not warm it and press the oil back out, then blot the powder between sheets of paper if any oil shows.
Sieve it, regrinding the coarse bits, until it runs light and dusty through the mesh.
Fold in the chilli, ginger, garlic, onion, cloves, ehuru, uda and salt, then sieve the whole blend once more so the cloves spread evenly.
Store it airtight in the dark and use it while the groundnut still smells sweet.

note: Groundnuts are half oil, which is exactly why yaji is built on kuli kuli, the cake left behind after the oil has been pressed out. Whatever oil remains will cake the mix into paste within a week and turn it rancid soon after. Dry the kuli kuli until it snaps, grind, sieve, and only then bring in the dry spices. Cloves carry the blend: three grams is already loud, six is medicine.

steps.text: Rub the butter into the flour, sugar, baking powder, nutmeg and salt until the mixture looks like damp sand.
Beat the eggs with the milk and bring the dough together, adding the liquid a spoon at a time and stopping while it is still firm and dry to the touch.
Rest the covered dough, then roll it to 3 mm and cut it into 1 cm squares with a knife or a pastry wheel.
Fry at 160C (320F) in batches, stirring so they colour evenly, until the loud fizzing drops to a whisper and the pieces are pale gold.
Drain on a rack and let them cool completely before they go into a tin, since they harden as they cool.

note: Crispness here comes from drying, not browning, so fry cool. At 160C (320F) the water has time to leave before the surface sets; at 180C the outside is gold in two minutes and the centre stays soft, then goes leathery in the tin overnight. ingredients.text: 600 g walu (Spanish mackerel) or mahi mahi fillet, skinned and pin boned
180 ml fresh lime juice, from about 8 limes
1 red onion, 120 g, sliced paper thin
2 ripe tomatoes, 200 g, seeded and cut into 1 cm dice
1 small cucumber, 150 g, seeded and cut into 1 cm dice
3 bird's eye chillies, deseeded and minced
a small handful of coriander leaves

steps.text: Cut the fish across the grain into 15 mm cubes so the pieces stay square instead of shredding, then toss with the salt and lime until every face is wet.
Cure in the coldest part of the fridge until the cubes have gone opaque, then cut one in half and stop while the very centre is still faintly translucent.
Drain the fish in a sieve and press it gently with the back of a spoon; throw away the milky lime, which is now watery and bitter.
Fold through the coconut cream, onion, tomato, cucumber, chilli and spring onion, then taste for salt; it will take more than you expect.
Scatter the coriander over and serve cold, in half coconut shells if you have them.

note: Lime does not cook the fish; the acid unfolds its proteins so they knit and go opaque, and it never stops. Twenty to thirty minutes is the window, and past about forty the cubes tighten to chalk. Drain hard before the cream goes in: leftover acid thins coconut cream and curdles it into oil and grit, so cure and dressing must never share a bowl.

ingredients.text: 2 mature brown coconuts, about 1.4 kg together, heavy in the hand and sloshing when shaken
500 ml water at 60C (140F), hand hot and no hotter

steps.text: Pierce the two soft eyes with a clean nail and drain the water into a glass; that is the drink, not the cream.
Tap the shell around its equator with the back of a heavy knife, turning the nut as you go, until it cracks open into two clean domes.
Grate the white meat straight out of the shell on a coconut scraper or the fine side of a box grater; you want a damp fluff, not shards.
Squeeze the bare gratings hard in both fists over a bowl until nothing more runs: that is the first pressing, about 250 ml, thick as single cream.
Work the warm water into the spent meat, leave it ten minutes, then wring it out through muslin into a second bowl: that is the second pressing, thin and blue white.
Keep the two apart and cold; within the hour the first pressing will set a firm cap of white fat on top, which you stir back in before use.

note: First pressing is a true emulsion, roughly a quarter fat, and it is a finishing cream: boil it and it breaks. Second pressing is mostly water carrying the fat the first squeeze could not reach, so it is the cooking liquid, thin enough to simmer fish or root crops without splitting. Keep the soaking water under about 70C (158F); hotter sets the coconut protein in the gratings and the yield falls.

ingredients.text: 250 ml first pressing coconut cream, cold
1 small red onion, 80 g, cut into 3 mm dice

steps.text: Salt the diced onion in the serving bowl and leave it to weep while you juice the limes; the salt takes the raw bite out of it.
Whisk the lime juice into the cold coconut cream a spoonful at a time until the sauce is smooth and the colour of milk, with no thin streaks.
Stir in the chilli and spring onion, then taste: it should read salty first, sour second, and the heat should arrive last.
Pour into a shallow bowl and serve within the hour, for dipping fish, taro and cassava.

note: Lime is what makes miti taste of the sea and also what kills it. Acid strips the charge holding the coconut emulsion together, so the cream thins and then curdles to oil and flakes. Adding the juice slowly into cold cream, whisking, keeps it whole long enough to reach the table. Capsaicin is fat soluble, so the heat climbs the longer the bowl stands. Never warm it.

ingredients.text: 6 squares of banana leaf, passed over a flame until glossy and pliable
6 sheets of foil, if no breadfruit leaf is to hand

steps.text: Wash the leaves and cut out the stem and the thick central rib, which hold the most oxalate and never soften.
Stack four leaves in your cupped palm, shiny side outward, and hold the edges up like a purse.
Stir the salt and onion into the coconut cream, ladle about 120 ml into each leaf cup, and gather the edges over the top to close it.
Wrap each parcel in banana leaf and then foil, seam upward so nothing runs out, and set them in a roasting tin.
Bake at 180C (350F) until the parcels smell nutty and a leaf pulled from the middle is limp, black green and falling apart under a fork.
Rest ten minutes before opening; inside, the cream will have parted into a spoonable curd and clear oil, and it is scalding.

note: Taro leaf carries needle crystals of calcium oxalate held in cells that only long moist heat destroys, and undercooked leaf prickles and itches in the throat for hours; no amount of salt or lime hides it. Two hours in the oven, minimum, and the test is textural rather than clock based: the leaf must be black green and collapsing, never tender crisp. The coconut cream is not garnish, it is the medium that carries the heat in.

ingredients.text: 1.2 kg mutton flap or lamb belly, cut into 4 cm pieces
40 young taro leaves (lu), ribs removed, about 800 g
banana leaves for lining, or a double layer of foil

steps.text: Trim only the hardest of the fat cap off the flap and leave a good 5 mm on; that fat is the cooking medium and, later, the sauce.
Line a deep pot with a double layer of banana leaf, then build alternating layers of taro leaf, mutton, onion and salt, finishing with a thick lid of taro leaf.
Pour the coconut cream over so it soaks down through every layer, fold the leaves across the top and put the lid on tight.
Cook at 160C (320F), or on the lowest flame the hob will hold, until the mutton pulls apart between finger and thumb and the leaves have gone to a dark sludge.
Open the parcel and stir once: the clear rendered oil sitting on top is stirred back through, never poured off.

note: Here the coconut cream is meant to break. Held for three hours it separates, and the freed coconut oil plus the mutton's own rendered fat is what fries the leaf and makes lu taste of Tonga rather than of milk. What cannot be short is the leaf: taro needs the same long heat as the meat to destroy the oxalate itch, so tough mutton and a burning mouth arrive together. Use flap, not lean leg, or the dish comes out dry and thin.

ingredients.text: 1 chicken, 1.8 kg, jointed into eight and rubbed with salt
1.5 kg dalo (taro corms), peeled and halved
1 kg cassava, peeled, cored and cut into 10 cm lengths
1 mature breadfruit, 2 kg, quartered and cored
6 parcels of taro leaf and coconut cream
20 banana leaves, passed over a flame until glossy
35 fist sized stones of dense volcanic or hard river rock, bone dry
earth or clean sand for sealing

steps.text: Dig a pit 60 cm across and 40 cm deep, build the hardwood fire in it with the stones sitting in the flames, and burn until the stones glow dull red and the wood has fallen to white ash.
Rake out the embers, level the hot stones with a green stick and lay a close bed of banana leaves straight onto them; they will hiss and scorch, and that is the seal forming.

Peel the dalo under running water to keep the sap off your hands, salt everything, and pack the pit densest first: dalo and cassava on the stones, breadfruit above, chicken and leaf parcels on top where the heat is gentler.
Spoon the coconut cream over the chicken, cover the whole load with a thick blanket of banana leaves, then the wet sacks, then shovel earth over the lot until not one wisp of steam escapes.
Open only when the pit has stopped breathing and the earth is cool to the palm; the chicken should be pulling from the bone and a knife should go through the dalo like soft butter.

note: A lovo is a steam oven, not a barbecue. Heat stored in the stones turns the wet leaves and the food's own water to steam, and the earth cap is the lid; one leaking vent bleeds the temperature and gives you smoke taint and raw dalo at the centre, so chase every wisp with more soil and then leave it alone. Reckon two hours to bring the stones up and three hours buried. Use dense dry stone: layered or porous rock holds water that flashes and bursts it across the pit.

ingredients.text: 1 mature breadfruit, about 2 kg, matt skinned, firm all over and with no soft patches
200 ml first pressing coconut cream, to serve

steps.text: Cut the stem out of the crown with the point of a knife and stand the fruit stem down for a few minutes to let the white latex bleed out.
Bury the whole fruit in the glowing embers of a burnt down wood fire and give it a quarter turn every ten minutes.
Cook until the skin is black and crazed all over and a skewer slides to the centre with no resistance; the fruit hisses steadily and then falls quiet as the steam finds its way out.
Roll it out of the ashes, scrape the charred skin away with the back of a knife, halve the fruit and cut out the fibrous core.
Slice thick, salt while hot and pour coconut cream over; breadfruit left to go cold turns hard and waxy and will not come back.

note: Breadfruit cooks in its own steam behind a skin that chars into a sealed crust, so the black layer is the cooking vessel: peel it first and the flesh dries to cork. Allow about forty five minutes in the embers. Pick the fruit mature but hard, since an unripe one stays rubbery and bleeds latex that gums the knife, while a fruit already yellowing collapses into sweet paste on the coals.

steps.text: Salt the fish steaks and leave them while you sweat the onion and ginger in a spoonful of the first pressing until the onion is soft and clear but has taken no colour.
Add the tomato and split chillies and cook until the tomato has slumped and turned glossy.
Pour in the second pressing, bring it to a bare shiver with no rolling bubbles, and lay the fish in in a single layer.
Poach uncovered, spooning liquid over the steaks, until the flesh parts from the bone at the thickest point and not a moment longer.
Pull the pan off the heat, count to sixty, then stir in the first pressing and the lime; the sauce should thicken to a coating without a single bead of oil showing.
Scatter the spring onion over and serve with dalo or cassava to mop the pan.

note: This dish is the argument for two pressings. The thin second pressing holds a simmer because it has too little fat to break, so it poaches the fish and takes on the ginger and tomato. steps.text: Melt the sugar with the 80 ml of water in a wide heavy pan and boil it without stirring until it darkens to the colour of strong tea and smells of toast.

Simmer the sauce, stirring, until it coats the back of a spoon and a slick of clear oil begins to show at the edge, then take it off the heat to cool to just warm.
Mix the flour, baking powder, salt and the 200 ml of water to a soft sticky dough and drop rough walnut sized lumps into a wide pan of boiling water.
Boil until the dumplings bob to the surface, then give them two minutes more so the centres are not raw; a split one should be white and open, not grey and dense.

Stir through the grated coconut, the coconut cream, the cold water and the sugar, then taste; it should be barely sweet, because the fruit keeps releasing sugar as it stands.

ingredients.text: 900 g lamb shoulder on the bone, in 5 cm pieces
700 g onions, half sliced thin, half chopped

steps.text: Pound peppercorns, garlic, netetou, parsley and the chopped onion to a coarse wet nokoss; work half of it into slits cut in the lamb.
Brown the lamb in the oil in a wide pot, turning only when each face releases itself and the pot smells toasted rather than steamy.
Add the sliced onion and the rest of the nokoss, then the tomato paste, and fry until the paste darkens from red to brick and oil beads out around it.
Pour in the water, drop in the whole chilli and the vegetables, and simmer until cassava gives to a knife with no resistance at the centre; lift out meat, chilli and vegetables and cover them.
Taste the broth: it should be a shade too strong and leave a film on the spoon. Reduce if it is thin, then stir in the rinsed broken rice.

Cook uncovered until the liquid drops to the level of the grains, then cover, drop the heat to the barest thread and steam until the surface is pitted with holes and a grain squashes clean. Pile the rice, crown with meat and vegetables.

Leave the lamb and vegetables in for that and they turn grey and collapse, so they come out first and the rice takes the pot to itself: gelatine, rendered onion, netetou, pepper. steps.text: Mix onions, lime juice, mustard, garlic, pepper and salt in a bowl, bury the fish in it and leave it cold for one to two hours, no longer.

Squeeze the onions dry, keeping every drop of marinade, and fry them in the oil over medium heat until they slump and the edges take a toffee colour.

ingredients.text: 400 g dried black eyed peas (ñebbe), soaked overnight

steps.text: Boil the drained peas in plenty of unsalted water with the bay until they crush easily between finger and thumb but still hold their shape; keep the cooking liquor.
Warm the palm oil until it clears to bright orange, then soften the onion and garlic in it until slumped and sweet.
Add the tomato paste, netetou and pepper and fry until the paste goes brick dark and oil separates around the edge.
Fold in the peas with a ladle of their liquor and the whole chilli, then mash about a quarter of them against the side of the pan and simmer until the sauce clings.
Salt now, sharpen with lime, and spoon into split bread hot.

note: Cook the ñebbe in plain water. Salt is survivable, but tomato or lime in the pot puts acid on the skins, and acid keeps pectin insoluble, so the peas stay squeaky however long they boil. Season once they crush between finger and thumb. There is no flour in the sauce: mash about a quarter of the cooked peas back in and their own starch thickens it, which is why ndambé holds in bread instead of soaking through.
techniques: Soaking dried goods back to life

ingredients.text: 1 whole head of garlic, cloves peeled
40 g flat parsley, thick stalks included

steps.text: Toast the netetou in a dry pan over low heat, shaking, until the sharp ammoniacal smell gives way to something malty and the beans darken a shade.
In a mortar, crush the peppercorns to a coarse grit first, then work in the netetou, then the garlic and chillies with the salt as an abrasive.
Add the parsley and pound until it is bruised into the paste, then the onion last, working only until it breaks down and no further.
Pack into a jar, level the surface and pour the oil over so it seals the paste from the air. Keep cold and spoon out with a dry spoon.

note: Pound in order of hardness: peppercorns, netetou, garlic and chilli against the salt, parsley, onion last and briefly. A blender reverses that order and shreds the onion cells first, flooding everything with juice, so the paste separates and sours within days. Toast the netetou before it goes in; dry heat drives off the ammoniacal top note and leaves the malty glutamate that is the point of it.

ingredients.text: 400 g thick soured milk (lait caillé) or plain whole yoghurt
150 g crème fraîche or soured cream

steps.text: Sprinkle the water and oil over the millet a little at a time, raking it through with spread fingers until every grain is damp and separate with no clumps.
Steam uncovered in a couscoussier over boiling water for twenty minutes, tip onto a tray, break up every lump with a fork and sprinkle again.
Steam a second time until a grain crushed on the tooth is tender all the way through with no chalky centre, then spread it out and cool it completely, fluffing as it goes.
Whisk the soured milk, crème fraîche, sugar, vanilla seeds, orange blossom water and salt until smooth and pourable.
Fold the cold millet and the raisins into the cold cream, chill an hour so the raisins swell, and grate nutmeg over at the table.

note: Steam the millet twice. One pass leaves a chalky core that no amount of sitting in milk will soften, because the grain has to hydrate and gelatinise in steam, not in cold acid. Then cool it completely. Fold warm thiéré into soured milk and the casein splits while the grains keep drinking, so a bowl that looked right turns dry and grainy within the hour. Cold into cold, then rest it cold.

steps.text: Rinse the calyces briefly in cold water to shift dust and grit, then drain; do not let them soak.
Heat the water to about 90C (195F), when the base of the pan is chattering but no rolling bubbles break the surface, and take it off the heat.
Pour the water over the calyces with the vanilla pod and steep until the liquid is a deep garnet and tastes bracingly sour, around twenty minutes.
Strain through a sieve without pressing or wringing the calyces, then stir the sugar, salt and orange blossom water into the warm liquid until fully dissolved.
Bruise the mint between your palms, drop it in, and chill hard. Taste again cold and adjust the sugar.

note: Colour and tartness are anthocyanins and organic acids, and they leave the calyces fast in water around 90C (195F). Boiling gains nothing and costs plenty: the perfume goes off with the steam and the seed fragments start giving up tannin, which lands as a dry, dusty finish. Steep off the heat and strain without wringing. Sweeten a shade past correct, because cold flattens sugar on the tongue.

teacher.label: The cuisine, deeper
teacher.sub: Technique films from the Senegalese kitchen

ingredients.text: 800 g coarsely minced lamb or beef
2 thick slices white bread, about 80 g
6 fresh lemon leaves, or 4 bay leaves

steps.text: Soak the bread in 150 ml of the milk until it is saturated and falling apart, then squeeze it out over the bowl; keep both the pulp and the milk it gives back.

Sweat the onions in butter over medium heat until slack, translucent and sweet at the edges; add garlic, ginger, curry powder and turmeric and fry only until the spices smell toasted and the pan looks dry, about a minute.

Raise the heat, add the mince and break it up until it has just lost its raw colour without browning hard, then stir in apricots, sultanas, vinegar, jam, salt and the bread pulp until the mixture is glossy and tastes sweet, then sour, then salty.
Press it into a buttered 25 cm dish, loosely rather than packed tight, and stand the lemon leaves upright in the surface.
Whisk the eggs into the remaining milk plus the milk squeezed from the bread, pour it over so it floods the surface evenly, and scatter the almonds.
Bake at 160C (320F) until the custard is set and lightly freckled at the edges but still trembles in the middle when the dish is knocked, 35 to 40 minutes; rest 10 minutes before cutting.

note: What separates this from a shepherd's pie is acid and sugar carried into the meat itself: vinegar, jam and dried fruit season the mince the way salt does, and the curry powder is bloomed in fat first so it tastes toasted rather than dusty. The topping is a custard, not a sauce. Egg sets around 82C (180F) and curdles just above, so keep the oven at 160C (320F) and pull it while the centre still trembles, or it splits and weeps water into the meat.

ingredients.text: 300 g dried samp, coarsely stamped white maize
250 g floury potatoes, in 2 cm dice

steps.text: Rinse samp and beans separately through several changes of cold water until it runs clear, then soak each overnight in plenty of cold water; the samp will swell to roughly three times its dry volume.

Drain the samp, cover with 1.5 litres of fresh water and bring to a bare shiver with the lid ajar; cook until every kernel has split open and there is no chalk left at the centre when you crush one, about 90 minutes.

Add the drained beans and carry on at the same shiver until they crush to a paste between finger and thumb while their skins stay whole, 45 to 60 minutes more, topping up with boiling water whenever the surface goes dry.
Stir in the onion, potato and salt and cook until the potato collapses and thickens the pot into a loose, soft porridge that just holds a spoon mark.
Beat in the butter off the heat until it disappears, add the pepper and check the salt; it should taste of sweet corn first and beans second.

note: Samp is maize with the hull knocked off and it wants a good ninety minutes longer than the beans, so start it alone or you end up with collapsed beans sitting in chalky corn. Salt and any acid firm up bean pectin, so both go in only once the beans crush easily. Keep the water at a shiver rather than a boil: rolling water strips the skins off the beans and turns the whole pot into grey glue.

ingredients.text: 1.5 kg lamb neck and shank on the bone, in thick pieces

steps.text: Set the three legged pot over a bed of coals and brown the lamb in the oil in batches until every face is properly dark; crowding steams it, so give each piece room, then lift it all out.
Soften the onions and garlic in the same fat until slack and browning at the edges, return the meat, and add wine, water, tomato paste, bay, thyme, pepper and half the salt.

Lid on, rake the coals down to a low glow you can hold a hand over for six seconds, and braise untouched until the neck meat gives when pushed with a spoon, about 2 hours; the lid should mutter, never rattle.
Now layer, and do not stir: potatoes straight onto the meat, then carrots, then butternut, then the green beans on top. Lid back on.

Cook until a skewer slides through the butternut without resistance and the beans are tender but still dark green, 45 to 60 minutes, then lift the pot off, tilt it and spoon gravy from the bottom over the top; serve in layers rather than mixed.

note: A potjie is a stacked steamer, not a stew. Only the meat sits in liquid; everything above it cooks in the steam rising off that liquid, which is why the vegetables go in by density and why lifting the lid to stir is the single thing that ruins the pot. Stir and they drop into the gravy, boil, shed their starch and go to mash. Keep the coals at a mutter; a hard boil does exactly the same damage from below.

ingredients.text: 1 whole snoek of about 2 kg, gutted and split flat down the back
4 garlic cloves, crushed to a paste
1 lemon, juiced, plus wedges to serve

steps.text: Salt the flesh side of the split fish heavily, leave it 30 minutes, then rinse and pat it absolutely dry; a wet surface is what welds a fish to the grid.
Melt the butter with the apricot jam, garlic, vinegar, lemon juice and pepper into a loose, pourable smeer and keep it warm at the side of the fire.
Burn the fire right down until the coals are grey coated with no flame licking through, then oil a hinged grid and clamp the fish in it skin side down.

Grill skin side down, a good hand span above the coals, for 15 to 20 minutes, brushing the flesh with smeer every few minutes once the surface has turned opaque; the skin should blister and char in patches.
Flip for only 2 to 3 minutes to set the glaze. It is done when the thick shoulder flesh lifts away from the two rows of pin bones in one clean sheet; serve with lemon and roosterkoek.

note: Snoek carries its oil in the skin and belly and dries out fast through the middle, so nearly all the time is spent skin side down: the skin is the pan. Flip it early and the flake tears straight through the grid. The smeer is not just sweetness, the jam sugars caramelise while the vinegar and lemon cut the oil, but brush it on only after the flesh has gone opaque or the sugar blackens long before the fish is cooked.

teacher.sub: Technique films from the South African kitchen

ingredients.text: 900 g mutton on the bone, in 4 cm pieces
6 garlic cloves and 20 g ginger, pounded to a paste
350 g ripe tomatoes, coarsely grated and skins discarded

steps.text: Heat the oil and crack the cassia and cardamom in it until they swell and the oil smells of them, then drop in the curry leaves and stand back while they spit.
Add the onions and fry with real patience until they are brown and jammy rather than merely golden; this browning, not the masala, is the body of the gravy.
Stir in the garlic and ginger paste until the raw smell goes, then the masala and turmeric with a splash of water so nothing scorches, and fry until oil beads red at the edge of the pan.
Add the mutton and salt and turn it until sealed all over, then the grated tomato and the water; simmer covered until the meat pulls away from the bone, about 90 minutes.
Add the potatoes and cook uncovered until they are soft and their starch has thickened the gravy enough that a spoon dragged through leaves a trail, 25 to 30 minutes; stir in the coriander.
Only now cut the loaf into quarters, pull the crumb out of each leaving 1.5 cm walls, ladle the curry in and cap it with the pulled crumb.

note: The loaf is the bowl and there is no plate underneath, so the gravy has to be thick enough to sit still. That comes from potato starch released in the last twenty minutes with the lid off, never from flour. Cut the bread at the last moment or the walls go damp and slump. And fry the masala until oil beads red at the pan edge; masala stirred into a wet pan tastes raw and dusty however long it simmers afterwards.

ingredients.text: 1.7 kg lean beef silverside, well trimmed and cold
300 g hard beef or sheep tail fat, never pork fat
20 g whole coriander seed, dry roasted and coarsely cracked
3 m narrow sheep casings, rinsed and soaked

steps.text: Chill the meat and fat until they are firm to the edge of frozen, then mince both once through a 6 to 8 mm plate; one coarse pass is what gives wors its open texture, a second fine pass gives you a hot dog.

Toss the mince with the cracked coriander, pepper, nutmeg, cloves, allspice, salt and chilled vinegar using your hands, only until it is evenly speckled; do not knead it, the protein must not turn sticky and bind.
Cover and rest in the fridge overnight so the salt and vinegar work through, then check the seasoning by frying a teaspoon of it.
Fill the sheep casings loosely and do not twist into links; a slack fill lets the sausage shrink inward as it dries instead of splitting its skin.

Hang the coils in a cool, dry place at 15C to 20C (59F to 68F) with a fan moving air over them, until the wors is hard at the surface and still gives faintly at the core, 2 to 4 days depending on thickness.

note: This is not jerky. Jerky is cooked dry with heat and usually smoke; wors and biltong are raw, and their safety comes from salt pulling water out while brown grape vinegar drops the surface pH below what spoilage organisms tolerate. So the drying stays cool with air always moving; warm still air grows mould in the folds first. Use beef or sheep fat only. Pork fat goes rancid within days of hanging and there is no rescuing it.
techniques: The overnight rest: letting a dish marry

ingredients.text: 30 g butter, softened, plus more to serve

steps.text: Mix the flour, yeast, salt and sugar, add the water and softened butter, and work to a slack, faintly tacky dough; knead until you can stretch a piece thin enough to see light through it without tearing, 8 to 10 minutes.
Prove covered until doubled and the dough springs back slowly and incompletely when pressed with a finger, 60 to 90 minutes in a warm room.
Divide into 12 pieces of about 70 g, roll each into a ball then flatten to a disc 2 cm thick, and prove again under a cloth until visibly puffed and light to lift.
Burn the fire down until the coals are grey and you can hold a hand at grid height for five or six seconds, then oil the grid and lay the discs on well spaced.

Grill, turning every 3 to 4 minutes and shifting them to cooler patches as they colour, until both faces are branded and mottled brown and the underside sounds hollow when knocked, 15 to 20 minutes; tear open and butter while hot.

note: Bread over coals bakes by heat conducting slowly inward, so the fire has to be well past flame. Over a hot bed the crust sets and blackens in three minutes while the middle is still raw dough, and no amount of extra time fixes a sealed crust. Hold your hand at grid height and count: five or six seconds is right. Turn often so neither face runs ahead, and knock the base; hollow means the crumb has set.

steps.text: Soak the chopped apricots in the vinegar and water until they plump and go soft at the edges, about 2 hours; they should squash easily against the side of the bowl.
Simmer the soaked fruit and its liquid with the onion, garlic, ginger, chilli and ground coriander over low heat until the apricots collapse into a rough puree, about 30 minutes.
Add the sugar and salt and stir until every grain has dissolved before you let the pot come back to a simmer; undissolved sugar sinks and catches on the base.
Cook uncovered, stirring more and more often as it thickens, until the surface turns from matt to glossy and a spoon dragged across the base leaves a channel that fills back slowly.
Stir in the sultanas and almonds off the heat, then jar into hot dry jars while the blatjang is still above 85C (185F) and seal at once.

note: Blatjang sets on apricot pectin held by sugar and acid, not on a boiling point, so judge it with the channel test rather than a thermometer. Dissolve the sugar completely before the pot returns to a simmer: crystals sink, scorch, and scorch cannot be stirred back out. Then leave it three weeks before opening a jar. The vinegar is harsh and one dimensional for the first fortnight and only rounds out after that.

ingredients.text: 600 g amaranth leaves, thick stalks stripped out
350 g ripe tomatoes, coarsely grated and skins discarded
40 g raw peanuts, roasted and coarsely pounded

steps.text: Strip the leaves off any woody stalk and wash them through three changes of water; grit sits in the leaf crowns and cooking will not shift it.

Fry the onion in the oil over medium heat until slack and just colouring, then add the chilli and grated tomato and cook until the tomato has gone from bright and watery to dark, thick and beading oil at the edges, about 10 minutes.
Pack the wet leaves in on top, put the lid on and let them collapse in their own steam, turning once when the top layer has wilted.
Uncover, add the water and simmer until the leaf stalks are tender and the pan liquid has reduced to a dark sauce that clings rather than pools.
Salt now, fold in the pounded peanuts off the heat, and serve against stiff maize pap.

note: Amaranth leaves are almost entirely water, so the tomato base has to be cooked down to a dark paste before they go in; a wet base plus wet leaves gives grey soup you cannot reduce back without overcooking the greens. Salt at the end for the same reason. The peanuts are not garnish: their fat carries the leaf bitterness and their protein thickens the sauce enough to cling to pap. Stop while the leaves are still dark green, khaki means the flavour has gone with the chlorophyll.

steps.text: Boil the sugar, water, cream of tartar, cinnamon, lemon peel, lemon juice and ginger for 5 to 8 minutes to a thin syrup that coats a spoon but still runs off freely, then cool and chill it overnight until it is ice cold; split it between two bowls and put one in the freezer.

Rub the cold butter into the flour, baking powder and salt to fine crumbs, beat the egg into the milk and bring it together to a soft dough, knead just 2 minutes until smooth, then rest it covered in the fridge for an hour.
Roll to 6 to 8 mm, cut strips 7 cm by 4 cm, slit each into three legs leaving the top joined, and plait tightly, pinching the tail hard so it cannot unravel in the oil.
Fry a few at a time at 175C (350F), turning, until deep golden right through the plait, 3 to 4 minutes; cooler oil soaks them and hotter oil browns the outside over raw dough at the crossings.

Lift each one straight from the oil, shake off the drips and plunge it immediately into the ice cold syrup, holding it under for 30 seconds before lifting onto a rack; swap to the frozen bowl the moment the first loses its chill.

note: The whole thing is a temperature gap. The koeksister leaves the oil at frying heat, its trapped steam condenses the instant it meets ice cold syrup, and the small vacuum that follows draws syrup deep into the crumb while the crust is chilled too fast to soften. Warm syrup soaks in slowly and evenly instead and you get a limp sweet doughnut with no crack to it. Keep the second bowl in the freezer and swap often. Cream of tartar inverts some sugar so the syrup never crystallises.

ingredients.text: 600 g smoked pork shoulder (palette fumée), in one piece
300 g smoked pork belly, in one piece
Strong mustard and grated horseradish, to serve

steps.text: Rinse the sauerkraut once under cold water and squeeze it dry in handfuls. Taste a strand; it should still make you wince.
Melt the goose fat in a deep pot and sweat the onions until slack and translucent with no colour, then pile in the kraut with the juniper, pepper, bay and cloves tied in muslin.

Bed the smoked shoulder and belly down in the kraut, pour in wine and water to two thirds depth, cover and cook at 150C (300F) until a strand crushes to nothing between finger and thumb, about two and a half hours.
Poach the Strasbourg and Montbéliard sausages in a separate pan of water held at 80C (176F) for 10 minutes, until plump and firm to a squeeze. Do not let it boil.
Boil the potatoes in well salted water until a knife enters with no drag, then pile kraut, sliced meats, sausages and potatoes on a hot dish.

note: Sauerkraut arrives already cooked and already sour; the oven only softens the strand and lets goose fat coat it. Poach the fine sausages apart at 80C (176F), because at a rolling boil the casings split and all their fat leaves them.

ingredients.text: 200 g fromage blanc, drained 2 hours in a sieve

steps.text: Work flour, water, oil and salt to a smooth dough that no longer tacks to the board, cover it, and heat a baking stone at the top of the oven at its maximum, 270C (520F) or hotter, for a full hour.
Beat the drained fromage blanc with the crème fraîche, nutmeg and pepper until it holds a ribbon on the whisk; a loose cream floods the base.
Roll the dough to 2 mm on a floured peel, thin enough to see your hand through, and spread the cream to within a finger of the edge.
Scatter the raw lardons and the onion in a single sparse layer, never a heap, and slide the tart onto the stone.
Bake 6 to 8 minutes, until the rim is blistered black in patches, the lardons have thrown their fat and the base lifts stiff and dry off the stone.

note: No yeast means no gas and no puff: this base exists to dry into a cracker in the time the cream takes to set, and only a fierce oven wins that race. ingredients.text: 400 g pork shoulder, in 4 cm cubes
400 g lamb shoulder, in 4 cm cubes
400 g beef chuck, in 4 cm cubes
1.2 kg waxy potatoes, in 5 mm slices
150 g plain flour, for the seal

steps.text: Marinate the three meats overnight in the cold with the wine, onion, leek, garlic, juniper, bay and thyme; by morning the meat looks grey and the wine has gone cloudy.
Layer the clay terrine potato, meat, potato, salting each layer, and pour in the strained marinade until it just glints between the top slices.
Knead the flour and water to a stiff rope, press it round the rim and set the lid into it, working the paste up over the join until no gap will whistle.
Bake at 160C (320F) for three hours without once lifting the lid. The seal is done when it has gone hard and pale gold.
Crack the seal at the table with a knife point. The escaping steam should smell of wine and juniper, and the top potatoes should still be whole and glossy, not dried at the edges.

ingredients.text: 1 free range chicken, 1.8 kg, jointed into 8

steps.text: Colour the chicken skin side down in the butter and oil over moderate heat until pale gold only, lifting it out before the butter smells nutty; a dark crust muddies a white braise.
Sweat the shallots and lardons in the same fat until the shallot is glassy, add the mushrooms and cook until they squeak and have given up their water.
Pour in the Riesling, scrape the pan clean and reduce by a third, until the smell loses its raw alcohol edge.
Return the legs, then the breasts twelve minutes later, and hold the pan at a bare tremble until the thigh joint runs clear and reads 74C (165F).

Lift the chicken out, stir in the crème fraîche and reduce until the sauce coats a spoon, then pull the pan off the heat and whisk in the yolk slaked with a spoonful of the hot sauce. Sharpen with lemon, scatter parsley.

note: Riesling is the acid in this dish, and acid plus dairy is where a white braise curdles. Crème fraîche at 30 percent fat holds because the fat shields the casein; single cream grains on contact. Reduce the wine before any dairy goes near it, and once the yolk is in keep the pan under 82C (180F) or the liaison scrambles into threads.

ingredients.text: 20 g fresh yeast, or 7 g dried
200 g soft butter, plus 30 g for the mould

steps.text: Soak the raisins in the kirsch until plump and the liquid is all but gone, then butter a cold earthenware mould heavily and drop one almond into each flute.
Mix flour, sugar, salt, yeast, milk and eggs, then work the dough until it slaps clean off the sides of the bowl and stretches to a window without tearing.
Add the soft butter in four additions, taking each fully in before the next, until the dough is glossy and slack. If it climbs past 24C (75F), chill it fifteen minutes and carry on.
Fold in the drained raisins, fill the mould one third full and prove until the crown sits a centimetre below the rim and shivers as one piece when nudged.
Bake at 180C (350F) to a deep chestnut crust reading 94C (200F) at the centre, turn out at once, and dust only when cold.

note: Forty percent butter is more than a raw dough can absorb, so build the gluten on milk and egg alone, then feed the butter in four goes. Hold the dough under 24C (75F): warmer and the butter melts out, greasing the crumb short instead of shreddable. Butter the mould cold, since a warm one sheds its film and the flutes tear on unmoulding. Allow two hours to prove and 45 minutes in the oven.

steps.text: Beat flour, eggs, milk, salt and nutmeg hard with a wooden spoon until the batter blisters and falls from the spoon in a sheet rather than in drops, then rest it 20 minutes.
Bring a wide pan of well salted water to a shiver, not a rolling boil, and hold it there.
Press the batter through a spaetzle plate or a wide holed colander straight onto the water, in batches, so the surface is never crowded.
Lift them out 30 seconds after they float and drain hard; they should be firm at the edge and still tender at the core.
Fry the onion in the butter until deep brown at the frill, add the spaetzle and toss over high heat until they take a lace of gold on one side.

note: Beat the batter until it blisters and hangs in a sheet, then rest it. Slack, unrested gluten frays into rags the moment it meets water. Keep the water at a bare shiver, because a rolling boil tears the strands before they set. They are cooked 30 seconds after they surface; longer and you carry waterlogged dumplings to the butter pan, where they steam instead of browning.

ingredients.text: 300 g rabbit, boned, in 3 cm batons
300 g chicken thigh, boned, in 3 cm batons
300 g veal shoulder, in 3 cm batons
300 g pork belly, in 3 cm batons
400 ml white beer or dry white wine
12 thin slices unsmoked streaky bacon, to line

steps.text: Marinate the four meats overnight in the beer, vinegar, onion, juniper, bay and pepper, turning once; the surfaces firm up and pale.
Line a terrine with the bacon, stand the batons upright and packed tight with the four meats alternating, and tuck the split trotter down one side.
Pour in the strained marinade to just below the top of the meat, cover with paper and a lid, and cook at 150C (300F) for three hours, until a baton parts under a fork with no spring left in it.
Spoon a little hot cooking liquid onto a cold saucer and wait five minutes: it must set to a firm wobble. If it slumps, dissolve the soaked gelatine into the pot.
Weight the terrine lightly, chill overnight until fully set, then turn out and slice thick, serving at cellar temperature with frites and mustard.

note: The jelly is collagen from the trotter and nothing else, and the vinegar earns its keep twice: it speeds collagen into gelatine and it stops cold fat tasting waxy. Always test a spoonful on a cold saucer before chilling, because a weak set collapses the moment you slice. Serve at about 14C (57F); fridge cold mutes the jelly and hardens the fat.

ingredients.text: 1.2 kg beef chuck or paleron, in 5 cm pieces
30 g vergeoise or dark brown sugar

steps.text: Dry the beef on cloth and brown it hard in the lard in uncrowded batches, until every face is mahogany and the pan floor is dark but not black.
Cook the onions in the same fat until they collapse to a deep gold jam, using the water they give up to lift the fond off the base.
Deglaze with the ale, add the stock, vergeoise, vinegar, bay and thyme, and bring to a bare simmer.
Spread the pain d'épices thickly with mustard, lay the slices mustard side down on the surface, cover, and cook at 150C (300F) for three hours, until the beef gives at the push of a spoon.
Whisk the softened bread through the sauce until it is glossy and coats, then taste and pull the bitterness back with a little more vergeoise or a few drops of vinegar.

note: Beer reduces, the alcohol leaves and the bitterness stays, so a hoppy ale turns acrid over three hours: use a brown Flemish ale and keep the lid on so the volume barely falls. There is no roux in this pot. The pain d'épices spread with mustard melts down and its starch does the thickening, while vergeoise and vinegar at the end are the brake on the bitter.

ingredients.text: 2 leeks, white only, in fine julienne

steps.text: Sweat the leek, carrot, celery and celeriac in the butter with a pinch of salt until the leek smells sweet and nothing has taken any colour.
Lay the chicken on the vegetables, pour in the stock, add the potatoes and hold at a bare shiver until the thigh reads 74C (165F) and a knife slides through the potato.
Lift out the chicken and the vegetables and keep them warm, then skim the fat off the broth and taste it for strength.
Whisk the yolks and cream together and slacken them with two ladles of hot broth poured in a thread, then return the mixture to the pan off the heat.
Stir over the lowest possible heat until the broth thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon, 78 to 82C (172 to 180F), then finish with lemon, chervil and parsley and ladle it over the chicken.

note: This is a broth thickened with egg rather than flour, which makes the whole pot a custard held just below the point where yolk protein sets hard. Temper the yolks with hot broth poured in a thread, and never take the pan past 82C (180F). One second of boiling and the liaison breaks into strands of sweet scrambled egg in thin soup.

ingredients.text: 1 whole farmhouse munster, about 400 g, in its box
1 head of frisée or a bowl of lamb's lettuce

steps.text: Take the cheese out of the cold a full hour ahead and leave it in its box; at fridge temperature the paste is rigid and it tastes of nothing but salt.
Boil the potatoes in their skins in heavily salted water until a knife slides in and out with no drag, then drain and keep them covered and hot.
Toast the seed in a dry pan over low heat, shaking, until it darkens a shade and smells of aniseed rather than dust, then crush it coarsely.
Warm the whole cheese in its box at 90C (195F) for 10 to 12 minutes, until the centre wobbles under a fingertip while the rind still stands up.
Dress the leaves with shallot, vinegar and oil, split the hot potatoes open and spoon the running cheese over them, finishing with the crushed seed and pepper.

note: A washed rind cheese has already been broken down by its own enzymes: it flows at 30 to 35C (86 to 95F) and wants no more heat than that. Push it past 60C (140F) and the fat splits out while the rind's ammonia concentrates into something acrid. The seed, caraway as often as true cumin in Alsace, is not decoration; its carvone reads straight across those ammoniacal notes and settles them.

ingredients.text: 200 g crumb from a day-old dense white loaf, torn
150 ml extra virgin olive oil, picual if you have it
1 small garlic clove, green germ removed
60 g jamón serrano, torn into strips

steps.text: Blitz the chilled tomatoes on their own to a purée, then tear in the bread and leave it 10 minutes, until the crumb collapses when you press it.
Add the garlic and salt and blend in short bursts until no flecks of skin remain, stopping if the jug starts to feel warm under your hand.
Drop to the lowest speed and pour the oil in a thin thread until the colour turns from red to pale coral and the surface reads matt rather than shiny.
Season with the vinegar and chill for two hours; it is right when a spoon drawn through leaves a track that closes slowly.
Serve in shallow bowls with the egg, the jamón and a last thread of oil.

note: There is no water in salmorejo: the body is tomato pulp thickened with bread starch, carrying about a fifth of its weight in oil as droplets. Two failures. Warm tomatoes give a thin, slack cream, so start cold. And a long blast of the blender shears the oil droplets small enough to release their phenolics, which turns the bowl bitter, so thread the oil in on the lowest speed and stop the moment it goes coral.

ingredients.text: 80 g crumb from a day-old white loaf
1 small garlic clove, green germ removed
150 ml extra virgin olive oil, a mild hojiblanca or arbequina
750 ml iced water, plus more to loosen
200 g Moscatel grapes, halved and seeded

steps.text: Soak the bread crumb in 100 ml of the iced water until sodden, then squeeze it lightly.
Grind the almonds with the garlic and salt to a paste, adding water a spoonful at a time; it is ready when a smear rubbed between finger and thumb feels smooth with no grain at all.
Add the soaked bread, then pour the oil in a slow thread on a low speed until the paste turns chalk white and glossy and thickens like loose mayonnaise.
Let the rest of the iced water down in stages to the thickness of single cream, stir the vinegar in by hand off the machine, and chill hard for two hours.
Serve very cold with the grapes scattered over and a thread of oil.

note: Almonds carry no starch, so this emulsion rests on almond protein with a little bread starch behind it. Grit means under milling: take the almonds to a smooth paste before any liquid joins them. Splitting means acid too early; vinegar and salt together drive the almond protein to clump and shed its oil, so the vinegar goes in last, by hand, into a cold finished base.

ingredients.text: 500 g waxy potatoes, peeled and cut in 1 cm slices
1.2 litres light fish stock or salted water
300 g hake fillet, in large pieces
300 g clams, purged in salted water
200 ml mild olive oil or sunflower oil
15 ml lemon juice, plus more to finish

steps.text: Simmer the potatoes in the stock until a knife slides out without lifting the slice, then slide in the hake and clams and poach until the clams gape and the hake flakes at a light push.
Lift out the fish, clams and potatoes and keep them warm; take the pan off the heat and let the broth go still.
Make a mayonnaise with the egg, a pinch of salt and the oil, working the oil in a thread until it holds the whisk marks, then slacken it with the lemon juice.
Whisk one ladle of the hot broth into the mayonnaise, then a second, then a third, before pouring the lot back into the pan off the heat.
Stir until the broth turns opaque ivory and thickens to single cream, return the fish and potatoes, scatter parsley and serve at once.

note: This is a mayonnaise stirred into hot broth, and yolk proteins begin coagulating around 65C (150F). Ladle broth into the mayonnaise a little at a time to bring it up gently, then return it to the pan off the heat; one trip back to the boil curdles it into greasy shreds in cloudy water. If it looks like breaking, whisk in a spoon of cold water. It will not survive reheating.

ingredients.text: 600 g mixed small fish: whole boquerones, small red mullet, hake tails, squid rings
300 g fine soft wheat frying flour, or 250 g plain flour sifted with 50 g chickpea flour

steps.text: Salt the fish lightly, leave it 10 minutes, then blot every piece dry; a wet surface will not take a thin coat.
Bring the oil to 180C (355F); a pinch of flour dropped in should fizz and rise at once rather than sink and sit.
Toss a handful of fish through the flour, shake it in a sieve until only a dusty veil clings, and lower it straight into the oil.
Fry in small batches so the oil never falls below 170C (340F); each piece is done when it floats and the loud bubbling drops to a whisper, 60 to 90 seconds for boquerones.
Lift onto a wire rack, salt while still glistening and eat within the minute, with lemon.

note: The coat is a veil, not a batter: finely milled soft wheat hydrates on the fish's own damp surface and dehydrates into a shell before the flesh can push steam out. That needs 180C (355F). Below about 165C the shell forms too slowly, water escapes through it and oil moves in to take its place, which is exactly why bad fried fish is limp and heavy. Small batches, and a rack, never stacked paper.

ingredients.text: 250 ml iced water, or half water and half clean sea water
60 g spring onion, very finely chopped
15 g flat leaf parsley, finely chopped
400 ml olive oil for shallow frying

steps.text: Whisk the two flours with the iced water and salt to a batter that runs off the ladle in an unbroken stream, thinner than instinct says, then rest it cold for an hour.
Stir in the shrimp, spring onion and parsley, keeping the bowl sitting on ice so the batter stays cold.
Heat 1 cm of oil to 185C (365F); a drop of batter should spit and lace immediately.
Pour a small ladle in close to the surface and spread it thin at once with the back of the ladle, so it opens into a ragged disc pierced with holes.
Fry until the edges are lace brown and the underside lifts free without tearing, turn once, then drain on a rack and salt.

note: The batter is meant to be as thin as crepe batter. Water flashing to steam is what blows the lace holes; a thick batter has nothing to blow and fries into a pancake. Chickpea flour brings no gluten, so nothing turns elastic and the starch sets brittle. Hold the oil at 185C (365F) and spread each ladleful thin on contact, or the tortillita puffs, drinks oil and stays raw in the middle.

ingredients.text: 1.6 kg oxtail, cut through the joints

steps.text: Salt the oxtail an hour ahead, dry it, dust it thinly with flour and brown it hard in the oil until every face is deep mahogany with no pale patches, then lift it out.

Soften the onion, carrot, pepper and garlic in the same fat until the onion is tawny and the pan base is sticky brown, then add the grated tomato and cook until it darkens and the oil runs clear at the edges.
Pour in the sherry and scrape the base clean, reducing until the sharp alcohol smell has gone and what rises is nutty and raisined.

Return the tail with the bay, peppercorns and clove, add stock to two thirds up the meat, and hold it at a bare tremble with the lid ajar for three hours, until a skewer meets no resistance and the meat has pulled back from the bone.
Cool overnight, lift off the set fat cap, then reduce the sauce until it coats a spoon and warm the tail through in it.

note: Oxtail is collagen, and collagen needs hours near 85 to 90C (185 to 195F) to turn to gelatine. At a rolling boil the muscle fibres wring themselves dry long before that happens, leaving shreds in thin liquid, so keep the surface barely trembling. Dry oloroso is the right wine because it carries oxidised, nutty depth with no residual sugar; reduce it hard before the stock goes in or a raw solvent edge stays in the sauce.

ingredients.text: 400 g cooked chickpeas, plus 200 ml of their cooking liquid
50 g day-old bread, in two thin slices

steps.text: Fry the bread and garlic in the oil until the bread is gold on both sides and the garlic smells nutty, pulling both out before either darkens.
Pound the bread, garlic, cumin and a good pinch of salt in a mortar, working in the vinegar, until the paste is stiff enough to hold a ridge.
Wilt the spinach in the same pan in batches, tip it into a sieve and press hard; it should give up a surprising amount of green water.
Take the pan off the heat, stir the pimentón through the warm oil for a few seconds only, then add the chickpeas, the pounded paste and the chickpea liquid.
Return to a low heat with the spinach and simmer until the sauce clings to the chickpeas instead of running around them, then check the salt and vinegar.

note: The mortar does the thickening: fried bread pounded with garlic, cumin and vinegar spreads gelatinised starch and oil through the chickpea liquor so the sauce clings rather than pools. Two failures. Pimentón scorches in hot oil within seconds and turns acrid, so it goes in off the heat. And spinach holds enormous water; squeeze it hard or the pan floods and nothing ever binds.

steps.text: Split the kidneys and cut out every scrap of white core and hard fat, then soak the pieces 20 minutes in cold water with the vinegar, rinse, and dry them until the surface feels tacky rather than wet.
Sear them in very hot oil one layer at a time, browned outside but rosy at the centre, lifting each batch out the moment it colours.
Lower the heat and soften the onion and garlic with the bay leaf until translucent and sweet.
Pour in the sherry and reduce by half, until the smell turns from sharp to nutty, then add the stock and reduce again to a glaze that coats the spoon.
Slide the kidneys and their resting juices back for 30 seconds only, just to warm through, then take the pan off the heat, add parsley and serve with bread.

note: Kidney is a sprint. Past about 60C (140F) the tissue contracts and squeezes out its residual urea in the juices, which is the ammonia note people blame on the offal itself, and it goes rubbery at the same moment. Sear hot in batches so they never steam, take them out rosy, and let them rejoin the sauce only to warm. Cut out every scrap of white core first, because that is where the taint lives.

ingredients.text: 500 g ripe tomatoes, grated, or passata
150 g green beans, cut short and blanched

steps.text: Fry the jamón and chorizo in the oil until the fat runs orange, lift them out, and soften the onion, pepper and garlic in that fat until slack and sweet.
Off the heat stir in the pimentón, then the tomato, and cook it down until the sauce darkens and a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a track that stays open.
Heat four earthenware cazuelas, divide the sofrito between them while it is still hot, and press two hollows into each with the back of a spoon.
Crack an egg into each hollow, ring them with the peas, beans, asparagus, jamón and chorizo, and bake at 200C (390F) for 6 to 8 minutes.
Pull them out while the whites are just opaque and the yolks still shiver; the earthenware finishes the cooking on the way to the table.

note: White sets around 62 to 65C, yolk around 65 to 70C, and that narrow gap is the whole dish. The sofrito must be properly hot when the eggs go in, so the underside of the white cooks from below while the oven works from above; on a cold base the whites are still slimy underneath by the time the yolks go chalky. Earthenware keeps cooking off the heat, so pull the dish early.

ingredients.text: 1 strip of lemon peel, no pith
60 g caster sugar for the caramel

steps.text: Cook the 60 g of sugar with its water to a light amber caramel and swirl it around a warm mould to coat the base and a finger's depth of the sides, then leave it to set hard.
Boil the remaining sugar and water with the lemon peel to 105 to 110C (220 to 230F), the point where a cooled drop pulled between finger and thumb draws a short thread.
Stir the yolks smooth without whisking air into them, trickle the hot syrup in slowly while stirring, then pass the mixture through a fine sieve.
Pour into the caramelled mould, cover with foil and bake in a bain marie at 150C (300F) for about 40 minutes, until the centre wobbles as one piece and a skewer comes out with only a film on it.
Cool, chill for four hours, then turn out so the caramel runs down the sides.

note: No whites, no cream, no gelatine: the only structure is yolk protein, which sets between 65 and 70C. So the syrup, at 105 to 110C (220 to 230F), goes onto the yolks in a slow thread with constant stirring, or it scrambles them on contact. The bain marie holds the custard near 85C; direct oven heat drives it past 90C and it curdles and weeps syrup. Stir without raising foam or the set turns spongy instead of dense.
