ingredients.text: 4 pieces salt cod loin, 160 g each, skin on, desalted
300 ml mild olive oil, arbequina or a soft picual
1 dried guindilla chilli, seeds shaken out
flaky salt, only if the cod needs it

steps.text: Blot the desalted loins bone dry on a cloth, skin down; any surface water will thin the gelatine and stall the sauce later.
Warm the oil with the garlic and chilli in a wide shallow cazuela over low heat until the slices turn pale straw and rise, then lift them out before they colour past gold.

Let the oil settle to 60 to 65C (140 to 150F), where a bead breaks the surface only every few seconds. Slide the cod in skin down and poach 6 to 8 minutes, until a white curd weeps from under the skin and the flakes shift when nudged.
Lift the cod to a warm plate. Pour the oil into a jug and leave the pan until it is hand warm; a milky layer of gelatine will have collected on the base.

Off the heat, add two tablespoons of oil to that gelatine and swirl the pan flat on the worktop in a slow circle. As it goes opaque, dribble in the rest of the oil in a thread, swirling without pause, until the sauce is ivory, glossy and coats the back of a spoon.
Return the cod skin up, tilt to flood it with sauce, and scatter the reserved garlic and chilli over the top.

note: No egg and no flour: the sauce is cod gelatine and olive oil alone. Skin and collagen release that gelatine only in a narrow band around 60 to 65C (140 to 150F); let the oil bubble and the protein tightens, the cod weeps water instead of gel, and nothing will emulsify. Build it off the heat and swirl the pan flat rather than stirring, because a spoon shears the oil droplets the swirl keeps whole. Desalting is 48 hours in cold water, changed four times.
techniques: The bare simmer: holding liquid below the boil

ingredients.text: 500 g hake kokotxas, the throats, grey membrane trimmed
8 small clams, purged in salted water
100 ml txakoli or another sharp dry white
30 g flat parsley leaves, very finely chopped

steps.text: Salt the kokotxas lightly, leave 10 minutes, then blot both faces on a cloth until the surface is matt rather than slippery.
Warm the oil with garlic and chilli in a wide cazuela over the lowest heat until the garlic is pale gold, then fish it out and set it aside.

Take the pan off the heat until the oil is hand warm, lay the kokotxas in skin side down in a single layer, and set it back on the barest heat for 3 minutes, until white beads of gel gather round each edge.

Off the heat again, swirl the pan flat and slow for 3 to 4 minutes; the oil and the seeping gel will bind and turn pale and cloudy. Add the wine and the clams, swirl over low heat until the shells gape and the sauce falls from the spoon in a ribbon.
Kill the heat, shower in the parsley, swirl once more so it stays bright green, and serve in the cazuela.

note: Kokotxas are almost pure collagen, so salsa verde is pil pil with parsley: the gel that seeps from the throats emulsifies the garlic oil. Above a bare tremble they clench, squeeze out water instead of gel, and the pan becomes a puddle of oil floating on fish juice. Keep the cazuela hand warm, swirl it flat on the worktop, and add the wine only once the sauce has already gone pale and thick.

ingredients.text: 2 spider crabs, about 1 kg each, or 500 g picked white and brown crab meat
250 g onion, in a very fine dice
1 leek, white part only, finely diced
2 tbsp choricero pepper pulp, scraped from 2 soaked dried peppers
200 ml txakoli or dry white wine
200 g tomato, grated on the coarse side and drained

steps.text: Cook the crabs in water salted to 35 g per litre at a bare shiver, 15 minutes per kilo, then cool. Pick every scrap of white meat and scrape the brown meat, coral and juices from the shell into a second bowl. Scrub the top shells and keep them.
Sweat the onion and leek in the oil with a pinch of salt over low heat for 25 minutes, until they slump into a pale jam that tastes sweet with no raw edge.

Stir in the garlic and choricero pulp for 2 minutes, add the brandy and cook it out until the fumes no longer catch the back of your throat, then the wine and tomato. Reduce until a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a track that stays open.
Off the heat, fold in the white meat and all of the brown, which is both the flavour and the binder. Correct with salt and a knife tip of cayenne; it should taste half a step too seasoned while hot.
Pack into the shells, cover with crumbs and dots of butter, and grill close to the element for 4 to 5 minutes, until the crust is dark gold and the edges bubble.

note: The brown meat is the sauce. Its fat and protein bind the sofrito and carry the iodine flavour, so picking only white meat leaves a dry, sweet, characterless filling. Fold everything in off the heat: crab protein is already fully cooked and a second hard simmer turns the strands to cotton wool. The grill is there for the crumb, not the crab, so keep it fierce and brief.

ingredients.text: 700 g bonito del norte loin, skinned and boned, in 3 cm cubes
3 tbsp choricero pepper pulp, from 3 soaked dried peppers
1.2 litres light fish stock or water

steps.text: Sweat the onion, green pepper and garlic in the oil with a good pinch of salt over low heat for 20 minutes, until everything is translucent and smells sweet rather than sharp.
Stir in the choricero pulp and cook 2 minutes, until it darkens a shade and the raw paste smell gives way to dried pepper.

Tear the potatoes rather than slicing them: push the knife tip in 2 cm and lever until the chunk snaps away, leaving a ragged face. Turn them through the sofrito, add the guindilla and cover with stock.
Simmer at a lazy blip for 20 to 25 minutes, until a potato crushes against the side of the pot with no resistance and the broth has thickened enough to cling to the spoon.

Season the bonito, take the pot off the heat entirely, submerge the cubes and clamp on the lid. After 5 minutes they should be opaque at the edge and still faintly rose at the centre; serve straight away.

note: Two things thicken this pot and neither is flour. Tearing the potato rips cells open so starch leaks into the broth, and choricero pulp adds body with its sweet dried pepper flavour. Bonito is very lean; its muscle proteins wring out moisture above roughly 55C (130F) and it goes chalky in seconds. Add it with the heat off and the lid on, and let residual warmth set it only to rosy.

ingredients.text: 12 piparra peppers in vinegar, the pale thin skinned ones, drained
12 Cantabrian anchovy fillets in olive oil

steps.text: Lay the piparras on a cloth, pinch off the stalks and leave them until the cloth stops darkening; blot the anchovies on the same cloth. Wet components let the vinegar bleed and the pintxo slides apart on the stick.
Fold each anchovy into a concertina of three, then thread piparra, anchovy, olive and a second piparra so the fish is trapped in the middle and nothing can spin.
Stand them in a shallow dish, spoon over the anchovy oil, and leave 10 minutes in a warm room until the oil runs clear and loose before eating.

note: Three tastes on one stick, each with a job: anchovy for salt and glutamate, piparra for acid, olive for fat and bitterness. It fails on temperature and on water. Fridge cold, the anchovy oil is stiff and only salt registers; straight from the jar, vinegar bleeds out and blurs everything. Blot dry, build, then let them stand ten minutes at room temperature.

ingredients.text: 16 whole piquillo peppers from Lodosa, drained but never rinsed
300 g salt cod, desalted, in pieces
1 onion, 150 g, in a fine dice
4 broken or torn piquillos, for the sauce
100 ml light fish stock or the poaching milk

steps.text: Poach the cod in the milk with the garlic clove at 70C (160F), just under a shiver, for 6 minutes, until the flakes part under a fork. Lift it out, keep the milk hot, and flake the fish, discarding skin and bone.

Sweat the onion in the oil until soft and blond, about 12 minutes. Scatter in the flour and cook 3 minutes until it smells of biscuit, then beat in the hot milk a ladle at a time until the bechamel pulls away from the base in one mass.
Fold in the flaked cod, season with nutmeg and salt, spread on a cold tray, press cling film onto the surface and chill until it is firm enough to hold a piped ridge.
Pipe the filling into each pepper through its open end, stopping just short of the rim so there is room to expand, and set them seam down in a wide pan.

Blend the broken peppers with the cream and stock, pour around the parcels, and warm at a bare tremble for 6 to 8 minutes, until the filling is hot through and the sauce has reduced to the colour of terracotta.

note: Piquillos from Lodosa are roasted over wood and peeled dry, never washed, so their smoke sits on the surface; rinsing them throws away the thing you paid for. The filling has to be a stiff bechamel, cooked until it leaves the pan in one mass and then chilled hard, because starch pastes loosen as they warm. Pipe a soft one and the pepper splits along its seam and empties into the sauce.

ingredients.text: 800 g leeks, white and pale green only, in 2 cm rings
1.2 litres water or a light vegetable broth
extra virgin olive oil, to finish

steps.text: Drop the leek rings into a bowl of cold water and swish, then lift them out with your hands so the grit stays behind. Drain them hard and shake dry; wet leeks steam instead of sweating.
Sweat the leeks and garlic in the oil with a good pinch of salt over low heat for 15 minutes, lid ajar, until they slump and turn silky without taking any colour at all.

Tear the potatoes with a knife tip so every face is ragged, add them with the carrot, cover with the water and simmer at a lazy blip for 25 minutes, until a potato collapses under the back of a spoon.

Crush a third of the potato against the side of the pot and stir it through; the broth should thicken to the weight of single cream. Rest 10 minutes off the heat, season, and finish each bowl with raw oil.

note: A soup of two ingredients has to be built out of texture. Tearing the potatoes gives ragged faces that shed starch into the water, and crushing a third of them at the end thickens the broth to the weight of single cream with no flour anywhere. The one real failure is colour: brown the leeks even slightly and the soup turns grey and faintly bitter. Sweat them salted and covered, and never let them sizzle.

ingredients.text: 1 aged rib chop on the bone, 1.2 to 1.4 kg, 5 cm thick, fat cap deep yellow
coarse sea salt, a generous handful
3 kg oak or holm oak charcoal, or dry vine cuttings

steps.text: Stand the chop uncovered on a rack until the centre is 18 to 20C (64 to 68F) and the surface is dry to the touch. A fridge cold core forces you to burn the outside to warm the inside.
Burn the charcoal down past the flames until the bed glows dull orange under a coat of grey ash and you can hold a hand 10 cm above the grill for three seconds, no longer.
Grill unsalted, 6 to 8 minutes a side for 5 cm, turning once, until the fat crackles and the crust is mahogany and dry. Hold the chop on its fat edge with tongs for a final 2 minutes to render it.
Rest on a warm rack, never a plate, for 12 to 15 minutes; it is ready when the surface stops steaming and the meat gives like the heel of your palm.
Carve the eye off the bone, slice across the grain in 1 cm strips, and salt the cut faces heavily with coarse salt at the table.

note: Salt goes on after carving, not before. On the raw surface it draws out water that has to boil off before a crust can form, so the meat greys; on the cut face it dissolves on contact and reads cleanly as seasoning. Grill over embers with no flame, because dripping fat that ignites lays down soot rather than smoke. Rest twelve minutes on a rack so the core, around 48C (118F), and the scorched outside meet in the middle.

ingredients.text: 300 ml double cream, at least 35 percent fat, very cold
1 strip lemon peel and 1 cinnamon stick
3 eggs, 90 g caster sugar and 90 g plain flour, for the sponge
100 ml water, 80 g sugar and 30 ml rum, for the syrup
100 g caster sugar, for the caramel

steps.text: Whip the cream with the icing sugar only to soft peaks that hold their shape but fold over as the whisk lifts, then spoon it into the base of six straight glasses and chill; this layer has to carry the sponge.

Infuse the milk with lemon peel and cinnamon. Whisk yolks, sugar and cornflour, temper with the hot milk, then cook it back in the pan, whisking hard, until it thickens and throws one heavy bubble; keep it there a full minute, then cool with film on the surface.
Whisk the eggs and sugar to the ribbon, fold in the sifted flour in three goes, bake in a shallow tin at 180C (350F) for 12 minutes until the top springs back, and cool.
Cut discs of sponge to fit the glasses, lay one on the cream and spoon over the rum syrup until the crumb is soaked through but no liquid pools at the edge.
Spread the cold pastry cream over the sponge and level it, chill an hour, then pour on thin caramel or dust with sugar and blowtorch to an amber sheet that cracks under a spoon.

note: Pastry cream is a starch gel and it has to boil. Cornflour granules only burst above about 95C (203F), and the same heat destroys the amylase in the yolks that would otherwise digest the set overnight. Pull it early and it looks thick in the pan, then thins in the fridge and floods the sponge. Whisk through that first heavy bubble and hold it there a full minute.

ingredients.text: 1.5 kg ripe quinces, hard and fragrant, grey down rubbed off
caster sugar, the same weight as the finished pulp, roughly 900 g
300 g Idiazabal, a well smoked wheel, in thin wedges

steps.text: Quarter the quinces without peeling or coring and cook them in barely enough water to cover, 30 to 40 minutes, until a knife slides through the flesh with no resistance. The cores and skins hold most of the pectin.
Lift them out, pull away cores and peel, and pass the flesh through a mouli. Weigh the puree and add an equal weight of sugar plus the lemon juice.

Cook over low heat in a heavy pan, stirring and standing clear of the spits, for 45 to 60 minutes, until the paste has turned from blush pink to deep brick and a spoon leaves a track that closes only slowly.
Pour into a lined tin to a depth of 3 cm, level the top, and leave uncovered at room temperature until it has skinned over and is firm enough to cut cleanly.
Slice 5 mm thick and serve with wedges of Idiazabal left out of the fridge for an hour, and the cracked walnuts alongside.

note: Quince sets on its own pectin, which needs acid, sugar and a long enough boil to link into a network. Cook the fruit with cores and skins on, because that is where the pectin sits, and add lemon with the sugar. Underdone, the paste stays tacky and slumps on the board; pushed well past deep brick it goes grainy. Stop at the slow closing track, and let the cheese warm up so its fat softens.

ingredients.text: 1 kg white onions, halved and sliced thin along the grain
400 g very ripe tomatoes, halved and grated on the coarse side, skins discarded

steps.text: Warm the oil in a wide low pan over the smallest flame, add the onions and the salt, and turn them through the oil. The salt pulls water out so they stew rather than fry.

Cook uncovered, stirring every ten minutes and scraping the base, until the onions have collapsed to a third of their bulk, lost every trace of white and gone the colour of weak tea. No browned frilly edges.
If a film sticks to the pan, splash in a spoon of water and scrape it back into the mass; that film is flavour, not damage.
Add the grated tomato and the bay leaf, lift the heat a little, and cook until the whole thing darkens to brick red.
Stop when the oil separates and pools clear around the edge and a spoon dragged through the middle leaves a track that fills back slowly. Discard the bay.

note: Sofregit is a water removal exercise, not a browning one. While the onions still hold water they sit at 100C (212F) and cannot caramelise, so pushing the heat only scorches the outsides bitter before the insides give up their liquid. Wait for the oil to separate and run clear at the edge: that split is the signal the water has gone. Allow 90 minutes in the pan.

ingredients.text: 30 g blanched almonds, toasted until they smell of biscuit
20 g day-old country bread, fried in olive oil until deep gold
a good pinch of saffron threads, dried in a warm pan and crumbled
1 ladle of the hot cooking liquid from the dish it will thicken

steps.text: Pound the garlic with a pinch of flaky salt in a stone mortar until it is a smooth white paste with no fibre. The salt crystals give the pestle grip.
Add the nuts a few at a time and grind, pressing and turning rather than striking down, until the paste is fine sand with no whole pieces left to catch on a tooth.
Work in the fried bread and the saffron until the mass takes a dull matte sheen and holds together in one lump on the pestle.
Bruise in the parsley last, only until the paste is streaked green, then slacken with the hot cooking liquid to the thickness of double cream.
Stir into the simmering dish in its final ten minutes and cook no longer.

note: A picada thickens by suspension, not by starch gelling: the nut and bread particles swell with liquid and the nut oils hold everything in a loose cloud. Put it in early and those oils cook out, the bread dissolves and the perfume of raw garlic, parsley and saffron boils away, leaving a muddy body and no lift. Ten gentle minutes binds it; longer undoes it.

teacher.sub: Technique films from the Catalonia kitchen

ingredients.text: 25 g garlic, about 4 fat cloves, green germ removed
250 ml mild olive oil, at room temperature
a few drops of lemon juice or warm water, only if needed

steps.text: Pound the garlic and salt in a heavy mortar, turning the pestle always in the same direction, until you have a slack ivory paste with no fibre left in it, three or four minutes of real work.
Start the oil literally drop by drop down the side of the pestle, never breaking the circular stroke and never stirring back and forth.
Watch for the paste to go pale, glossy and thick enough to climb the pestle. That is the emulsion taking hold; only now move to a thin unbroken thread of oil.
Stop the moment the allioli stands in a peak that does not slump. If it slackens, weeps a bead of oil or looks grainy, add no more oil.
To rescue a split batch, pound one fresh clove with salt in a clean mortar and beat the broken sauce into it a teaspoon at a time.

note: Garlic brings no egg lecithin, so the only emulsifiers are its own mucilage and pulverised protein, and every drop of oil has to be sheared into droplets before the next arrives. Pour fast, use fridge-cold oil, or reverse the pestle stroke and the droplets merge and the sauce weeps. Bitterness is a separate fault: hard shearing of a peppery oil shatters its polyphenols, so choose a mild one.

ingredients.text: 4 nyora peppers, stems and seeds shaken out

steps.text: Cover the nyoras with warm water and leave them until the flesh is soft and slippery, then open each one flat and scrape the pulp off the skin with a teaspoon. Keep the pulp, bin the skin.
Oil the tomatoes and the garlic head and roast at 200C (390F) until the tomato skins blister and split and a clove squeezed from the head comes out like paste.
Fry the bread and the nuts in a little of the oil until deep gold and smelling toasted, then drain them on paper.
Pound the nuts and bread to fine sand in the mortar, then work in the nyora pulp, the roast garlic, the peeled tomato flesh, the herbs and the salt.
Beat in the rest of the oil in a slow thread, then the vinegar, until the sauce is orange-red and falls from the spoon like loose cream. Rest it an hour before serving.

note: Nyora is a dried sweet pepper, not a chilli, and its whole flavour sits in a thin flesh glued to a leathery skin that no blender will ever break down. Blitz the pepper whole and the sauce is gritty and tastes of cardboard: soak it for 30 minutes, scrape the pulp off with a spoon, discard the skin. The nut and bread sand is what keeps the oil from splitting back out.

ingredients.text: 24 calçots, or 24 slim spring onions with at least 3 cm of white bulb
vine cuttings or dry hardwood for the fire
newspaper or clean brown paper, for wrapping

steps.text: Burn the wood down to leaping flame over glowing cuttings. You want live fire here, not the settled embers you would bank down for a slow roast.
Trim the roots and cut the green tops back to a hand's length, then lay the calçots straight across the grate, touching each other.
Char hard, turning once, until the outer two layers are black the whole way round and the point of a knife slides into the bulb with no resistance.
Stack them hot into newspaper, fold the parcel shut and leave it 20 minutes. The trapped steam lifts the burnt sheaths off the sweet core.
To eat, hold the green top in one hand, pinch the black sheath at the base with the other and pull down. Salt the pale stem, drag it through salvitxada and lower it in from above.

note: The black is not a mistake, it is a sacrificial layer. A calçot holds enough water to steam its own middle while the outside burns, so the fire must be fierce and the cooking short. Grill them gently instead and the sugars set into a scorched crust welded to the flesh, and nothing peels cleanly. The paper wrap is the real second cooking stage; skip it and the skins tear off in shreds.

ingredients.text: 4 tbsp Arbequina olive oil, plus more to finish

steps.text: Set the vegetables whole, dry and unoiled straight over coals or a gas flame. Do not prick them: the skin is the cooking vessel.
Turn them every few minutes until the pepper skin is blistered black and lifting away in sheets and the aubergine has slumped, hissing steam and feeling light for its size.
Pull each one as it is ready. The aubergine is done when a finger sinks in with no bounce back; the onions take longest, until a knife slides to the centre.
Pile everything hot into a bowl, cover it, and let the steam work on the skins for 15 minutes.
Peel with your fingers, never under a tap. Tear the flesh into long strips along the grain, salt it, and dress with the oil, the raw garlic and every drop of smoky juice left in the bowl.

note: Escalivar means to cook in the ashes. The skin is a sealed bag: inside it the flesh steams in its own water at 100C (212F) while the outside burns away, which is exactly why you must not pierce or oil it first. Rinsing the char off afterwards is the usual ruin, because water carries away the smoke and the concentrated juices with it. Wipe your fingers on a cloth instead.

ingredients.text: 300 g salt cod loin, thick cut
100 g sweet onion, sliced as thin as paper

steps.text: Rinse the crust of salt off the cod, then soak it submerged in cold water in the fridge, changing the water four times, until a raw shred tastes seasoned rather than salty.
Drain and press the loin dry in a cloth, then pull it apart with your fingers, following the grain, into rough splinters. Do not touch it with a knife.
Salt the diced tomato lightly, let it sit ten minutes and pour off the water it gives up, so the salad cannot go slack.
Toss the cod with the oil first, coating every shred, then add the tomato, onion, green pepper and olives and only then the vinegar. Grind over black pepper.
Rest 15 minutes, then taste before adding any salt at all. The cod almost always brings enough.

note: Esqueixar means to tear. A knife cuts across the muscle blocks and leaves wet chips that shed liquid into the bowl, while tearing follows the natural seams so each splinter keeps its collagen sheath and stays firm. Oil before vinegar for the same reason: the fat coats the fibres so the acid cannot draw more water out. Desalting takes 36 to 48 hours in the fridge and has no shortcut.

ingredients.text: 400 g fideus number 2, the short hollow noodles
1.2 L rockfish and prawn head stock, held at a bare simmer
300 g monkfish tail, in 3 cm pieces
250 g cuttlefish, cut in squares and lightly scored
1 tsp nyora pulp, scraped from a soaked pepper
a pinch of saffron, dried and crumbled

steps.text: In a wide shallow pan, fry the prawns in the oil for 30 seconds a side, until the shells turn scarlet, and lift them out. Do the same with the cuttlefish until its edges curl, and set that aside too.
Drop the heat and toast the dry fideus in that same oil, stirring without pause, until they are the colour of amber and smell like baked biscuit. This is the rossejat and it takes about five minutes.
Stir in the sofregit, the nyora pulp and the saffron, then pour in all the hot stock at once and season. It should sit just level with the noodles.
Boil hard for 4 minutes, then drop to a simmer for 5 more, tucking in the monkfish and cuttlefish. From the moment the stock goes in, do not stir.
Spoon the picada over the surface, shake the pan to settle it, and cook 2 minutes more, until the liquid is gone and the noodles at the surface stand up on end like bristles.
Lay the prawns on top, rest the pan off the heat for 5 minutes and serve with allioli.

note: Toasting the fideus is what separates a fideuà from a wet noodle stew: dry heat sets a shell of dextrins on each tube so it drinks the stock slowly and stays a separate strand. Stir once the liquid is in and you rub that shell off into the pan, and the dish turns to paste. Noodles standing on end mean the stock has gone; leave them any longer and the base burns rather than crisps.

ingredients.text: 1 free range chicken, 1.6 kg, jointed into 8
100 ml vi ranci, or a dry oxidised white wine
1 bay leaf and 1 sprig of thyme
1 slice of bread fried in olive oil
a pinch of saffron, dried and crumbled

steps.text: Salt the chicken and brown it hard in the oil, skin down and unmoved, until the skin releases itself from the pan and is the colour of mahogany. Set it aside.
Sear the langoustines in the same fat for 40 seconds a side, just until the shells redden, and lift them straight out. They finish in the sauce later.
Pour off half the fat, add the sofregit and the herbs, then the vi ranci, scraping the base and reducing until the pan no longer smells of alcohol.
Return the chicken with the stock, cover, and simmer gently until the thigh meat pulls away from the bone at a fork, about 35 minutes.
Pound the almonds, hazelnuts, garlic, fried bread, saffron and chocolate to a paste with a ladle of the sauce, stir it in and simmer 10 minutes, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon.
Slide the langoustines back in, cover, and leave them off the heat 3 minutes, until the tail meat is just opaque to the middle.

note: Mar i muntanya works because prawn shells and browned chicken skin throw off the same families of roasted amino acids, so the two palettes stack instead of fighting. The shellfish is the fragile half: langoustine tail sets at about 55C (130F) and shreds into cotton wool by 65C (150F), so it goes in twice and briefly, and it never simmers alongside the bird.

ingredients.text: 150 g sweet potato, boiled in its skin, peeled and riced

steps.text: Rice the sweet potato while hot and spread it out to cool completely, then knead it with the almonds, sugar, lemon zest and enough egg white to make a stiff, barely tacky marzipan.
Wrap the paste and rest it overnight in the fridge so the almond oil and the sugar syrup even out and it stops sticking to your hands.
Roll into 20 g balls. Rinse the pine nuts and drain them damp, then roll each ball through them, pressing so the nuts bed in halfway and stand upright.
Brush with beaten egg and bake on the top shelf at 200C (390F) for 8 to 10 minutes, until the pine nut tips are gold but the base is still pale.
Cool them on the tray without moving them; they are fragile hot and set firm as they come down to room temperature.

note: Panellets fail on the bench or in the oven, and both faults are water. Too much sweet potato and the paste slumps and sheds its pine nuts; too little and it cracks as you roll. Bake hot, high and fast: the aim is to colour the nuts before the heat reaches the centre, because almond paste that dries through goes sandy and hard instead of staying fudgy. Rest the paste overnight.

ingredients.text: 120 ml cold kombu and katsuobushi dashi

steps.text: Grate the nagaimo to a slippery paste, whisk it into the flour, cold dashi and one egg until only just smooth, then chill the batter for an hour; it should ribbon thickly off the whisk.
Cut the cabbage into 1 cm squares rather than shreds and blot it dry; fine shreds weep and turn the middle to soup.
Fold the cabbage, tenkasu, beni shoga, spring onion and remaining eggs in with a lifting motion, stopping while the mixture still looks loose and airy.
Ladle a 2 cm mound onto a griddle at 180C (355F), drape the pork belly over the top, and cook until the edge sets matt and the underside is deep gold.
Flip once and never press down; it is ready when a skewer pushed into the centre comes out clean and hot against your lip.
Sauce, then mayonnaise, then aonori, and the katsuobushi last so the flakes lift and curl in the steam.

note: Grated nagaimo is a mucilage: long chain glycoproteins that hold water and trap air, so the middle sets as custard rather than pancake. Two habits kill it. Beat the batter and you build gluten; press with the spatula while it cooks and you squeeze out the steam that is doing the lifting. Flip once, then leave it alone.

ingredients.text: 150 ml cold kombu and katsuobushi dashi
300 g Japanese negi or thin spring onion

steps.text: Whisk the flour, cold dashi and egg to a thin pourable batter, barely thicker than single cream, then slice the negi 5 mm thick, greens and all.
Oil a medium hot plate, spread a thin disc of batter, and bury it under a deep drift of negi, squid, tenkasu and beni shoga; the onion should outweigh everything else in the bowl.
Spoon a little more batter over the pile to glue it down and cook until the underside is set and freckled and the onion smells sweet instead of raw.
Flip once, tidy only the edges flat, and cook until the second side is patched brown and the squid has turned opaque.
Slide onto a board, fold in half, cut into fingers and dress with usukuchi soy sharpened with citrus juice; shichimi at the table.

note: Negiyaki is not okonomiyaki with onion in it. Cabbage holds its shape, so its batter can be thick; negi collapses and leaks sugary water, so the batter here is only glue, roughly one part flour to two and a half parts dashi. Thicker and you get a doughy pancake. Those same onion sugars scorch, so keep the iron moderate and finish with soy and citrus, never sweet sauce.

ingredients.text: 250 g beef sirloin or top round
150 ml thin Japanese Worcestershire style sauce

steps.text: Cut the beef into 25 g cubes and the onion into layered wedges, keeping each ingredient on its own skewer with the last 3 cm left bare as a handle.
Crush the panko under a rolling pin to the texture of coarse sand, and whisk the flour, egg and cold water to a batter that runs off a skewer in a thin sheet.
Dip, let the excess drain back into the bowl, then roll in the crumb and pat it on; the coat should be about 2 mm and you should still read the shape underneath.
Fry at 170C to 180C (340F to 355F) in small batches until the bubbling quietens and the crust is pale gold, about 90 seconds for beef and a little longer for the vegetables.
Stand them upright to drain and serve with one communal pot of sauce and the raw cabbage alongside.

note: Two rules, both physical. Crush the panko fine: coarse crumb builds armour that soaks oil and shatters into the shared sauce. And the batter is a thin cream, not a paste; paste steams the food and the crust lifts away as a hollow shell. Never dip twice, because the pot is communal, which is exactly what the raw cabbage is for: use a leaf to scoop your second helping.

ingredients.text: 800 g beef sinew (suji) or shin with tendon

steps.text: Cover the sinew with cold water, bring to the boil and drain the moment grey scum rises, then rinse each piece; that first water carries the smell that would otherwise settle into the miso.
Return it with the ginger, sake and dashi and hold at a bare tremble around 90C (195F) for two to three hours, until a skewer slides through and the tendon has gone glassy.
Tear the konnyaku into rough lumps rather than cutting it, so the sauce grips the torn faces, and simmer 15 minutes.
Slacken both misos with a ladle of the hot liquid, stir them back in with the mirin and sugar, and cook at a whisper until the sauce clings to the meat.
Rest off the heat to thicken, then serve with spring onion and shichimi.

note: Two clocks run here. Collagen in sinew only becomes gelatine after two hours or more at a bare tremble near 90C (195F); rush it and the suji chews like elastic. Kansai white miso is the opposite: low in salt, high in sugar and volatile aroma, so it goes dull and grainy at a boil and its sugars catch on the base. Simmer the meat first, stir the miso in last, never let it bubble.

steps.text: Whisk the flour, dashi and salt to a batter the thickness of pouring cream and chop the squid into 1 cm pieces.
Bring a heavy pan to 220C (430F), oil it, pour a thin round of batter and scatter the squid over straight away.
Cover with a second heavy pan or a foil wrapped weight and lean on it for 60 seconds; steam should hiss from the edges and the disc should compact to about 3 mm.
Lift the weight, crack the egg on top and spread it thin, then fold the sheet in half as soon as the egg has just set.
Brush with sauce, scatter beni shoga and eat immediately, while the rim is still lace crisp.

note: Pressure and speed are the whole dish. Squeezing the batter between hot iron drives out steam and forces contact with the metal, so it sets as a chewy crisp sheet instead of a fluffy pancake. Squid sets the clock: its collagen contracts between roughly 60C (140F) and 100C (212F) and only relaxes again after a long braise, so cook it under two minutes or for half an hour. Nothing in between works.

ingredients.text: 400 g seasoned sushi rice (shari), at body temperature

steps.text: Use mackerel that has been frozen at -20C (-4F) for at least 24 hours. Bury the fillets in salt, skin and flesh, and leave 45 minutes, until the surface firms and beads liquid.
Rinse off the salt, pat dry, then steep in the rice vinegar with the sugar and kombu for 20 minutes, until the outer 2 mm has turned opaque white.
Peel the fine translucent membrane off the skin, working from tail to head; it should lift in one sheet. Slice the fillet to an even 8 mm, keeping the trimmings.
Wet a wooden oshibako, lay the fish skin side down with trimmings filling the gaps, smear a whisper of wasabi, and pack the shari on top to just over the rim.
Fit the lid and press with steady weight until it stops sinking, rest 20 minutes, then unmould and drape with the softened white kombu sheet.
Cut with a wet blade, one clean pull per slice, wiping the steel between cuts.

note: Salt before vinegar, always. Salt pulls water out by osmosis and firms the muscle, so the vinegar then soaks in evenly and whitens only the outer few millimetres. Go straight to vinegar on a wet fillet and you get a chalky rim over a raw, slack middle that weeps in the box. Press once with steady weight until the lid stops giving; pumping it mashes the shari to paste.

steps.text: Wipe the kombu with a dry cloth and leave the white bloom on it; that is glutamate and mannitol, not dirt. Steep it in the cold water for 30 minutes.
Bring it slowly to 60C (140F), hold there 45 minutes, then lift the kombu out before the pot reaches 80C (175F).
Take the water to 85C (185F), kill the heat, scatter in both shavings and leave until they sink, about 2 minutes.
Strain through damp muslin without pressing; squeezing pushes bitter fines through and clouds a broth whose whole point is clarity.
Simmer the mirin alone for 30 seconds to drive off the alcohol, add the usukuchi and salt, stir into the dashi and bring to 80C (175F) without boiling it again.
Taste from a spoon: it should read one notch too salty, because the noodles it will dress are boiled in plain unsalted water.

note: Kansai broth is pale, not weak. Usukuchi runs around 18 percent salt against koikuchi's 16, and its lighter colour comes from that extra salt restraining fermentation and browning, not from dilution. Season this by eye and you will oversalt it. Measure. Keep the kombu under 80C (175F) as well; hotter and it sheds alginates, turning the dashi slippery and faintly bitter.

steps.text: Pour boiling water over both sides of the abura-age, press it flat between your palms, and cut it into 5 mm strips.
Heat the kombu and dried shiitake in the water to 65C (150F), hold 45 minutes, lift the kombu out before the pot reaches 80C (175F), then strain.
Simmer the mirin 30 seconds, add the usukuchi and salt, stir into the dashi and hold at 80C (175F).
Boil the udon in unsalted water until the white core has just gone, then rinse under cold water until the strands stop feeling slippery and dunk them back in hot water for 10 seconds.
Bowl the udon, pour the broth down the side, and pile on the abura-age, green onion and ginger.

note: Abura-age is fried in oil that keeps oxidising on the shelf; skip the boiling water rinse and that oil surfaces as a film which flattens the dashi aroma and coats the tongue. Kizami is the unsweetened cousin of kitsune: no sugar simmered pouch to hide behind, so the fat must be clean and the ginger sharp. Rinse the boiled udon too, or its surface starch clouds and thickens the broth.

steps.text: Tear the sake lees into a bowl, ladle over 200 ml of the hot dashi, and leave until it mashes smooth against the side with no grains left.
Cut the daikon and carrot into 3 mm quarter rounds and shave the burdock straight into water so it does not brown.
Simmer the roots in the remaining dashi until the daikon edge goes translucent and a skewer meets no resistance.
Add the salted salmon in 3 cm pieces and the abura-age in strips, and cook until the fish flakes at a nudge.
Whisk the lees slurry and the white miso in through a ladle, add the usukuchi, and hold at 80C to 85C (175F to 185F) for 5 minutes; the surface should shiver, never bubble.
Finish with spring onion and shichimi.

note: Sake lees is unpressed rice, koji and yeast: raw starch, protein and roughly 8 percent alcohol. Stirred in dry it stays gritty and tastes of raw spirit. Soften it in hot dashi and mash it smooth first, then hold the pot at 80C to 85C (175F to 185F), hot enough for the alcohol to leave, cool enough that the sweet koji smell and the white miso do not boil away.

ingredients.text: 10 g katakuriko or kudzu starch slaked in 20 ml water

steps.text: Rub the two rice flours together, work in the hot water a little at a time, and knead until the dough is as soft as an earlobe and stops cracking at the edges when rolled.
Roll 15 g balls, boil until they float, give them two minutes more, then drop them into iced water so the surface firms.
Thread four to a skewer and dry them thoroughly on a cloth; a wet dango steams instead of blistering.
Grill dry over a naked flame or on a bare pan, turning, until brown blisters patch the surface and the skin squeaks under the tongs.
Simmer the water, sugar, mirin and koikuchi soy, used here for colour and roast where the rest of this chapter uses usukuchi, then rain in the starch slurry while whisking.
Cook the glaze until it turns from cloudy to glossy and coats a spoon, then spoon it over the hot skewers and serve at once.

note: Two flours, two jobs. Joshinko is milled from ordinary rice and gives bite plus a skin that can take a scorch; shiratamako alone would slump on the grill and pull into strings. Dry the boiled dango before it meets the flame or it steams rather than blisters. The glaze needs a full simmer after the starch goes in: pull it while still cloudy and it will thin out and slide off.

ingredients.text: 600g kinugoshi tofu, the softest you can buy

steps.text: Steep the kombu and shiitake in the cold water for an hour. Lift the shiitake out and keep their soaking water; the kombu stays in the pot.
For the tare, warm 200ml of the shiitake water with the shoyu and mirin until it steams and the raw alcohol smell has gone, then hold it warm in a jug.
Bring the kombu water to 70 to 75C (158 to 167F): the surface should shiver and throw a thin plume, and never break into bubbles.
Cut the tofu into 5cm blocks and slide them in. They sink, then rise and sway as they warm through, three to four minutes.
Lift each block out the moment it floats and wobbles, before any pitting shows on the surface, and serve in the warm tare with daikon, negi, ginger and grated yuzu.

note: Tofu is a protein gel holding water, and above about 80C (176F) the gel contracts and squeezes that water back out: the block honeycombs, goes rubbery and tastes of nothing. Hold the kombu water at 70 to 75C (158 to 167F), a surface that trembles but never bubbles, and lift each block as soon as it floats.

ingredients.text: 1.2 L unsweetened soymilk, at least 10 percent solids and nothing added

steps.text: Lay the kombu in a wide shallow pan and pour the soymilk over it to a depth of 3 to 4cm. Surface area makes yuba, not volume.
Hold the milk at 75 to 80C (167 to 176F). The surface dulls, then wrinkles at the edge when you breathe across it: that is the film, five to eight minutes.
For kumiage yuba, slide a flat ladle under the film and lift it away loose, with a little milk beneath it, into a chilled bowl.
For hikiage yuba, run a bamboo skewer along the far edge, lift the whole sheet in one unbroken movement and hang it a minute to drain.
Keep going for as long as the pot allows; each sheet comes thinner and sweeter than the last as the protein is used up. Serve with wasabi, a few drops of shoyu, or salt alone.

note: The skin is soy protein and fat setting at the air interface as surface water evaporates, so it needs a still surface, 75 to 80C (167 to 176F) and milk of at least 10 percent solids. Boil it and the churn stops any film forming: you get grey scum and a scorched base. Thin milk with added emulsifiers never skins at all.

steps.text: Soften the yuba: wipe each sheet with a damp cloth, or dip it for ten seconds in water at about 40C, until it bends without cracking. Hot water turns it to shreds.
Cook the shiitake, carrot and mitsuba in 100ml of the dashi with the salt until the carrot bends but still grips the tooth; drain and cool.
Roll the filling in the yuba, seal each seam with a smear of kuzu slurry and cut the rolls into 4cm lengths.
Season the rest of the dashi with shoyu and mirin, bring it to a bare tremble and poach the rolls three minutes; lift them into warm bowls.

Slake the kuzu in the cold water, stir it into the dashi off the heat, then bring it just to a boil until it turns from cloudy to clear and coats the back of a spoon. Pour over, add ginger and grate yuzu on top.

note: Kuzu has to be slaked cold, then taken just to a boil: the sauce turns from cloudy white to clear as the granules swell, and that is the signal the raw starch taste has gone. Hold it at a rolling boil and the chains shear apart and it thins back towards water. Dried yuba is the other trap; soak it tepid, never hot, or it dissolves.

ingredients.text: 1 kamo nasu, about 300g, or 2 small round aubergines
1 shogoin kabu, about 400g, or 2 small turnips

steps.text: Steep the kombu in the cold water for an hour, bring it to 60C (140F) and hold it there half an hour, then lift the kombu out before it reaches 80C (176F). Divide the dashi between three pans.

Peel the taro into clean flat facets, salt and rinse off the slime, and parboil it in the rice rinsing water until a skewer meets slight resistance. Finish it in the first pan with mirin, sake and half the shoyu under a drop lid.

Score the cut faces of the aubergine and fry them in the sesame oil until the skin is glossy and blackish purple, then simmer in the second pan with the rest of the shoyu, so the oil never reaches the other pots.
Peel the turnip thickly, past the fibrous ring under the skin, and simmer it in the third pan seasoned with salt alone, so it stays white and tastes of turnip.
Blanch the mangetout in salted water and cool them at once. Leave every element sitting in its own liquid until service.
Set each vegetable in its own quarter of the bowl and pour a little of the palest broth around them, not over them. Grate yuzu at the table.

note: Takiawase means cooked apart, served together. Aubergine leaks oil and dye, taro leaks starch and slime, turnip leaks sulphur: one pot and everything tastes of everything, brown. Give each its own dashi. Draw the kombu at 60C (140F) and lift it before 80C (176F), past which it gives up alginates and the broth goes slippery and smells of the shore.

ingredients.text: 300g Manganji togarashi, or long thick-walled sweet green peppers

steps.text: Pour a kettle of boiling water over both sides of the abura-age and press it between your palms until it stops dripping, then cut it into 1cm strips.
Pierce each pepper once behind the stem so steam has a way out and it cannot burst; leave them whole.
Blister the peppers in the sesame oil over a high heat until the skin bubbles and goes khaki in patches, two to three minutes.
Add the dashi, sake, mirin and sugar, then the shoyu, lay a drop lid on and simmer until the peppers slump and the abura-age is heavy with broth, eight to ten minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and leave it until it is no warmer than the room, then scatter the sesame and serve.

note: Two things make this obanzai and not a stir fry. Pour boiling water over the abura-age first: the frying oil on it is old and oxidised, and it will slick the broth and taste stale. Then let the pot cool. Seasoning travels into the peppers as they contract on cooling, which is why this is cooked in the morning and eaten at noon.

ingredients.text: 400g saikyo miso, the sweet pale one

steps.text: Salt the fillets lightly and leave them half an hour, then blot away the beads of moisture that rise; the fishy note leaves with them.
Beat the miso with the mirin and sake to the thickness of soft butter.
Spread half of it in a tray, lay muslin over it, the fish on that, muslin again and the rest of the miso; cover and refrigerate two to three days.
Wipe the fillets clean with the back of a knife and a dry cloth. Do not rinse them, or you undo the cure with water.

Grill skin side first, set well back from a moderate heat, until the surface is mahogany in patches and the flesh springs back, about four minutes a side. Rest two minutes and serve with hajikami and sudachi.

note: The cure runs two to three days and it is gentle: saikyo miso holds only about 5 percent salt against a great deal of rice koji, so osmosis firms the flesh while koji enzymes turn protein into savoury amino acids. Its sugars are also why fish burns here. Wipe the miso off, never rinse, and grill well back from the heat, or the surface blackens before the centre is warm.

ingredients.text: 20ml mirin, boiled to drive off the alcohol

steps.text: Lay a fillet skin down and cut straight down through flesh and bone every 3mm, feeling for the moment the edge touches skin and stopping there. Free a piece every 3cm.
Bring the water and salt to 90C (194F): a surface that shivers, with no rolling bubbles.
Drop in four or five pieces at a time. In twenty to thirty seconds the flesh turns white and the cuts fan open into a flower.
Lift them straight into ice water for ten seconds only, then drain skin down on a cloth; any longer and the flesh drinks and goes flabby.
Whisk the umeboshi with the mirin, dashi and shoyu, and serve the hamo cold on ice with shiso and sudachi.

note: Hamo carries thousands of fine forked bones that cannot be pulled, so honekiri cuts them instead: the blade goes down every 3mm and stops at the skin, which holds the slice together. Cut through the skin and the piece falls to bits in the pot. Drop it into water at 90C (194F), not boiling; collagen between the cuts contracts and the slice opens like a peony.

ingredients.text: 1.2 L dashi of kombu and katsuobushi
2 kujo negi, sliced on the angle

steps.text: Soak the herring in the rice rinsing water in a cool place, changing it once, until a fingernail dents the flesh; scrape off any scales and rinse.
Simmer it in the bancha for twenty minutes to strip the old surface fat, then throw the tea away.

Set the herring in the sake, sugar and ginger under a drop lid at a bare tremble for an hour, then add the koikuchi shoyu and mirin and carry on until the liquid is syrupy and a chopstick pushes through the backbone.
Season the dashi with the usukuchi shoyu, mirin and salt and hold it just below a simmer. Taste it pale and frankly salty; it has plain noodles to meet.
Boil the soba in a large pot of unsalted water until the core is no longer chalky, drain, rinse under cold water to strip the surface starch, then dip it back into hot water to reheat.
Ladle the broth over the noodles, lay a piece of herring on top and finish with kujo negi.

note: The herring soaks a day or two in rice rinsing water to soften, then loses its rancid surface fat in weak bancha. After that, simmer it in sake and sugar for an hour before any soy goes near it: salt is a small molecule, it reaches the flesh first and tightens it, and a tightened fish never softens and its bones never yield.

ingredients.text: 1 kg small aubergines, or kamo nasu in wedges
200g red shiso leaves, stripped from the stems
56g fine sea salt, 4 percent of the total weight

steps.text: Quarter the aubergines lengthwise, skin on, and weigh everything together; the salt is 4 percent of the combined weight of vegetables and shiso.
Rub the shiso hard with a third of the salt until it gives up a dark, bitter liquid. Squeeze that out and throw it away, then rub again with a second third until what runs is clear purple.
Layer the aubergine, myoga and cucumber with the shiso in a crock, salting each layer with what is left.
Weight it with twice the vegetables' weight. Brine must cover everything within two days; if it does not, add more weight rather than water.
Keep it at 15 to 20C (59 to 68F) until the liquid smells sour like yoghurt and the flesh has gone rose right through, three to six weeks. Squeeze, slice and serve cold.

note: Kyoto pickles are salt and time, three to six weeks of it, and no vinegar. Salt pulls the water out and lactobacilli in the brine make the acid; that acid is what flips red shiso from murky violet to crimson and what keeps the crock. Vinegar gets the colour in an afternoon and tastes of it. Keep the weight heavy or the tops sit dry and go slimy.

flavor.sentence: Leads with fresh herbs arguing happily on top, acid holding everything up to the light, leaving a faint perfume.

steps.text: Melt the kurozato in its water over a low heat to a loose syrup and leave it to cool. Sift the kinako with the matcha and icing sugar.
Whisk the warabiko, sugar and water together cold until no grit drags on the whisk, then pass it through a sieve; true bracken starch comes in hard lumps.
Cook over a medium heat, stirring without stopping. It goes from milk white to grey and lumpy in patches, then pulls together into one mass.
Once it is translucent all through, keep working it over the heat another three to five minutes until it is glossy and heavy on the spatula. This is the step people cut short.
Drop spoonfuls into ice water for half a minute, or pour into a wetted tray and cut with a wet scraper. Roll in the kinako and matcha, and pour the kuromitsu at the table.

note: Bracken starch sets into a soft gel that retrogrades fast: chill it and the chains re-associate, so it whitens and turns grainy within hours. Make it the day you eat it and keep it at room temperature. Stopping at first translucency is the other error; it leaves a raw starch taste and the mochi weeps water on the plate.

flavor.sentence: A quiet dish that lets its main ingredient speak: season well and stand aside.

teacher.label: The cuisine, deeper
teacher.sub: Technique films from the Kyoto & Kaiseki kitchen

ingredients.text: 300 g pike fillet, skinned, pin boned and well chilled
500 g whole freshwater crayfish, live or frozen
60 g butter, for mounting the sauce

steps.text: Panade: boil the milk with the 60 g butter and half the salt, draw off the heat and rain in the flour, then dry the paste over low heat, beating hard, until it balls up and films the base of the pan. Spread it thin on a tray and chill until stone cold.

Blend the pike to a smooth paste with the rest of the salt, work in the cold panade, then the eggs and yolks one at a time, then the diced cold butter. Keep the bowl on ice throughout; the mixture must stay below 12C (54F) and hold a soft peak on the spatula. Rest it two hours in the fridge.

Sauce: roast the crayfish until scarlet, pick the tails, crush shells and heads and sweat them with the carrot, shallot and tomato purée, flame with the marc, add wine and cream and simmer 20 min. Press hard through a fine sieve, add the tarragon, then mount with the 60 g butter off the heat.

Shape quenelles between two wet spoons and slide them into salted water held at 78 to 80C (172 to 176F), so the surface only shivers. Turn once. They are ready when they have doubled, roll over on their own and feel springy under a finger, about 12 min.
Drain on a cloth, set in a buttered dish, nap with the Nantua and scatter over the crayfish tails.
Bake at 200C (390F) until the sauce blisters at the edges and the quenelles swell again, about 8 min.

note: The panade is flour already gelatinised in hot milk: the granules have drunk their water, so in the poach they swell instead of dissolving while the egg sets a mesh around them. That swelling is the lift, not any raising agent. Hold the water at 78 to 80C (172 to 176F); at a boil the trapped steam escapes faster than the egg can set and the quenelles tear open.

ingredients.text: 1 coarse pork cooking sausage with pistachios, about 400 g
1 egg yolk beaten with 10 ml milk, to glaze

steps.text: Mix flour, salt, sugar, yeast and the cold eggs to a shaggy dough and work it 10 min until it slaps clean off the bowl. Add the butter piece by piece and keep working until the dough is glossy and stretches to a windowpane. Chill overnight.
Poach the sausage in water held at 80C (176F), never bubbling, until a skewer meets no resistance, about 30 min. Cool it in its liquid, peel off the skin, pat dry and chill until firm.

Roll the cold dough to a rectangle 1 cm thick, paint the sausage with the mustard, dust it with flour and roll it up, sealing the seam and pinching the ends closed. Set it seam down in a lined loaf tin.
Prove at around 24C (75F) until the dough springs back slowly from a fingertip and has filled the tin by half again, about 90 min. Glaze twice.
Bake at 180C (355F) until deep chestnut and the core reads 65C (150F), about 35 min. Rest 20 min before cutting or the crumb drags.

note: Poach the sausage first and chill it hard. Wrapped raw it shrinks as it bakes and leaves a cavity between meat and crumb, and the fat it renders soaks the base to paste. Keep the poaching water at 80C (176F) so the forcemeat's fat stays emulsified, dry the peeled sausage, then paint it with mustard: dough grips a tacky surface and slides off a wet one.

ingredients.text: 2 heads frisée, pale hearts only, about 250 g
180 g smoked poitrine, cut into thick lardons
80 g stale pain de campagne, in cubes
30 ml red wine vinegar, plus 20 ml for the poaching water
fine salt and coarse black pepper

steps.text: Wash the frisée hearts and dry them hard in a cloth; water left on the leaves dilutes the hot dressing to nothing.

Render the lardons from cold in a dry pan until the fat runs clear and the edges crisp but the centres still yield. Lift them out, fry the bread cubes in the fat until gold, then rub them with the cut garlic.
Poach the eggs one at a time in water at 82C (180F) with the 20 ml vinegar, until the white is opaque and set but the yolk still swings loose inside it, about 3 min. Slip them into cold water.
Off the heat, whisk the mustard, shallot, the 30 ml vinegar and the oil into the hot pan fat; it should turn cloudy and slightly thick rather than separating into pools.
Pour the hot dressing over the frisée and toss until the leaves slump but still crackle, add lardons and croutons, sit an egg on each plate and grind the pepper at the table.

note: The dressing is rendered lardon fat deglazed with vinegar and poured on hot, so the leaf has to have rib: frisée hearts wilt without collapsing, soft lettuce turns to slime. Poach the eggs at 82C (180F) in barely moving water; a boil shreds the white before the yolk thickens. The yolk must stay liquid, because it is the second half of the dressing.

steps.text: Slice the potatoes 3 mm thick on a mandoline and do not rinse or soak them; the starch clinging to the cut faces is the only binder in the dish.
Rub the gratin dish hard with the cut garlic until the surface smells of it, then butter it heavily.
Bring the milk, salt, nutmeg, pepper and the garlic halves to a simmer, add the slices and cook, moving them gently, until the milk has visibly thickened and coats the back of a spoon, about 10 min.
Layer the slices flat and overlapping into the dish, pour over the thickened milk, then the cream, and press the top down until the liquid rises just level with the potatoes.
Bake at 150C (300F) until a knife slides through with no resistance and the top is bronzed and set, about 1 h 15 min. Rest 20 min so it will cut.

note: No cheese and no egg in the Dauphiné, so potato starch is the only thickener. Never rinse the slices, and simmer them in the milk first so the amylose leaches out and the liquid thickens before it meets the oven; rinsed potatoes bake into a puddle with the cream floating on top. Hold the oven at 150C (300F), because hotter curdles the milk proteins into grains.

ingredients.text: 750 ml red Burgundy, a young Pinot Noir
40 g butter for the pan, plus 40 g softened and 30 g cold

steps.text: Render the lardons in the 40 g pan butter and lift them out, glaze the small onions with the sugar until burnished, then fry the mushrooms until they squeak and colour. Reserve all three together; this is the garniture.

In the same pan sweat the shallot and crushed garlic, add the wine, thyme and bay and boil hard to reduce by half, until it smells of fruit rather than alcohol. Add the stock and reduce again to about 400 ml.

Poach the eggs one at a time in a small pan of that wine held at 82C (180F), spinning the liquid first, until the whites are firm and stained purple, about 3 min. Lift them out, trim the ragged skirts, and tip the wine back into the sauce.

Knead the 40 g softened butter with the flour and whisk it into the simmering sauce in small knobs; hold it at a simmer two minutes, until it coats a spoon and no longer tastes raw of flour, then strain.
Return the garniture to warm through, take the pan off the heat and swirl in the 30 g cold butter until the sauce turns glossy and clings.
Toast the bread, rub it with the garlic clove, sit an egg on each and spoon the meurette over so it pools around rather than soaks in.

note: Wine is acid, tannin and no body at all. Reduce it alone by half to drive off the raw alcohol, then build weight with brown stock and a beurre manié simmered two minutes so it loses its floury taste. Push the reduction too far and the tannins turn inky and astringent. Poach the eggs in the wine itself: its acidity sets the white fast, so no vinegar is wanted.

ingredients.text: 1.2 kg unsmoked salted ham hock, on the bone
bouquet garni of thyme, bay and parsley stalks
2 garlic cloves, crushed to a paste with salt
2 leaves gelatine, only if the test spoon will not set

steps.text: Soak the hock in cold water overnight, changing it twice, to pull the cure back out; the last water should taste barely salty.

Cover hock and trotter with the wine and enough water to submerge, add vegetables, bouquet and peppercorns, and simmer at a bare tremble, skimming, until the meat pulls from the bone under a fork, about 3 h.

Lift out the meat. Strain the stock, boil it down to about 600 ml and chill a spoonful on a cold plate: it must set firm enough to hold a fingerprint. Only if it stays slack, soften the gelatine and whisk it in.

Tear the warm ham into coarse shreds with some of its fat, discarding rind and bone. Let the stock cool to a thick syrup, then stir in the parsley chopped at the last moment, the garlic, shallots, vinegar and pepper.

Pack meat and green jelly into a terrine in alternating spoonfuls so the parsley marbles rather than layers, press lightly, and chill overnight until firm. Cut in thick slices and serve with pickles and bread.

note: The set comes from the trotter's collagen, not a packet: simmer it alongside the hock and test a spoonful on a cold plate before you commit the mould. Fold the parsley in only once the jelly has cooled to syrup; stirred into hot stock the chlorophyll goes khaki and tastes of boiled grass. Tear the ham into shreds rather than dicing it, so the fibres interlock and the slice holds together.

ingredients.text: 400 g fromage blanc, at least 20 percent fat
30 ml dry white wine, Aligoté or Mâcon
2 shallots, chopped as fine as gravel
1 small garlic clove, crushed with salt
800 g small waxy potatoes, boiled and hot, to serve

steps.text: Line a sieve with muslin, tip in the fromage blanc and drain it in the fridge until it holds a ridge from the spoon and the whey has stopped dripping, at least 4 h.
Beat the drained curd with the crème fraîche and salt, then trickle in the oil while whisking until the mixture is glossy and thick enough to keep the whisk marks.
Let it down with the vinegar and then the wine, a little at a time, until it drops slowly from a spoon; stop before it pours.
Fold in the shallot, garlic and all the herbs, chopped only now, grind on plenty of pepper and serve within the hour with the hot potatoes.

note: Fromage blanc is mostly water held loosely by casein. Drain it in muslin for several hours, then beat the oil in first, to a body like thick mayonnaise, and only after that let it down with vinegar and wine; in the other order the acid thins the curd to a grey slop that weeps in the dish. Herbs go in last, because salt and acid draw their water out and they go limp within the hour.

ingredients.text: 600 g cooked honeycomb ox tripe, gras-double
55 g Dijon mustard, 40 g for the marinade and 15 g for the sauce
20 g tarragon, chervil and parsley, chopped

steps.text: Cut the tripe into 8 palm sized pieces and marinate overnight in the wine, the 40 g mustard, the juice of one lemon and the pepper, turning once.
Drain and pat every piece bone dry on cloth, then pass it through flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs, pressing the crumbs on firmly. Chill uncovered an hour so the coat sets and dries.

Gribiche: mash the cooked yolks with the raw yolk and the 15 g mustard to a smooth paste, then drive in the oil drop by drop until it grips and in a thin stream once it thickens. Slacken with the vinegar, then fold in the chopped whites, cornichons, capers and herbs.
Fry in the clarified butter at 170C (340F), a few pieces at a time, until the crust is deep gold and crackles under the back of a spoon, about 3 min a side. Drain on a rack, never stacked on paper.
Salt at once and serve with the gribiche and the second lemon in wedges.

note: Tripe reaches you already cooked and saturated, so pat it bone dry before it meets the flour: wet tripe sheds its crust into the pan as the gelatine underneath melts. Fry in clarified butter at 170C (340F), since whole butter's milk solids blacken well before the crumb colours. The gribiche emulsifies on the raw yolk alone, the cooked yolks only give body, so start the oil drop by drop.

ingredients.text: 1.5 kg mixed river fish: pike, perch, tench and a piece of eel, cleaned and cut into thick sections
40 g softened butter, for the beurre manié
bouquet garni of thyme, bay and parsley stalks
1 garlic clove, for rubbing the croutons

steps.text: Render the lardons, then brown the small onions and the mushrooms in the same fat until glazed and squeaking. Lift the garniture out and hold it aside.
Sweat the sliced onion and crushed garlic in the 50 g butter without letting them colour, add the wine, bouquet and 250 ml water and simmer 20 min, until the broth no longer smells sharp.

Slide the fish in by firmness: eel first, pike and tench four minutes later, perch last. Keep the pan at a shiver and lift each piece out the moment the flesh parts from the bone at a fork's nudge. Keep them warm.
Whisk a beurre manié of the softened butter and flour into the broth in small knobs, simmer two minutes until it coats a spoon, then add the cream and reduce to a light nappé.
Warm the marc, flame it into the sauce, return the garniture to heat through and correct the salt.
Fry the bread in butter, rub it with the garlic clove, and serve the fish in warm bowls under the sauce with the croutons alongside.

note: A garniture bourguignonne is lardons, button mushrooms and small glazed onions, and that trio is what makes a dish Burgundian; here the wine is white, from the Saône valley, not red. Cook the garnish apart and add it at the end or the mushrooms bleed grey through the broth. Add the fish by firmness, eel first and perch last: they are five minutes apart, and river fish poached past that goes to cotton.

steps.text: Peel the pears, leaving the stalks on, and rub them all over with the cut lemon so they do not brown before they go into the pan.
Bring the wine, sugar, cinnamon, zest, peppercorns and clove to a simmer and stir until no grain of sugar is left on the base; undissolved sugar scorches there and turns the syrup bitter.

Lower the pears in on their sides, cover with a paper cartouche and a small plate to keep them under the surface, and poach at a bare shiver, turning once, until a skewer meets only slight resistance at the core, 20 to 35 min according to ripeness.
Cool the pears in the syrup, then chill them in it overnight; the colour keeps travelling inward as they sit.
Lift the pears out, boil the syrup with the cassis until glossy and just coating a spoon, cool it and pour it back over them.

note: Hold the syrup at a shiver. At a boil the pears knock about and the anthocyanins that are colouring them leach straight back into the pan. Sugar matters as much as wine: below roughly a fifth by weight the flesh loses water to the syrup and goes woolly. Lift the pears out before you reduce, or the ten minutes of hard boiling that glazes the syrup will cook them to mush.

ingredients.text: 6g fine salt, for drawing the goya
300g shima dofu, or the firmest tofu you can buy

steps.text: Halve the goya lengthwise and scrape out the seeds and every trace of the cottony white pith with a spoon, then slice 3mm thick across.

Toss the slices with the 6g salt and leave 10 minutes, until water beads on them and a slice bends instead of snapping. Squeeze once, hard, in your fist and do not rinse. Taste a piece: it should still be plainly bitter.
Tear the tofu into 3cm lumps and fry them undisturbed in a hot oiled pan until the torn faces are gold and squeak against the spatula. Lift out.
Fry the pork in the same pan until its fat runs clear and the edges crisp, then add the goya and toss over the highest heat for 90 seconds, until the green brightens and the cut edges blister.
Return the tofu, splash in the awamori and soy, season with salt and white pepper, then pour the egg round the edge of the pan and fold twice.
Kill the heat while the egg is still glossy and barely set, pile it up, and scatter the katsuobushi so it curls in the steam.

note: Salting works osmotically: it pulls water out of the goya and the bitter momordicins leave dissolved in that water. Ten minutes and one squeeze takes out roughly a third, which is all you want. Blanch it, or salt it for an hour, and you have a limp green courgette and no reason to have cooked it. The other failure is a wet pan: tofu that was not pressed and browned first floods the heat, and champuru becomes a stew.

ingredients.text: 1kg skin-on pork belly, in one piece

steps.text: Boil the belly whole with the ginger and leek greens in water to cover for 40 minutes, skimming the grey scum until the surface runs clear. Lift out, rinse under hot water and cool enough to handle.
Cut into 4cm squares, skin left on every piece: the skin is the dish, not a trimming.

Boil the awamori hard in a wide pan for 2 minutes, until the raw spirit smell has burned off and what rises smells of rice. Add the dashi and the pork, lay on a drop lid, and hold at a bare shiver, about 85C (185F), for 90 minutes, until a skewer slides through the fat with no resistance at all.
Only now stir in the kokuto, and 20 minutes later both soy sauces.
Simmer uncovered another 30 minutes, spooning the liquid over the pieces, until it darkens to a gloss on the skin and falls off the spoon in a slow ribbon.
Cool in the pan, lift off the set fat cap, and rewarm to serve with a dab of karashi.

note: Awamori, not sake, is what separates this from kakuni. It is distilled from long grain rice with black koji and lands at 30 percent or more, so it unwinds collagen faster than any brewed alcohol, and it carries no sugar of its own. That is why the kokuto goes in late. Sugar and salt raise the osmotic pressure of the braise and draw water out of the muscle fibres, tightening the meat before its collagen has had time to melt. Sweeten early and it stays stringy for hours.

ingredients.text: 800g pork spare ribs, cut into 5cm lengths
600g Okinawa soba noodles (wheat, alkaline, no buckwheat)
koregusu (island chillies steeped in awamori), to serve

steps.text: Cover the neck bones with cold water, bring to the boil, then throw the water away and scrub both bones and pot clean of grey scum. Refill with 3 litres cold water and the kombu, pull the kombu out just before it boils, and hold at a lazy simmer for 3 hours.

Meanwhile simmer the ribs in the awamori with water to cover for 1 hour, then add the kokuto and soy and cook down 30 minutes more, turning them, until they are sticky and the meat has drawn back from the bone.
Strain the pork broth, bring it to 80C (176F), cut the heat, drop in the katsuobushi and leave 3 minutes. Strain again through a cloth without pressing, and salt it to just past what tastes right.
Boil the noodles in unsalted water until they are springy rather than soft, drain, and rinse briefly in warm water to wash the surface alkali off.
Load the bowls with noodles, hot broth, ribs, kamaboko, spring onion and a pinch of beni shoga. Koregusu goes on at the table, drop by drop.

note: Okinawa soba holds no buckwheat: it is wheat raised with alkaline water, and the high pH tightens the gluten and yellows the flour, which is why the strand stays springy sitting in hot broth. The broth is the other local marker, half pork and half katsuobushi rather than one or the other. Boil the bonito and you pull out bitterness and cloud; hold the pot near 80C (176F) for three minutes and you get the savour and nothing sour.

steps.text: Drain the peanuts, rub off any clinging skins, and blend with the water in two batches until the liquid is chalk white and no grit rolls between your fingers.
Wring the puree through a doubled cloth, hard, until the pulp left in your hand is dry and crumbly. You want about 550ml of milk.
Whisk the sweet potato starch and salt into the cold milk until nothing settles out, then set the pan over low heat and stir with a spatula, corners included, without stopping.

It thickens all at once around 70C (158F) into a pale paste. Keep it moving a full 15 minutes past that, until it turns from matt to glossy, gathers away from the sides in one mass, and drags heavily on the spatula.
Scrape into a wetted mould, tap out the air, cover the surface and set at room temperature for an hour. Turn out, cut, and spoon over the kombu dashi simmered with the soy, sugar and ginger.

note: Nothing here is coagulated. No nigari, no soy beans: this is a starch gel, and the peanut protein and fat are passengers in it. Sweet potato starch swells near 70C (158F), but the granules must be cooked well past that and worked constantly before the paste goes glossy and will hold a cut edge. Stop at the first thickening and it sets soft and weeps overnight. Eat it the day you make it; the starch retrogrades in the cold and turns chalky.

ingredients.text: shima rakkyo or spring onion, to serve

steps.text: Scrape the ears with the back of a knife under running water and singe off any bristles over a flame, wiping them away as they char.

Simmer in water with the 50ml awamori and the ginger, lid ajar, for 90 minutes, until a skewer passes easily through the fleshy base while the cartilage at the rim still resists and clicks under the point.
Lift out, press flat between two plates and chill until cold and firm, at least 2 hours.
Pound the peanuts to a coarse rubble, then work in the miso, sugar, vinegar and dressing awamori to a thick, spoonable paste.
Slice the cold ear across into 2mm ribbons, toss with the cucumber and just enough peanut miso to coat, and scatter with shima rakkyo. Dress at the last moment so it clings rather than soaks.

note: A pig's ear is skin wrapped round elastic cartilage, and the two parts want different times. Ninety minutes at a simmer melts the skin collagen to gelatine and turns it silky, while the cartilage, which is elastin, keeps its crunch. Run it to two hours and that crunch slackens into rubber. The chilling is not for convenience either: cold sets the gelatine hard enough to take a 2mm slice, and a warm ear only shreds.

ingredients.text: 700g pork small intestine, split and rough cleaned

steps.text: Work the flour and salt into the intestine in a big bowl, kneading it like dough for two minutes, until your hands are gloved in grey paste. Rinse and repeat three times, until the flour comes away white and the rinse water runs clear.
Cover with cold water, boil hard 10 minutes, drain and wash each piece under the tap. Do that twice more with fresh water.
Cut into 3cm strips and simmer in the dashi with the shiitake, konnyaku and awamori for 90 minutes, until a piece gives under the tooth with no chew left but still holds its tube.
Season with the salt and only a trickle of light soy. The broth should stay pale and read clean, not brown.
Ladle out, grate the ginger over each bowl at the table, and finish with sesame.

note: Flour is an abrasive here, not a flavouring. Salt and water slide over the mucus and fat that carry the smell, while a stiff flour paste grips and lifts them, and the starch adsorbs the indole and skatole as it goes. Three scrubs, then three changes of hard boiling water. Skip a round and the soup tastes of the animal the whole way through, and no amount of ginger at the end will cover it. Keep the broth clear: this is a salt soup, never a miso one.

ingredients.text: soy sauce, rice vinegar and shikuwasa juice, to dip

steps.text: Whisk the flour, kombu dashi, eggs and salt to a batter the body of single cream, thin enough to run off the whisk in an unbroken thread, and rest it 10 minutes while you cut the nira.
Stir in the nira and carrot. It should look like greens held loosely in liquid, not a thick dough with things buried in it.
Set a 24cm pan over medium heat with a slick of oil, pour in half the batter and tilt it out to a 3mm layer.

Cook about 3 minutes, until the top loses its wet shine and the edge lifts away dry, then flip and give it 2 minutes more, until both faces are freckled tan and the chives inside have gone soft and dark instead of squeaking.
Slide out, cut into six wedges and eat at once with the dip, the second one cooking while you do.

note: This is not okonomiyaki. No cabbage, no yam, no thickener, and that absence is the whole discipline: a slack batter with almost no gluten worked into it stays floppy and folds, where a stiff one bakes into a chewy pad. Keep the pan at medium. Hot enough to blister the outside fast and the chives inside are still raw and squeaking, and that raw allium bite is the one flavour a pancake this thin cannot carry.

steps.text: Beat the eggs with the kokuto until the sugar has dissolved and the mix ribbons off the whisk, then beat in the oil and milk.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt over the top and fold with a spatula, stopping the moment no dry flour is left. The dough should be stiff, sticky and a little shaggy, never smooth and elastic.
Rest it 20 minutes covered while the oil comes to 160C (320F). Hold it there; that number is the recipe.
Oil your hands, squeeze the dough up between thumb and forefinger into 4cm balls and slide them in, four or five at a time. They sink, then rise.

Fry 7 to 8 minutes, turning, until each has split across the crown into three or four seams and the dough exposed in the cracks has browned. Still smooth at 5 minutes means the oil is too hot: pull the pan off the heat and let it fall.
Drain on a rack rather than paper, and eat warm.

note: The split is the doneness gauge, and it only happens slowly. At 160C (320F) the crust stays pliable long enough for steam and the baking powder to swell the ball and tear it open from inside, and by the time it has torn the centre is cooked. At 180C (356F) the surface sets first, the ball stays round and smooth, and you bite into raw batter. Below 150C (302F) it simply drinks oil.

steps.text: Keep the umibudo out of the fridge from the moment you buy it, on the counter, loosely covered.
Warm the kombu dashi, vinegar, shikuwasa, soy and sugar only until the sugar dissolves, then cool the sanbaizu to room temperature and stir in the grated daikon.
Rinse the umibudo in a bowl of room temperature water for 20 seconds, moving it with your fingers, until the beads plump and go from dull olive to translucent green. Lift it out and drain on a cloth.
Pile it on a plate and set the sanbaizu beside it in a small dish. Dip at the table, a forkful at a time, and listen for the beads going off like small shot.

note: Sea grapes are single algal cells holding water under pressure, and that pressure is the pop. Two things burst it. Cold shrivels the beads and they never recover, so this is the one thing in the kitchen that must never see the fridge or iced water. And salt or vinegar draws the water straight out osmotically: leave them sitting in the dressing two minutes and you serve limp string. Dip, do not dress.
