ingredients.text: 600g hot cooked Japanese short grain rice

steps.text: Brown the beef in a dry pan without stirring until one face has a crust and the fat has run, then break it up and add the onion and garlic, cooking until the onion turns translucent.
Add the spices to the hot fat for 30 seconds, until they smell toasted rather than dusty, then the tomato puree, soy, Worcestershire and water.
Simmer and stir until the pan is nearly dry and a spoon dragged across the base leaves a track that fills back slowly. Keep going past the point it looks ready.
Build in order: hot rice, cheese straight onto it so it slumps, then the hot mince over the cheese.
Only now the cold lettuce and tomato, with salsa and koregusu at the table.

note: Post-war food, built round American mince and island rice, and the rice is exactly why the mince has to be reduced almost dry. A tortilla carries sauce; short grain rice does not. Its surface starch takes up free liquid on contact and the bowl goes to porridge under the topping. Build hot to cold as well: cheese onto rice hot enough to slump it, salad last, or the lettuce wilts into the meat before it reaches the table.

ingredients.text: 2 kg small rock fish (rascasse, weever, small wrasse, gurnard, a green crab or two), gutted
1 fennel bulb, sliced, plus 1 tsp fennel seed
2 wide strips dried orange peel, white pith scraped away
1 tsp fine sea salt, plus more to finish
1 waxy potato (150 g), boiled soft in the soup and lifted out
1 small hot dried red chilli, soaked and skinned
200 ml olive oil for the rouille
A pinch of saffron for the rouille
1 thin baguette, sliced and dried out in the oven

steps.text: Sweat the onions, fennel and garlic in the olive oil over low heat until translucent and quite without colour, then add the fennel seed and wait until the pan smells of aniseed.
Raise the heat, turn the whole fish in the hot oil until the flesh whitens and begins to fall off the frames, then add tomatoes, orange peel and saffron and stir until the tomatoes slump.
Pour on the water, bring it to a bare shiver and hold it there for 30 minutes; the surface should tremble, never roll.
Pass everything, bones and all, through the coarse plate of a food mill, pressing until only dry pulp remains, then push that liquid through a conical sieve and salt it harder than feels polite.
For the rouille, pound the garlic and chilli to a smooth paste with salt, work in the boiled potato and saffron, then the yolk, then dribble in the oil until it stands up around the pestle.
Reheat the soup to just under a boil and serve it with the dried bread, letting each person melt rouille off a croûton into the bowl.

note: Saffron, fennel and dried orange are the spine of this soup, not its garnish; without them you have made fish broth. The body is gelatine milled out of small bones, held in suspension by the oil, which is why a hard boil ruins it: it shears the fat out and the soup turns grey and greasy. Keep it shivering, and use a food mill, never a blender, which grinds bone to grit.

ingredients.text: 400 g salt cod fillet, soaked 24 hours in cold water changed four times
8 fat garlic cloves, green germ removed
400 ml olive oil at room temperature, half fruity and half mild

steps.text: Poach the soaked cod in barely moving water with the bay until it flakes at a fork, about 8 minutes, and lift it out before the flakes tighten and go stringy.
Boil the eggs 9 minutes, and cook each vegetable separately in salted water: potatoes and carrots to a knife tip, beans and cauliflower still squeaking against the tooth.
Pound the garlic with the coarse salt in a mortar until it is a wet sticky cream with no fibre left in it, then work in the yolks.

Dribble in the oil in a thread, the pestle always turning the same way, until the sauce climbs the sides of the mortar and holds the pestle upright; loosen with the lemon juice and a teaspoon of warm water.
Bring everything to the table warm or at room temperature on one platter with the mortar in the middle, and eat it slowly.

note: Garlic is as much the emulsifier here as the yolk: crushing it releases a mucilage that keeps oil droplets apart. Two things break the sauce. Oil poured faster than it can be taken up pools and splits, and the fix is to start a fresh yolk and beat the broken sauce into it a spoon at a time. And a blender shears the oil so hard that bitter phenolics flood out, so pound by hand.

ingredients.text: 1.6 kg beef cheek or shin, in 6 cm pieces
750 ml young red wine from the Rhône
200 g unsmoked salt pork belly, in lardons
2 wide strips dried orange peel, white pith scraped away
1 bouquet of thyme, bay, parsley stalks and a piece of dried fennel stalk
150 g black olives from Nyons, stoned

steps.text: Marinate the beef overnight in the wine with the onions, carrots, garlic, cloves and bouquet; next day lift the meat out and dry every face of every piece, or it will steam rather than brown.
Brown the lardons in the olive oil in a heavy casserole, then the beef in unhurried batches until each side is properly dark, and set it aside.
Soften the drained marinade vegetables in that fat, return the meat, pour on the strained wine with the tomatoes, tuck in the orange peel and bouquet and bring it to a bare tremble.
Cover and hold at 85C (185F) in the oven for 4 hours; look in once an hour and confirm the surface is still only trembling.
Add the olives for the last 20 minutes, then cool the daube overnight, lift off the set fat, reheat it gently and sharpen it with the vinegar at the last moment.

note: Collagen becomes gelatine from around 70C, but slowly, and four hours at 85C (185F) buys meat that slumps into its own melted connective tissue. Let it boil and the muscle fibres contract and wring themselves dry: stringy meat in a thin sauce. Scrape the orange peel too. The coloured zest perfumes the wine; the white pith turns the whole pot bitter over a cook this long.

ingredients.text: 250 g fresh white coco beans, shelled, or soaked dried white beans
150 g fresh red borlotti beans, shelled
250 g green beans, in 2 cm lengths
80 g small pasta, coquillettes or broken vermicelli
For the pistou: 80 g basil leaves, from three large bunches
80 g hard sheep's cheese made with vegetarian rennet, finely grated
1 ripe tomato, peeled and seeded, Nice style (optional)

steps.text: Simmer the shelled beans in the salted water until their skins are tender and the insides no longer chalky, 30 to 40 minutes depending on how freshly they were picked.
Add potato, carrot and leek, then ten minutes later the green beans, courgette and tomato, so that everything arrives at tender together instead of the soft ones dissolving.
Cook the pasta in the soup itself; the starch it sheds is what gives the broth its cling.
Pound the garlic to a paste with a pinch of salt, add the basil a handful at a time and work it to a dark green cream, then the cheese, then the oil in a thread.
Pull the pot off the heat, let it stop bubbling, and only then stir in half the pistou; the rest goes on the table in the mortar.

note: Basil's scent lives in volatile oils that boil away, and its phenols oxidise to a blackish grey the moment they meet sustained heat. So the pistou goes in off the flame, never simmers, and reheated leftovers want a fresh spoonful. Note also that there are no pine nuts: that is Genoa. Here it is garlic, basil, cheese and oil, pounded in that order so the salt and garlic can grind the leaves.

ingredients.text: 1 kg very ripe tomatoes, peeled, seeded and roughly chopped

steps.text: Salt the aubergine cubes, leave them 30 minutes and press them dry in a towel; once their cells have collapsed they drink far less oil.
Reduce the tomatoes in a wide pan with the thyme, bay and a spoonful of oil until they hold their shape on a spoon and no water weeps out around them.
In a second pan, very hot, fry the aubergine in batches in the rest of the oil until the cubes are bronzed and floppy, adding onion and garlic to the last batch.
Fold the aubergine into the tomato, cook five minutes more so they trade flavour, then take it off the heat and let it fall to warm before adding the parsley.

note: This is the ratatouille lesson taught in two pans. Aubergine only browns above about 140C (285F), and a pan full of tomato water cannot pass 100C (212F), so cooked together nothing browns: the aubergine simply boils in juice until its cell walls give way and the whole thing is one grey purée. Reduce the tomato to a paste, fry the aubergine hot and separate, marry them at the end.

ingredients.text: 80 ml olive oil, plus more for the top
60 g hard sheep's cheese made with vegetarian rennet, grated

steps.text: Salt the grated courgette, leave it 20 minutes, then wring it out hard in a cloth over a bowl and keep the green juice.
Soften the onion and garlic in the olive oil without letting them colour, add the courgette and cook until it stops steaming and begins to catch on the pan.
Stir in the raw rice, the reserved juice topped up with water to 200 ml, then the eggs, cheese, basil and plenty of pepper.
Spread it no deeper than 4 cm in an oiled earthenware tian, trickle oil over the surface and bake at 180C (350F) until the top is crusted brown and a knife comes out clean, about 50 minutes.

note: The rice is not filler, it is there to drink. Courgette is over ninety percent water, and a tian is a wide shallow dish precisely so that water can leave as steam. Pile it deep, or leave the rice out, and you get green soup under a brown lid. Salt and wring the courgette first, keep the squeezed juice for the rice to swell in, and hold the layer under 4 cm.

ingredients.text: 60 ml olive oil, plus more for the tin
2 kg onions, halved and finely sliced
24 salted anchovy fillets, rinsed and split lengthways
24 small black olives from Nice, left whole with their stones

steps.text: Work the flour, salt, yeast, water and oil into a slack dough, knead it smooth and leave it to double.
Cook the onions with thyme, bay, oil and a pinch of salt under a lid on the lowest heat for at least an hour, stirring now and then, until they are a pale gold jam with no liquid left in the pan.
Press the dough into an oiled shallow tin of about 30 by 40 cm, no thicker than a finger, and let it puff for 30 minutes.
Spread the cooled onions right to the edges, lay the anchovies in a lattice, drop an olive into each diamond and grind over pepper.
Bake at 220C (430F) until the underside is crisp and the anchovies have darkened, 20 to 25 minutes.

note: The onions are dried rather than fried: an hour under a lid drives their water off and concentrates the sugar, and the pale gold comes from that, not from a hot pan. Hurry them and they scorch at the rim while staying wet in the middle, and that water soaks the base into a sog. Spread them cold, and salt nothing else on the tart; the anchovies carry all the salt it needs.

ingredients.text: 250 g black Tanche olives from Nyons, stoned

steps.text: Rinse the capers and anchovies, soak them ten minutes and taste one of each; if either is still fierce, soak and taste again before anything else happens.
Pound the garlic and thyme first, then the anchovies, then the capers, then the olives, adding each only once the one before has broken down.
Work in the oil a spoonful at a time so it is absorbed rather than pooling, then the lemon and the marc, and finish with pepper alone.
Leave it an hour before serving; it should stay rough enough that you can still see the olive skins in it.

note: The name comes from tapeno, the caper, so capers are half the flavour and not a garnish. They and the anchovies both arrive packed in salt, and the only way to know how much salt is already in the bowl is to rinse and taste before pounding; add none of your own. Pound in order of hardness so each thing breaks down, and skip the blender, which whips the lot into a flat, greasy black emulsion.

ingredients.text: 3 tbsp olive oil, plus 800 ml for frying

steps.text: Whisk the chickpea flour into the cold water off the heat until not one lump remains; added to hot water the flour sets a skin around each lump and locks it in.

Bring it to the boil stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, add the salt and the 3 tbsp oil, and cook about 10 minutes, until the spoon leaves a clean trail across the pan floor and the paste pulls away from the sides.
Pour it at once into oiled saucers or a shallow tray to a depth of 1.5 cm, smooth the top and leave it to set cold and firm, at least two hours.
Cut into thick chips and fry in olive oil at 175C (350F) until crisp and pale gold, then drain, salt coarsely, pepper heavily and serve with lemon.

note: Chickpea starch must gelatinise fully before it will set, which is why the paste is cooked until it leaves the pan sides; underdone, it sets soft and the water still trapped inside flashes to steam in the fryer and bursts the panisse open. Fry in olive oil rather than beside it: sound low acidity oil smokes near 200C (390F), so 175C (350F) sits comfortably below trouble.

ingredients.text: 1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tsp water, to glaze

steps.text: Work everything into a firm, barely tacky dough; it should feel dry against any biscuit dough you know, and should stop being worked the moment it is smooth.
Rest it wrapped and cool for an hour so the gluten slackens.
Roll 30 g pieces into little spindles, pinch the ends to points, and cut one deep slit down the length of each, well into the dough.
Glaze them and bake at 180C (350F) for 18 to 20 minutes, until each slit has opened into a boat and the undersides are the colour of pale straw.
Cool them completely on a rack; they firm as they cool and keep for weeks in a tin.

note: There is no raising agent and almost no water here, so the only lift comes from steam and the slit is the vent that decides where it escapes. Cut it shallow and the dough seals over in the oven, then splits along the flank instead. Skip the rest and the spindles retract into lumps as the gluten pulls back. Orange flower water is volatile, so be generous; half its perfume leaves in the heat.

ingredients.text: 700 g piments doux verts (long sweet green peppers), deseeded and cut in 1 cm strips
600 g ripe tomatoes, peeled, deseeded and roughly chopped
1.5 tsp piment d'Espelette, plus a pinch to finish

steps.text: Sweat the onions and garlic in the olive oil over low heat with a pinch of salt until they are slack and glassy with no colour at all.
Add the green peppers and cook on until they slump and lose their squeak; a strip should bend double without snapping.
Add the tomatoes and the Espelette and cook uncovered until a spoon dragged across the base leaves a clean channel and no watery juice runs back into it.
Pull the pan to the lowest possible heat, pour in the beaten salted eggs and stir slowly and constantly, scraping the base, until the mass thickens and turns glossy.
Take it off while it still looks slightly too loose, since it carries on setting in the hot pan, and dust with Espelette.

note: Espelette is not paprika under a French name: the pods are dried whole and milled coarse, so it carries fruit and a slow warmth near 4,000 SHU rather than sweet red dust. The eggs are the fragile part. They set from 62C (144F) and weep water past 75C (167F), so the vegetables must be reduced dry and the heat right down before the eggs go in, or you get scrambled egg sitting in a puddle.

ingredients.text: 100 g jambon de Bayonne, cut in 5 mm lardons
450 g piments doux verts, in 1 cm strips
300 g red peppers, in 1 cm strips
150 ml dry white Irouléguy or another crisp white

steps.text: Salt the chicken and lay it skin down in the duck fat over medium heat; leave it until the skin is deep gold and lifts from the pan by itself, then set it aside.
Render the ham lardons in the same fat, then add the onions and both peppers and cook until they have collapsed and the edges are catching brown.
Stir in the garlic and Espelette for thirty seconds, until the fat stains red and smells sweet, then deglaze with the wine and reduce until the pan smells of wine and not of alcohol.
Add the tomatoes and herbs, return the legs and thighs so the skin stands proud of the sauce, and simmer bare and gentle for 25 minutes.
Tuck in the breast pieces for the last 12 minutes, until the juices at the thigh joint run clear and the flesh pulls from the bone with a little coaxing. Rest off the heat for 10 minutes.

note: Capsaicin and the carotenoids that carry Espelette's flavour are fat soluble, so the powder goes into the hot fat for half a minute, never straight into the tomato water, where it stays dusty and tastes raw. Keep the chicken skin standing above the sauce as it simmers. Submerged skin rehydrates into slack rubber, and no amount of later reduction will crisp it again.

ingredients.text: 1.2 kg veal shoulder, trimmed and cut by knife into 1 cm dice
600 g piments doux verts, in 1 cm dice
1 dried Espelette pod, crumbled, or 1 small green chilli
300 ml light veal or chicken stock

steps.text: Cut the shoulder into dice with a knife, never a machine, and keep every piece about a centimetre so they cook at one rate.
Colour the veal in the duck fat in a wide pan in two or three batches, gold on two faces only; if the pan hisses quietly instead of cracking, it is too crowded.
Sweat the onions, diced peppers and garlic in the same fat until they are melting and sweet and the brown fond has dissolved off the base.
Return the meat with both Espelettes and stock barely to cover, then hold it covered at a lazy blip for about an hour and a quarter, until a dice crushes between finger and thumb with no spring left.
Uncover and reduce until the sauce pools around the meat rather than running off it, and salt only now.

note: Shoulder is collagen rich, and collagen only unwinds into gelatine above about 70C (158F) held for an hour or more. That gelatine is what makes axoa glossy with no flour in it. Mince the meat instead of dicing it and you rupture the fibres, so the juices run out in the first minutes and the finished pan is grainy and dry. Keep the dice at a centimetre and the pot at a blip, never a rolling boil, which wrings the fibres tight.

ingredients.text: 1 kg hake and monkfish heads and bones, gills cut out, rinsed until the water runs clear
600 g hake, in 4 thick pieces on the bone
8 slices of baguette, toasted and rubbed with raw garlic

steps.text: Cover the heads and bones with cold water, bring them to a bare tremble, skim the grey scum until the surface runs clear, hold twenty minutes only, then strain without pressing the bones.
Fry the langoustines hard in the olive oil until the shells turn brick and the pan smells toasted, lift them out, and sweat the onion, leek and garlic in that same fat until slack.
Add the tomatoes and wine and reduce until the pan smells of fruit rather than alcohol, stir in the Espelette, pour in the strained fumet and simmer ten minutes.
Drop the heat until the surface only shivers, around 85C (185F), and stage the fish: monkfish first, hake three minutes behind it, mussels and langoustines last.
It is done when the hake parts into white curd along its flakes and the mussels have just gaped. Ladle over the garlic toasts.

note: Fish bones give up their gelatine in about twenty minutes; past that the heads leach bitterness and cloud the pot, so a long fish stock is a worse one. In the broth, fish protein sets near 50C (122F) and starts squeezing out moisture by 60C (140F), and a rolling boil batters the flakes apart before the centre is even warm. Hold it at a shiver and stage by density: monkfish is dense and slow, hake is fragile and fast.

ingredients.text: 2 magrets de canard of 350 to 400 g each, skin on

steps.text: Score the fat in a 1 cm lattice, cutting down to the meat but not into it, salt the skin, leave it fifteen minutes and blot away the beads of moisture that rise.
Lay the magrets skin down in a cold dry heavy pan and set it over low heat; listen for a whisper, not a sizzle, and press the breasts flat with a spatula for the first minute.
Spoon or pour the rendered fat into a bowl every few minutes, keeping it, and continue for 12 to 15 minutes until the skin is thin, amber and stiff and only a few millimetres of fat remain under it.
Raise the heat, turn the breasts and give the flesh two to three minutes, to 52C to 54C (126F to 129F) at the core for rosé.
Rest them skin up on a rack for eight minutes, then carve across the grain in 5 mm slices and finish with flaky salt and Espelette.

note: A magret carries a centimetre of fat under thick skin, and that fat has to melt from around 35C (95F) and then escape through the skin before the skin can dry out and brown. A hot pan browns and sets the outer skin first, trapping the fat so it steams the meat grey. Cold and slow renders in stages: melt, drain, dehydrate, brown. Pour the liquid fat off as it comes, or the breast begins to confit itself and the skin stays flabby.

ingredients.text: 4 slices of raw duck foie gras, 2 cm thick, about 70 g each, cut from a chilled deveined lobe
fine salt and coarsely cracked black pepper

steps.text: Cut the slices with a knife dipped in hot water and wiped, then lay them on a cold plate and return them to the fridge until the pan is ready.
Heat a dry heavy pan until a flicked drop of water skitters and vanishes, and season the slices only as they leave the fridge.
Sear 45 to 60 seconds a side without moving them, until a lacquered brown crust has formed and the slice yields under a fingertip but is still cool at its centre; lift onto warm plates.
Pour off all but a spoonful of the fat, deglaze off the heat with the verjus and Armagnac, add the stock and reduce over heat to a light syrup, then spoon it over and serve on the brioche.

note: Foie gras is roughly half fat, held in cells that rupture from about 45C (113F); once they let go the slice pours into the pan and leaves you a wafer. The defence is contrast: liver straight from the fridge, a pan hot enough to brown in under a minute, and salt applied at the very last second, since salt draws moisture that cools the surface and stalls the crust. If the slice slumps and the fat floods, the pan was too cool.

ingredients.text: 1 kg duck gizzards, silverskin and gristle trimmed away
walnut oil and bitter leaves, to serve

steps.text: Toss the gizzards with the salt, pepper, garlic and herbs, cover and cure them in the fridge overnight, until they feel firm and faintly tacky.
Rinse the cure off completely and dry the gizzards very well; any water left on them will spit in the fat and shorten their keeping.

Melt the fat, submerge the gizzards and hold the pot at 85C (185F), the surface trembling with only an occasional lazy bubble, for two and a half to three hours, until a skewer slides in with no resistance.
Cool them in their fat, then pack into a jar under at least 2 cm of fat with nothing breaking the surface, and pour off the meat juices that settle to the bottom as jelly.
To serve, lift out, wipe, and crisp in a dry hot pan for two minutes a side until the edges brown, then slice over leaves dressed with walnut oil.

note: Confit was storage long before it was a texture. Salt pulls out free water and lowers water activity, the long bath at 85C (185F) pasteurises and drives off more, and the fat cap then locks out air. Two rules keep it keeping: no meat may break the surface of the fat, and the juices that settle into jelly at the bottom of the jar are water, not fat, so pour them off before you store. Cold and sealed they hold for months.
techniques: Resting meat & slicing against the grain

flavor.sentence: Leads with an earthy, grounding base, toasted, nutty warmth throughout, lifted green at the very end.

ingredients.text: 1 ham hock of about 700 g, or a jambon de Bayonne bone
250 g haricots tarbais, soaked overnight in cold water
800 g green cabbage, cored and cut in wide ribbons
300 g carrots and 200 g turnips, in large pieces
1 bouquet of thyme, bay and parsley stalks
a glass of dry red wine, to finish at the table

steps.text: Cover the hock and the drained beans with 3 litres of cold water, bring up slowly and skim the grey foam until the surface runs clear, then add the clove onion, garlic and bouquet and hold at a murmur for an hour.
Add the carrots, turnips and leek and cook until a knife enters a turnip with just a little resistance left.
Add the potatoes and cabbage and cook on until the cabbage is dark and silky rather than squeaky, about 25 minutes.
Warm the confit legs, pull the meat into large shreds and stir them in for the last ten minutes so their fat glosses the broth.
Crush some of the potato against the side of the pot until a spoon stood upright in the middle stays standing, then season with Espelette and taste for salt only now.
Serve, and let each person pour red wine into the last inches of broth in the bowl.

note: Garbure is measured by the spoon: it should stand up in the bowl. That body comes from potato starch and long cooked cabbage, not flour, which is why the potatoes go in as thick slices and are crushed against the pot at the end. Salt right at the finish. A ham hock leaches salt into the broth for the whole cook, and a pot seasoned early will be inedible by the time it has reduced.

flavor.sentence: Leads with warm spice humming through the middle, aromatics blooming from the first bite, lifted green at the very end.

ingredients.text: 300 g fine white maize flour, neither coarse polenta nor nixtamalised masa

steps.text: Mix the flour and salt, pour the hot water in all at once and stir with a spoon until it gathers into a mass.
Knead it in the bowl as soon as you can bear the heat, a minute or two, until it is smooth and takes a fingerprint without cracking at the rim; rest it covered for fifteen minutes.
Divide into six, roll each into a ball, and press between two sheets of baking paper into discs 2 mm thick and about 18 cm across, patching any split edge with a wet thumb.
Cook on a dry iron griddle over medium high heat for one to two minutes a side, until pale gold freckles rise and the disc puffs in patches when you press the centre with a folded cloth.
Stack them under a cloth as they come off so their own steam keeps them pliable.

note: Maize has no gluten, so nothing holds a talo together but gelatinised starch, and starch only gelatinises in hot water. That is why the water goes in near 80C (176F). Mixed cold, the dough is sandy, cracks at the rim and falls to pieces on the griddle. Work it while it is hot, keep the disc thin and even, and eat them within the hour: as they cool the starch retrogrades, and reheating never fully undoes the chalkiness.
techniques: Resting dough: the pause that does the work

flavor.sentence: A quiet dish that lets its main ingredient speak: season well and stand aside.

ingredients.text: 300 g thick black cherry jam from Itxassou
1 yolk beaten with 1 tsp water, to glaze

steps.text: Cream the butter and sugar to a pale soft paste, beat in the egg, yolk, rum and salt, then fold in the flour, almonds and baking powder just until no dry flour shows.
Scrape the dough into two flat discs between sheets of paper and chill at least two hours, until it is firm enough to pipe but not hard.
Spread or pipe half into a buttered 22 cm ring, taking it 1 cm up the sides, then spread the jam inside a clean 1.5 cm border of bare dough.
Pipe the second half over in a tight spiral, smooth it, and seal the rim by pressing all round with a wet fingertip until you cannot see the join.
Glaze, chill 20 minutes, glaze again and score a crosshatch with a fork, then bake at 175C (350F) for 40 to 45 minutes, until it is deep chestnut brown and firm in the centre.
Cool completely in the tin before cutting, since the crumb sets only as it cools.

note: This is a cake batter behaving as a pastry: nearly three quarters butter to flour and no added water, so almost no gluten develops and it can be piped but never rolled. Two faults spoil it. A loose jam boils, finds the seam and bursts out, so use a properly set jam and seal a bare border. And an underbaked gâteau is pasty at the middle; take the colour to deep chestnut, not gold.
techniques: Chilling to firm: the fridge as binder
